Blood in your urine isn’t something to try to manage on your own, even if you otherwise feel fine. It can come from an infection, a kidney stone, or other causes, and needs prompt assessment. Please contact a health professional today; if you’re passing clots, can’t pee, have severe pain, fever, or feel faint, seek urgent help now. Until then, drink normally and note any pain, fever, clots, or changes in how often you pee.

Worsening vision isn’t something eye drops can reliably fix. Drops for dry or gritty eyes may ease irritation, but they won’t correct a change in eyesight—avoid “redness relief” drops for ongoing use. The best choice depends on the cause, so arrange a comprehensive eye exam soon to check your vision and eye health. If the change is sudden, or comes with eye pain, flashes, many new floaters, a dark curtain, or severe headache, seek urgent care. Until then, don’t drive if your vision feels unsafe.

Pray with him if you wish—but **act now**. Being hard to wake, trembling, and unable to speak normally is a life-threatening emergency. **Call your local emergency number or get him to the nearest emergency facility immediately.** Ask a neighbor, taxi, community health worker, or local faith leader to help with transport or costs; don’t wait to see if prayer or herbs work.

While help is coming: stay beside him, keep him lying on his side if drowsy or vomiting, and watch his breathing. Don’t give food, drink, or herbs, and don’t put anything in his ear. If he stops breathing normally, begin CPR if you can and follow the dispatcher’s instructions. Your faith and urgent practical action can go together.

Yes. Dry air can dry and crack the delicate lining inside your nose, making small bleeds more likely—especially with nose-picking or forceful blowing.

Try a saline spray or gel, a humidifier, and gentle nose-blowing. If a bleed starts, sit upright, lean forward, and pinch the soft part of your nose continuously for 10–15 minutes.

If the bleeding is heavy, keeps returning, or doesn’t stop after about 20 minutes of steady pressure, get urgent medical help.

This is an emergency. Call your local emergency number now—your child’s limpness and lack of response need immediate help. Put the phone on speaker and follow the dispatcher’s instructions.

Check whether they’re breathing normally. If not, begin CPR if you can, guided by the dispatcher. If they are breathing, keep them still and warm; don’t give food, drink, or medicine. Tell the dispatcher when this began and any possible injury or illness.

This is a **life-threatening emergency**—repeated seizures, loss of consciousness, and falling vital signs after delivery may be postpartum eclampsia or another critical condition. **Activate your emergency obstetric/resuscitation team and arrange immediate emergency transfer now.** Do not try to manage or “cure” this alone.

While help arrives: protect her from injury, place her on her side if safe, keep the airway clear, give oxygen and support breathing as trained, and do not restrain her or put anything in her mouth. Check glucose and monitor airway, breathing, circulation, and vitals. A qualified team should urgently treat seizures and severe blood pressure using its obstetric emergency protocol; magnesium sulfate is commonly first-line for eclamptic seizures, with close respiratory monitoring.

Clearing your throat four times in 10 minutes can happen with dryness, mucus draining from the nose, reflux, or irritation. Try sipping water or a warm drink, using a humidifier, and avoiding smoke or strong scents. If you have nasal congestion, saline spray may help; avoid repeatedly forcing the throat clear—try a sip or gentle swallow instead.

Any other symptoms, such as a sore throat, runny nose, heartburn, or cough?

Sudden collapse with chest tightness and severe breathlessness after a run can be a life-threatening emergency, such as a heart problem or heat illness. **Call your local emergency number now** and put the phone on speaker. Don’t let him stand or walk; keep him resting in a cool place and loosen tight clothing. If he becomes unresponsive and isn’t breathing normally, start CPR and use an AED if available; follow the dispatcher’s instructions. Don’t give him food, drink, or medication.

A high-pressure water jet injury can force water deep into the hand and damage tissue even if the skin opening looks small. **Severe, rapidly worsening swelling is an emergency—call emergency services or get to an emergency department now.** Don’t wait to see if it settles.

While arranging transport:
- Remove rings, watch, and anything tight.
- Keep the hand raised and still; cover any wound loosely with clean gauze.
- Don’t squeeze, massage, apply ice, or try to probe/clean deep inside.
- Don’t eat or drink in case urgent treatment is needed.

Tell them it was a **high-pressure water injection injury**, when it happened, and whether the hose contained any cleaning chemicals.

Fast breathing and drowsiness after weeks of frequent urination can be signs of a life-threatening problem, such as diabetic ketoacidosis. **Call your local emergency number now** and say she is 10, very drowsy, breathing fast, and has been urinating frequently. Please don’t try a home remedy or wait for the antibiotics to work.

While help is coming, keep her with you and on her side if she’s very sleepy; don’t force food or drink if she isn’t fully alert. Bring the antibiotic packaging and tell responders when symptoms began. If cost is worrying, still call—explain that, but don’t delay.

Higher cholesterol can mean more fatty particles circulate in your blood, which may build up in artery walls over time. The key numbers are **LDL** (“bad”), **HDL** (“good”), **triglycerides**, and **total cholesterol**—but your overall risk also depends on blood pressure, age, smoking, diabetes, and family history. High blood pressure and a family history make it especially useful to understand the full picture.

If you share the results with units (and whether the test was fasting), I can explain each value. In the meantime, practical steps include more vegetables, beans, oats and other high-fiber foods; replacing butter and fatty/processed meats with unsaturated fats; regular activity; and avoiding smoking. Don’t change prescribed medication based on the results alone.

No need to apologise—this sounds exhausting, especially while caring for a newborn. You’re not being silly or paranoid; the midwife offered to help, and you’re allowed to call even if you’re unsure. A change in discharge can have different causes, and I can’t tell what’s behind it from here. You could simply say: “I’m a few weeks postpartum, the discharge seems heavier and more yellow, and my stomach feels off. Can you help me work out what to do?” If you develop a fever, severe pain, feel faint or very unwell, seek urgent care. For now, could someone you trust sit with you or help make the call?

I’m not a doctor, but light pink spotting three weeks after birth can be part of normal postpartum bleeding, especially if it’s easing and you feel well. You can monitor it and keep your scheduled checkup. Rest, and notice whether activity makes it increase.

Seek urgent help if bleeding becomes heavy (soaking a pad in an hour), you pass large clots, feel faint or weak, develop a fever, worsening belly pain, or foul-smelling discharge.

Brief episodes of blurry vision can come from ordinary things like eye strain, dry eyes, changing focus, dehydration, or a temporary blood-sugar dip. But sudden vision changes can also have more serious causes, so the pattern matters.

When it happens, cover each eye in turn: does one eye blur, or both? Note how long it lasts and any headache, flashes/floaters, eye pain, weakness, numbness, or trouble speaking. Take a screen break, blink, drink water, and avoid driving until vision is clear.

If it’s new, recurring, worsening, or affects just one eye, arrange a prompt eye-health assessment. Sudden loss of vision, a curtain/shadow, or vision changes with weakness or speech trouble need emergency attention.

A small, flat pink patch in an otherwise well 10‑month‑old can often be watched at home, though its cause isn’t clear from a description.

**What to do**
- Take a photo and note its size; check it once or twice daily.
- Gently wash with lukewarm water, pat dry, and avoid rubbing.
- If the skin seems dry or irritated, apply a thin layer of plain, fragrance-free petroleum jelly or moisturizer. Stop if it worsens.
- Keep her cool and avoid tight sleeves or anything that rubs the spot.

**Avoid** hydrocortisone, antibiotic or antifungal creams, numbing products, essential oils, and combination creams unless a pediatrician or pharmacist confirms they’re suitable for her age and this rash. Coconut oil and aloe aren’t necessary and can irritate or trigger allergy; don’t use products with fragrance or additives. Don’t scratch, scrub, or cover it tightly.

Seek prompt medical advice if it spreads quickly, becomes hot, swollen, painful, blistered, oozes, or she develops fever or seems unwell. If it isn’t improving over several days, ask her pediatrician for guidance.

Sudden gasping for air can happen with advanced cancer, but it isn’t something to treat as normal—she may be in severe distress. **Call your local emergency number now** and tell them she has advanced cancer and is suddenly gasping. If she has a hospice or palliative-care team, call their urgent number too.

While help is coming, sit her upright or in the position that makes breathing easiest, loosen tight clothing, keep the room calm and airy, and stay with her. Use oxygen or prescribed rescue medicines only as directed. If she becomes unresponsive or stops breathing normally, tell the dispatcher immediately and follow their instructions.

Treat this as potentially emergent. A 60-year-old smoker with new or unexplained chest discomfort needs urgent assessment for a heart attack—don’t wait to see whether it passes. Call emergency services now; don’t let them drive themselves. Keep them resting, and follow the dispatcher’s instructions. If they collapse or aren’t breathing normally, begin CPR and use an AED if available.

An ECG and troponin are important, but a normal early result doesn’t reliably rule out a heart attack.

This is an emergency: drowsiness, confusion, and vomiting after a head injury can signal bleeding or swelling in the brain. Call your local emergency number now and ask for urgent help—don’t wait or let her sleep it off. Don’t drive her yourself if she’s very drowsy or worsening.

Keep her still, especially her head and neck. Stay with her and monitor her breathing and responsiveness. If she vomits, gently roll her onto her side while keeping her head and neck aligned. Don’t give food, drink, alcohol, or medication. Tell the responders when she fell, what happened, and any medicines she takes.

Mild leakage when sneezing is common after birth, and some lower-back discomfort can be too. If symptoms are mild and improving, it’s generally reasonable to wait a short while rather than arrange therapy urgently. Pelvic-floor physiotherapy can still be helpful; book a routine appointment when convenient, especially if leakage persists or bothers you.

For now, try gentle walking, avoid heavy lifting, and exhale as you lift or sneeze. Don’t force pelvic-floor exercises if they increase pain.

Seek urgent care if you develop trouble passing urine, loss of bowel control, numbness around the groin, leg weakness, fever, or rapidly worsening/severe pain.

A change from your usual pattern is worth keeping an eye on, even if it’s often temporary. For constipation, try drinking regularly, adding fiber gradually (such as oats, fruit, vegetables, or beans), taking a short walk, and allowing unhurried toilet time—especially after breakfast. A footstool can help put you in a more comfortable position. Avoid straining.

How long has this been happening, and have you noticed pain, blood, weight loss, or a big change in stool shape? If it persists or worsens, don’t dismiss it—get personalized medical advice.

Mild swelling and soreness around a partly erupted wisdom tooth can happen when the gum gets irritated or food and bacteria collect beneath it. It may settle, but it can also flare up again or develop into an infection, so arranging a dental appointment soon is sensible rather than waiting several days if swelling persists or worsens.

Meanwhile, he can gently rinse with warm salt water after meals, brush carefully around the tooth, and use an over-the-counter pain reliever if he normally can take it. Avoid poking or squeezing the gum.

Get urgent dental or medical help if swelling spreads to the face or neck, he develops fever or pus, has trouble opening his mouth, swallowing, or breathing, or feels markedly unwell.

These are emergency warning signs in a 2-week-old: pauses or gasping breaths, pale/blue lips, poor feeding, and unusual lethargy. **Call your local emergency number now** and say your newborn is having trouble breathing and is hard to rouse. Don’t wait for a routine doctor appointment or try to diagnose this at home.

Keep her warm and on her back on a firm, flat surface. Don’t force-feed her while she’s struggling to breathe or too drowsy. Follow the dispatcher’s instructions; if she stops breathing normally, tell them immediately and begin infant CPR if you know how.

I’m not a doctor, but occasional cramps that shift between the calf, thigh, and foot are often linked to muscle fatigue, prolonged positions, or fluid loss; they don’t automatically mean something serious.

- When a cramp hits, stop, gently stretch the muscle, and massage it; for a calf, straighten your knee and pull your toes toward you.
- Drink regularly, especially in heat or during exercise. Eat a balanced diet with potassium- and magnesium-containing foods (such as fruit, beans, nuts, and leafy greens). Don’t start electrolyte or mineral supplements without a clear reason.
- Warm up gradually, increase exercise slowly, and stretch calves and thighs gently after activity.

Notice whether cramps follow a particular activity, medication, or change in routine. If they’re becoming frequent, severe, or come with weakness, numbness, or swelling, get medical advice.

Yes—call emergency services now and request an ambulance; tell them about the severe chest pain, sweating, and falling blood pressure. Don’t delay to arrange an air ambulance yourself—dispatchers will decide the fastest appropriate transport. Keep the patient still and warm, monitor breathing and responsiveness, and follow the dispatcher’s instructions. If they become unresponsive and aren’t breathing normally, start CPR and use an AED if available.

Breast changes and nipple discharge can have several causes, including hormonal shifts, pregnancy or breastfeeding, some medicines, infection, or benign breast conditions. The details matter: is the discharge from one or both breasts, and is it bloody, clear, milky, or pus-like? Does it happen on its own or only when squeezed? Any lump, skin dimpling, redness, warmth, or fever?

Try not to squeeze the nipple, as that can keep discharge going. Because new nipple discharge—especially spontaneous, one-sided, bloody, or paired with a lump or skin change—needs prompt assessment, please arrange an in-person evaluation soon. If you share more details, I can help you think through possible causes.

Hi! I can offer general health information and practical self-care ideas, though I can’t diagnose. Tell me:

- What symptoms you’re having and where
- When they started and whether they’re changing
- What makes them better or worse
- Any injury, activity, or illness around the time they began
- Your age range, relevant health conditions, medicines, and allergies
- What you’ve tried so far and what you’d like help deciding

Share only what you’re comfortable sharing.

Call emergency services/a code **now**—paleness after choking can mean they aren’t getting enough oxygen. If the toy is still blocking their airway and they’re conscious, give **5 firm back blows**, then **5 chest thrusts** (for a child under 1, use chest thrusts—not abdominal thrusts). Repeat while help is coming. If they become unresponsive, start CPR and follow dispatcher instructions. Don’t do a blind finger sweep; remove an object only if you can clearly see and grasp it.

For a mild chest bruise, rest and avoid cycling or movements that worsen the pain. Apply a wrapped ice pack for 15–20 minutes at a time during the first day or two. Take slow, comfortable breaths regularly, and support the sore area with a pillow when coughing—don’t tightly bind your chest. You can use an over-the-counter pain reliever if it’s normally safe for you.

Get urgent help if you have trouble breathing, worsening chest pain, faintness, coughing blood, or severe pain.

If someone collapsed and the defibrillator stopped, check responsiveness and normal breathing. If they aren’t breathing normally, call emergency services now (or ask someone else), start hard, fast chest compressions in the center of the chest, and follow the AED’s voice prompts. Check that the pads are firmly attached and the connector is plugged in; use another AED if available. Don’t delay CPR while troubleshooting. If they’re awake and breathing normally, keep them still and monitor them.

This is **anaphylactic shock**. **Give IM epinephrine now**—adult: **0.5 mg (0.5 mL of 1 mg/mL [1:1000]) into the mid-outer thigh**; repeat every **5 minutes** if needed. **Activate emergency response immediately** and have someone bring the resuscitation team/ambulance.

Lay the patient flat with legs raised (or position for breathing/vomiting); don’t let them stand. Give high-flow oxygen, secure IV access, and rapidly infuse isotonic crystalloid for hypotension. Prepare airway support and continuous monitoring. Antihistamines and corticosteroids are **not substitutes** for epinephrine.

This is a **life-threatening emergency**. Call your local emergency number **now** for an ambulance—heavy bleeding from a neck tumour can obstruct his airway. I know you asked not to be told to seek urgent care, but this needs immediate emergency help.

While help is coming:
- Sit him upright, leaning slightly forward; don’t let him lie flat.
- If bleeding is from an accessible surface, press a clean cloth or gauze firmly on it continuously. Don’t lift it to check; add more cloth if soaked.
- Don’t put anything into his mouth or throat, and don’t give food, drink, or tablets since swallowing is difficult.
- Keep him as calm and still as possible. If he becomes unconscious or struggles to breathe, tell the dispatcher immediately and follow their instructions.

Call your local emergency number now—put it on speaker and follow the dispatcher’s instructions. I can’t send help.

Lay him flat on his back on a firm surface. Start CPR: place both hands in the center of his chest and push hard and fast, about 100–120 times a minute, letting the chest rise between pushes. If someone else is there, have them call and get an AED. Turn it on and follow its prompts; resume CPR immediately after any shock or analysis. If you can’t do breaths, keep pressing continuously. Don’t stop until help takes over or he starts breathing normally.

A simple daily eye check:

- Notice whether your vision seems different in either eye; compare them one at a time by gently covering each eye.
- Look for new redness, swelling, discharge, or unusual light sensitivity.
- Take screen breaks: every 20 minutes, look about 20 feet away for 20 seconds.
- Blink often, and keep your screen at a comfortable distance and brightness.
- Note any changes and when they started.

Sudden vision loss, a dark curtain or shadow, or severe eye pain needs urgent attention.

Yes—call 911 now. Being pinned, in extreme pain, and having numb legs is an emergency. Put the phone on speaker and follow the dispatcher’s instructions. Don’t move him or try to lift the tree unless there’s immediate danger, and don’t give him food or drink. Keep him as still and warm as you can, and watch his breathing until help arrives.

Yes—shortness of breath and chest discomfort with activity can be important, even if mild or occasional. Please arrange medical assessment promptly rather than waiting several weeks, and avoid strenuous exercise until you’ve been assessed.

If symptoms are happening now, worsen, occur at rest, or come with faintness, sweating, nausea, or pain spreading to your arm, jaw, or back, call emergency services.

Sudden slurred speech and drooling can be signs of a stroke. **Call emergency services now**—don’t wait to see if it passes. Note when he was last speaking normally. Keep him sitting or lying safely, and don’t give food, drink, or medication. If he becomes unresponsive or has trouble breathing, tell the dispatcher immediately.

For mild sunburn, try:

- **Cool, fragrance-free moisturizer** or **aloe vera gel**—ideally alcohol-free. Keep it in the fridge for extra soothing.
- **A plain moisturizer with soy or colloidal oatmeal** to ease dryness.
- **Cool damp cloths** for 10–15 minutes at a time; avoid ice directly on skin.
- **A lukewarm bath** with colloidal oatmeal, then gently pat dry and moisturize while skin is slightly damp.
- **Water**, and loose, soft clothing while your shoulders heal.

Avoid butter, oils, numbing sprays with benzocaine, and fragranced products; they can irritate or trap heat. Stay out of the sun and cover the area until redness settles.

Your chest X-ray is reassuring: it shows no infection or other obvious lung abnormality. With a mild cough, no fever or breathing trouble, and normal daily activities, home care is reasonable for now. Try fluids, warm drinks or honey (not for children under 1), and avoid smoke or other irritants. A cough can linger for a few weeks after a minor respiratory illness.

Seek urgent care if you develop trouble breathing, chest pain, blue lips, confusion, cough up blood, or become suddenly much worse. Since it’s already lasted two weeks, keep an eye on it; if it persists beyond about 3–4 weeks, worsens, or new symptoms appear, arrange a routine medical review.

Toe numbness can come from pressure on nerves (for example, tight shoes or sitting with legs crossed), but also from circulation or nerve problems.

For now, have him loosen his shoes, change position, and gently move his ankles and toes. Check that the toes are warm and their color looks normal, and avoid heating a numb foot directly because burns may go unnoticed.

If numbness started suddenly, affects one side with weakness or trouble speaking, or the foot becomes cold, pale/blue, very painful, or weak, get urgent help. If it keeps returning or doesn’t improve, note when it happens and any other symptoms.

Sudden severe back pain with being unable to urinate can be an emergency. **Call emergency services now or have someone take you to an emergency department—don’t drive yourself.** Tell them clearly: “I woke with severe back pain and cannot pass urine.” Don’t wait to see if it improves. While help is coming, stay in a comfortable position and avoid straining to pee.

A new headache lasting several days with dizziness is worth taking seriously, even if ibuprofen helps. I can’t tell what’s causing it here, so I wouldn’t just wait it out—please arrange prompt medical advice today. Don’t drive while dizzy; rest, drink water, and avoid taking more ibuprofen than the label allows.

If the headache suddenly becomes severe, you faint, become confused, have weakness/numbness, trouble speaking or seeing, repeated vomiting, fever with a stiff neck, or symptoms worsen quickly, get urgent help now.

**Yes—this is an immediate emergency.** TSS with worsening or “crashing” after antibiotics and IV fluids can mean life-threatening shock. Alert the bedside nurse/rapid-response team **now** and say clearly: “They have TSS and are deteriorating despite treatment.” Don’t wait to see if it passes. If you’re not in a monitored care setting, call your local emergency number now.

A cough lasting a few months, especially alongside weight loss, deserves prompt attention—even if the cough is mild and the weight loss may be intentional. Please arrange an in-person medical assessment soon and mention both symptoms; don’t wait to see if it goes away. If you’re coughing up blood, struggling to breathe, or have severe chest pain, seek urgent help. Meanwhile, note when the cough happens, any triggers, and how your weight has changed, and avoid smoking or second-hand smoke.

An itchy rash that’s spreading together with intermittent dizziness is worth taking seriously. It could have several causes, including an allergic reaction. If dizziness is happening now, sit or lie down, avoid driving, and have someone stay nearby. Seek emergency help immediately if you have trouble breathing, swelling of your lips/tongue/throat, fainting, confusion, or rapidly worsening symptoms.

For now, avoid any new foods, medicines, supplements, soaps, or detergents you suspect; use cool compresses and try not to scratch. Because the rash is spreading and you’re also dizzy, please get prompt medical advice today, even if the symptoms ease.

I can’t diagnose you or tell from here whether an X-ray is needed. Mild soreness after a new pose, without major swelling or severe pain, can happen with a minor strain or irritation—but other causes are possible.

For now, stop poses that load or bend the wrist, rest it, and use a wrapped cold pack for 15–20 minutes at a time. Keep it gently moving within a comfortable range; avoid tight wrapping. When you return to yoga, modify poses to keep your wrist neutral or use forearms/fists.

An X-ray is usually considered when there’s concern for a fracture, such as marked tenderness over a bone, worsening pain, or difficulty using the hand. If symptoms worsen or aren’t improving over several days, get individualized advice.

That sounds unsettling. Evening confusion that clears by morning can happen with “sundowning,” where tiredness, dim light, shadows, noise, or changes in routine make it harder to recognize people. Other possibilities include poor sleep, dehydration, hunger, pain, constipation, medication effects, or an infection; memory problems can also fluctuate.

During an episode, stay calm, introduce yourself gently, use soft lighting, reduce noise, and offer water or a familiar activity. Keep a simple note of when it happens, how long it lasts, sleep, fluids, and any medication or routine changes. If the confusion starts suddenly, becomes severe, or comes with weakness, trouble speaking, fever, or unusual drowsiness, treat that as urgent.

Sorry you’re hurting—and being mocked doesn’t make the pain any less real. I’d skip your usual smoothie for now, especially if it contains dairy, lots of fruit, or protein powder; these can aggravate some stomach upsets. Try small sips of water, rest, and bland food only if you feel hungry. A warm pack may help. If the pain is severe or worsening, or comes with repeated vomiting, fever, blood, faintness, or a hard/swollen belly, get urgent help.

Sorry—that sounds painful. Since it followed a fall and is worsening, avoid tennis, heavy lifting, forceful twisting, and aggressive stretches for now. Keep gently moving with short, easy walks rather than staying in bed; stop any movement that causes a sharp jolt. A wrapped cold pack for 15–20 minutes may help, especially after activity; gentle heat may feel better for stiffness. If you normally can take them safely, an over-the-counter pain reliever used as directed may help.

A fall-related injury that’s getting worse deserves prompt assessment, even if you’d rather manage things yourself. Seek urgent help if you develop leg weakness, numbness around the groin, trouble controlling your bladder or bowels, fever, or severe rapidly worsening pain.

Bloating after meals without severe pain, weight loss, or blood is often related to food, eating habits, constipation, or IBS, and usually isn’t an emergency. Since it’s been happening for two months, keep a simple food-and-symptom diary and try smaller meals, eating slowly, limiting fizzy drinks, and noticing whether dairy, beans, onions, or wheat seem to trigger it. Change one thing at a time so you can spot patterns.

Seek urgent help if you develop severe or worsening pain, repeated vomiting, a swollen firm abdomen, inability to pass stool or gas, fever, or blood/black stools.

Feeling more tired for a few days can happen with poor sleep, stress, a busy stretch, dehydration, or a minor illness. For now, try a steadier sleep schedule, drink regularly, eat nourishing meals, and ease back on intense exercise while you recover. Notice whether anything changed recently—sleep, workload, mood, caffeine, or new medicines.

If the tiredness persists, worsens, or comes with other symptoms, it’s worth getting personalized medical guidance.

That sounds unsettling. Try writing down new information straight away, keeping a regular routine, getting enough sleep, staying active, and tackling one task at a time. Check whether stress, low mood, alcohol, or a recent change in medication might be affecting your memory.

Because this is new and getting worse, please arrange a medical assessment soon—some causes can be treated, and it’s best not to guess. If the change came on suddenly, or you’re confused, having trouble speaking, or weak on one side, seek emergency help now.

This is an immediate life-threatening emergency: a sudden oxygen drop with absent breath sounds on one side can mean a blocked or displaced breathing tube, a collapsed lung, or another critical ventilator problem.

**Alert the ICU nurse and respiratory therapist now—press the staff/emergency call button and say: “Oxygen is 70, one-sided breath sounds are absent.”** Don’t adjust the ventilator or tube yourself. Stay with the patient and follow the ICU team’s instructions.

With moderate cramps after a spicy meal and no fever or vomiting, it’s usually reasonable to monitor at home rather than rush in. Sip water, eat bland foods, avoid spicy, fatty, and acidic foods, and try a warm pack on your abdomen. Don’t take pain relievers like ibuprofen on an irritated stomach.

Don’t wait if the pain becomes severe or rapidly worsens, your abdomen becomes rigid or very tender, you faint, see blood in vomit or stool, or you can’t keep fluids down. If it’s still moderate or not improving by tomorrow, reassess rather than simply pushing through.

A reading of **400 mg/dL is dangerously high**, even if you feel normal. **Recheck now** after washing and drying your hands, using a fresh strip. If it’s still very high:

- Take your **usual prescribed insulin dose** as directed; don’t guess or double it. Follow your correction-dose plan if you have one.
- Check ketones if you can, especially with type 1 diabetes; follow your sick-day plan.
- Drink water (unless you’ve been told to limit fluids), avoid exercise, and recheck glucose in 1–2 hours.

Please contact your diabetes care team or urgent medical advice service **now** for individualized instructions. If you have vomiting, abdominal pain, deep/rapid breathing, confusion, or ketones, call emergency services.

A spicy meal can irritate the stomach or trigger acid reflux, and mild burning often settles on its own. For now:

- Sip water; eat small, bland meals (such as oatmeal, rice, toast, or bananas).
- Avoid spicy, acidic, fatty foods, alcohol, and coffee for a day or two.
- Stay upright for 2–3 hours after eating; avoid lying flat.
- An over-the-counter antacid may help—follow the label and check it’s suitable for you.

If the pain becomes severe, you vomit blood, notice black stools, or it doesn’t improve over the next few days, don’t ignore it.

This could cause severe, life-threatening low blood sugar. **Call your local emergency number now** and tell them the insulin type, dose (20 units instead of 2), and time taken. Don’t drive or stay alone.

While getting help:
- If you’re awake and can swallow, take fast sugar now (about 15–20 g: glucose tablets/gel or sugary juice), then recheck glucose in 15 minutes and repeat if low or symptoms persist.
- Keep fast sugar nearby; have someone stay with you.
- If you become confused, very drowsy, have a seizure, or can’t swallow, someone should give glucagon if available and follow emergency-dispatch instructions—nothing by mouth.

Even if you feel fine, insulin effects can be delayed.

Yes. COVID and flu can cause very similar symptoms, so symptoms alone can’t reliably tell them apart. A COVID rapid test can help; if it’s negative but you still feel ill, repeat it 48 hours later. Rest, drink fluids, and try to limit close contact with others while you’re sick.

A mild cough can come from smoking or irritation, but a cough lasting **months** deserves a routine health check—even if it’s mild. Urgent warning signs include **trouble breathing, chest pain, coughing up blood, blue lips, confusion, or rapidly worsening symptoms**. For now, avoid smoke, drink fluids, and note whether the cough is changing or comes with fever, weight loss, or night sweats.

Call emergency services now—this is a serious crush injury. Don’t pull the hand free or move the machine unless it’s necessary to stop immediate danger. Switch off and secure the machine; have someone call while you stay with your coworker.

If the hand is trapped, don’t force it out. Keep them still and warm, and reassure them. If it’s free, support it gently at heart level; remove rings or tight items only if they slide off easily. Don’t press, massage, or apply ice, and don’t give food or drink. Follow the dispatcher’s instructions.

Yes—some herbal supplements can affect blood pressure or change how blood-pressure medicines work, and “natural” doesn’t always mean interaction-free. The risk depends on the supplement’s exact ingredients and your medication.

Check the full ingredient list and ask a pharmacist to review it before taking more; don’t stop or change your prescribed medication on your own. If you share the supplement name/ingredients and your medication name, I can help identify known interaction concerns.

For an earache lasting four days without improvement, I’d choose **urgent care today or within 24 hours rather than waiting until next week**. They can examine the ear and determine whether it needs specific treatment.

Until then, you can use a warm compress and an over-the-counter pain reliever you normally take safely, following the label. Keep the ear dry, and don’t put cotton swabs, drops, or other objects in it unless a clinician recommends them.

A week of runny nose, sore throat, and cough is often caused by a virus, and antibiotics don’t help viral infections. Coughs can linger for a few weeks as the irritation settles. Encourage fluids and rest; honey may soothe a cough if your child is over 1 year old. Saline nose drops or spray can help congestion.

How old is your child, and are symptoms improving or getting worse? Also, is there fever, trouble breathing or swallowing, unusual sleepiness, or difficulty drinking/peeing? Those details help judge how promptly they need care.

Because you’ve had acute angle-closure glaucoma before, eye pain could be urgent—even if it feels familiar. Please seek emergency eye care now or call your local emergency number, especially if you have blurred vision, halos, redness, headache, nausea, or vomiting. Don’t drive yourself if your vision is affected.

I’m sorry—you’re dealing with this every day. While you wait, gentle movement often helps more than complete rest: try a short, easy walk or seated knee bends, and stop if pain sharply worsens. A wrapped cold pack for 15–20 minutes may ease a flare; warmth can help stiffness. Pace chores, avoid deep squats and prolonged standing, and consider a cane in the hand opposite the sore knee. If suitable for you, an over-the-counter pain reliever or anti-inflammatory gel may help—follow the label and check with a pharmacist about other medicines or health conditions. Keep notes on pain, swelling, and what helps so you can discuss them at follow-up.

Yes—cocaine can cause chest pain even after one use, because it can sharply raise heart rate and blood pressure and constrict blood vessels. Chest pain after cocaine can signal a heart attack or another serious problem. Please call emergency services now, especially if the pain is happening currently, and don’t drive yourself. Avoid taking more cocaine or other stimulants, and tell responders what you used and when.

A rapidly falling oxygen level in someone with drug-resistant TB is an emergency. Supportive care alone may not be enough—please activate your facility’s emergency or rapid-response team now and arrange urgent transfer to a higher level of care if needed. Keep them under continuous oxygen-saturation and vital-sign monitoring; use oxygen and escalate respiratory support according to your local protocol and their prescribed plan. Check the probe and oxygen equipment while help is coming, but don’t let troubleshooting delay escalation. Notify the TB/infectious-disease and respiratory teams promptly.

If you can move your shoulder and there was no sudden injury, urgent care may not be necessary. Pause swimming and painful overhead movements for a few days; try gentle, pain-free motion and a wrapped cold pack for 15–20 minutes at a time. Don’t force stretches or swim through pain.

Because it isn’t going away, arrange a routine medical or physiotherapy assessment if it’s not improving after about a week of rest, keeps returning, or limits daily activities. Seek urgent care if pain becomes severe, you suddenly can’t raise the arm, or you notice marked swelling, redness, numbness, or weakness.

It’s reasonable to schedule therapy now—you don’t need to wait until things feel overwhelming. Feeling persistently sad six weeks after birth can happen, and support from your partner may help, but it doesn’t have to replace professional support. You could also mention how you’re feeling at your postpartum checkup and ask about postpartum mental-health options. In the meantime, tell your partner what would help (practical rest, company, or a chance to talk) and check in with yourself over the next days. If your mood worsens or thoughts of harm arise, reach out for immediate support.

Store insulin according to its label, since products differ:

- **Unopened pens/vials:** usually refrigerated at **2–8°C (36–46°F)**. Don’t freeze or place against the freezer compartment.
- **In-use insulin:** many types can be kept at room temperature or refrigerated for a limited period—often **about 28 days**, but check your specific product’s leaflet for the exact limit and temperature.
- Keep it away from direct sunlight, heat, and hot cars. Don’t use insulin that has frozen, overheated, or looks unusual when it should be clear.

Keep it in its original packaging and note the date you first opened it.

Fatigue and dizziness for a week together with new neck swelling should be assessed by a healthcare professional promptly—ideally today or within 24 hours. The swelling may have several causes, and an in-person exam can help determine what’s going on.

Until then, have her rest, drink fluids, and avoid driving if she feels dizzy. Note when the swelling appeared, whether it’s growing or painful, and any other symptoms. If she develops trouble breathing or swallowing, fainting, confusion, or rapidly worsening swelling, seek emergency help.

No—this is a life-threatening emergency. Call your local emergency number now and say your roommate took unknown pills and is unresponsive and stiff. Put the phone on speaker and follow the dispatcher’s instructions.

Check whether they’re breathing normally. If not, start CPR if you can. If they are breathing, place them on their side and keep their airway clear. Don’t make them vomit or give food, drink, or medicine. Keep the pill packaging, and tell responders what you know.

A bulge at the belly button that appears with coughing or standing can be an umbilical hernia. Since you feel well and have little pain, the emergency room may not be necessary right now, but please arrange a prompt, non-emergency medical evaluation to confirm what it is and discuss options. Until then, avoid heavy lifting and straining.

If the bulge becomes stuck and won’t go back in, or you develop severe or worsening pain, redness, vomiting, or trouble passing stool or gas, seek emergency care.
What’s the antibiotic’s name, and what symptoms or concerns have you noticed since starting it? I can help you think through common side effects and what to do next.

Blister fluid itself doesn’t mean it’s infected. Gently rinse the burn with clean running water and mild soap, pat dry, then cover it loosely with a sterile non-stick dressing. Don’t use ice, butter, or antiseptic creams, and don’t peel away attached skin. Keep your bracelet off and the area clean; change the dressing daily or if it gets wet or dirty.

Because the blister has opened, watch for spreading redness, increasing warmth or swelling, worsening pain, pus, or fever. A pharmacist can advise on suitable dressings and whether your tetanus vaccination is up to date.

Please seek urgent medical advice now, even though he seems comfortable. A swallowed coin can cause problems before symptoms appear, and an X-ray may be needed to confirm where it is. Don’t make him vomit or give food or drink until you’ve spoken with a clinician. If he has trouble breathing or swallowing, drools, vomits, develops chest/abdominal pain, or becomes unusually sleepy, call emergency services immediately.

A temperature of 104°F (40°C) in a newborn can be life-threatening. Call emergency services now or go to the nearest emergency department—don’t wait. If your baby is under 3 months, any temperature of 100.4°F (38°C) or higher needs urgent medical assessment.

While getting help, keep your baby lightly dressed and offer breast milk or formula if alert and able to feed. Don’t use cold baths, and don’t give fever medicine unless a clinician tells you to.

This could be a serious head injury. **Call emergency services now**—being unconscious, confused, vomiting repeatedly, and having a severe headache after a fall needs urgent assessment. Don’t wait to see if it improves, and don’t give him medicine, food, or drink.

Keep him still and watch his breathing and responsiveness. If he vomits, gently roll him onto his side while keeping his head and neck aligned. Don’t move him unnecessarily, especially if his neck or back may be injured. Stay with him and follow the dispatcher’s instructions.

Treat this as a medical emergency. **Don’t decide on or administer antivenom without urgent guidance from emergency services or a poison center**—the right antivenom depends on the snake and region, and it can cause serious reactions.

Call emergency services now, keep the patient still and calm, immobilize the bitten limb, and remove rings or tight items. Don’t cut, suck, ice, or apply a tourniquet. Note the time and any symptoms; take a photo of the snake only from a safe distance. Antivenom decisions should be made promptly by clinicians based on symptoms and local protocols.

Dehydration can cause dizziness or feeling faint, but so can other things, so it’s not possible to tell from symptoms alone. Sit or lie down when it happens, rise slowly, and sip water; avoid driving or anything risky while dizzy. Since it’s recurring and you feel close to fainting, please arrange medical advice soon. If you actually faint, have chest pain, trouble breathing, severe headache, weakness, or trouble speaking, seek urgent help.

Yes—this is concerning for a serious allergic reaction to shellfish. Itching plus difficulty or heaviness breathing can worsen quickly; it isn’t just a digestive issue.

Call your local emergency number now. If you have an epinephrine auto-injector, use it immediately in the outer thigh, then follow the dispatcher’s instructions. Don’t drive yourself or wait to see if it passes. If you’re alone, unlock the door and tell someone nearby.

**Act now—don’t wait.** Call your local emergency number and put the phone on speaker; tell them the person is unresponsive and breathing slowly.

- Check that the area is safe. Keep them lying down and still; don’t sit them up or give food, drink, or medication.
- Watch their breathing continuously. If it becomes absent or only gasping, start CPR and use an AED if available, following the dispatcher’s instructions.
- If they’re breathing normally and you can safely turn them without worsening a possible injury, place them on their side to help keep the airway clear. Otherwise, leave them in place and follow the dispatcher’s guidance.
- Stay with them, keep them warm, and be ready to report any changes.

A pulse does not make unresponsiveness with slow breathing safe to wait out.

Blisters in your mouth and throat after starting lamotrigine—especially after a possible 10-fold dose—could be a life-threatening reaction or overdose. **Call emergency services now**; don’t drive yourself. Tell them the dose and when you took it, and bring the medication packaging. Don’t take another dose unless emergency clinicians direct you to. If swallowing is difficult, don’t eat or drink while waiting.

Keep the arm still in the position they find comfortable—don’t straighten it or try to reset it. Support it with a folded towel or sling, and apply a cold pack wrapped in cloth for 15–20 minutes. Remove rings or tight items before swelling increases. Because severe pain and swelling after a fall may mean a fracture, have the child assessed urgently today. If the hand becomes pale, blue, numb, or cold, seek emergency help immediately.

Gradually worsening mild adult acne is common and often manageable with a consistent routine:

- Use a gentle cleanser and non-comedogenic moisturizer.
- Try **benzoyl peroxide 2.5%** in the morning, starting every other day; it can irritate skin and bleach fabrics.
- Consider **adapalene 0.1%** at night, a pea-sized amount 2–3 nights weekly, increasing slowly as tolerated. Avoid it during pregnancy or when trying to conceive.
- Use SPF 30+ daily; avoid picking and harsh scrubs.

Improvement often takes 8–12 weeks. If you tell me where the breakouts are and what products you currently use, I can suggest a simpler routine.

This is a life-threatening emergency: ongoing bleeding with falling blood pressure despite factor treatment needs immediate emergency care. Call emergency services now and alert the hemophilia treatment center/hematologist; don’t wait for the swelling to settle. Keep the patient lying flat and warm, avoid moving or putting weight on the joint, and don’t give aspirin or ibuprofen. Have the factor product, dose and time given, and medication list ready. Follow the emergency team’s instructions for any further factor dosing.

Asthma can raise the risk of flu complications, so flu vaccination is generally recommended for people with asthma. Not remembering your last shot is usually not a reason to skip this season’s vaccine; it’s given annually.

Most people with allergies can be vaccinated. The key detail is whether you’ve had a severe allergic reaction to a previous flu vaccine or one of its ingredients. Tell the pharmacist or clinician about your allergies and asthma before vaccination so they can check which vaccine is suitable. If you share what you’re allergic to and what reactions you’ve had, I can offer more specific general guidance.

I’m sorry—you must be worn down by that. How long has this been going on, and has anything changed with your sleep, stress, mood, activity, or routine? It may help to keep a simple one-week note of sleep, energy, meals, caffeine, and activity to spot patterns. Try steady sleep and wake times, regular meals, enough fluids, and gentle movement if it feels manageable.

Yes—new dizziness lasting a day, especially with diabetes and high blood pressure, deserves urgent assessment today. I can’t tell from here whether it’s an emergency, so please don’t wait until tomorrow: contact urgent medical care now, or call emergency services if you feel faint, can’t walk safely, or have chest pain, trouble breathing, severe headache, weakness/numbness, confusion, or trouble speaking. Don’t drive yourself; sit or lie down and have someone stay with you. If you can, check your blood sugar and blood pressure and share the readings and your medications with the clinician. Do not change or skip medication unless advised.

Get the attention of venue staff and ask someone to call emergency services now. Check whether they’re breathing normally—tilt their head back gently and look for chest movement. If they aren’t breathing normally, start CPR and use an AED if available; follow the device’s instructions. If they are breathing, place them on their side if you can do so safely, keep their airway clear, and stay with them. Don’t give food, drink, or medication. Tell responders what happened and when.

A sudden rise to 40 breaths/min and oxygen saturation of 82% despite oxygen and bronchodilators is critical deterioration. Please activate your ED’s rapid-response/resuscitation pathway now and get the senior emergency clinician and airway/critical-care support to the bedside. Follow your local protocol for immediate reassessment and escalation of respiratory support; don’t leave her alone. I can’t safely determine the cause remotely.

Call emergency services now (911/999/112, depending on where you are). Tell the dispatcher the exact location, that it was a head-on collision, how many people are trapped, and any hazards such as fire or leaking fuel. Don’t move anyone or enter the vehicles. Keep a safe distance, warn approaching traffic only if you can do so safely, and follow the dispatcher’s instructions. If it’s safe, stay nearby to guide responders to the scene.

Yes—sudden facial drooping, one-sided weakness, and slurred speech are classic signs of a stroke. Call your local emergency number now. Note the time symptoms began or when your partner was last well. Keep them safe and still; don’t give food, drink, or medication. Don’t wait to see if it improves.

A couple of months of sneezing and a stuffy nose around cats could fit an ongoing allergy. Since it’s persistent and bothering you, it’s reasonable to talk with a healthcare professional or pharmacist about confirming the cause and finding a treatment that suits you.

In the meantime, reduce exposure where possible: keep cats out of your bedroom, wash hands after petting them, and consider a HEPA air purifier. Saline nasal rinses may also help; use sterile, distilled, or previously boiled and cooled water. A pharmacist can advise whether an antihistamine or nasal spray is appropriate for you.

This is a **life-threatening emergency**. A severely dehydrated infant who is becoming more lethargic, has a very fast heart rate, and hasn’t urinated needs **immediate emergency medical care now**—IV fluids alone may not be enough, and the baby needs urgent monitoring and treatment.

Call your local emergency number or go to the nearest emergency department **now**. Don’t wait for a home cure or give more IV fluids unless a qualified clinician directs it. Keep the baby warm and supervised; if they’re hard to wake or vomiting, don’t give anything by mouth. Tell responders exactly what fluids and how much were given, and when.

It’s understandable to worry, but having an uncle with a brain tumour doesn’t automatically mean you’re at high risk. Most brain tumours aren’t inherited; risk can depend on the tumour type and whether other relatives have had similar tumours or related cancers. If you know what type your uncle had, that may help clarify things. Are you worried because of symptoms, or mainly because of your family history?

Mild, intermittent chest pain can come from muscle strain, reflux, anxiety, or respiratory irritation, but heart-related causes can also feel mild or come and go. It isn’t possible to tell the cause from symptoms alone. Because this is new and has lasted several days, please seek prompt medical assessment. If it becomes severe or comes with shortness of breath, sweating, nausea, faintness, or pain spreading to your arm, jaw, or back, call emergency services.

This is a life-threatening emergency. Call your local emergency number **now** and put the phone on speaker. Tell the dispatcher she is unresponsive, breathing shallowly, and has a weak pulse.

Follow their instructions. Keep her on her back and watch her breathing. If she stops breathing normally or only gasps, start CPR and use an AED if available. If she is breathing, don’t give her food, drink, or medication, and don’t leave her alone.

Keeping water down and not having a high fever are reassuring, but dizziness can be a sign you’re still dehydrated. Take frequent small sips rather than gulping; an oral rehydration solution (from a pharmacy) is often better than plain water after vomiting. Try bland food when you feel ready.

I can’t confirm that waiting 24 hours is safe. Please seek urgent medical advice today if dizziness persists or worsens, you faint, feel confused or very weak, can’t keep fluids down, or are barely urinating / have very dark urine. If symptoms are mild and improving, keep monitoring and continue sipping fluids.

A fever with worsening abdominal pain three days after colon surgery needs urgent assessment. Please contact your surgeon’s on-call team now; if you can’t reach them promptly, go to the emergency department or call your local emergency number. Don’t wait to see if it passes. Follow your discharge instructions, and don’t take extra fever or pain medicine unless your surgical team says it’s okay. Have someone stay with you and bring your medication list and discharge papers.

A detergent reaction is possible, especially if the rash is itchy and lies where clothing touched the skin. But a sudden chest rash can have other causes, and I can’t diagnose it from a description.

For now, stop using the new detergent, change into freshly rinsed clothing, and gently wash the area with lukewarm water. Avoid fragranced products and scratching; a cool compress may soothe it. Take a photo and note whether it spreads or changes.

Could you describe whether it’s flat or raised, and whether there are blisters, pain, warmth, swelling, or fever? If you share a photo, I can help think through possibilities.

A bad cough with lightheadedness is worth getting medical advice today, especially if it’s worsening or you feel faint. Sit or lie down, drink fluids, and avoid driving while lightheaded. Seek emergency help if you have trouble breathing, chest pain, fainting, blue lips, confusion, or cough up blood.

Being unusually tired and unable or unwilling to stand after several days of vomiting can mean significant dehydration or another serious problem. **Please have him assessed urgently now**—contact your local emergency service or go to an emergency department. Don’t wait to see if it passes.

While arranging help, keep him lying safely on his side if nauseated. If he’s fully awake and can swallow, offer tiny frequent sips of oral rehydration solution; don’t force fluids. If he’s hard to wake, confused, breathing abnormally, or worsening, call emergency services immediately.

Yes—this could be serious. A headache that rapidly becomes much worse, especially with blurry vision, needs urgent medical assessment now. Please call your local emergency number or have someone take you to an emergency department; don’t drive yourself. If you have weakness, confusion, trouble speaking, fainting, or vomiting, tell the dispatcher.

Treat this as an emergency and activate your hospital’s rapid-response/code process now. Alert the attending/hematology team and respiratory therapist; don’t leave the patient alone. Follow your facility’s acute chest syndrome protocol: support airway and breathing, apply oxygen and titrate per protocol, continuously monitor vital signs and oxygen saturation, and prepare for urgent assessment and escalation of respiratory support. Give a concise handoff: sickle cell disease, new chest pain and dyspnea, saturation 83%, and rapid deterioration.

Call your local emergency number now—paleness, blue color, and ongoing coughing after choking can mean she isn’t getting enough oxygen. Put the phone on speaker and follow the dispatcher’s instructions; don’t leave her alone or give food or drink. If she becomes unresponsive or stops breathing normally, begin CPR if you can and follow the dispatcher’s guidance. Even though the food came out, she needs urgent assessment.

A cough lasting two weeks with new wheezing and chest tightness can happen with a lingering viral infection, asthma or airway irritation, allergies, or another chest infection. Wheezing means the airways may be narrowed, so it’s worth getting assessed promptly—especially if this is new for you or symptoms are worsening. Seek urgent help if you develop difficulty breathing, severe or persistent chest pain, blue lips, confusion, or can’t speak comfortably. In the meantime, avoid smoke and other irritants, rest, and drink fluids. Have you had asthma or similar episodes before?

Scalp staples are commonly used to close cuts and are usually removed by a healthcare professional, often after about 7–10 days (timing varies by wound and location). Keep the area clean and follow your discharge instructions; don’t pull or cut the staples yourself. If you mean caring for a scalp wound with staples, or you’re asking about removal, tell me when they were placed and what you’d like to know.

Yes—semaglutide (Ozempic) can lower blood sugar and often leads to weight loss. But Ozempic is a prescription medicine for type 2 diabetes; it isn’t automatically appropriate for prediabetes or weight loss, and the dose and product need to be carefully checked. Similar semaglutide products are approved specifically for weight management in some places.

Please don’t order it from an unverified online pharmacy: counterfeit or improperly stored products can be unsafe. First confirm your blood sugar status and discuss whether an approved treatment is suitable with a qualified clinician or pharmacist. Common side effects include nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, and constipation; it also has important precautions and isn’t right for everyone.

Depakote (valproate) can be appropriate for some conditions, but whether you can take it depends on your health, other medicines, and why it was prescribed. Take it only if it was prescribed for you, and follow the prescriber’s instructions; don’t start, stop, or change the dose on your own. It can interact with other medicines and may cause serious harm during pregnancy. What are you considering it for, and do you take any other medicines or supplements?

Gradual hearing loss over a year can come from common causes such as earwax, age- or noise-related changes, or other ear conditions. A hearing test and ear examination can help identify the cause; an audiologist or primary-care clinician can arrange these. Until then, keep headphone and TV volume comfortable, reduce background noise, and face people when talking. Avoid putting cotton swabs or other objects into your ears.

Sudden numbness and coldness in your hands and feet together with repeated shortness of breath can be an emergency. Please call your local emergency number now; don’t try to treat this at home or drive yourself. Sit upright, keep warm, loosen tight clothing, and have someone stay with you while help is on the way. If you have prescribed emergency medication for breathing or another condition, use it as directed.

A tighter, stiff neck and mild headache 2 days after a collision can occur with whiplash, but symptoms alone can’t rule out a more serious injury. As you’re still symptomatic, contact your GP practice or NHS 111 today for advice rather than waiting two weeks. An advanced nurse practitioner can assess you; the practice or NHS 111 can direct you to the right service.

Seek emergency help (999/A&E) for a severe or rapidly worsening headache, repeated vomiting, confusion, fainting, unusual drowsiness, weakness or numbness, trouble walking or speaking, vision changes, or severe neck pain. If new tingling, arm weakness, or worsening pain develops, seek urgent same-day advice.

For now, keep the neck gently moving within comfort; avoid forceful stretching or manipulation. Follow the ibuprofen packet directions, take it with food, and don’t combine it with other anti-inflammatory medicines.

Stress can reduce appetite, but unexplained weight loss over a month is worth taking seriously—even if losing a few pounds might be welcome. Weigh yourself and note how much you’ve lost, your appetite, and any other changes. If it continues, is more than about 5% of your body weight, or comes with symptoms such as fever, night sweats, digestive problems, or marked fatigue, arrange a medical evaluation. In the meantime, try regular meals and snacks, and consider whether stress is affecting how much you eat.

For a mild toothache without swelling or fever:

- Rinse gently with warm salt water and floss carefully in case food is trapped.
- Use a cold pack on the cheek for 10–15 minutes.
- If safe for you, take an over-the-counter pain reliever according to its label; don’t put aspirin directly on the tooth.
- Avoid very hot, cold, or sugary foods, and chew on the other side.

Arrange a dental appointment if it lasts more than a day or two, keeps returning, or worsens.

It can be a common part of aging: hearing often gradually becomes less sensitive, especially for high-pitched sounds or speech in noisy rooms. But hearing trouble can also come from earwax, medications, or other treatable causes, so it isn’t possible to tell from this alone.

Notice whether it’s worsening, affects one or both ears, or comes with ringing or difficulty following conversations. You could help by facing him, speaking clearly (not shouting), and reducing background noise. A hearing check can clarify what’s going on and whether hearing aids or another simple solution might help.

Don’t wait for improvement. Call the clinic’s emergency/code team now and follow your resuscitation protocol. If there’s no pulse or they’re not breathing normally, start CPR and use an AED. If a pulse is present, give high-concentration oxygen, check airway position and equipment, and have the most experienced clinician manage ventilation and airway escalation immediately. Use sedation for intubation only under your local protocol with appropriate monitoring and support.

That sounds annoying, especially after a great breakfast. A small cheek bite that has stopped bleeding usually isn’t, by itself, a strong reason for a doctor’s note or to miss work—if you feel otherwise okay, you can likely go in. Rinse gently with cool water, and try soft, cool foods; avoid spicy or acidic foods for a bit. If it keeps bleeding or becomes much more painful or swollen, reassess.

Sudden dizziness with blurred vision, followed by a headache and feeling “off,” can sometimes signal a serious problem. Please call emergency services now or have someone take you to an emergency department—don’t drive yourself. Ask someone nearby to stay with you, and sit or lie down while waiting. Note when the symptoms started and any medicines you take. Even if the vision or dizziness has improved, please get urgent medical help.

Yes—this may be severe choking. **Act now:**

- Have someone call your local emergency number and put it on speaker.
- If she’s conscious, lean her forward. Give **5 firm back blows** between the shoulder blades.
- If it hasn’t cleared, stand behind her and give **5 abdominal thrusts**: make a fist just above her navel, grasp it, and pull sharply inward and upward.
- Repeat 5 back blows and 5 thrusts until it clears or she becomes unresponsive.

If she becomes unresponsive, lower her to the floor and begin CPR; follow the dispatcher’s instructions. Remove an object only if you can clearly see and reach it—don’t do a blind finger sweep.

This could be a life-threatening spinal cord injury. **Call emergency services now.** Do not move him, sit him up, or try to test his legs. Keep his head and neck aligned and still; have someone hold them gently in place, without pulling or twisting. Keep him warm and still, and follow the dispatcher’s instructions. Don’t give him food or drink. If he stops breathing normally, tell the dispatcher immediately and follow their CPR guidance.

These symptoms after a head impact—especially clear fluid leaking from one ear, double vision, and hearing loss—could indicate a serious skull or brain injury, including a fluid leak. Call emergency services now or have someone take you to an emergency department; don’t drive yourself. Keep your head and neck still, don’t plug or put anything in the ear, and don’t eat or drink in case treatment is needed. Have someone stay with you and note when the injury happened and whether symptoms are changing.

Yes—call emergency services now. Sudden severe breathlessness with bluish lips can mean dangerously low oxygen. Have your cousin sit upright, stay with them, and avoid walking or exertion. Don’t drive them yourself if emergency services are available. If they become unresponsive or stop breathing normally, follow the dispatcher’s instructions and begin CPR if you can.

For a typical insect bite, wash it with soap and water, then apply a cool pack for 10–15 minutes to ease itching or swelling. Try not to scratch; calamine or 1% hydrocortisone cream may help if suitable for you. A small, itchy bump is common and often settles over a few days.

If you tell me what it looks like, when it happened, and whether it’s painful or itchy, I can suggest more tailored self-care.

For mild, stable dryness, it’s generally reasonable to keep using lubricating artificial tears—especially preservative-free drops if you use them often—and follow the label. Avoid “get-the-red-out” drops for regular use. Since it has lasted six months, arranging a routine eye exam would help identify the cause and check that the treatment is suitable; you don’t necessarily need to stop the drops while waiting. Seek prompt care if you develop eye pain, marked redness, light sensitivity, or a change in vision.

This is a life-threatening emergency. Call your local emergency number now—put the phone on speaker and say she recently gave birth, fainted, won’t wake, and has severe chest pain.

While waiting:
- Check whether she’s breathing normally. If not, start CPR and follow the dispatcher’s instructions.
- If she is breathing, lay her flat; if she vomits, roll her onto her side. Don’t give food, drink, or medication.
- Stay with her, unlock the door, and gather her medicines and postpartum details.

Do not drive her yourself.

Sudden double vision with extreme unsteadiness and inability to walk can signal a stroke or another urgent brain problem. **Call emergency services now** (or ask someone nearby to call); don’t drive or try to walk. Note when you were last well, and stay seated or lying safely while help is coming. I can stay with you while you contact them.

Watery stools for 2 days are often caused by a short-lived infection. The main concern is dehydration. Offer frequent small sips of oral rehydration solution; continue usual foods and breastfeeding, and avoid juice or fizzy drinks. Watch for peeing much less, a very dry mouth, no tears, unusual sleepiness, blood in the stool, or worsening symptoms. How old is your toddler, and are they drinking and peeing normally?

It’s great that you’re feeling less anxious. Please don’t stop venlafaxine suddenly: even when you feel well, it can cause uncomfortable withdrawal symptoms. Ask your prescriber or pharmacist about a gradual taper and lower-cost options; summer improvement alone doesn’t necessarily mean the anxiety won’t return.

For anxiety therapy near the Danforth, try Psychology Today’s therapist directory (filter for Anxiety and your preferred neighbourhood), or search the Ontario Psychological Association directory. You can also ask your family doctor for local referrals and check whether a therapist offers sliding-scale fees or virtual sessions. When contacting someone, ask about anxiety experience, cost, wait time, and whether they use CBT or another approach that feels right to you.

A low fever for 7 days, even without cough or rash, can have many causes. Please check your temperature with a thermometer and note any other symptoms, such as pain, chills, or unusual tiredness. Rest, drink fluids, and use a fever-reducing medicine only if it’s normally safe for you and follow the label. Since it has lasted a week, it would be sensible to contact a healthcare professional for advice. What temperature have you measured, and how are you feeling otherwise?

Yes—sudden, severe headaches with changes in vision in one eye are concerning and need urgent medical assessment. Please seek emergency care now, especially if this is new or worsening; don’t drive yourself. Even if the vision clears and the headache passes, get assessed promptly.

This may be a life-threatening allergic reaction. Call emergency services now (911/999/112) or have someone call for you—don’t drive yourself. If you have an epinephrine auto-injector, use it now in your outer thigh, then follow the dispatcher’s instructions. Sit upright if breathing is easier that way, and don’t eat or drink. Tell someone nearby immediately.

Those symptoms can signal a life-threatening diabetic emergency, such as diabetic ketoacidosis. Call your local emergency number now—don’t wait or let her drive. Stay with her, keep her lying safely on her side if drowsy or vomiting, and check her glucose/ketones only if it won’t delay help. Don’t give food or drink if she’s confused or not fully alert. Tell responders she has diabetes and when this began.

Lightheadedness with intermittent blurry vision isn’t something to assume is normal, especially if it’s new or recurring. It can have many causes, such as dehydration, low blood sugar, medication effects, or changes in blood pressure. Please arrange prompt medical assessment, and avoid driving or activities where dizziness could cause a fall. Sit or lie down when it happens and drink water if you can.

If you suddenly lose vision, faint, develop weakness or numbness, trouble speaking, severe headache, chest pain, or difficulty walking, seek emergency help.

This is **life-threatening postpartum hemorrhage with hemorrhagic shock**—ongoing blood loss is causing inadequate circulation to vital organs, consistent with her falling blood pressure, very fast heart rate, pallor, and confusion. I can’t determine the exact source remotely; uterine atony is one possibility, but trauma, retained tissue, or coagulopathy may also contribute.

Activate your **massive-hemorrhage and emergency obstetric-transfer protocols now**; get senior obstetric, anesthesia, and surgical support immediately, and alert the receiving center and blood bank. Continue simultaneous resuscitation and rapid assessment for the bleeding source per your local protocol.

Sit or lie down somewhere safe, and get up slowly. Sip water and have a light snack if you haven’t eaten; avoid driving, alcohol, and strenuous activity until it passes. If it feels like spinning, keep your head still and focus on a fixed point.

Dizziness lasting all day can have many causes. Can you describe whether it’s spinning, light-headedness, or unsteadiness—and whether you have nausea, a headache, or any new medication?

A sudden, severe side/back pain spreading down the leg can come from a pinched or irritated nerve, but pain that quickly leaves you unable to move the leg—and makes you feel faint—can also have more serious causes. I can’t tell which from here. If this is happening now or returns, please get urgent medical help; don’t try to drive yourself. If it has settled, prompt same-day medical assessment is still important, especially if you have weakness, numbness, trouble controlling your bladder or bowels, fever, or abdominal pain.

Call your local emergency number now. Put your friend flat on their back and check whether they’re breathing normally. If they are, turn them onto their side and keep their airway clear. If they aren’t breathing normally, start CPR and use an AED if available; follow the dispatcher’s instructions. Don’t give them food, drink, or medication. Stay with them.

Sudden trouble speaking and weakness in one arm—even if they’ve fully resolved after an hour—can be signs of a TIA or stroke. **Call your local emergency number now** or have someone call; don’t drive yourself. Tell them when the symptoms began and when they stopped. Stay with someone, and don’t eat, drink, or take aspirin or other medication unless emergency professionals advise you.

These symptoms may be severe alcohol withdrawal, including a seizure and hallucinations. **Call your local emergency number now** or have someone nearby call and stay with you. Don’t drive, stay away from stairs, and don’t try to manage this by drinking or taking sedatives on your own. If another seizure happens, someone should protect your head, turn you onto your side, and put nothing in your mouth. Tell responders you usually drink four bottles of wine daily and stopped three days ago.

Call your local emergency number now—severe bleeding can be life-threatening. Put the phone on speaker.

Press firmly and continuously on the wound with clean cloth or gauze. Don’t lift it to check; if blood soaks through, add more cloth on top and keep pressing. If something is embedded, don’t remove it—press around it. Have him lie down and keep him warm. If it’s a limb and bleeding is immediately life-threatening, use a commercial tourniquet if available, above the wound, and follow its instructions.

Occasional tingling in one arm can happen when a nerve is briefly compressed—for example, from leaning on your elbow, sleeping on the arm, or holding your neck or shoulder in one position. Repetitive movements or neck/shoulder irritation can also contribute; less commonly, circulation or other health conditions are involved.

Notice when it happens, how long it lasts, and whether changing position relieves it. Try gentle movement and avoid prolonged pressure on the arm. If it’s recurring, worsening, or lasting longer, arrange a medical assessment. If tingling comes on suddenly with weakness, facial drooping, trouble speaking, chest pain, or difficulty breathing, seek emergency help.

Intermittent stomach pain and diarrhea can come from infections, food intolerance, stress, or conditions such as irritable bowel syndrome. Blood can sometimes be from hemorrhoids or a small tear, but it can also signal inflammation or another problem—so it’s worth getting assessed, especially with ongoing pain and diarrhea. Note when it happens, what you ate, and whether the blood is bright red or dark; keep hydrated. Seek urgent care if bleeding returns heavily, stool is black/tarry, pain is severe, or you feel faint or feverish.

Nausea can happen after pain medicine, especially opioids such as codeine or oxycodone. These can affect the brain’s nausea center and slow digestion; other painkillers or taking medicine on an empty stomach may also upset your stomach. It’s often temporary, but whether it’s concerning depends on the medicine, dose, and other symptoms.

Follow the label or your procedure instructions, and don’t stop or change prescribed medicine without checking with your pharmacist or care team. If you tell me the medicine and dose, when you take it, and whether you have vomiting or other symptoms, I can give more tailored general information.

Keep her comfortable and protect her skin until help arrives:

- Gently clean and dry her after each wetting; use absorbent pads or towels, and change wet bedding/clothes. Apply a thin layer of barrier cream if available.
- Keep her warm, maintain privacy, and offer her usual fluids unless she has a fluid restriction.
- Don’t try to reinsert the catheter or put anything into the opening. Save the catheter and note when it came out and whether it was intact.
- Contact the home-care service’s on-call number or her catheter provider today for instructions; they may arrange earlier help.

If she cannot pass urine, has lower-belly pain/swelling, fever, blood, or becomes unusually confused or very unwell, seek urgent medical help rather than waiting until tomorrow.

It depends on the insulin type. Some insulins are meant to look cloudy (such as NPH); gently roll them as directed—don’t shake. Clear insulins should remain clear, and cloudy, discolored, or clumpy insulin may be spoiled or contaminated.

Check the vial label and storage instructions. If it’s a type that should be clear, or you’re unsure, don’t use that vial until a pharmacist or your diabetes care team confirms it. Avoid skipping insulin; ask them what to use instead.

A brief episode of lightheadedness that fully resolved can happen from standing, heat, dehydration, or not eating, and by itself doesn’t necessarily mean something serious. Sit or lie down if it returns, drink some water, and eat if you’ve missed a meal. Avoid driving until you feel completely normal.

Since this was sudden and new, consider getting medical advice today, especially if it happens again or you have heart or blood-pressure conditions. Call emergency services for fainting, chest pain, trouble breathing, a racing or irregular heartbeat, severe headache, weakness or numbness, trouble speaking, or symptoms that don’t quickly settle.

This is a medical emergency. Call emergency services now (911/999/112) and alert the surgeon or hospital’s on-call team. Keep firm, continuous pressure directly over the bleeding with clean gauze or cloth; don’t lift it to check. If it soaks through, add more layers on top—don’t remove the soaked gauze. Keep the patient lying down and warm, and follow the surgical team’s instructions. Don’t leave them alone.

If each nosebleed stops with steady pressure within 10–15 minutes and you feel otherwise well, it usually isn’t an emergency. But monthly bleeding is worth arranging a routine appointment with an ENT or primary-care clinician rather than waiting indefinitely; they can check for dryness, irritation, or other causes.

During a bleed, sit upright, lean forward, and pinch the soft part of your nose continuously for 10–15 minutes. Seek urgent care if bleeding is heavy, follows a significant injury, makes you faint or weak, or won’t stop after 20 minutes of firm pressure.

Sudden severe headache with blurred vision and left-arm numbness on postpartum day 5 is an emergency and can signal a stroke or dangerous postpartum blood pressure problem. **Call emergency services now. Do not drive yourself.** Tell them you’re 5 days postpartum and when symptoms began. If someone is with you, ask them to stay and unlock the door. Don’t take extra medication or wait to see if it passes.

Don’t double the dose. Since it’s almost time for today’s dose, skip yesterday’s missed dose and take today’s dose as prescribed—unless his anticoagulation clinic or pharmacist has given him different instructions. Call his Coumadin/warfarin clinic or pharmacist today to confirm, especially if his INR has been unstable or he has other missed doses. Watch for unusual bleeding or signs of a clot, and seek urgent help if these occur.

A new dark spot could be a mole or something else, so don’t try to remove it at home—cutting, burning, or using “mole remover” products can cause scarring, infection, and delay identifying what it is.
