Get them out of the heat, move them to a cool place, and loosen extra clothing. Keep them lying on their side if drowsy or vomiting, and stay with them. Don’t give food, drink, or medication, and don’t put them in an ice bath. Follow the dispatcher’s instructions.

Don’t put water in your ear or use fingers, cotton buds, or tweezers—the insect may move deeper, and water can make it harder to remove. Tilt your head with the left ear facing upward and wait briefly; you can gently shine a light near the opening, but don’t insert anything. If it doesn’t come out quickly, or you have pain, bleeding, dizziness, or reduced hearing, seek urgent medical care so it can be removed safely.

Itchy throat and a neck rash after eating can signal a food allergy. Avoid the suspected foods and arrange an appointment with a healthcare professional or allergist to identify the cause. Keep a note of what you ate and when symptoms started.

If you develop trouble breathing or swallowing, throat/tongue/lip swelling, dizziness, or feel faint, use prescribed epinephrine if you have it and call emergency services immediately. Don’t wait to see if it passes.

This is a **life-threatening emergency** and could be thyroid storm. **Call emergency services now** and tell them she has hyperthyroidism, a heart rate over 180, fever above 40°C, and rapidly worsening symptoms. Do not drive her yourself if emergency transport is available. Keep her with someone, monitor breathing and responsiveness, and follow the dispatcher’s instructions. Don’t give extra thyroid or heart medication unless a clinician or emergency dispatcher directs you.

Wash the scratch thoroughly with soap and running water for 15 minutes, then apply an antiseptic and keep it clean and covered. Don’t let your dog lick it. Check for increasing redness, warmth, swelling, pain, pus, or fever; seek medical care if these develop.

Even vaccinated dogs can rarely transmit infection, and rabies risk depends on your location and the circumstances. Contact a healthcare professional or local public-health service promptly if the dog is acting unusually, cannot be observed, or the scratch may have been contaminated with saliva. Ask whether your tetanus vaccination is up to date.

I can’t diagnose enlarged tonsils remotely, but if your child is comfortable, breathing and swallowing normally, and has no fever or pain, it’s usually reasonable to arrange a routine appointment with their pediatrician rather than seek urgent care. They can check whether the tonsils are truly enlarged and review the child’s growth, sleep, and infection history. Don’t give antibiotics or use throat treatments unless advised; encourage fluids and observe.

Note snoring, pauses or gasping during sleep, restless sleep, daytime tiredness, repeated throat infections, or worsening size, and share these with the clinician. Seek urgent medical care if breathing or swallowing becomes difficult, they can’t handle saliva, or they become very unwell.

I’m so sorry—this could be a life-threatening infection. Call emergency services now or take her to the ER immediately; don’t wait. Tell them about the cut, fever, confusion, and racing heart. Keep her with someone, and don’t let her drive herself.

New numbness around the genitals together with back pain and trouble walking can signal serious pressure on nerves. **Please go to the emergency department now**—don’t wait for an appointment or try exercises. Have someone take you; don’t drive if walking is difficult. If you can’t get there safely, call emergency services.

That sounds unsettling. Dizziness triggered by reading can have several causes, including eye strain or an outdated glasses prescription, neck posture, dehydration, or problems with balance—but I can’t diagnose it here.

Take regular breaks from reading, keep the text well lit and at a comfortable distance, adjust your posture, and drink fluids. Since it’s been happening for a week, arrange a routine check with an optometrist or healthcare professional, especially if it continues or worsens. Note what triggers it and whether you feel spinning, unsteadiness, or light-headedness.

Seek urgent care if you develop severe or sudden dizziness, fainting, trouble walking, weakness or numbness, difficulty speaking, vision loss, chest pain, or a severe headache.

Vomiting blood—even a streak—needs urgent medical assessment. Please go to the emergency department now or call emergency services, especially since you feel unwell. Don’t drive yourself if you feel weak or dizzy.

While arranging help, if you’re fully alert and not actively vomiting, you can take tiny sips of water; don’t gulp or force fluids. If vomiting resumes, stop drinking and get help immediately.

No—don’t try to sleep this off. New or severe squeezing chest tightness can be a medical emergency, even if anxiety is possible. Call emergency services now (911/999/112, depending on where you are), and don’t drive yourself. Sit and rest while you wait; if someone is nearby, ask them to stay with you.

Getting breathless on stairs for several weeks deserves a medical check, even if you recover quickly. Please arrange an appointment with a clinician soon, especially if this is new or worsening. Until then, take stairs slowly and avoid pushing through symptoms.

If you’re breathless at rest, have chest pain, fainting, blue lips, or severe/worsening difficulty breathing, seek emergency care now.

A brief warm flush and metallic taste are common effects of CT contrast, and they often fade on their own. Since they eased and your heart rate and blood pressure were stable, this sounds less like a serious reaction.

Get emergency help now if you develop trouble breathing, throat or facial swelling, widespread hives, fainting, or severe dizziness. If you have a rash, ongoing vomiting, or symptoms that worsen or don’t settle, contact the imaging center or your healthcare provider for advice.

This is life-threatening shock. **Arrange emergency evacuation to the advanced facility now—do not delay for more treatments or advice.** Call emergency services or the receiving facility while transport is organized; send someone ahead if possible. Keep monitoring and give them your observations and what fluids were given.

While waiting and during transport:
- Keep him lying flat, warm, and as still as possible; do not let him walk.
- Apply firm pressure to severe bleeding; use a tourniquet for life-threatening limb bleeding if trained, noting the time.
- Cover the open wound with a clean dressing; don’t push bone back in or manipulate the leg.
- Check breathing and responsiveness continuously. Give nothing by mouth. If breathing stops, begin CPR if trained.

Your care matters. You can pray or ask someone to pray alongside you, but let that support—not delay—urgent transfer.

Brief, occasional twitches or shivers during sleep can be normal in babies, but it’s not possible to tell from a description whether these are seizures. Please contact your baby’s pediatrician promptly, especially since this is new or increasing; a video of an episode can help.

If an episode won’t stop, repeats without her returning to normal, involves trouble breathing or blue/gray color, or she’s hard to wake or unusually unresponsive, call emergency services or go to the ER now. Don’t restrain her or put anything in her mouth.

Yes—this could be life-threatening, such as a heart attack or stroke. **Call emergency services now** (911/999/112 or your local number). Put the phone on speaker, tell them he has severe chest pain, a pounding heart, slurred speech, and reduced alertness, and follow their instructions.

Keep him still and don’t give food, drink, or medication unless the dispatcher advises it. Check whether he’s breathing normally. If he becomes unresponsive and isn’t breathing normally, start CPR and use an AED if available. Don’t drive him yourself.

Mild stomach cramps after takeout can happen from indigestion or a foodborne illness. Sip water and rest; eat bland foods if you feel hungry. Seek medical care urgently if the pain is severe or worsening, you have blood in vomit or stool, repeated vomiting, a high fever, fainting, or signs of dehydration. If symptoms don’t improve within a day or two, contact a healthcare professional.

Try drinking water, eating something if you’ve skipped a meal, and resting in a quiet, dim room. A cool cloth or a usual over-the-counter pain reliever may help—follow the label and avoid it if it’s unsafe for you.

Get emergency care now for a sudden, extremely severe headache, or one with weakness, numbness, confusion, fainting, trouble speaking, vision loss, fever with a stiff neck, or after a head injury. If it’s new, worsening, keeps returning, or doesn’t improve, contact a healthcare professional.

A sudden droopy face can be a sign of a stroke. **Call emergency services now**—don’t wait to see if it improves. Note the time it started, keep your partner safe and comfortable, and don’t give food, drink, or medication. If they become unresponsive or have trouble breathing, tell the dispatcher immediately.

Call emergency services now. Press firmly on the wound with clean cloth or gauze and keep continuous pressure—don’t lift it to check. If blood soaks through, add more cloth on top. Have him lie down and keep the arm raised if that doesn’t worsen the injury. Don’t remove anything embedded in the wound. If bleeding is life-threatening and you have a tourniquet, apply it high and tight above the wound and note the time. Keep him warm and still; don’t give food or drink.

This is an emergency. **Call your local emergency number now**—don’t wait to see if it passes or drive her yourself. Severe abdominal pain, fainting, pale skin, and reduced responsiveness can signal a life-threatening problem.

While help is coming:
- Check whether she’s breathing normally. If not, follow the dispatcher’s CPR instructions.
- If she is breathing, keep her lying still and warm; if she vomits, turn her onto her side.
- Don’t give food, drink, or medication. Stay with her and follow the dispatcher’s directions.

Blood in your urine needs prompt medical assessment, even if it’s only a little or happens once. Please contact a clinician or urgent care today to find the cause; don’t wait to see if it clears. Go to the emergency room now if you have heavy bleeding or clots, can’t urinate, severe back/side pain, fever, feel faint, or feel very unwell. Possible causes include infection, stones, or other urinary problems, but an exam and urine tests are needed.

Worsening vision at 65 needs an eye exam rather than choosing drops—drops usually won’t correct changes such as cataracts, glaucoma, or a prescription change. Please arrange an appointment with an optometrist or ophthalmologist soon, especially if the decline is ongoing. Avoid “redness-relief” drops unless a clinician recommends them.

If vision worsens suddenly, or you have eye pain, marked redness, flashes/floaters, a curtain or shadow, or sudden loss of sight, seek emergency care right away.

**Get emergency medical help now.** Slipping in and out of consciousness, trembling, and being unable to speak clearly are danger signs—not symptoms to wait out. Call your local emergency number or arrange the fastest safe transport to the nearest hospital. Ask a neighbor, community or faith leader to help with transport or costs; tell the hospital about your financial limits.

While help is coming, stay with him, keep him on his side if drowsy or vomiting, and watch his breathing. Don’t give food, drink, herbs, or medicine while he’s barely responsive, and don’t put anything in his ear.

Prayer can be part of supporting him, but please don’t let it delay urgent care. You can pray as you get help—acting quickly is a way to protect his life.

Yes. Dry air can irritate and crack the delicate lining inside your nose, causing nosebleeds—especially with nose-picking or forceful blowing. A humidifier, saline spray or gel, and gentle nose-blowing may help.

If bleeding starts, sit upright, lean forward, and pinch the soft part of your nose continuously for 10–15 minutes. Seek urgent care if it’s heavy, you feel faint or weak, it followed an injury, or it won’t stop after 20 minutes. Since you’ve had several recently, consider checking with a healthcare professional, particularly if you take blood thinners or have easy bruising.

This is an emergency. Call your local emergency number now—your child’s limpness and lack of response could be life-threatening. Don’t wait or try exercises.

Check whether they’re breathing normally. If not, follow the dispatcher’s CPR instructions. If they are breathing, keep them still and warm, and don’t give food or drink. Stay with them until help arrives.

This is a life-threatening emergency—possible postpartum eclampsia or another critical cause. **Call emergency services and activate the hospital’s obstetric emergency/rapid-response team now. Do not wait or try to treat this at home.**

While help is coming: protect her from injury, turn her onto her side if possible, clear nearby objects, and time the seizure. Don’t restrain her or put anything in her mouth. Check breathing and follow dispatcher instructions; begin CPR if she isn’t breathing normally and you’re trained.

She needs immediate hospital resuscitation and urgent clinician-directed treatment.

Clearing your throat about four times in 10 minutes can happen with a dry throat, postnasal drip, reflux, or irritation. Sip water, try a warm drink, and notice whether it improves or comes with congestion or heartburn. How long has this been happening, and do you have any other symptoms?

This could be a life-threatening emergency, such as a heart problem or severe heat illness. **Call emergency services now** and say he collapsed after running, has chest tightness, and can’t speak full sentences. Don’t let him walk or drive; keep him still and cool, and follow the dispatcher’s instructions. If he becomes unresponsive and isn’t breathing normally, start CPR and use an AED if available. Even if he seems to improve, he needs urgent medical assessment.

This is a **medical emergency**. High-pressure water can force fluid and bacteria deep into the hand, causing serious tissue damage—even if the skin opening looks small. **Go to an emergency department now**; don’t wait or try to treat it at home. Call emergency services if transport is difficult.

Keep the hand still and raised, remove rings or tight items, and cover any wound loosely with clean gauze. Don’t squeeze, massage, or apply ice. Tell the clinicians it was a **high-pressure water injection injury** and when it happened.

This is an emergency. **Fast breathing and drowsiness, after weeks of frequent urination, can signal diabetic ketoacidosis or another serious illness. Call your local emergency number now or go to the emergency department immediately.** Don’t wait for the antibiotics to work, and don’t try a home remedy.

Tell the dispatcher she is 10, has been urinating frequently for weeks, is breathing fast and drowsy, and is taking antibiotics. If cost is a concern, emergency services can advise you—please don’t delay seeking help. Keep her with you; don’t give food or drink if she’s very drowsy or struggling to breathe.

Sure. Please share the numbers and units for **total cholesterol, LDL, HDL, and triglycerides**, plus whether the test was fasting. These help put “higher than normal” in context.

Cholesterol results don’t determine risk on their own. Your age, blood pressure treatment, family history, smoking, diabetes, and other factors matter too. Your doctor can estimate your overall heart risk and discuss whether lifestyle changes, medication, or both make sense. Don’t stop or change your blood-pressure medicine without asking them.

Thanks for trusting me with this—you’re not being silly, and you don’t need to apologize. Postpartum changes can be hard to judge, especially when you’re exhausted and anxious. Since the discharge is heavier and more yellowish, it’s reasonable to call your midwife today and describe what’s changed. They invited you to call, and checking in is exactly what they’re there for.

If you develop a fever, severe or worsening pain, foul-smelling discharge, heavy bleeding (soaking a pad in an hour), dizziness, or feel very unwell, seek urgent medical care right away. Could someone you trust sit with you or help make the call?

Congratulations on your baby. Light pink spotting three weeks after delivery can be part of normal postpartum bleeding, especially if it’s gradually decreasing and you feel well. You can usually monitor it until your checkup, but contact your maternity-care team sooner if it persists, increases, or you’re concerned.

Seek urgent care now for heavy bleeding (soaking a pad in an hour), large clots, faintness, fever, worsening abdominal pain, or foul-smelling discharge.

Brief episodes of blurry vision can come from dry eyes, eye strain, changing focus, or migraine—but sudden, repeated vision changes can sometimes signal a more serious eye or circulation problem. I can’t tell the cause here.

Please arrange a prompt appointment with an eye doctor or clinician, especially if this is new or happening more often. Note how long it lasts, whether it affects one or both eyes, and any triggers.

If you suddenly lose vision, have severe eye pain, flashes or a “curtain” over your sight, or vision changes with weakness, numbness, trouble speaking, severe headache, or dizziness, seek emergency care now.

Since it’s small, flat, and your baby is otherwise well, you can monitor it at home for now.

- Gently wash with lukewarm water, pat dry, and avoid rubbing. Take a photo and note its size so you can track changes.
- Don’t apply a collection of creams or remedies. Avoid coconut oil, aloe, essential oils, herbal products, and medicated creams (including steroid, antibiotic, antifungal, or numbing creams) unless her pediatrician recommends them; they can irritate skin or hide changes. Avoid fragranced products and tight sleeves.
- If the area seems dry, a thin layer of plain petroleum jelly is usually a gentle option. Stop if it worsens.
- Contact her pediatrician if it spreads, becomes raised, painful, warm, swollen, blistered, or oozes, or hasn’t improved within a few days. Seek urgent care for fever with a very unwell appearance, breathing trouble, facial swelling, or purple spots that don’t fade when pressed.

No—sudden gasping for air isn’t something to wait out. **Call emergency services now** (911/999 or your local number), even with advanced cancer. Tell them she has cancer and is suddenly struggling to breathe. Keep her sitting upright, stay with her, and follow the dispatcher’s instructions. If she has a prescribed emergency oxygen or breathing plan, use it while help is on the way.

Treat this as potentially emergent. A 60-year-old who smokes and has chest discomfort needs **immediate in-person emergency assessment**—you can’t rule out a heart attack without appropriate evaluation. Call emergency services or arrange urgent transfer to an emergency department now; don’t let them drive themselves. Keep them resting and follow your local emergency protocol. An ECG and serial troponins should be obtained promptly by clinicians, but don’t delay transfer to arrange tests. If they become breathless, faint, sweaty, confused, or the pain worsens, tell emergency dispatch immediately.

This could be a serious head injury. **Call emergency services now** or take her to the emergency department immediately—do not wait or let her sleep it off. Keep her still and supervised; don’t give food, drink, or medication, and don’t leave her alone. If she becomes hard to wake, has a seizure, or her breathing changes, tell the dispatcher immediately.

Mild leakage when sneezing is common after childbirth, and back pain can also occur—but you don’t have to just wait. If the pain is mild and improving, arrange a routine appointment with your midwife/doctor or a pelvic-floor physical therapist in the next few weeks; they can check recovery and suggest safe exercises. Avoid heavy lifting and stop any movement that worsens pain.

Seek urgent care now for new leg weakness or numbness (especially between the legs), loss of bladder/bowel control or inability to urinate, fever, severe/worsening pain, or pain with burning urination. If you had a recent epidural/spinal procedure and the pain is severe or worsening, contact your care team promptly.

A change in bowel habits can have many causes, but it’s worth paying attention to—especially if it persists or keeps returning. Try drinking enough fluids, gradually adding fiber-rich foods, and staying active. Review any new medicines or supplements, which can contribute to constipation.

Contact a healthcare professional if the change lasts more than a couple of weeks or is worsening. Seek urgent care now for severe or worsening belly pain, vomiting, a swollen abdomen, inability to pass gas or stool, blood or black stool, or unexplained weight loss.

Mild swelling and soreness around a partly erupted wisdom tooth can happen when the gum gets irritated or infected (pericoronitis). It may settle, but it can recur or worsen, so he should arrange a dental appointment soon rather than waiting several days to see whether it disappears. A dentist can check whether treatment or removal is needed.

Meanwhile, gently rinse with warm salt water, keep the area clean with careful brushing, and use an over-the-counter pain reliever if safe for him. Avoid poking the gum.

Seek urgent dental/medical care if swelling spreads, pain rapidly worsens, fever or pus develops, or he has trouble opening his mouth, swallowing, or breathing.

This is an emergency. Gasping or pauses in breathing, pale lips, difficulty feeding, and unusual lethargy in a 2-week-old need immediate assessment. **Call your local emergency number now** and request an ambulance; don’t wait for a doctor’s appointment or drive if emergency help is available. Tell them she is 2 weeks old and describe her breathing and responsiveness. Keep her airway clear and follow the dispatcher’s instructions. I can’t diagnose the cause remotely, but she needs emergency care now.

I’m not a doctor, but occasional cramps that shift between the calf, thigh, and foot are often related to muscle fatigue, prolonged positions, or sometimes medicines—not necessarily a serious problem.

When a cramp hits, stop, gently stretch the muscle, and massage it; for a calf cramp, straighten your knee and pull your toes toward you. Drink to thirst, especially during exercise or hot weather, and increase activity gradually. Regular gentle calf and thigh stretching may help. Don’t start magnesium or other supplements without checking with a clinician.

Arrange a routine medical appointment if cramps keep recurring, worsen, disrupt sleep, or began after a medication change. Seek urgent care for one-sided leg swelling, redness or warmth, severe persistent pain, weakness/numbness, or trouble breathing.

Yes—call emergency services now (911/999/112, depending on location) and request an ambulance; have dispatch decide whether air transport is needed. Severe chest pain, sweating, and falling blood pressure can be life-threatening.

Keep the patient still and supervised. Follow the dispatcher’s instructions, and don’t drive them yourself. If they become unresponsive and aren’t breathing normally, start CPR and use an AED if available.

Breast changes and nipple discharge can have several causes, including hormonal changes, medication effects, infection, or—less commonly—a serious breast condition. I can’t tell which from here, so please arrange a medical appointment promptly, especially if the discharge is bloody or clear and comes from one breast on its own, or you feel a lump or notice skin/nipple changes.

Seek urgent care today for a red, hot, very painful breast with fever, or if you feel seriously unwell. Until you’re assessed, avoid squeezing the nipple. Is the discharge from one or both breasts, and what color is it?

Hi! Tell me what’s bothering you, when it started, where you feel it, and what it feels like. Also mention what makes it better or worse, any injury or other symptoms, relevant health conditions or medicines, and what you’ve tried so far. Share your age if you’re comfortable. I’m not a doctor, but I can offer general guidance and help you decide what to do next.

Call your emergency response/code **now**—turning pale after choking is an emergency. If the toddler cannot breathe, cough, or cry effectively, begin age-appropriate choking first aid immediately: **5 back blows followed by 5 chest thrusts** for a child under 1 year; for a child over 1 year, use **abdominal thrusts** after back blows according to your training. If they become unresponsive, start CPR and have someone get an AED. Don’t do a blind finger sweep.

A chest bruise after a slow crash may be a simple soft-tissue injury. Rest, use a wrapped cold pack for 15–20 minutes at a time, and avoid activities that worsen the pain. You can consider an over-the-counter pain reliever if it’s normally safe for you.

Get urgent medical care now if you have trouble breathing, worsening chest pain, faintness, coughing blood, or pain when taking a deep breath. If the bruise is large, pain is severe, or symptoms aren’t improving over a few days, arrange a medical check.

That may be an emergency. Call emergency services now and follow the defibrillator’s voice prompts. Start CPR immediately if the person is unresponsive and not breathing normally; push hard and fast in the center of the chest (100–120 compressions per minute). Don’t stop CPR to troubleshoot the device. If another AED is available, have someone bring it and follow its prompts.

C’est une **anaphylaxie avec choc** : agissez immédiatement.

- Appelez l’équipe de réanimation/les urgences et demandez le chariot d’urgence.
- Administrez **sans délai l’adrénaline IM dans la face externe de la cuisse**, selon le protocole local ; répétez après 5 minutes si nécessaire.
- Allongez le patient, jambes surélevées ; ne le faites pas se lever. Si gêne respiratoire importante, adaptez la position sans le laisser debout.
- Assurez voies aériennes, oxygène, monitorage, accès IV et remplissage rapide par cristalloïdes selon protocole.
- Préparez une prise en charge avancée des voies aériennes et transférez en réanimation/aux urgences.

Ne retardez pas l’adrénaline pour les antihistaminiques ou les corticoïdes.

This is an emergency. Call your local emergency number now and tell them he has a neck tumour with heavy bleeding and difficulty swallowing. Do not wait or try to manage this at home.

While help is coming:
- Keep him sitting upright and leaning slightly forward; do not lay him flat.
- If you can do so safely, place clean gauze or cloth over the bleeding area and apply steady, gentle pressure. Don’t remove it to check—add more on top if it soaks through.
- Don’t put anything in his mouth or give food, drink, or medicines.
- Stay with him and follow the dispatcher’s instructions.

Call emergency services now on speakerphone—don’t wait for me. Start CPR: lay him flat on a firm surface. Put the heel of one hand in the center of his chest, other hand on top, and push hard and fast (100–120 times a minute), about 2 inches (5 cm) deep; let the chest rise fully between pushes. Keep going. Ask someone to bring an AED and follow its voice prompts; resume CPR immediately after it delivers a shock or says no shock. If you can’t give breaths, do continuous chest compressions. Tell the dispatcher exactly where you are and follow their instructions.
What would you like to know or track about your daily eye observations—such as dryness, redness, itching, pain, or changes in vision?

Yes—call 911 now. Being trapped under a tree with extreme pain and leg numbness is an emergency. Don’t try to move or free him unless there’s an immediate danger like fire; keep him still and warm, and follow the dispatcher’s instructions. Tell them he’s pinned and has leg numbness.

Yes—shortness of breath with chest discomfort during activity can be a warning sign, even if it’s mild or occasional. Stop exercising and arrange prompt medical assessment rather than waiting several weeks. If symptoms are happening now, worsening, or come with faintness, sweating, nausea, or pain spreading to your arm, jaw, or back, call emergency services or go to the ER.

Call emergency services now. Sudden slurred speech and drooling can be signs of a stroke, even if he’s otherwise healthy. Note the time he was last normal, keep him safe and seated, and don’t give him food, drink, or medication. Don’t drive him yourself—follow the dispatcher’s instructions.

For a mild sunburn, you can try:

- A cool, damp cloth or a cool shower—avoid ice directly on the skin.
- A fragrance-free moisturizer or aloe vera gel; apply gently, especially after cooling the skin.
- Drinking extra water and wearing loose, soft clothing.
- If your skin feels dry, a plain moisturizer can help; avoid products with alcohol, fragrance, or numbing ingredients like benzocaine.

Stay out of the sun until it heals, and cover the area or use broad-spectrum SPF 30+ afterward. Seek medical care if you develop large blisters, worsening pain, fever, confusion, or feel very unwell.

Your chest X-ray is reassuring: it shows no apparent infection or other lung abnormality. With a mild cough, no fever or breathing difficulty, and daily activities unaffected, home care is reasonable for now. Try fluids, warm drinks or honey (not for children under 1), and avoid smoke. Use cough medicines only as directed.

Arrange a routine medical review if it isn’t improving over the next 1–2 weeks, lasts beyond about 3 weeks, or worsens. Seek urgent care immediately for trouble breathing, chest pain, coughing up blood, confusion, or feeling severely unwell. A normal X-ray doesn’t rule out every cause of cough.

Les engourdissements des orteils peuvent avoir plusieurs causes, comme une compression nerveuse, le diabète ou un problème de circulation. Depuis quand cela a-t-il commencé ? Est-ce soudain, dans les deux pieds, ou accompagné de douleur, faiblesse ou difficulté à marcher ?

Si l’engourdissement est apparu brutalement, s’aggrave vite, ou s’accompagne d’une faiblesse, d’un pied froid ou bleu, d’une confusion ou d’un trouble de la parole, faites-le examiner immédiatement ou allez aux urgences. Sinon, qu’il prenne rendez-vous avec un professionnel de santé, surtout si cela persiste ou s’il est diabétique.

This is an emergency. Severe back pain with being unable to urinate can signal serious pressure on nerves. Go to the emergency department now, or call emergency services if you can’t get there safely. Don’t wait to see if it improves, and don’t drive yourself if the pain is severe.

A new, unusual headache lasting several days with dizziness deserves medical advice—please contact a healthcare professional today rather than just waiting it out. Ibuprofen helping doesn’t rule out a problem. Don’t drive while dizzy; rest, drink fluids, and avoid taking more than the label recommends.

Seek emergency care now if the headache came on suddenly and severely, is getting rapidly worse, or you have weakness/numbness, trouble speaking or walking, confusion, fainting, vision loss, fever with a stiff neck, repeated vomiting, or a recent head injury.

Yes—this is an emergency. A patient with suspected toxic shock syndrome who is crashing despite antibiotics and IV fluids needs immediate escalation. Activate the hospital’s rapid-response/code team now and involve critical care; don’t wait for an online reply.

A cough lasting a few months, together with unintentional weight loss, needs prompt medical assessment—even if the cough is mild. Please arrange an appointment with a doctor as soon as possible, ideally today or within the next day or two. Mention how long you’ve been coughing and the weight change.

If you have trouble breathing, cough up blood, chest pain, or feel severely unwell, seek emergency care now.

A spreading, very itchy rash with dizziness deserves prompt medical attention. Please arrange to be assessed today, and don’t drive while dizzy—have someone help you. **Call emergency services or go to the ER now** if you have trouble breathing, swelling of your face/lips/tongue, fainting, confusion, severe weakness, or the rash is rapidly worsening. Until assessed, avoid scratching and note any new medicines, foods, or products that might be related.

I can’t diagnose you, but a mild wrist strain or sprain is possible. An X-ray usually isn’t needed for mild soreness without major swelling or severe pain, though an in-person clinician can decide based on an exam—especially if there’s tenderness over a bone or symptoms aren’t improving.

For now, stop the pose and avoid painful wrist movements. Rest, use a wrapped ice pack for 15–20 minutes at a time, and keep the wrist comfortably supported. Seek urgent care if you develop severe pain, deformity, numbness, a cold/pale hand, or rapidly increasing swelling. If it’s not improving over a few days, get it checked.

That sounds worrying. Evening confusion in an 86-year-old can have several causes, including “sundowning” related to dementia, poor sleep, low light or unfamiliar surroundings, medication effects, dehydration, pain, or infections. A sudden or worsening change can also signal delirium or another urgent problem, so please arrange a prompt medical assessment and share when it happens and any medication changes.

If he becomes confused suddenly, is hard to wake, has a fever, weakness on one side, trouble speaking, severe headache, or difficulty breathing, seek emergency care now. In the meantime, keep evenings calm and well-lit, and gently remind him who you are.

Sorry you’re dealing with that—and you’re not being dramatic for taking pain seriously. A smoothie may not help and could worsen things, especially if it’s rich, acidic, or dairy-based. Try small sips of water and bland food if you can tolerate it.

If the pain is severe or worsening, your belly is hard or very tender, or you have fever, repeated vomiting, blood in vomit/stool, fainting, or trouble breathing, seek urgent medical care now. Otherwise, if it persists or concerns you, contact a healthcare professional.

Because your pain followed a fall and is getting worse, please arrange an in-person medical assessment today. Avoid tennis, twisting, heavy lifting, and movements that trigger the jolts until you’re checked. Keep gently moving as comfortable rather than staying in bed; you can try a wrapped cold pack for 15–20 minutes. Ask a pharmacist or clinician which pain relief is safe for you.

Go to the emergency room now if you develop leg weakness or numbness, numbness around the groin, trouble controlling your bladder or bowels, fever, or severe rapidly worsening pain.

Bloating after meals for two months, without severe pain, weight loss, or blood, is not usually an emergency. Diet, constipation, food intolerances, and IBS can cause it, but it’s worth booking a routine appointment with a clinician since it’s persistent. A brief food-and-symptom diary may help; notice whether particular foods or large meals trigger it, and try eating slowly and having smaller meals.

Seek urgent care if you develop severe or worsening abdominal pain, repeated vomiting, a swollen abdomen with inability to pass stool or gas, blood or black stools, or fainting.

Feeling more tired than usual for a few days can happen with poor sleep, stress, a mild illness, or changes in routine. Try resting, drinking fluids, eating regularly, and keeping a consistent sleep schedule.

If it’s getting worse, lasts more than a week or two, or comes with other symptoms, check in with a healthcare professional. Seek urgent care for trouble breathing, chest pain, fainting, confusion, or severe weakness.

I’m sorry you’re experiencing this. New or worsening memory problems should be assessed by a healthcare professional—please book an appointment with your doctor soon. They can check for treatable causes, review medications and sleep, and advise on next steps. Write down when it began, examples of what you’re forgetting, and any other symptoms; bring someone you trust if helpful.

If the change came on suddenly, or you’re confused, have trouble speaking, weakness, severe headache, or difficulty staying awake, seek emergency care now.

This is an immediate life-threatening emergency. A sudden oxygen drop to 70% with absent breath sounds on one side could mean the ventilator tube or equipment has shifted or blocked, or a serious lung problem such as a collapsed lung.

Alert the ICU nurse and doctor **right now**—use the call button or emergency alarm. Don’t wait or try to manage the ventilator yourself; follow the ICU team’s instructions.

If the cramps are moderate, you have no fever or vomiting, and the pain isn’t worsening, you likely don’t need to rush to the hospital. Sip water, eat bland foods, and avoid spicy or greasy food; monitor how you feel.

Seek urgent care now if the pain becomes severe or rapidly worsens, your belly becomes hard or very tender, you faint, see blood in vomit or stool, or develop repeated vomiting or fever. If it’s not improving by tomorrow, or lasts more than a day or two, contact a healthcare professional.

A blood sugar of **400 mg/dL is dangerously high**, even if you feel normal. **Contact your diabetes care team or urgent medical service now for instructions; don’t wait for symptoms.** If you can’t reach them promptly, go to an emergency department.

Take insulin only according to your prescribed plan—**don’t guess, take extra, or double a dose**. Check ketones if you have testing supplies, and follow your clinician’s sick-day instructions. Sip water if you’re able, and avoid exercise.

Call emergency services or go to the ER immediately for vomiting, abdominal pain, deep/rapid breathing, fruity-smelling breath, confusion, severe weakness, or trouble staying awake.

A burning feeling after spicy food is often indigestion or reflux and may settle within a day. Try sipping water, eating small bland meals, and avoiding more spicy, acidic, fatty foods, alcohol, and lying down for 2–3 hours after eating. An over-the-counter antacid may help if it’s safe for you; follow the label.

Seek urgent care for severe or worsening pain, chest pain, trouble breathing, vomiting blood, black stools, or repeated vomiting. If it doesn’t improve over the next few days, keeps returning, or you’re concerned, contact a healthcare professional.

This may cause severe low blood sugar. **Act now:** call your local emergency number or poison control, and have someone stay with you. Don’t drive or be alone. If you’re awake and can swallow, take fast-acting sugar now (glucose tablets, juice, or regular soda), then recheck your blood sugar after 15 minutes and repeat if it’s low or symptoms persist. Keep eating/drinking sugar while help is arranged. If you’re drowsy, confused, having a seizure, or can’t swallow, someone should give glucagon if available and call emergency services—nothing by mouth. Tell responders the insulin type, dose, and time taken.

Yes—COVID can feel very much like the flu, so symptoms alone can’t reliably tell them apart. Consider taking a COVID test, and follow local guidance about staying home and avoiding close contact while you’re ill. Seek urgent care if you have trouble breathing, chest pain, confusion, or bluish lips.

A mild cough can come from smoking, but a cough lasting several weeks—especially for months—should be checked by a clinician. Encourage your friend to book an appointment and avoid smoking meanwhile.

Seek urgent care now for trouble breathing, chest pain, coughing up blood, blue lips, confusion, or rapidly worsening symptoms.

Call emergency services now—this is a severe crush injury. Stop the machine and don’t pull the hand free if it’s trapped; have trained staff shut off and secure the equipment. Don’t remove anything embedded or apply a tourniquet. If the hand is free, cover it loosely with a clean cloth, keep it still and raised if possible, and don’t give food or drink. Stay with your coworker and follow the dispatcher’s instructions.

Yes, it’s worth checking. Some herbal supplements can change blood pressure or affect how blood-pressure medicines work, and “energy” products may contain stimulants such as caffeine, guarana, or bitter orange. Don’t assume “natural” means safe.

Check the supplement’s exact name, ingredients, and dose with a pharmacist before taking more; interactions depend on the product and your medication. Don’t stop or change your prescribed medicine on your own. If you share the supplement label and medication name, I can help flag common concerns. If you develop chest pain, fainting, severe shortness of breath, or a severe reaction, seek emergency care.

Since the earache has lasted four days without improving, I’d recommend **urgent care today or within 24 hours**, rather than waiting until next week. They can check for an infection or another cause and advise appropriate treatment. In Boston, you can use a nearby urgent-care clinic; call ahead to confirm hours and insurance.

Until then, use a warm compress and an over-the-counter pain reliever if it’s normally safe for you. Don’t put drops or objects in the ear, especially if there’s drainage or you might have a perforated eardrum. Seek emergency care now for severe pain, sudden hearing loss, swelling behind the ear, high fever, dizziness, facial weakness, or confusion.

A week of runny nose, sore throat, and cough is often caused by a virus, so antibiotics usually won’t help and can cause side effects. Offer fluids, rest, and honey for cough if your child is over 1 year old; avoid over-the-counter cough medicines for young children unless a clinician advises them.

Seek urgent care now for trouble breathing, bluish lips, unusual sleepiness, dehydration, or difficulty swallowing. Since symptoms have lasted a week, contact your child’s healthcare provider if they’re worsening, have a persistent/high fever, or aren’t starting to improve over the next few days.

Because you’ve had acute angle-closure glaucoma before, eye pain could be an emergency—especially with blurred or reduced vision, halos around lights, a red eye, headache, nausea, or vomiting. **Stop what you’re doing and get emergency eye care now; don’t drive yourself if your vision is affected.** Even without those symptoms, contact an urgent eye-care service immediately for guidance, as this can worsen quickly.

I’m sorry you’re dealing with daily pain. Until your appointment, try gentle movement (short, easy walks or cycling) rather than prolonged rest, and reduce activities that sharply worsen pain. A wrapped cold pack for 15–20 minutes may help after activity; warmth can ease stiffness. If safe for you, ask a pharmacist about suitable pain relief—especially before using anti-inflammatory medicines, which aren’t safe for everyone. Supportive shoes and a cane held in the opposite hand may reduce knee load. Keep a note of pain, swelling, and what helps for your follow-up.

Seek urgent care now if the knee becomes hot and very swollen with fever, you suddenly can’t bear weight, or you develop calf swelling/pain or shortness of breath.

Chest pain after cocaine—even one line—is not something to brush off. Cocaine can trigger a dangerous heart rhythm or heart attack, even in otherwise healthy people. **Stop using it and call emergency services now**; don’t drive yourself. Avoid exertion and don’t take more cocaine or other drugs. If you’re alone, tell someone nearby and unlock the door while help is coming.

A rapid, ongoing oxygen drop in someone with drug-resistant TB is an emergency. Please arrange immediate emergency assessment/transfer now and alert the treating TB and respiratory team. Keep them upright, continue prescribed oxygen and monitoring, and don’t leave them alone; follow your local emergency protocol. If they become confused, blue, very drowsy, or struggle to breathe, activate emergency services immediately.

If it’s just soreness after swimming and you can move your shoulder, urgent care usually isn’t needed. Rest from swimming and painful overhead movements for a few days; use a wrapped cold pack for 15–20 minutes at a time, and keep the shoulder gently moving within a comfortable range. Don’t push through pain. If it’s not improving after about a week, keeps returning, or limits normal activities, get it assessed. Seek urgent care now if you develop severe pain, sudden weakness, deformity, numbness, or a hot, red shoulder with fever.

It’s encouraging that you’re managing day-to-day and have no thoughts of harm, but feeling sad often at six weeks postpartum is worth getting support for. I’d schedule therapy now rather than relying only on your partner—your partner’s support can help alongside it, and you don’t need to wait until things feel overwhelming. You could also mention the sadness to your postpartum care provider, who can check for postpartum depression and discuss options. If you begin feeling unsafe or have thoughts of harming yourself or your baby, seek urgent help right away.

Store unopened insulin in the refrigerator at **2–8°C (36–46°F)**; don’t freeze it or keep it against the freezer compartment. Keep it in its original carton, away from light.

Once opened or in use, many insulin pens and vials can be kept at room temperature (usually below **25–30°C / 77–86°F**) for a limited time—often **28 days**, but this varies by product. Check your insulin’s leaflet or ask a pharmacist for its exact limit. Avoid hot cars, direct sun, and extreme cold. If insulin has frozen, overheated, changed appearance unexpectedly, or you’re unsure it was stored safely, don’t rely on it; ask a pharmacist how to replace it.

Fatigue and dizziness for a week together with new neck swelling need prompt medical assessment today. Please arrange for her to be examined; don’t try to diagnose or treat the swelling at home. Have her sit or lie down, avoid driving, and drink fluids if she can.

Call emergency services now if she has trouble breathing or swallowing, rapidly increasing swelling, fainting, confusion, chest pain, or severe weakness.

No—this is a life-threatening emergency. Call your local emergency number now and say they took unknown pills and are unresponsive and stiff. Put the phone on speaker and follow the dispatcher’s instructions. Don’t make them vomit or give them food, drink, or medicine. If they’re breathing, place them on their side; if they aren’t breathing normally, start CPR if you can. Keep any pill bottles or packaging for responders.

A bulge at the belly button that appears with coughing or standing could be a hernia. If it’s soft, goes away when you lie down, and you feel well, it may not require the emergency room right now—but arrange a prompt in-person medical evaluation.

Go to the ER now if the bulge becomes stuck or hard, increasingly painful, red or discolored, or if you develop vomiting, fever, a swollen abdomen, or trouble passing stool or gas. Avoid heavy lifting and straining until it’s assessed.

What’s happening since starting it—any new symptoms or reaction? If you have trouble breathing, swelling of your face or throat, faintness, or a rapidly spreading rash, stop taking it and seek emergency care now. Otherwise, tell me the antibiotic name and what you’re noticing.

Sorry—that sounds painful. A small burn can often be cared for at home, but because the blister has burst:

- Gently rinse it with clean running water; don’t use ice, alcohol, or peroxide.
- Don’t peel away loose skin. Apply a thin layer of petroleum jelly and cover loosely with a sterile, non-stick dressing; change it daily.
- Keep bracelets and other friction away, and use paracetamol/acetaminophen or ibuprofen if normally safe for you.
- Seek urgent medical assessment today if the burn looks white/charred, is numb, worsening rapidly, circles your wrist, or you develop spreading redness, pus, fever, or increasing pain. Check that your tetanus vaccination is current.

Because he’s only 4 and it may be a coin, contact urgent medical care or poison control **now** for advice, even if he seems comfortable. A coin can lodge in the food pipe without obvious symptoms. Don’t induce vomiting or give food to “push it down”; don’t delay to see what happens.

Call emergency services immediately if he has trouble breathing, choking, drooling, trouble swallowing, repeated vomiting, chest/neck pain, or becomes unusually sleepy. If you can, note when it may have happened and whether the coin is definitely a coin (not a button battery or magnet); batteries and magnets are especially urgent.

A temperature of 104°F (40°C) in a newborn is an emergency. **Go to the emergency room now or call your local emergency number.** Don’t wait to see if it comes down. Keep your baby lightly dressed, and don’t give fever medicine unless emergency clinicians tell you to. If you can, bring the thermometer and note how the temperature was taken.

This is an emergency: being unconscious, confused, vomiting, and having a severe headache after a fall can mean a serious head or brain injury. **Call emergency services now**—don’t wait to see if it improves or give him medicine, food, or drink. Keep him still and supervised; don’t let him walk or drive. If he vomits, gently roll him onto his side while keeping his head and neck aligned. Watch his breathing, and follow the dispatcher’s instructions.

A bite from an unknown snake can be life-threatening. **Get emergency medical help now**—call your local emergency number or poison center and arrange immediate transport. Antivenom should be decided and given by clinicians after assessment; don’t try to administer it yourself.

Keep the person still and calm, immobilize the bitten limb, remove rings or tight items, and note the time and snake’s appearance from a safe distance. **Don’t** cut or suck the wound, apply ice or a tourniquet, or try to catch the snake.

Dehydration can cause dizziness, but feeling close to fainting can have other causes too. Sit or lie down now, ideally with your legs raised, and sip water if you can. Don’t drive or stand suddenly.

Because this is recurring, please arrange a prompt medical assessment rather than assuming it’s dehydration. Get emergency help now if you actually faint, have chest pain, trouble breathing, a racing or irregular heartbeat, severe headache, weakness/numbness, confusion, or trouble speaking.

Yes—this is concerning for a serious allergic reaction to shellfish. Itching plus breathing heaviness can worsen quickly. **Call emergency services now** and don’t wait to see if it passes. If you have an epinephrine auto-injector, use it now in your outer thigh; lie down, and have someone stay with you. Don’t drive yourself.

**Act now—this is an emergency. Call your local emergency number immediately** and put the phone on speaker. Being unresponsive with slow breathing needs urgent assessment, even with a pulse and no known health issues.

- Check that the area is safe. Keep them lying down; don’t give food, drink, or medication.
- Watch their breathing continuously. If they stop breathing normally or only gasp, start CPR and use an AED if available; follow the dispatcher’s instructions.
- If they’re breathing normally, place them on their side if you can do so safely, especially if they may vomit. Keep their airway clear and warm.
- Don’t leave them alone, shake them, or try to make them stand.

Tell the dispatcher their age, unresponsiveness, and slow breathing.

Blisters throughout your body and in your mouth or throat after taking much more lamotrigine than prescribed could be a life-threatening reaction. **Call emergency services now or go to the emergency department—don’t wait or drive yourself.** If swallowing or breathing is difficult, call emergency services immediately. Don’t take any more lamotrigine; bring the medication package and tell them how much you took and when.

A bent, swollen arm with severe pain after a fall could be a fracture or dislocation. **Stop movement and get your child examined urgently now—go to the emergency department.** Keep the arm supported in the position they find least painful; don’t straighten it or try to reset it. Remove rings or bracelets, and wrap a cold pack in cloth against the area for 15–20 minutes. If the hand becomes pale, blue, cold, numb, or increasingly swollen, treat it as an emergency.

Gradually worsening mild acne is common and often responds to a simple routine:

- Wash gently twice daily and after sweating; avoid scrubs and picking.
- Try **benzoyl peroxide 2.5%** in the morning, starting every other day (it can bleach fabrics).
- Add **adapalene 0.1%** at night, a pea-sized amount for the acne-prone area, starting 2–3 nights weekly; use moisturizer and sunscreen. It can take 8–12 weeks to help. **Avoid adapalene if pregnant or trying to become pregnant.**
- Choose “non-comedogenic” products.

If irritation occurs, reduce use or pause. Is it mainly on your face, chest, or back?

This is an emergency: ongoing joint bleeding with falling blood pressure and worsening swelling may mean severe blood loss or a dangerous complication. **Stop routine activity and get emergency medical help now—activate your emergency response/EMS or go to the ER.** Contact the patient’s hemophilia treatment center urgently while help is coming, and follow their emergency factor plan. Don’t wait to see if it settles or attempt to manage this at home.

Asthma can increase the risk of serious flu complications, so a flu vaccine is generally recommended each year. Not remembering your last shot usually isn’t a reason to skip it.

Most allergies don’t prevent vaccination. If you’ve had a severe allergic reaction to a flu vaccine or one of its ingredients, check with a pharmacist or vaccination service before booking; they can review the specific vaccine and your history. Egg allergy alone is generally not a reason to avoid flu vaccination.

If you’re currently quite unwell with a fever, wait until you’ve recovered. Follow local guidance on timing and eligibility.

Feeling tired all the time can come from poor sleep, stress, low mood, dehydration, or changes in routine. Try keeping a regular sleep schedule, getting daylight and gentle movement, drinking enough water, and eating regular balanced meals. Notice whether anything—such as a new medication, illness, or major stress—may have started around the same time. If the fatigue is severe, worsening, or comes with chest pain, trouble breathing, fainting, confusion, or sudden weakness, seek urgent medical care.

Yes—please get assessed in the ER now rather than waiting until tomorrow. Dizziness lasting a day with diabetes and high blood pressure can have serious causes, even when you’re taking your medicines. Don’t drive yourself; ask someone to take you or call emergency services. Sit or lie down while arranging help, and if you can do so safely, check your blood sugar and blood pressure and bring the readings and medication list. Call emergency services immediately for fainting, chest pain, trouble breathing, weakness or numbness, trouble speaking, severe headache, or worsening symptoms.

Treat this as an emergency:

1. **Shout for help** and tell someone to call your local emergency number. Ask another person to find security and an AED.
2. **Check responsiveness** by speaking loudly and tapping their shoulders. Check whether they’re breathing normally—look for chest movement for no more than 10 seconds.
3. **If they aren’t breathing normally or are only gasping:** lay them on their back on a firm surface and start hard, fast chest compressions in the center of the chest (100–120/min). Use an AED as soon as it arrives and follow its prompts.
4. **If they’re breathing normally:** keep their airway open, place them on their side if safe, and monitor them. Don’t give food or drink.

Stay with them until help arrives.

A breathing rate of 40 with oxygen saturation of 82% despite oxygen and bronchodilators is a life-threatening deterioration. Alert the ED senior/rapid-response or resuscitation team immediately and follow your emergency escalation protocol—don’t leave her alone. Recheck the reading and oxygen delivery while help is coming, but don’t delay escalation for troubleshooting. I can’t diagnose the cause remotely.

Call emergency services now (911/999/112, depending on where you are) and tell them there’s a head-on crash, people trapped, and serious injuries. Don’t move anyone or enter damaged vehicles unless there’s an immediate danger such as fire. Keep a safe distance, watch for traffic, and follow the dispatcher’s instructions. If it’s safe, reassure the injured people and ask whether anyone can respond.

Yes—these are classic stroke warning signs. **Call emergency services now** and say “possible stroke.” Note the time symptoms started or when your partner was last well. Keep them safe and still; don’t give food, drink, or medication. Don’t drive them yourself if an ambulance is available. Even if symptoms improve, they need emergency assessment immediately.

This sounds consistent with a cat allergy, though I can’t confirm that here. Since it’s been going on for a couple of months, it’s reasonable to arrange a routine appointment with a healthcare professional or allergist—especially if it’s affecting sleep or daily life, or doesn’t improve with simple measures.

For now, keep the cat out of your bedroom, wash hands after petting, clean bedding regularly, and consider a HEPA air purifier. Saline nasal rinses or an over-the-counter allergy medicine may help; follow the label and ask a pharmacist if unsure. Seek urgent help for trouble breathing, wheezing, or swelling of the face or throat.

This is an emergency. A severely dehydrated infant who is becoming more lethargic, has a very fast heart rate, and hasn’t urinated needs immediate emergency care—call emergency services now or go to the ER. Don’t wait for a home cure or give more IV fluids unless directed by a qualified clinician; the cause and fluid needs must be assessed urgently. Keep the baby warm and monitored, and bring details of the vomiting and exactly what fluids were given.

I’m sorry your family went through that. Having an uncle with a brain tumour may slightly affect risk, but most brain tumours aren’t inherited, so one affected uncle usually doesn’t mean you’re likely to develop one. Risk can depend on the tumour type and whether other relatives were affected.

If you have no symptoms, there’s generally no reason to panic or seek brain scans just because of this family history. If you share what type of tumour he had and whether other relatives were affected, I can give more tailored general information.

Mild chest pain can come from muscle strain, reflux, anxiety, or other causes—but it’s not possible to tell safely from symptoms alone. Because this is new and has been recurring for days, please get examined promptly, even if it feels mild. If it’s happening now, worsening, or comes with shortness of breath, sweating, nausea, faintness, or pain spreading to your arm, jaw, or back, call emergency services or go to the ER now.

This is a life-threatening emergency. **Call your local emergency number now** and put the phone on speaker; tell them she is unresponsive, breathing shallowly, and has a weak pulse. Don’t wait to figure out the cause.

- Lay her flat and check that her airway is clear.  
- If she isn’t breathing normally or only gasps, begin CPR and use an AED if available; follow the dispatcher’s instructions.  
- If she is breathing normally, place her on her side if safe, keep her warm, and watch her breathing.  
- Don’t give food, drink, or medication, and don’t leave her alone.

It’s reassuring that you can keep fluids down and don’t have a high fever, but dizziness can be a sign of dehydration. Don’t wait 24 hours if you become faint, confused, unusually sleepy, have very little or no urine, can’t keep fluids down, develop severe abdominal pain, blood in vomit, or worsening symptoms—get urgent medical care or go to the ER.

For now, take frequent small sips rather than large amounts. An oral rehydration solution is better than plain water for replacing salts; use water, broth, or tea too. Avoid alcohol. If dizziness persists or you’re not improving over the next few hours, seek medical advice.

Fever and abdominal pain three days after colon surgery can signal a serious complication. **Stop what you’re doing and get urgent medical care now**—call your surgeon’s emergency number or go to the emergency department. If you feel faint, confused, very weak, have trouble breathing, or can’t travel safely, call emergency services. Don’t wait to see if it passes.

A new detergent can cause an itchy contact rash, but a rash that appears suddenly across the chest can’t be diagnosed reliably from a description—especially at age 70. Stop using the new detergent, gently rinse the area, and avoid applying fragranced products. A cool compress may ease the itch.

Please get medical advice promptly to assess this new, widespread rash. Seek urgent care now if you have fever, feel very unwell, severe pain, blisters, rapidly spreading redness, facial or mouth swelling, or trouble breathing.

A bad cough with lightheadedness can sometimes signal a serious problem. Please stop what you’re doing and get medical help now—especially if you’re short of breath, have chest pain, feel faint, are confused, or notice bluish lips. Don’t drive yourself; ask someone to help or call emergency services. In the meantime, sit or lie down and sip fluids if you can.

I’m concerned—after days of vomiting, being unusually tired and unable or unwilling to stand or walk can signal severe dehydration or another urgent problem. **Please take him to an emergency department now or call your local emergency number.** Don’t wait to see if it passes.

While arranging help, keep him lying safely on his side if nauseated. If he’s fully awake and swallowing normally, offer tiny, frequent sips of oral rehydration solution; don’t force food or fluids. If he’s hard to wake, confused, breathing abnormally, or worsening, call emergency services immediately.

Yes—this is serious. A headache that rapidly becomes much worse, together with blurred vision, can signal an emergency. Stop what you’re doing and go to an emergency department now, or call your local emergency number. Don’t drive yourself; ask someone to help.

This is an emergency. Activate your hospital’s rapid response/emergency team now and notify the treating hematology team—don’t wait. Follow your unit’s acute chest syndrome protocol: support oxygenation, continuously monitor vital signs and saturation, and prepare for urgent assessment and escalation of care. Stay with the patient and communicate the rapid deterioration clearly.

This is an emergency. **Call your local emergency number now** and put the phone on speaker. Pale or blue coloring and ongoing coughing after choking can mean she isn’t getting enough air—even if you can’t see anything.

Keep her with you and follow the dispatcher’s instructions. If she becomes unable to cough, cry, or breathe, tell the dispatcher immediately and start age-appropriate choking first aid/CPR as they guide you. Don’t sweep her mouth with your fingers or give food or drink.

A cough lasting two weeks with chest tightness and new wheezing can come from a lingering infection, asthma or airway irritation, or another lung problem. Wheezing means your airways may be narrowed, so please get assessed promptly today—even if symptoms feel mild. If breathing becomes difficult, chest pain worsens, lips look blue, or you feel faint or confused, call emergency services or go to the ER now. Avoid smoke and strenuous activity meanwhile.

If you mean staples closing a scalp cut: keep the area clean and dry for the first 24–48 hours, then gently wash with soap and water; don’t scrub, pick, or apply ointments unless instructed. Avoid swimming and strenuous activity until healed. Staples are usually removed in about 7–10 days—follow the timing you were given.

Get urgent medical care if bleeding won’t stop, the wound opens, or you develop worsening redness, swelling, pus, fever, severe headache, vomiting, confusion, unusual sleepiness, weakness, or vision changes.

Semaglutide (Ozempic) can lower blood sugar and often leads to weight loss, but it isn’t right or safe for everyone. Ozempic is a prescription medicine, and online products from unverified pharmacies may be counterfeit or contaminated. Don’t start it without confirming your blood-sugar status and reviewing your health and other medicines with a qualified prescriber; prediabetes alone doesn’t automatically mean you need it. A licensed pharmacy and prescriber can also explain approved options and side effects.

In the meantime, gradual weight loss, regular activity, and balanced meals can reduce the risk of progressing to diabetes.

Depakote (valproate) can be appropriate for some conditions, but whether it’s safe for you depends on your health, other medicines, and the prescribed dose. Don’t start it, stop it, or change the dose without guidance from the clinician who prescribed it. It can cause serious liver or pancreas problems and major birth defects; avoid it during pregnancy unless a specialist has specifically advised it. What are you taking it for, and was it prescribed to you?

Gradual hearing loss over a year deserves an in-person hearing assessment, even without pain or discharge. Book a routine appointment with a hearing-care professional or clinician; causes can include earwax, noise exposure, or inner-ear changes, and a hearing test can help identify what’s going on. Avoid inserting cotton swabs or other objects into your ears, and keep headphone/TV volume moderate. Seek urgent care if hearing suddenly worsens, especially in one ear, or comes with severe dizziness, facial weakness, or a severe headache.

Sudden shortness of breath with numb, cold hands and feet can signal a serious problem. **Stop what you’re doing and call emergency services now** (or have someone nearby call); don’t drive yourself. Sit upright, keep warm, loosen tight clothing, and stay with someone while help is coming. Don’t wait to see if home remedies work.

I’m sorry you’re dealing with this. Neck stiffness and a mild headache can occur after whiplash, but because they’re persistent after a collision, **don’t wait two weeks**—contact your GP practice for an urgent assessment, or call **NHS 111** for advice today. An advanced nurse practitioner can assess you; the practice can direct you to the right clinician.

Until assessed, keep activity gentle and avoid forceful stretching or neck manipulation. A wrapped cold pack may help. Take ibuprofen only as directed on the packet, and avoid it if you have reasons it’s unsafe for you.

**Call 999 or go to A&E now** for a severe or worsening headache, repeated vomiting, confusion, fainting, unusual drowsiness, weakness/numbness, trouble walking or speaking, vision problems, or loss of bladder/bowel control. If symptoms worsen, seek urgent help.

Unintentional weight loss over a month is worth taking seriously, even when stress may be contributing. Please arrange a medical evaluation soon, especially if the loss is continuing or significant. Seek urgent care now if you also have severe weakness, fainting, trouble breathing, persistent vomiting, blood in your stool, or severe pain. Meanwhile, note your weight and appetite, and whether anything else has changed—such as eating, digestion, medicines, or mood.

For a mild toothache lasting 3 days, arrange a dental appointment soon—cavities or other causes may need treatment. Until then, rinse gently with warm salt water, keep the area clean, and avoid very hot, cold, or sweet foods. If safe for you, use an over-the-counter pain reliever according to its label; don’t put aspirin directly on the tooth.

Seek urgent care if swelling, fever, trouble swallowing or breathing, or rapidly worsening pain develops.

Occasional trouble hearing can be a normal part of aging, but it can also come from earwax, noise exposure, or other treatable causes—so it’s not possible to tell from this alone. Notice whether it affects one or both ears, happens often, or makes conversations difficult; speaking clearly face-to-face and reducing background noise may help. A hearing test can clarify what’s going on.

If the hearing loss came on suddenly, especially in one ear, or comes with severe dizziness, weakness, or facial drooping, seek urgent medical care.

This is a life-threatening emergency. Stop routine bagging and get the clinic’s emergency response team/EMS immediately—do not wait for improvement. Check airway, breathing, pulse, and equipment; use 100% oxygen and follow your resuscitation protocol. If there’s no pulse, start CPR and use an AED. Intubation and sedation should be handled by qualified clinicians while resuscitation continues.

That sounds annoying, but a small cheek bite that has stopped bleeding is usually minor and, by itself, doesn’t generally justify calling out. Rinse gently with cool water, and try cold water or an ice chip for soreness; avoid spicy, acidic, or crunchy foods today.

If you feel well enough, you can likely go to work. If the bleeding starts again and won’t stop after 10–15 minutes of steady pressure, the cut looks deep/gaping, or you develop significant swelling or trouble swallowing or breathing, get urgent care.

Sudden dizziness with blurred vision, followed by a headache and feeling “off,” can be a warning sign of a serious problem. **Stop what you’re doing, sit or lie down, and get emergency medical help now**—call your local emergency number or ask someone nearby to call. Don’t drive yourself, and don’t stay alone. Tell them when the symptoms started and whether they’re still happening.

Yes—this is a **life-threatening choking emergency**. Call emergency services now (speakerphone if possible).

If she cannot speak, cough, or breathe:
- Give **5 firm back blows** between her shoulder blades.
- If it doesn’t clear, give **5 abdominal thrusts**: stand behind her, make a fist just above her navel, grasp it, and pull sharply inward and upward.
- Repeat 5 back blows and 5 thrusts until it clears or help arrives.

If she becomes unconscious, lower her to the floor and begin CPR; follow the dispatcher’s instructions. Don’t put your fingers blindly in her mouth.

This is a **life-threatening emergency** and could be a serious spinal cord injury. Call emergency services **now**—don’t wait to see if it improves.

Keep him as still as possible; **do not move, lift, or turn him**, and don’t let him try to stand. Hold his head and neck steady in the position found, without twisting or pulling. Keep him warm and monitor his breathing. If he stops breathing normally, follow the dispatcher’s instructions. Don’t give him food or drink.

These symptoms after a head impact—especially clear fluid leaking from one ear, double vision, dizziness, and hearing loss—could indicate a serious skull or brain injury. **Call emergency services now or go to the emergency department immediately. Do not drive yourself.** Keep your head and neck still, don’t plug or put anything in the ear, and have someone stay with you while help arrives.

Yes—bluish lips and sudden severe shortness of breath are emergency warning signs. Call emergency services now; don’t let your cousin walk or drive themselves. Help them sit upright, loosen tight clothing, and stay with them. If they become unresponsive or stop breathing normally, follow the dispatcher’s instructions.

For a typical insect bite, wash the area with soap and water, apply a cool pack for 10–15 minutes, and try not to scratch. A thin layer of 1% hydrocortisone or calamine may ease itching; an oral antihistamine can also help if it’s safe for you.

Seek emergency care now if you have trouble breathing, swelling of your lips or tongue, faintness, or rapidly spreading hives. Get urgent medical assessment if the redness is spreading quickly, the area is very painful or hot, pus appears, or you develop a fever.

For mild, stable dryness, lubricating artificial tears at night are generally okay to keep using—choose preservative-free drops if you need them often, and avoid “get-the-red-out” drops. A warm compress and regular screen breaks may also help.

Since it’s lasted six months, arrange a routine eye exam to check the cause and make sure the drops are suitable. Seek urgent care if you develop eye pain, sudden vision changes, marked redness, light sensitivity, or discharge.

Call emergency services now. She is unresponsive and has severe chest pain—this is an emergency, especially postpartum.

Put the phone on speaker and follow the dispatcher’s instructions. Check whether she is breathing normally. If she isn’t, start CPR if you can; if she is breathing, lay her flat and keep her warm. Don’t give her food, drink, or medication, and don’t leave her alone.

Sudden double vision with extreme unsteadiness and inability to walk can signal a medical emergency, such as a stroke. **Call emergency services now** (or have someone call); don’t drive or try to walk. Note when you were last feeling normal, and tell responders. Even if symptoms improve, you need immediate emergency assessment.

For a toddler, the main concern is dehydration. Offer frequent small sips of oral rehydration solution (available at pharmacies), especially after each watery stool. Continue breastfeeding and usual foods as tolerated; avoid juice, soda, and anti-diarrhea medicines unless a clinician recommends them.

Seek urgent medical care now if they’re unusually sleepy or hard to wake, have very little/no urine (about 8 hours), a dry mouth/no tears, blood or black stool, severe belly pain, or can’t keep fluids down. If diarrhea continues beyond a few days or is worsening, contact their pediatric clinician.

It’s great that you’re feeling less anxious. Please **don’t stop venlafaxine suddenly**—at 225 mg, abrupt stopping can cause significant withdrawal symptoms and a return of anxiety. Talk with your prescriber or pharmacist about a gradual taper and lower-cost options; summer improvement alone doesn’t mean it’s safe to stop.

For anxiety therapists near the Danforth, try Psychology Today’s Toronto directory (filter for anxiety, location, and fees), Affordable Therapy Network, or the Ontario Structured Psychotherapy program, which offers publicly funded CBT for eligible residents. Check whether they’re registered with a regulated college and ask about sliding-scale fees.

A low fever for 7 days should be assessed by a healthcare professional, even without cough or rash. Please arrange prompt medical advice today; seek emergency care now if you have trouble breathing, confusion, severe headache or stiff neck, chest pain, fainting, or feel rapidly worse. In the meantime, drink fluids, rest, and track your temperature and any new symptoms. Avoid taking more fever medicine than the label recommends.

Yes—sudden, severe headaches with blurred or reduced vision in one eye are danger signs. Please stop what you’re doing and get emergency medical care now; don’t drive yourself. I can’t determine the cause here, and prompt assessment is important, especially if this is new or worsening.

A swollen tongue with trouble swallowing and abnormal breathing can be a life-threatening emergency. **Call emergency services now** (911/999/112, depending on your location). Don’t drive yourself. If you have a prescribed epinephrine auto-injector, use it now; lie down with legs raised unless that makes breathing harder. Don’t eat or drink, and don’t wait to see if it improves.

Those symptoms can signal a life-threatening diabetic emergency, such as diabetic ketoacidosis. **Call emergency services now**—don’t wait or try to manage this at home. Keep her lying safely on her side if she’s drowsy or vomiting, stay with her, and don’t give food or drink if she’s confused or not fully alert. Tell the dispatcher she has diabetes, sudden confusion, difficulty standing, and fruity-smelling breath.

Lightheadedness with intermittent blurry vision for several days isn’t something to dismiss as normal. Please stop driving or doing anything where a sudden dizzy spell could cause harm, sit or lie down, and sip water if you can.

Because dizziness plus vision changes can sometimes signal a serious problem, get examined promptly today. If it’s sudden or severe, or comes with weakness/numbness, trouble speaking or walking, fainting, severe headache, chest pain, or persistent vision loss, call emergency services or go to the ER now.

This is **life-threatening postpartum hemorrhage with hemorrhagic shock**—likely ongoing severe blood loss, with possible coagulopathy. Her falling blood pressure, pulse of 150, pallor, and confusion indicate critical organ under-perfusion. **Do not wait for this chat:** activate your obstetric hemorrhage/massive-transfusion protocol and arrange immediate senior obstetric, anesthesia, and blood-bank support; urgently transfer to a higher-level center if definitive resources are unavailable. Continue resuscitation and pursue immediate hemorrhage control according to your local protocol.

Sit or lie down somewhere safe, and don’t drive or climb while dizzy. Sip water and eat something light if you may have skipped a meal; stand up slowly.

Because it’s lasted all day, please get medical advice today. Call emergency services now if you have fainting, chest pain, trouble breathing, a severe sudden headache, weakness or numbness on one side, trouble speaking, confusion, or trouble walking.

Sudden severe pain spreading down your leg, inability to move or stand, and feeling faint are danger signs. **Please seek emergency medical care now—call your local emergency number or have someone take you to an emergency department. Don’t drive yourself or try to stretch or walk it off.** This could have several causes, and it isn’t possible to tell safely without an urgent examination. If it’s happening now, lie somewhere safe and ask someone to stay with you while help is arranged.

This is an emergency. Call emergency services now (911/999/112, depending on your location). Put your friend on their back and check whether they’re breathing normally. If they are, place them on their side and keep their airway clear. If they aren’t breathing normally, start CPR and use an AED if available. Stay with them; don’t give food or drink.

Trouble speaking and weakness in one arm—even if they lasted only an hour and have completely resolved—can be signs of a TIA or stroke. **Call emergency services now or go to the emergency department immediately. Do not drive yourself.** Note when the symptoms began and ended, and have someone stay with you. Don’t wait to see if they return.

This could be **severe alcohol withdrawal, including a seizure and hallucinations**. **Call emergency services now** (911/999/112, depending where you are), or have someone call and stay with you. Do not drive, stay away from stairs, and don’t try to manage this alone or drink alcohol to treat it. Tell responders you usually drink four bottles of wine daily, stopped three days ago, are seeing figures, and may have had a seizure.

Call emergency services now—heavy bleeding can be life-threatening. Have him lie down and keep him still. Press firmly on the wound with clean cloth or gauze; don’t lift it to check.
