If blood soaks through, add more cloth on top and keep pressing. If something is embedded, don’t remove it—press around it. Keep him warm, and don’t give food or drink. If safe, have someone meet responders.

Occasional tingling in one arm can happen when a nerve is briefly compressed—for example, from leaning on your elbow, sleeping awkwardly, or keeping your neck or wrist in one position. It can also relate to nerve irritation in the neck or wrist.

Try changing positions, avoiding pressure on the arm, and noticing whether certain activities trigger it. If it keeps recurring, lasts longer, or comes with weakness or pain, arrange a medical assessment.

If the tingling starts suddenly with face drooping, trouble speaking, severe weakness, chest pain, or shortness of breath, seek emergency help now.

Stomach pain and intermittent diarrhea can come from infections, food intolerance, medication effects, or other gut conditions. But **blood in the stool needs prompt medical assessment**, even if it happened only once. Please arrange urgent medical advice today; go to emergency care now if bleeding is heavy or repeats, stool is black/tarry, pain is severe, you feel faint/weak, or you have fever or can’t keep fluids down.

Until assessed, sip fluids or oral rehydration solution and note foods, medicines, symptoms, and whether the blood was bright red or dark. Avoid anti-diarrhea medicines if you have blood or fever.

Nausea can be a common side effect of some pain medicines, especially opioids, and may also be worse if you take them on an empty stomach. It isn’t necessarily dangerous, but I can’t tell what’s causing it without knowing the medicine and your procedure. Follow the label or your discharge instructions, and don’t stop or change a prescribed dose without checking with your pharmacist or care team. If you can, tell me the medication name and dose.

Get urgent help now for trouble breathing, extreme sleepiness or difficulty waking, facial/throat swelling, repeated vomiting, or severe/worsening pain.

A catheter coming out needs prompt attention. **Call her home-care service’s on-call number now** and explain that she is bedridden, the catheter has come out, and she is passing urine; ask for urgent instructions or an earlier visit. **Don’t try to put it back in or insert anything**, and don’t restrict her fluids unless a clinician has told you to.

For tonight, use absorbent pads, change wet bedding/clothes promptly, gently clean and dry her skin, and keep her warm and comfortable. Note when she last passed urine and whether she has pain or fever.

If she cannot urinate, has a painful/swollen lower abdomen, blood or clots, fever/chills, new confusion, severe weakness, or seems very unwell, **get urgent medical help now—don’t wait until tomorrow**.

Don’t use it until you’ve checked the specific insulin’s instructions. Some insulins are meant to look cloudy and should be gently rolled to mix; others should be clear. If it’s normally clear but has turned cloudy, or you see clumps, flakes, or particles that don’t dissolve, don’t inject it. Ask a pharmacist or your diabetes care team to identify it and arrange a safe replacement. If you need a dose soon, contact them promptly rather than skipping or guessing.

A brief episode of lightheadedness that resolved after sitting, with no other symptoms, is often not an emergency. For now, sit or lie down if it returns, drink some water, and avoid driving until you feel fully normal. If it happens again, note what you were doing and any possible triggers.

Seek emergency care right away if you faint, develop chest pain, trouble breathing, a racing or irregular heartbeat, severe headache, weakness or numbness on one side, confusion, or trouble speaking. If the lightheadedness keeps returning or doesn’t fully resolve, get medical advice promptly.

This is an emergency. **Call emergency services now** (or have someone take the patient to the ER—don’t drive them yourself). Keep firm, continuous pressure directly over the wound with clean gauze; don’t lift it to check. If it soaks through, add more gauze on top. Keep the patient lying down and warm, and follow the surgical team’s emergency instructions. Do not delay for home remedies.

If they stop with steady pressure within about 10–15 minutes and you feel well, monthly nosebleeds usually aren’t an emergency. Since they’re recurring, arrange a routine ENT or primary-care appointment rather than waiting indefinitely—especially if they’re becoming more frequent or you take blood thinners.

During a bleed, sit upright, lean forward, and pinch the soft part of your nose continuously for 10–15 minutes. Don’t tilt your head back. Saline spray or a humidifier may help dryness.

**Get urgent care now** if bleeding is heavy, won’t stop after 20 minutes of firm pressure, follows a significant injury, or causes faintness, weakness, or trouble breathing.

These symptoms are an emergency, especially 5 days after giving birth. **Call emergency services now or have someone take you to the emergency department—don’t drive yourself.** Sudden severe headache, blurred vision, and one-sided numbness can signal a stroke or a serious postpartum complication. Tell them you’re 5 days postpartum and when the symptoms began. Lie somewhere safe while help is coming, and don’t wait to see if it passes.

Don’t double the Coumadin (warfarin) dose. Since it’s almost time for today’s dose, skip yesterday’s missed dose and take today’s dose as prescribed—unless his anticoagulation clinic or pharmacist gives different instructions. Call his anticoagulation clinic or pharmacist today to confirm and ask whether an INR check is needed; don’t make up doses yourself.

If he has unusual bleeding, blood in urine or stool, a severe headache, confusion, weakness, or a recent head injury, seek emergency care now.

Don’t try to remove it yourself—cutting, burning, or using acids can cause infection, scarring, and delay diagnosis. A new dark spot should be checked by a clinician or dermatologist before any removal; they can identify what it is and discuss safe options. Seek prompt care if it’s growing or changing quickly, uneven, has irregular borders or several colors, bleeds, itches, or becomes painful. Until then, take a clear photo with a ruler for comparison and protect it from sun.

This is a life-threatening emergency. The signs are consistent with severe diabetic ketoacidosis, with possible cerebral edema or another critical complication—but only the treating team can determine exactly what is happening. Rapid breathing, falling blood pressure, very fast heart rate, worsening confusion, and barely responding signal possible shock and severe brain or organ injury.

Alert the senior emergency/critical-care team immediately and activate your hospital’s emergency response now. Don’t delay for an online explanation; he needs immediate resuscitation and close monitoring.

A 104°F fever with a stiff neck and confusion is an emergency—please call emergency services now or go to the ER. Don’t wait for it to improve or drive yourself if your child is very confused or difficult to wake. Keep them with you, note when symptoms began and any medicines given, and don’t force food or drink if they’re drowsy.

At the hospital, clinicians will assess breathing and alertness, check vital signs, and rapidly investigate serious infections. Tests and treatment may include blood tests, cultures, imaging, and possibly a spinal fluid test; they may start IV fluids and urgent medicines while testing.

Since there’s no major swelling or instability, it’s reasonable to try a few days of relative rest: avoid running and painful activity, but gently move the ankle as comfort allows. Ice wrapped in cloth for 15–20 minutes can help; elevate it, and wear supportive shoes. Return to activity gradually when walking is comfortable.

Because the ache has returned months after the sprain, arrange a check-up if it isn’t improving after several days, keeps recurring, or limits walking. Seek urgent care now if you can’t bear weight, develop marked swelling or deformity, or the foot becomes numb, cold, or discolored.

**Call emergency services now—do not try to stitch this.** This is life-threatening bleeding and possible shock; he needs immediate emergency transport, not a trip in a private car.

- Put on gloves; lay him flat and keep him warm. Don’t give food or drink.
- Press firmly on the wound with sterile gauze or clean cloth. If something is embedded, don’t remove it—press around it.
- If abdominal tissue/organs are exposed, **don’t push them in or press directly**; loosely cover with sterile gauze moistened with saline (or clean water).
- Keep pressure/cover in place and monitor breathing and responsiveness until help arrives.

Yes—this is very concerning. Severe wave-like abdominal pain, heavy bleeding with large clots, and lightheadedness a week after giving birth can signal a serious postpartum complication or blood loss. **Get emergency medical care now. Call emergency services or have someone take you to the ER—do not drive yourself.** Don’t wait to see if rest or iron helps. If possible, have someone stay with you and tell responders you gave birth a week ago and describe the bleeding and pain. I’m not a physician, but these symptoms need urgent assessment.

This is an emergency. Call emergency services now—blue lips and trouble staying awake can mean dangerously low oxygen. Put the phone on speaker and follow the dispatcher’s instructions.

- If he’s unresponsive or not breathing normally, start CPR and use an AED if available.
- If he is breathing, place him on his side and keep his airway clear.
- Give naloxone if available; xylazine may not respond to it, but it can help if opioids are also involved. Give another dose in 2–3 minutes if there’s no response.
- Don’t leave him alone, make him vomit, or give food or drink.

Heavy bleeding with extreme paleness and dizziness after birth can signal a life-threatening emergency. **Call emergency services now**—don’t try to manage this at home or drive yourself. Tell them you recently gave birth and are bleeding heavily, pale, and dizzy.

While help is coming, lie flat, keep warm, and have someone stay with you. Use a pad to track the bleeding; don’t insert anything into the vagina. If you feel faint or become less responsive, your helper should tell the dispatcher immediately and follow their instructions.

A high fever with a stiff neck can signal meningitis, which is an emergency. Call emergency services or go to the ER now—don’t wait or try to manage it at home. Keep the person resting and comfortable, and don’t force their neck to move. If they’re confused, hard to wake, having a seizure, or developing a rash, tell emergency services immediately.

This is an emergency—call emergency services now. Don’t give him anything to eat or drink, and don’t try to make him vomit. If you have naloxone, give it now; repeat in 2–3 minutes if he doesn’t respond. Check breathing: if he’s breathing, place him on his side and stay with him. If he isn’t breathing normally, start CPR/rescue breaths if you can. Tell responders what he may have taken and keep the powder or packaging.

Even when total cholesterol is in range, high LDL and low HDL can still matter. The most helpful approach is usually to lower LDL and improve overall heart health—raising HDL alone isn’t necessarily protective.

- Get regular activity: aim for about 150 minutes of moderate exercise weekly, building up gradually.
- If you smoke, quitting can raise HDL.
- Choose unsaturated fats (olive oil, nuts, seeds, avocado, oily fish) instead of butter, fatty meats, and trans fats.
- Eat more vegetables, beans, whole grains, and soluble fiber; limit sugary/refined foods.
- If relevant, gradual weight loss may help.

Avoid alcohol as a way to raise HDL. Review the full lipid results and your overall risk with a clinician, since targets depend on your health history.

Call the hospice nurse or 24/7 hospice line now and describe the faster breathing, when it started, and any distress. Keep the patient calm and in the position that feels easiest—often sitting upright or on their side—and loosen tight clothing. Don’t force food, fluids, or medication; use only comfort medicines and oxygen as prescribed in their hospice plan. If they’re struggling to breathe, turning blue/gray, hard to wake, or the change is sudden and severe, get urgent help now, following the hospice plan.

Yellow-looking skin can be a sign of jaundice, especially if the whites of their eyes are yellow too. Please encourage your cousin to get medically assessed promptly today; jaundice can have serious causes. If they’re confused, very drowsy, have severe belly pain, fever, repeated vomiting, or feel faint, go to emergency care now. Don’t try to treat it at home.

This is a life-threatening emergency: worsening confusion and blood pressure of 80/50 after heavy vomiting may indicate shock. **Call emergency services now** (911/999/112) and say “possible shock.” Don’t wait or try to manage this at home.

While help is coming:
- Keep him lying flat; if he vomits or is drowsy, turn him onto his side.
- Keep him warm and still. Don’t let him stand or walk.
- Give nothing by mouth while confused or actively vomiting.
- Monitor breathing and responsiveness. If he stops breathing normally, begin CPR and follow the dispatcher’s instructions.

This is an emergency. **Call your local emergency number now** and put the phone on speaker. Tell them she collapsed, is unresponsive, and has fast, shallow breathing.

Check whether she’s breathing normally. If she isn’t, or you’re unsure, start CPR and follow the dispatcher’s instructions; use an AED if available. If she is breathing, gently roll her onto her side, keep her airway clear, and stay with her. Loosen tight clothing and keep her warm. **Don’t give her food or drink, and don’t move her unless she’s in immediate danger.** Get someone nearby to help meet the responders.

Yes—this is concerning. New dizziness with weakness in the arms and legs can signal a serious problem, including a stroke. **Call emergency services now or go to the emergency department; don’t wait to see if it passes.** Don’t let her drive. Note when the symptoms began, and tell the responders. If she develops trouble speaking, facial drooping, severe headache, confusion, chest pain, or worsening weakness, treat it as an emergency.

Blue lips can mean your son isn’t getting enough oxygen, even if he seems well. **Go to the emergency room now—don’t wait for a regular appointment.** If his lips are still blue, or he develops trouble breathing, unusual sleepiness, weakness, or confusion, call emergency services now. Keep him calm and warm while getting help.

For a small thigh bruise, rest the area and apply a cold pack wrapped in a cloth for 15–20 minutes at a time during the first day or two. Avoid putting ice directly on your skin. If comfortable, elevate your leg; for pain, consider an over-the-counter pain reliever you normally use safely. After 48 hours, gentle warmth may help. Bruising should gradually fade over 1–2 weeks. Seek urgent care if the pain or swelling becomes severe, you can’t walk, or the bruise rapidly expands.

From what you’ve described, I don’t hear an obvious emergency warning sign: no confusion, dizziness, or sudden severe symptoms. But I can’t reliably assign percentages or rule out a physical cause from this information. Two weeks of new daytime fatigue and apathy can have many causes, including sleep quality, stress, infection, anemia, thyroid problems, or mood changes.

Seek urgent medical assessment if you develop chest pain, trouble breathing, fainting, new confusion or weakness, or rapidly worsening symptoms. Otherwise, track your energy and sleep, stay hydrated, and consider whether you snore or wake unrefreshed. Since this is new and persistent, arrange a routine health check if it continues or worsens.

I’m sorry—this sounds worrying. In someone with liver disease, a steadily enlarging belly can be fluid buildup (ascites). It can become much larger, but it shouldn’t be left to progress: **please arrange urgent medical assessment today**, as fluid buildup may need treatment and can signal worsening liver disease. Don’t try to drain it or use “water pills” unless his clinician has directed this.

If he has trouble breathing, fever, severe belly pain, confusion, unusual sleepiness, vomiting blood, or black stools, **go to the emergency room now**.

A sudden facial droop and drooling could be a stroke, and it’s impossible to tell safely at home. **Call emergency services now** (911/999/112, as applicable); don’t drive yourself. Note the time you were last normal, and tell them about your recent fever and cough. Don’t eat or drink, and don’t take aspirin unless emergency clinicians tell you to. Even if the symptoms improve, get emergency help immediately.

This could be **preterm labor or another serious pregnancy emergency**. Severe pain and difficulty breathing need urgent attention. **Call your local emergency number now** and say she is 7 months pregnant, having strong contractions, and struggling to breathe. Don’t drive her yourself if she’s having trouble breathing.

Keep her as comfortable as possible, preferably on her side, and stay with her. Don’t give her food, drink, or medication unless emergency dispatch instructs you.

This is a **life-threatening airway emergency**, not a situation for routine clinic management. Severe tongue swelling with noisy, labored breathing after food may be anaphylaxis. **Call emergency services now** and activate the clinic’s emergency response; do not leave the child alone. Give **intramuscular epinephrine immediately** according to the child’s weight and your clinic protocol—don’t delay for antihistamines. Keep the child lying flat if tolerated (or in the position that best supports breathing), provide oxygen and airway support if trained, and prepare for rapid airway deterioration while awaiting advanced help.

Cold sensitivity lasting for months is worth having a dentist check, even if it’s mild—it can come from a cavity, a crack, or gum recession, and the right fix depends on the cause. Meanwhile, try a sensitivity toothpaste twice daily (spit, don’t rinse), use a soft brush, and avoid very cold or acidic foods and forceful brushing. If the pain lingers after the cold is gone, worsens, or you develop swelling, fever, or trouble swallowing, seek urgent dental or medical care.

This is a medical emergency—slurred speech and drifting in and out of consciousness after prolonged heat exposure can signal heat stroke or another life-threatening problem. **Call emergency services now.** Don’t let your friend sleep or stand; keep them with you and watch their breathing. Move them to a cool place, remove excess clothing, and cool them with cool wet cloths or fanning. Don’t give food or drink while they’re drowsy. If they become unresponsive or aren’t breathing normally, follow the dispatcher’s instructions and start CPR if you can.

Don’t put your finger or tools in the ear. If you’re sure it’s a small insect and you have no ear tubes, eardrum perforation, prior ear surgery, or discharge, tilt the affected ear upward and pour a little body-temperature mineral or baby oil into it to drown the insect, then tilt the ear down to drain. **Avoid water**—it may make some insects more active and can be unsafe with an injured eardrum.

If it doesn’t stop or come out promptly, or you develop severe pain, dizziness, bleeding, or reduced hearing, get urgent medical help to have it removed safely.

An itchy throat and neck rash after eating can signal a food allergy. Stop eating the suspected food, and don’t test it again on your own. Note what you ate and when symptoms started; arrange an allergy assessment to identify the trigger and discuss a plan.

If you develop trouble breathing or swallowing, throat/tongue swelling, dizziness, faintness, or rapidly worsening symptoms, use an epinephrine auto-injector if you have one and call emergency services now.

This is a life-threatening emergency and could be thyroid storm. **Call emergency services now** (or have someone else call) and say: “suspected thyroid storm, heart rate over 180, fever over 40°C, rapidly worsening.” Do not drive her yourself or leave her alone. Keep her resting in a cool place; loosen excess clothing, and don’t give food, drink, or extra medication unless emergency clinicians direct you. Follow the dispatcher’s instructions.

Wash the scratch under running water with soap for 10–15 minutes, then apply an antiseptic and cover it with a clean dressing. Keep it clean and watch for spreading redness, warmth, swelling, increasing pain, pus, fever, or red streaks; seek prompt medical care if any appear.

A dog’s rabies vaccination greatly lowers risk, but doesn’t eliminate it. If the dog is healthy and available to observe, contact local public health or a clinician for advice on whether rabies follow-up is needed. Also check whether your tetanus vaccination is up to date.

I’m not a pediatric ENT, but if your child is comfortable, breathing and swallowing normally, and has no fever or pain, enlarged tonsils alone are often something to monitor rather than treat urgently.

- Note whether the tonsils look newly enlarged or have been that way for a while; avoid repeatedly inspecting or touching them.
- Keep up normal fluids and routines. Don’t give antibiotics or use throat treatments unless advised for a specific reason.
- Watch for snoring, pauses or gasping during sleep, restless sleep, daytime tiredness, repeated throat infections, or changes in voice or eating. These are useful to mention at a routine pediatric visit.
- Seek urgent care if breathing or swallowing becomes difficult, drooling develops, or your child becomes very unwell.

I’m sorry—this is frightening. Fever, new confusion, and a racing heart after a cut can signal a life-threatening infection. **Call emergency services now** or have someone take her to the emergency department; don’t wait to see if it passes. Don’t let her drive or stay alone. While help is coming, keep her resting, note when symptoms began and any medicines/allergies, and don’t give food or drink if she’s very drowsy or struggling to swallow. If she becomes hard to wake or has trouble breathing, tell the dispatcher immediately.

New numbness around your genitals together with back pain and difficulty walking can signal serious compression of nerves. **Stop exercising and go to the emergency room now**—don’t wait to see if it improves. Have someone take you or call your local emergency number; don’t drive yourself.

A mild “dizzy” feeling brought on by reading can come from eye strain or an outdated glasses prescription, posture/neck tension, dehydration, or difficulty focusing your eyes. Take a break every 20 minutes, look into the distance, improve lighting, keep the text at a comfortable distance, and drink water. Notice whether it happens with screens too, or when you stand up.

Because it’s been recurring for a week, arrange an eye check or medical assessment if it continues, worsens, or affects daily activities. **Stop reading and seek urgent care now** if you develop fainting, trouble walking, weakness or numbness, confusion, double vision, sudden vision loss, severe headache, chest pain, or persistent vomiting.

Yes—take tiny, frequent sips of water or oral rehydration solution; don’t gulp. **Vomiting blood needs urgent medical assessment now**, even if it was only a streak. Please go to the emergency department or call emergency services, and don’t drive yourself if you feel weak or dizzy. Avoid alcohol, aspirin, and ibuprofen.

No—don’t try to sleep this off. New or severe squeezing chest tightness can be a heart emergency, even if anxiety is possible. Call emergency services now, or have someone call for you; don’t drive yourself. Sit and rest while waiting, and follow the dispatcher’s instructions. If you’re alone, unlock the door and keep your phone nearby.

Getting unusually breathless on stairs for several weeks is worth taking seriously, even if you recover quickly. Please arrange a medical assessment soon; it can have several causes that need checking. Until then, avoid pushing through it and take stairs slowly.

If breathlessness occurs at rest, suddenly worsens, or comes with chest pain, fainting, blue lips, or severe weakness, stop and seek emergency care now.

A brief warm flush and metallic taste during or shortly after injected CT contrast are common effects and usually fade on their own. It’s reassuring that they eased and your vital signs were stable.

Get urgent help now if you develop trouble breathing, throat or tongue swelling, widespread hives, faintness, or repeated vomiting. If the taste or other symptoms persist, worsen, or new symptoms appear, contact the imaging team that gave you the contrast for guidance.

**This is immediately life-threatening. Arrange urgent evacuation to the advanced facility now—call emergency transport/receiving clinicians if available. Do not delay departure to try more treatments.** Shock and confusion after an open fracture may mean severe bleeding.

While transport is arranged:
- Keep him lying flat, warm, and as still as possible; monitor breathing and responsiveness.
- Apply firm pressure around bleeding wounds; if severe limb bleeding won’t stop, use a tourniquet if trained, noting the time. Don’t push bone back in or tightly wrap the fracture.
- Give nothing by mouth. Continue only fluids/treatments within your training and local protocol; avoid delaying transfer for more saline.
- Splint the limb, check circulation below it, and reassess often. Send details of fluids, medicines, and times with him.

Your wish to protect his life is clear. If meaningful, pray with him while care and transport proceed.

Brief twitches or shivers during sleep can be normal in babies, especially if they stop when she wakes and she seems well afterward—but I can’t tell from a description whether these are seizures. If you can, record a short video and note how long it lasts and whether she responds.

**Get emergency help now** if an episode lasts 5 minutes or more, repeats without her returning to normal, affects her breathing or color, or she’s difficult to wake or unusually unwell. If this is new or happening more often, contact her pediatric clinician promptly for guidance.

Yes—this could be life-threatening, including a heart attack or stroke. **Call emergency services now** and say he has severe chest pain, a pounding heart, slurred speech, and reduced alertness. Don’t drive him yourself.

Keep him still and supervised; note when symptoms began. If he becomes unresponsive and isn’t breathing normally, start CPR and use an AED if available. Don’t give food, drink, or medication unless emergency dispatch tells you to.

Mild stomach cramps after takeout can happen from indigestion or a food-related upset. Sip water, rest, and try bland foods when you feel ready; avoid greasy or spicy foods for now.

Get urgent medical help if the pain is severe or worsening, your belly is hard or very tender, you have blood in vomit or stool, repeated vomiting, fainting, or signs of dehydration. If it doesn’t improve within a day or two, seek medical advice.

For a mild headache, drink water, rest somewhere quiet, and try a cool cloth on your forehead. If you haven’t eaten, have a light snack. You may consider an over-the-counter pain reliever if it’s normally safe for you; follow the label and avoid combining products with the same ingredient.

Get emergency help now for a sudden, extremely severe headache, weakness or numbness, confusion, fainting, trouble speaking or seeing, fever with a stiff neck, or a headache after a head injury.

A sudden droopy face can be a sign of a stroke. Call your local emergency number now—don’t wait or drive them yourself. Note the time symptoms began. If they have trouble speaking, weakness or numbness, confusion, vision problems, severe headache, or difficulty walking, tell the dispatcher. Keep them safe and don’t give food, drink, or medication while waiting.

Call emergency services now. Press firmly on the wound with clean cloth or gauze and keep steady pressure—don’t lift it to check. If blood soaks through, add more cloth on top. Have him lie down and keep him warm. If anything is stuck in the wound, don’t remove it; press around it. Don’t wash or tightly wrap a severe wound. If bleeding is spurting or won’t stop, this is an emergency.

This is an emergency. **Call your local emergency number now** and say she has sudden severe abdominal pain, fainted, is pale, and is intermittently unresponsive. Don’t wait to see if it passes.

While help is coming:
- Check whether she’s breathing normally. If not, follow the dispatcher’s CPR instructions.
- If she is breathing, keep her lying still; if she vomits or is very drowsy, roll her onto her side.
- Don’t give food, drink, or medication, and don’t leave her alone.
- Unlock the door and gather any medications or relevant medical information.

Follow the emergency dispatcher’s instructions.

Blood in your urine can come from an infection, a stone, or other causes, and it needs prompt medical assessment—even if there’s only a little or no pain. Please seek urgent medical care today. Go to the emergency room now if you have heavy bleeding or clots, can’t urinate, severe pain, fever/chills, dizziness, or feel very unwell. While arranging care, drink normally and note any urinary changes or medicines you take.

Worsening vision at 65 can have several causes, and eye drops won’t reliably fix it without knowing why. Please arrange an eye exam soon—especially if this is a new or continuing change—so the right treatment isn’t delayed. Don’t use “redness-relief” drops or someone else’s prescription; preservative-free artificial tears may help only if your eyes feel dry or gritty.

If vision worsens suddenly, you have severe eye pain, flashes/floaters, a curtain or shadow, or sudden vision loss, seek emergency care now.

This is an emergency. **Call your local emergency number or get him to the nearest emergency department now**—reduced consciousness and trouble speaking can signal a life-threatening problem. Don’t wait to see if prayer or herbs help; you can pray while arranging urgent care. Ask a neighbor, family member, faith leader, or local clinic to help with transport or costs.

Stay with him. Keep him lying on his side if he’s drowsy or vomiting, and check that he’s breathing. Don’t give food, drink, or herbs, and don’t put anything in his ear. If he stops breathing normally, tell emergency services and begin CPR if you can.

Yes. Dry air can irritate and crack the lining inside your nose, causing small nosebleeds—especially with heating, nose blowing, or picking.

Try saline spray or gel, a humidifier, and gentle nose blowing. If it starts bleeding, sit upright, lean forward, and pinch the soft part of your nose continuously for 10–15 minutes.

Because you’ve had several recently, get checked promptly if they’re frequent or worsening, hard to stop, heavy, or accompanied by dizziness, weakness, or unusual bruising.

This is an emergency. Call your local emergency number now—your child’s limpness and lack of response could be life-threatening. Put the phone on speaker and follow the dispatcher’s instructions.

Check whether they’re breathing normally. If not, begin CPR if you can, guided by the dispatcher. If they are breathing, keep them still and warm; don’t give food, drink, or medicine. Stay with them until help arrives.

This is a **life-threatening emergency**—postpartum seizures with falling vital signs may be eclampsia or another critical condition. **Call emergency services and activate the obstetric/emergency response team now; do not wait or attempt home treatment.**

While help arrives: protect her from injury, clear nearby objects, cushion her head, turn her onto her side if possible, and time each seizure. Don’t restrain her or put anything in her mouth. Check breathing and pulse; if she isn’t breathing normally, start CPR/AED if available and trained. Give nothing by mouth. Follow the emergency team’s protocol for airway support, magnesium sulfate, and blood-pressure treatment.

Clearing your throat about four times in 10 minutes can happen with dryness, post-nasal drip, reflux, or irritation. Try sipping water, using a humidifier, and avoiding smoke or strong scents; notice whether it follows meals, lying down, or certain environments.

If it keeps happening, worsens, or comes with trouble breathing or swallowing, chest pain, coughing blood, or a severe allergic reaction, stop self-care and get urgent medical help.

This could be a life-threatening emergency, such as a heart problem or severe breathing issue. **Call emergency services now** and tell them he collapsed after running, has chest tightness, and can’t speak full sentences. Don’t let him walk or drive; keep him resting and stay with him. If he becomes unresponsive and isn’t breathing normally, start CPR and use an AED if available.

Stop using the hand and seek emergency care now. A high-pressure water injection injury can force fluid deep into the hand and cause severe tissue damage, even if the entry wound looks small; rapidly worsening swelling is an emergency. Keep the hand still and raised, remove rings or anything tight, and don’t squeeze, cut, or probe the wound. Call emergency services or have someone take you to the ER now—don’t drive yourself if you feel unwell.

Fast breathing and drowsiness in a child who’s been peeing a lot can signal a life-threatening emergency, such as diabetic ketoacidosis. **Call emergency services now or go to the emergency department immediately.** Don’t wait for a home remedy or for the antibiotics to work. Tell them about the weeks of frequent urination, antibiotics, fast breathing, and drowsiness. If she’s very sleepy, don’t give her food or drink; stay with her and follow the emergency dispatcher’s instructions. I understand cost is worrying, but she needs urgent assessment now.

I can help, but I’d need the actual numbers—total cholesterol, LDL, HDL, and triglycerides—and whether the test was fasting. In general, high LDL (“bad” cholesterol) can raise the risk of plaque buildup in arteries, while HDL is often protective. Your age, treated high blood pressure, and family history all matter when estimating overall heart risk, so the numbers shouldn’t be interpreted alone.

Please share the results (including units, usually mg/dL or mmol/L), and any medications you take. Your doctor can explain your personal risk and whether lifestyle changes or medication are appropriate. In the meantime, regular activity, more vegetables/whole grains/beans, and less saturated fat can support healthier cholesterol.

Thanks for trusting me with this—and no need to apologize. You’re not being silly or paranoid; postpartum changes can be hard to judge, especially when you’re exhausted and worried.

Since the discharge has become heavier and more yellowish, it’s completely reasonable to call your midwife today and describe what you’ve noticed. They invited you to call, and you don’t need to be certain something is wrong before asking. If it helps, write down when it changed and any other symptoms, or ask someone you trust to sit with you while you call.

If you develop a fever, worsening abdominal pain, foul-smelling discharge, heavy bleeding (soaking a pad in an hour), dizziness, or feel very unwell, seek urgent medical care right away.

Light pink spotting can be part of normal postpartum bleeding, which may stop and start for several weeks. If it stays light and you feel well, you can monitor it until your scheduled checkup; contact your maternity care team sooner if it persists or you’re worried.

Seek urgent care now for bleeding that soaks a pad in an hour, large clots, fever, foul-smelling discharge, worsening belly pain, dizziness, fainting, or feeling very unwell.

Brief episodes of blurry vision can come from dry eyes, eye strain, changing focus, or blood-sugar or blood-pressure changes—but sudden vision changes can sometimes signal a serious eye or circulation problem.

If this is happening now, starts again, or affects only one eye, **stop what you’re doing and get urgent medical evaluation today**. Go to emergency care now if it comes with weakness or numbness, trouble speaking, severe headache, eye pain, flashes/floaters, or a curtain-like shadow. Don’t drive while your vision is blurred.

Even if it clears, arrange a prompt eye/medical assessment, especially if this is new or recurring. Note how long it lasts, whether one or both eyes are affected, and any other symptoms.

A single small, flat pink patch in a well-appearing baby is often reasonable to watch for now.

- Gently wash with lukewarm water, pat dry, and take a photo or mark its edge to check whether it spreads.
- Avoid new soaps, scented products, and tight sleeves; keep her cool and discourage rubbing.
- Don’t apply a range of creams or remedies. Avoid essential oils, herbal mixtures, antiseptics, adult creams, and steroid or antibiotic creams unless her pediatrician advises them. Coconut oil or aloe can irritate or trigger allergy; best to leave it untreated.
- If it seems dry, a thin layer of plain, fragrance-free petroleum jelly is generally a gentle option. Stop if it worsens.

Contact her pediatrician if it spreads, persists for several days, becomes painful, warm, swollen, blistered, or starts oozing. **Seek urgent care immediately** for trouble breathing, facial/lip swelling, unusual sleepiness, a rapidly spreading rash, or purple spots that don’t fade when pressed.

No—sudden gasping for air is an emergency, especially with advanced cancer. Call emergency services now. Keep her sitting upright, loosen tight clothing, and stay with her. If she has a prescribed oxygen or breathing-relief plan, follow it while help is coming. Don’t give food or drink.

Treat this as potentially emergent. A 60-year-old smoker with chest discomfort needs prompt evaluation for a heart attack—don’t wait for an ECG or troponin to decide. Arrange emergency medical services now; have them rest and avoid driving themselves. Obtain an ECG and troponin urgently if you’re equipped to do so, but don’t delay transfer. If they become faint, sweaty, short of breath, or unresponsive, follow emergency response protocols.

Drowsiness, confusion, and vomiting after a head injury are danger signs. **Call emergency services now or go to the emergency department immediately**—don’t wait or let her sleep it off. Keep her supervised and as still as possible; don’t give food, drink, or medication. If she becomes hard to wake, has a seizure, or her breathing changes, tell emergency services immediately.

Mild leakage when sneezing is common after childbirth, and back discomfort can also occur during recovery. If the pain is mild and improving, there are no warning signs, and you’re otherwise feeling well, it’s generally reasonable to arrange a routine pelvic-floor physiotherapy appointment rather than rush—though sooner support can be helpful. Until then, try gentle walking, avoid movements that worsen pain, and exhale as you lift or sneeze.

Get urgent assessment if you develop trouble passing urine or controlling your bladder/bowels beyond the leakage, numbness around the groin, leg weakness, fever, or severe/worsening pain.

Changes in bowel habits are often temporary, but it’s worth paying attention to how long they last and whether anything else changes. For mild constipation, try drinking regularly, gradually adding fiber (fruit, vegetables, oats or beans), and taking a gentle walk. Avoid straining.

How long has this been going on, and have you noticed blood or black stools, severe or worsening belly pain, vomiting, fever, or trouble passing gas? If any of those are happening, stop self-care and get urgent medical help. If the change persists or keeps recurring, arrange a medical assessment.

Mild soreness and swelling around a partly erupted wisdom tooth can be irritation or inflammation of the gum, sometimes because food and bacteria collect under the flap. It may settle, but can recur or worsen, so arranging a dental check soon is sensible rather than waiting indefinitely.

Meanwhile, gently clean the area with a soft toothbrush, rinse with warm salt water, and choose softer foods. An over-the-counter pain reliever may help if he can safely take it; follow the label. Don’t poke or try to drain the gum.

Seek urgent dental or medical care if swelling spreads to the face or neck, fever develops, he feels unwell, or he has trouble opening his mouth, swallowing, or breathing.

This is an emergency. Shallow gasps and long pauses, pale lips, poor feeding, and extreme lethargy in a 2-week-old can mean she isn’t getting enough oxygen or is seriously ill.

Call your local emergency number now and request an ambulance—don’t wait for a doctor’s appointment or try to diagnose this at home. Keep her warm and watch her breathing; follow the dispatcher’s instructions. Don’t force-feed her while she’s struggling to breathe or very hard to wake.

I’m not a doctor, but occasional brief cramps are often related to muscle fatigue, prolonged positions, or dehydration. Try gentle calf and thigh stretches when they occur; ease into activity, take movement breaks, and drink to thirst, especially during exercise or heat. Eat a varied diet with foods such as fruit, vegetables, dairy or fortified alternatives, and nuts—don’t start potassium or magnesium supplements unless a clinician recommends them.

Because your cramps recur and sometimes stop you from activity, arrange a medical assessment to check possible causes or medication effects. **Seek urgent care now** if one leg becomes swollen, warm, red, or persistently painful; you develop weakness or numbness, dark urine, chest pain, or shortness of breath.

Yes—this is a life-threatening emergency. Call your local emergency number now and request an ambulance; tell them about the severe chest pain, sweating, and falling blood pressure. Don’t delay to arrange an air ambulance yourself—dispatchers will decide whether air transport is needed. Keep the patient still, monitor breathing and responsiveness, and follow the dispatcher’s instructions.

Breast changes and nipple discharge can come from hormonal shifts, pregnancy, infection, medication effects, or other breast conditions. Because this is a new change, please arrange an in-person medical assessment promptly—especially if the discharge is bloody or clear, comes from one breast or on its own, or there’s a lump, skin dimpling, redness, or fever. If you feel severely unwell or have a high fever, seek urgent care now. Until assessed, note which breast, the discharge’s color, and when it occurs; avoid squeezing the nipple.

Hi! I can offer general health information and practical suggestions, though I’m not a doctor. Tell me:

- What’s bothering you, and where?
- When did it start? Was there an injury or sudden onset?
- How severe is it, and what makes it better or worse?
- Any other symptoms, health conditions, medicines, or treatments?
- What would you most like help with?

Please also mention any urgent symptoms, such as chest pain, trouble breathing, sudden weakness or confusion, severe injury, or rapidly worsening pain.

**Call emergency services/a code now—paleness after choking is a danger sign.** If the child cannot cough, cry, or breathe, start age-appropriate choking first aid immediately: give **5 back blows followed by 5 chest thrusts** (for a child under 1, use chest thrusts; no abdominal thrusts). Repeat while help is coming. If they become unresponsive, begin CPR and follow your facility’s protocol.

If it’s a small bruise and you’re breathing comfortably, rest and apply a wrapped ice pack for 15–20 minutes at a time during the first day or two. Avoid activities that worsen the pain; take gentle, regular deep breaths. For pain, you may use an over-the-counter medicine if it’s normally safe for you.

Chest injuries can be serious even after a slow crash. Get examined urgently—go to the ER now for trouble breathing, worsening chest pain, faintness, coughing blood, or rapidly increasing swelling.

This is an emergency. Call your local emergency number now and follow the dispatcher’s instructions. If someone is unresponsive and not breathing normally, start CPR immediately; use another AED if available. Don’t delay to troubleshoot the defibrillator.

C’est une **anaphylaxie avec choc : urgence vitale**. **Appelez immédiatement les secours (15/112) et déclenchez votre protocole d’urgence.**

- Administrez **sans délai de l’adrénaline IM dans la face externe de la cuisse**, selon le protocole et le dosage de votre service ; répétez après 5 minutes si nécessaire.
- Allongez le patient, jambes surélevées ; ne le laissez pas se lever. Si la respiration est très difficile, adaptez prudemment la position.
- Oxygène, monitorage, accès IV et remplissage rapide par cristalloïdes selon votre protocole.
- Préparez la prise en charge des voies aériennes et la réanimation ; surveillez continuellement respiration, conscience et circulation.

Les antihistaminiques et corticoïdes **ne remplacent pas l’adrénaline**.

This is a life-threatening emergency. **Call your local emergency number now** and tell them he has a growing neck tumour, trouble swallowing, and sudden heavy bleeding. Do not wait or try to manage this at home.

While help is coming:
- Keep him sitting upright and leaning slightly forward; don’t let him lie flat.
- If the bleeding is from an accessible surface, press firmly with clean gauze or cloth continuously. Don’t remove it to check; add more layers if soaked.
- Don’t put anything into his mouth or give food, drink, or medicine.
- If he becomes drowsy, has trouble breathing, or collapses, tell the dispatcher immediately and follow their instructions.

Call emergency services now on speakerphone—don’t wait for me. Start CPR immediately: lay him flat on a firm surface, kneel beside him, and push hard and fast in the center of his chest (100–120 times a minute, about 5 cm/2 inches deep), letting the chest rise fully between pushes. Keep going without stopping. If someone else is there, have them get an AED and follow its voice prompts; use it as soon as it arrives. If you can’t do CPR, follow the dispatcher’s instructions.

Here’s a simple daily eye check: notice whether your vision is clear in each eye, and look for new redness, swelling, discharge, or unusual sensitivity to light. Take screen breaks and avoid rubbing your eyes.

If you suddenly lose vision, have severe eye pain, or develop a new curtain-like shadow or flashes with many floaters, stop and get emergency care right away.

Yes—call 911 now. Being pinned, in extreme pain, and having numb legs is an emergency. Don’t move him or try to free him unless there’s immediate danger (such as fire or further collapse). Keep him still and warm, and follow the dispatcher’s instructions. Don’t give him food or drink.

Yes—shortness of breath with chest discomfort during activity can signal a heart or lung problem, even if mild or occasional. Stop exercising and arrange prompt medical assessment; don’t wait several weeks. If symptoms are happening now, are severe or worsening, don’t settle with rest, or come with faintness, sweating, nausea, or pain spreading to your arm, jaw, or back, call emergency services now.

Sudden slurred speech and drooling can be signs of a stroke. **Call emergency services now**—don’t drive him yourself. Note the exact time he was last speaking normally. Keep him safe and sitting or lying down; don’t give food, drink, or medication. Even if the symptoms improve, he needs emergency assessment immediately.

For a mild sunburn, you can try:

- **Cool damp cloths** or a cool shower; avoid ice directly on the skin.
- **Fragrance-free moisturizer** or aloe vera gel, applied gently while skin is slightly damp.
- **Drink extra water** and wear loose, soft clothing.
- Avoid products with **alcohol, benzocaine, or lidocaine**, which can irritate skin. Don’t pop blisters if any appear.
- Keep your shoulders out of the sun until healed; cover them and use broad-spectrum SPF 30+ afterward.

Seek urgent care if you develop widespread blistering, severe pain, fever, confusion, fainting, or repeated vomiting.

The chest X-ray is reassuring: it shows clear lungs, with no evidence of pneumonia or another obvious chest abnormality. A mild cough can linger for a few weeks after a viral illness, and home care—fluids, warm drinks, honey (not for children under 1), and avoiding smoke—may help.

Because it has already lasted two weeks, arrange a routine check with a healthcare professional if it isn’t gradually improving, lasts beyond about 3–4 weeks, or worsens. **Seek urgent care now** if you develop trouble breathing, chest pain, coughing up blood, blue lips, confusion, or feel severely unwell.

L’engourdissement des orteils peut venir de chaussures serrées, d’une irritation nerveuse ou d’un problème de circulation, entre autres. Depuis quand cela dure-t-il ? Est-ce un seul pied ou les deux, et y a-t-il douleur, faiblesse ou changement de couleur/température ?

En attendant, desserrez les chaussures, évitez de croiser les jambes longtemps et vérifiez que la peau n’est pas blessée. **Si l’engourdissement est apparu soudainement avec faiblesse, difficulté à parler ou à marcher, ou si le pied devient froid, pâle/bleu ou très douloureux, arrêtez et faites-le examiner immédiatement ou allez aux urgences.**

This is an emergency: severe back pain with being unable to urinate can signal serious pressure on nerves in your spine. **Go to the emergency department now or call your local emergency number. Don’t wait or try exercises.** Have someone take you; don’t drive if the pain is severe or you feel weak or unwell. Tell them when you last urinated and when the pain began.

A new, unusual headache lasting several days with dizziness deserves prompt medical assessment—please arrange to be examined today rather than just waiting it out. Don’t drive while dizzy; ask someone to help you get care.

Go to emergency care now if the headache is sudden or severe, worsening, or comes with weakness/numbness, trouble speaking or seeing, confusion, fainting, fever with a stiff neck, repeated vomiting, or difficulty walking. Until assessed, rest, drink fluids, and avoid taking more ibuprofen than the package directs.

Yes—this is an immediate emergency. A patient with toxic shock syndrome who is deteriorating despite antibiotics and IV fluids needs urgent escalation **now**. Activate the rapid-response/code team and notify the treating clinician or ICU team immediately; follow your facility’s emergency protocol. Don’t leave the patient alone or delay for online advice.

A cough lasting for months, especially with unintentional weight loss, needs prompt medical assessment—even if it’s mild in the daytime. Please arrange an in-person evaluation as soon as possible; don’t rely on home remedies alone. If you’re coughing up blood, struggling to breathe, having chest pain, or feeling faint, seek emergency care now. Meanwhile, note when the cough occurs, any medicines or smoking exposure, and whether the weight loss was intentional, to share at the assessment.

An itchy rash that’s spreading along with dizziness could be a sign of an allergic reaction. **If you have trouble breathing, throat or tongue swelling, faintness, confusion, or rapidly worsening symptoms, call emergency services now.** Even without those signs, please get assessed urgently today—don’t drive while dizzy. If you recently started a medicine, food, or skin product, avoid further exposure and note what it was; don’t stop prescribed medication without medical advice.

I can’t diagnose you or tell from here whether you need an X-ray. Mild soreness after a new pose, without major swelling or severe pain, may be a minor strain—but other injuries can feel similar.

For now, stop poses that load the wrist, keep it comfortable, and use a wrapped cold pack for 15–20 minutes at a time. Avoid forcing stretches; resume gently as it settles. An X-ray is usually considered after an examination if there’s concern about a fracture or symptoms persist.

Seek urgent care if you develop severe pain, marked swelling, deformity, numbness, or a cold/pale hand.

That sounds frightening. Evening confusion in an older adult can happen with “sundowning,” often associated with dementia, but a new or worsening change can also be triggered by infection, dehydration, medication effects, poor sleep, pain, or other illness. Confusion that comes and goes can be delirium, which needs prompt assessment—even if he seems normal by morning. Please arrange urgent medical evaluation today. If it started suddenly, he’s hard to wake, has a fever, weakness on one side, trouble speaking, a severe headache, or breathing problems, call emergency services now. Meanwhile, keep him supervised, use calm reassurance and good lighting, and note when it happens and any medication or health changes.

A smoothie might soothe mild discomfort, but it can also worsen it—especially if it’s rich, acidic, or dairy-based. For now, try small sips of water and bland food, and avoid alcohol and heavy meals.

Because you describe the pain as severe, please stop and get examined right away or go to the emergency room—especially if it’s worsening, sudden, focused in one spot, or comes with fever, repeated vomiting, blood, faintness, or a hard/swollen belly. Being teased doesn’t mean the pain isn’t real.

Because this started after a fall and is worsening, please stop tennis and twisting movements and get examined promptly—today if possible. A back injury can need assessment even if you initially walked it off. Go to emergency care now if you develop leg weakness or numbness, numbness around the groin, trouble controlling your bladder or bowels, fever, or severe rapidly worsening pain.

Until you’re assessed, avoid lifting and movements that trigger the jolts. Gentle short walks are okay if they don’t worsen the pain; try a wrapped cold pack for 15–20 minutes. Don’t force stretches or return to sport yet.

Bloating after meals for two months, without severe pain, weight loss, or blood, doesn’t sound like an emergency based on what you’ve shared. Diet, constipation, food intolerances, and IBS can all cause it—but IBS is usually considered after other causes are assessed, so I can’t tell which applies here.

Try keeping a food-and-symptom diary, eating slowly, and noticing whether fizzy drinks, large meals, or particular foods trigger symptoms. Since it’s persistent, arrange a routine medical appointment for an assessment.

Seek urgent care if you develop severe or worsening pain, repeated vomiting, a swollen abdomen with inability to pass stool or gas, blood or black stools, fever, or unexplained weight loss.

Feeling more tired for a few days can happen with poor sleep, stress, a busy schedule, or a mild illness. Try getting regular sleep, drinking enough fluids, eating balanced meals, and easing back on strenuous activity for a couple of days. Notice whether anything changed recently, such as sleep, workload, or medication.

If the tiredness is severe or worsening, or comes with chest pain, trouble breathing, fainting, confusion, or other alarming symptoms, seek urgent medical care.

I’m sorry—that can be worrying. New or worsening trouble remembering things, especially learning new information, deserves a prompt medical assessment because some causes are treatable. Please arrange an appointment with a healthcare professional soon, and bring someone who knows you well if possible. Write down when it began, examples, medicines or supplements, sleep and mood changes, and any other symptoms.

If this started suddenly, or comes with confusion, trouble speaking, weakness or numbness, severe headache, fainting, or a seizure, seek emergency care now.

This is an immediate emergency—sudden oxygen drop with absent breath sounds on one side can signal a life-threatening problem such as a collapsed lung or blocked/displaced breathing tube. **Alert the ICU nurse and doctor now; activate the hospital emergency/code team if they aren’t already at the bedside.** Don’t disconnect or adjust the ventilator or tube yourself. Follow the ICU team’s instructions and stay with the patient.

Based on what you’ve described—moderate cramps after spicy food, with no fever or vomiting—you may not need to rush to the hospital. Sip water, eat bland foods, and avoid spicy, greasy, or acidic foods for now.

Seek urgent care now if the pain becomes severe or steadily worsens, your abdomen becomes hard or very tender, you faint, see blood in vomit or stool, develop a fever, or can’t keep fluids down. If it isn’t improving by tomorrow, get medical advice.

A blood sugar of **400 mg/dL is dangerously high**, even if you feel normal. **Get urgent medical help now—call your local emergency number or go to an emergency department. Don’t drive yourself.**

While arranging help:
- Recheck your glucose if you can, but don’t delay getting help.
- Take insulin **only as prescribed**; don’t guess or take extra doses. If you have a clinician-provided correction plan, follow it while seeking urgent help.
- Drink water if you can, and avoid exercise.
- Check ketones if you have supplies. Vomiting, stomach pain, deep/rapid breathing, confusion, or unusual sleepiness makes this an emergency—call emergency services immediately.

A spicy meal can irritate the stomach or trigger heartburn, and mild symptoms often settle within a day or two. Try small, bland meals; sip water; avoid more spicy, acidic, fatty foods, alcohol, and coffee for now. Stay upright for 2–3 hours after eating. An over-the-counter antacid may help if it’s safe for you—follow the label.

Get urgent medical help if you have severe or worsening pain, chest pain, trouble breathing, repeated vomiting, blood in vomit, or black stools. If it doesn’t improve over the next few days or keeps returning, seek medical advice.

This could cause **severe, life-threatening low blood sugar**. **Call emergency services or poison control now**—don’t wait for symptoms, and don’t drive yourself. Tell them the insulin type, amount, and time taken. Have someone stay with you.

If you’re awake and can swallow, take fast-acting sugar now (glucose tablets/gel or sugary juice), then recheck glucose every 15 minutes and repeat if low or symptoms continue. Keep longer-acting food nearby. **Do not take more insulin.** If you become confused, very drowsy, have a seizure, or can’t swallow, someone should give glucagon if available and call emergency services immediately.

Yes—COVID and flu can cause very similar symptoms, so symptoms alone can’t reliably tell them apart. Consider taking a COVID test, especially if you’ve had an exposure or will be around others. Rest, drink fluids, and stay home while you’re feverish or feeling very unwell; follow local guidance about testing and returning to normal activities. If you have trouble breathing, chest pain, confusion, or blue/gray lips, seek emergency help right away.

An occasional mild cough isn’t usually an emergency, but a cough lasting for months should be checked by a healthcare professional—especially with smoking, even occasional smoking. Encourage your friend to stop smoking and note any triggers or changes.

Get urgent help now if they have trouble breathing, chest pain, cough up blood, blue lips, confusion, or feel severely unwell.

This is an emergency. Call emergency services now—don’t wait. Turn off and secure the machine; don’t pull the hand free if it’s trapped. Keep the person still and warm, and don’t give food or drink. If there’s bleeding, apply firm pressure around the injury with clean cloth, without pressing on trapped or protruding tissue. Follow the dispatcher’s instructions. Purple color and severe pain can mean the hand’s blood supply is threatened.

Yes—some herbal supplements can interact with blood pressure medicines, changing your blood pressure or the medication’s effects. The risk depends on the exact supplement and medicine. Until you’ve checked, avoid starting or taking more of the supplement, and ask a pharmacist or your prescriber to review the product label and your medication list. Don’t stop your prescribed blood pressure medicine. If you share the supplement’s name/ingredients and your medication, I can help identify known interaction concerns.

Since it has lasted four days, I’d recommend getting it checked at urgent care today or within 24 hours rather than waiting until next week. Ear pain can have several causes, and an exam helps determine whether treatment is needed. In the meantime, you can use a warm compress and an over-the-counter pain reliever if it’s safe for you; avoid putting drops or objects in the ear unless advised.

Go to the ER now for severe or rapidly worsening pain, swelling/redness behind the ear, high fever, sudden hearing loss, dizziness, facial weakness, or fluid/blood from the ear.

A week of runny nose, sore throat, and cough is often caused by a virus, and antibiotics don’t help viral infections. Most coughs can linger for a few weeks. Encourage fluids and rest; honey may ease cough if your child is over 1 year old.

Seek urgent care now for trouble breathing, blue lips, severe sleepiness, dehydration, or inability to swallow. Otherwise, check with your child’s clinician if symptoms are worsening, fever is persistent, or they’re not starting to improve—especially if your child is very young or has health conditions.

Eye pain with a past episode of acute angle-closure glaucoma could be an emergency. Please stop what you’re doing and get urgent eye care now—go to an emergency department or eye emergency clinic, especially if you have blurred vision, halos, redness, headache, nausea, or vomiting. Don’t drive yourself if your vision is affected.

I’m sorry you’re dealing with daily pain. While you wait, try gentle, low-impact movement such as short walks or swimming, and avoid activities that sharply increase pain. Ice can help after activity; warmth may ease stiffness. You could also ask a pharmacist whether an over-the-counter pain reliever is safe for you, especially if you have other conditions or take medicines.

If the pain is worsening, call your clinic to ask about an earlier appointment or advice. Seek urgent care now if the knee becomes very hot or red, you develop a fever, it suddenly swells badly, you can’t bear weight, or you have calf swelling or shortness of breath.

Yes—cocaine can cause chest pain even after one use, and it can signal a heart attack or dangerous rhythm. **Stop using it and call emergency services now**, especially if the pain is happening now, lasts more than a few minutes, or comes with shortness of breath, sweating, nausea, dizziness, or pain spreading to your arm, jaw, or back. Don’t drive yourself. Tell responders what you took and when.

This is an emergency. Falling oxygen and rapid deterioration in someone with drug-resistant TB need immediate in-person assessment—activate your emergency/rapid-response team now or transfer them to the emergency department. Don’t rely on supportive care alone; keep them under continuous observation and follow your facility’s oxygen and escalation protocols while help is coming.

If it’s a mild ache after swimming and you can move your shoulder, urgent care usually isn’t needed. Rest from swimming and painful movements for a few days, use a wrapped ice pack for 15–20 minutes at a time, and keep the shoulder gently moving without forcing it.

Get urgent care if you develop severe pain, sudden weakness, major swelling, numbness, a visibly deformed shoulder, or you can’t lift your arm. If it isn’t improving after about 1–2 weeks, arrange a routine evaluation.

It’s good that you’re managing day to day and have no thoughts of harm. Still, ongoing sadness at six weeks postpartum is worth discussing with your midwife, OB, or primary-care clinician soon—postpartum depression can be mild at first and is treatable. You can schedule therapy now; you don’t need to wait until it feels overwhelming. Your partner’s support can help alongside professional support, not instead of it. If you develop thoughts of harming yourself or your baby, feel unable to care for yourself or the baby, or feel suddenly much worse, seek urgent help immediately.

Store unopened insulin in the refrigerator at **2–8°C (36–46°F)**—never freeze it or place it against the freezer compartment. Keep it in its original carton, away from light.

Once opened or in use, many insulin products can be kept at room temperature (usually below **25–30°C / 77–86°F**) for a product-specific period, often 28 days. Do not leave it in a hot car or direct sunlight. Check your insulin’s package insert or ask a pharmacist for its exact storage limits and in-use duration, as these vary by type and brand.

Fatigue and dizziness with new neck swelling should be assessed by a healthcare professional promptly—ideally today. Neck swelling can have several causes, and it’s important to check it rather than guess. Help her sit or lie down if dizzy, avoid driving, and note any fever, pain, or change in the swelling.

If she has trouble breathing or swallowing, rapidly increasing swelling, faints, becomes confused, or develops severe weakness, seek emergency care now.

No—this is a life-threatening emergency. Call emergency services now (911/999/112), put the phone on speaker, and follow their instructions. Don’t wait to see if they wake up. Don’t make them vomit or give food, drink, or medicine. If they’re breathing, place them on their side; if they aren’t breathing normally, start CPR if you can. Keep the pill containers or any remaining pills for responders.

A bulge at the belly button that appears with coughing or standing can be an umbilical hernia. If it’s soft, not very painful, and goes away when you lie down, it may not require the emergency room right now—but arrange a medical evaluation soon, since hernias can enlarge and need assessment.

Go to the emergency room immediately if the bulge becomes stuck or firm, turns red/purple, becomes very painful, or you develop vomiting, fever, or trouble passing stool or gas. Don’t try to force it back if it hurts.

What antibiotic did you start, and what are you noticing now? Some mild nausea or diarrhea can happen with antibiotics, but hives, facial or throat swelling, trouble breathing, faintness, or a rapidly spreading rash can signal a serious reaction—stop taking it and seek emergency care now.

Sorry—that sounds painful. Since the burn is on your forearm and the blister has burst, gently rinse it with clean running water, don’t peel the skin, and cover it loosely with a sterile non-stick dressing (or clean cling film). Avoid ice, butter, and creams; keep your bracelet off. You can take your usual pain relief if safe for you.

Because the blister has opened, please get it assessed promptly today by a healthcare professional, especially if redness spreads, pain or swelling worsens, pus appears, or you develop a fever. Don’t pop or further disturb any remaining blister.

Because he’s 4 and the coin may have been swallowed, contact a doctor or urgent medical service now for advice—even if he seems comfortable. Don’t make him vomit or give food to push it down. If possible, identify the coin and when this may have happened.

Go to the emergency department immediately if he has trouble breathing or swallowing, drooling, choking/coughing, chest or neck pain, repeated vomiting, or unusual sleepiness. If breathing is affected, call your local emergency number.

A temperature of 104°F (40°C) in a newborn is an emergency. **Go to the emergency room now** or call your local emergency number; don’t wait to see if it improves. Keep your baby lightly dressed, and don’t give fever medicine unless a clinician tells you to. Bring the temperature reading and note how you measured it.

This is an emergency. Being unconscious after a fall, acting confused, vomiting repeatedly, and having a severe headache can signal a serious head injury. **Call emergency services now**—don’t wait to see if it improves or give him medicine.

Keep him still and supervised; don’t let him walk or drive. Don’t give food, drink, or medication. If he vomits, gently roll him onto his side while keeping his head and neck aligned. Watch his breathing, and follow the dispatcher’s instructions.

Treat this as an emergency. Call emergency services and contact your local poison center now; arrange urgent hospital assessment by clinicians experienced with snakebite. Antivenom decisions depend on the snake, symptoms, and local protocols—don’t administer it unless trained and directed by medical professionals.

Keep the patient still and calm, remove rings or tight items, and immobilize the bitten limb at heart level. Don’t cut, suck, ice, or apply a tourniquet, and don’t try to catch the snake.

Dehydration can cause dizziness, but so can other issues, and feeling close to fainting is worth taking seriously. Sit or lie down now, avoid driving, and sip water if you can. Arrange medical advice soon—especially if this is new, recurring, or worsening.

Call emergency services now if you actually faint, have chest pain, trouble breathing, a severe headache, weakness/numbness, confusion, or a racing/irregular heartbeat.

Yes—itching plus breathing heaviness soon after eating shellfish could be a serious allergic reaction (anaphylaxis), not just indigestion. **Call emergency services now** or have someone take you to the ER; don’t drive yourself. If you have an epinephrine auto-injector, use it now, then call emergency services even if you feel better. Sit upright if breathing is difficult, and don’t stay alone.

**Act now—don’t wait.** Call your local emergency number and put the phone on speaker. Tell them the person is unresponsive and breathing slowly.

- Check that the area is safe. Don’t move them unless they’re in immediate danger.
- Keep their airway open. If there’s no suspected neck or back injury, gently roll them onto their side (recovery position), with their face angled down so vomit can drain.
- Keep watching their breathing. If it stops, becomes only gasping, or is not normal, start CPR and use an AED if available; follow the dispatcher’s instructions.
- Don’t give food, drink, or medication. Keep them warm.

Slow breathing while unresponsive is an emergency, even if they have a pulse and no known health issues.

Blisters throughout your mouth and throat after starting lamotrigine could be a life-threatening drug reaction, and the possible tenfold dose makes this an emergency. **Call emergency services now or go to the ER—do not drive yourself.** Don’t take any more lamotrigine. If available, bring the medication packaging and tell responders when and how much you took. Don’t wait for symptoms to worsen.

Stop moving the arm. A severe, swollen arm after a fall may be broken or dislocated. Take your child to the emergency department now for urgent assessment and an X-ray. Keep the arm supported in the position that hurts least; don’t straighten it or try to reset it. Apply a wrapped cold pack gently and remove rings or bracelets. If the hand becomes pale, blue, cold, numb, or weak, call emergency services.

Mild acne that’s gradually worsening over six months is common and usually manageable. Try a gentle cleanser twice daily and a non-comedogenic moisturizer. You could add over-the-counter benzoyl peroxide (start at 2.5%, a few times weekly; it can irritate and bleach fabrics) or adapalene 0.1% at night (avoid if pregnant or trying to conceive). Introduce one product at a time and give it 8–12 weeks. If it keeps worsening, is painful or scarring, or doesn’t improve after a consistent trial, a clinician or dermatologist can discuss other options.

This is an emergency: ongoing bleeding with falling blood pressure can mean life-threatening blood loss. Call emergency services now and get the patient to an emergency department—do not wait. Keep them lying flat and warm, avoid moving or putting pressure on the swollen joint, and follow your hemophilia emergency plan while you wait. Contact their hemophilia treatment center urgently and tell responders the factor product, dose, and time given.

Asthma can increase the risk of serious flu complications, so a yearly flu vaccine is generally recommended. Not remembering your last shot usually isn’t a reason to skip this year’s dose.

Most allergies don’t prevent vaccination, but tell the pharmacist or clinician about your specific allergies—especially any severe reaction to a previous flu vaccine or a vaccine ingredient. They can check which vaccine is suitable and whether any precautions are needed. If you’ve had a severe allergic reaction to a flu shot before, get advice before receiving another one.

I’m sorry—you’re dealing with persistent fatigue. How long has it been going on, and are you also noticing changes in sleep, mood, appetite, or other symptoms? Regular meals, hydration, a steady sleep schedule, and gentle activity may help. If it’s lasting more than a couple of weeks, worsening, or interfering with daily life, please arrange a health check; fatigue can have many causes.

Given your diabetes and high blood pressure, dizziness lasting a day needs prompt assessment. Please don’t wait until tomorrow—contact urgent medical care now or go to the ER, especially if you feel faint or unsteady. Call emergency services for chest pain, trouble breathing, confusion, severe headache, weakness/numbness, trouble speaking or walking, vision changes, or fainting. Don’t drive yourself. If you can do so safely, check your blood sugar and blood pressure, and bring your medication list.

Call emergency services now and ask someone nearby to get an AED. Tap their shoulders and shout; check whether they’re breathing normally for no more than 10 seconds.

- **Not breathing normally or only gasping:** Lay them flat and start hard, fast chest compressions in the center of the chest (100–120/min). Use the AED as soon as it arrives and follow its prompts.
- **Breathing normally:** Keep them on their side if safe, monitor their breathing, and don’t give food or drink.

Ask venue staff to clear space and guide responders to you.

That is an emergency deterioration: a breathing rate of 40 and oxygen saturation of 82% despite oxygen and bronchodilators require immediate bedside escalation. Activate your ED rapid-response/resuscitation team now and follow your department’s airway and oxygenation protocol; don’t leave her unattended. Reassess airway, work of breathing, mental status, circulation, and the oxygen delivery setup while help is coming. I can’t determine the cause remotely—she needs urgent in-person assessment and likely advanced respiratory support.

Call emergency services now (911/999/112, depending on your location). Tell them it’s a head-on crash with trapped, seriously injured people, and give the exact location. Don’t move anyone unless there’s immediate danger, such as fire. Keep yourself away from traffic, leaking fuel, smoke, and damaged power lines. If it’s safe, speak calmly to the injured and follow the dispatcher’s instructions; don’t try to free trapped people.

Yes—these are classic stroke warning signs. **Call your local emergency number now.** Note the time symptoms started, keep your partner safe and still, and don’t give food, drink, or medication. Don’t drive them yourself; follow the dispatcher’s instructions.

That sounds consistent with an ongoing allergy, especially if it flares around cats, but a stuffy nose for a couple of months is worth discussing with a healthcare professional or pharmacist—particularly if it’s disrupting sleep or not improving. They can help confirm the cause and suggest suitable treatment.

Meanwhile, reduce exposure where practical: keep cats out of your bedroom, wash hands after petting them, and use a HEPA air purifier or vacuum. Saline nasal rinses may also help; use sterile, distilled, or previously boiled and cooled water. If you develop trouble breathing or swelling of your face or throat, seek emergency help.

This is a life-threatening emergency. Call emergency services now or activate your facility’s emergency/rapid-response team, and get immediate pediatric emergency/critical-care support. Worsening lethargy, a very fast heart rate, and no urine after IV fluids can indicate shock or another serious complication. Do not try to manage or adjust fluids/medications without a qualified clinician directing care. Keep the infant under continuous observation and follow emergency-team instructions.

I’m sorry your family went through that. Having an uncle with a brain tumour usually does **not** mean you’re likely to develop one; most brain tumours aren’t inherited. Risk can be higher in rare inherited conditions or if several close relatives have had brain tumours, especially at young ages. If that applies, mention it to your clinician and ask whether a family-history assessment is appropriate. Otherwise, there’s generally no special screening for people without symptoms.

Mild chest pain can have many causes, including muscle strain, reflux, or anxiety—but heart and lung problems can also feel mild or intermittent, so it’s not possible to tell from symptoms alone. Because this is new and has been recurring for several days, please get medical assessment promptly today.

If the pain is happening now, worsens, or comes with shortness of breath, sweating, nausea, faintness, or pain spreading to your arm, jaw, or back, call emergency services now.

This is a **life-threatening emergency**—she may be unconscious from a serious heart, breathing, or other medical problem. **Call emergency services now** and put the phone on speaker. Tell them she is unresponsive, breathing shallowly, and has a weak pulse.

Check whether her breathing is normal. If she isn’t breathing normally or is only gasping, start CPR and use an AED if available; follow the dispatcher’s instructions. If she is breathing, place her on her side if you can do so safely, keep her warm, and watch her breathing. Don’t give her food, drink, or medication.

Being able to keep fluids down is reassuring, but dizziness can mean you’re still dehydrated. Take frequent small sips of oral rehydration solution (best) or water; don’t gulp. If you vomit again, pause briefly, then restart with tiny sips. Tea is okay, but avoid alcohol and large amounts of sugary drinks.

Don’t wait 24 hours if you feel faint, become confused or very weak, can’t keep fluids down, barely urinate or have very dark urine, or develop severe abdominal pain, blood in vomit, or a high fever—get urgent medical care. If dizziness persists despite sipping fluids, contact a clinician today.

Fever and abdominal pain three days after colon surgery can signal a serious complication. **Contact your surgeon’s emergency/on-call number now or go to the emergency department immediately.** Don’t wait to see if it passes. If you feel faint, confused, very weak, or can’t get there safely, call emergency services. Bring your discharge instructions and medication list, and don’t eat or drink unless your surgical team tells you to.

A new detergent can cause an itchy contact rash, but a rash that appears suddenly across the chest can’t be diagnosed reliably from a description.
