Stop using the new detergent and wash the area and recently washed clothing with a familiar, fragrance-free product. Avoid scratching; a cool compress may help.

Because she is 70 and the rash appeared overnight, contact a clinician today for advice, especially if it is spreading or worsening. Seek emergency care now if she has trouble breathing, swelling of the face or tongue, fever, severe pain, blisters, purple spots, confusion, or feels very unwell.

A bad cough with lightheadedness can have several causes, but it’s best to contact a healthcare professional today—especially if the lightheadedness is persistent or worsening. Sit or lie down, rise slowly, and sip fluids; don’t drive while lightheaded. Seek emergency care now if you’re struggling to breathe, have chest pain, faint, feel confused, or notice blue/gray lips.

Not standing or walking after several days of vomiting is a **danger sign**. He could be severely dehydrated or have another serious problem. **Please take him to an emergency department now**; call emergency services if he’s hard to wake, unusually weak, confused, or you can’t transport him safely.

While arranging help, don’t force him to stand or eat. If he’s fully awake and swallowing normally, offer tiny, frequent sips of oral rehydration solution. If he’s difficult to wake or can’t swallow safely, give nothing by mouth.

Yes—this could be serious. A headache that rapidly becomes much worse together with blurred vision needs urgent assessment. Stop what you’re doing and go to an emergency department now, or call your local emergency number. Don’t drive yourself; ask someone to stay with you and take you.

Treat this as an emergency: activate your hospital rapid-response/code team now and notify the attending/provider immediately. A saturation of 83% with new chest pain and breathing difficulty in sickle cell disease may be acute chest syndrome or another life-threatening problem.

Stay with the patient, assess airway and breathing, give oxygen and support per your unit’s emergency protocol, and continuously monitor vital signs and oxygen saturation. Bring emergency equipment and prepare for urgent evaluation and escalation of care. Don’t delay for a routine review.

This is an emergency. Call your local emergency number now and put the phone on speaker. Pale or blue color and ongoing coughing after choking can mean she isn’t getting enough oxygen, even if you can’t see food.

Keep her with you and follow the dispatcher’s instructions. If she becomes unable to breathe, cough, or cry, begin age-appropriate choking first aid/CPR if you know how, or let the dispatcher guide you. Don’t do a blind finger sweep or give food or drink. Don’t drive alone if emergency services can come.

A persistent cough with chest tightness and new wheezing can come from asthma or another airway irritation, a respiratory infection, or other causes. Because the wheezing is new and symptoms have lasted two weeks, please arrange prompt medical assessment today.

If you’re struggling to breathe, can’t speak full sentences, have blue/gray lips, severe chest pain, confusion, or rapidly worsening symptoms, stop what you’re doing and go to the emergency room or call emergency services now.

If you mean you have staples closing a cut on your scalp: keep the area clean and follow the discharge instructions. Don’t pull at the staples; avoid soaking the wound, and ask the clinic when they should be removed (often around 7–10 days). Seek urgent care for worsening redness or swelling, pus, fever, the wound opening, or a severe/worsening headache, vomiting, confusion, or unusual sleepiness.

Are you asking how to care for them, when they come out, or whether a scalp cut needs staples?

Ozempic (semaglutide) can help some people lose weight and improve blood sugar, but it’s a prescription medicine—not suitable for everyone, and it isn’t usually prescribed specifically for prediabetes. The right choice depends on your health history, current weight, and confirmed blood-sugar results.

Please don’t order it from an unverified online pharmacy: counterfeit or improperly stored injections can be dangerous. Arrange a clinician or pharmacist review to confirm your results and discuss approved options; lifestyle changes can also substantially lower the risk of type 2 diabetes. Common side effects include nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, and constipation.

Depakote (valproate) can be appropriate for some conditions, but whether it’s safe for you depends on your diagnosis, other medicines, and health history. Don’t start it, stop it, or change the dose without the prescriber’s guidance. It can cause serious liver or pancreas problems and major birth defects if taken during pregnancy. Was it prescribed to you, and what are you considering taking it for?

Gradual hearing loss over a year can have several causes, including earwax, noise exposure, or age-related changes. Please arrange a hearing test and an appointment with a clinician or audiologist soon; don’t try to remove wax with cotton swabs. In the meantime, keep headphone and TV volume at a comfortable level and use captions if helpful. Seek urgent care if hearing suddenly worsens, especially in one ear, or you develop severe dizziness, facial weakness, or other new neurological symptoms.

Sudden numbness and coldness in your hands and feet together with shortness of breath can be an emergency. **Stop what you’re doing and call your local emergency number now** (or have someone call); don’t drive yourself. Sit upright, keep warm, and loosen tight clothing while you wait. If you’re alone, unlock the door. Don’t wait to see whether home remedies help.

I’m sorry you’re dealing with this. Neck stiffness and mild headaches can occur after a collision, but because symptoms have persisted for two days, don’t wait two weeks: seek **same-day advice** from your GP practice or NHS 111. An advanced nurse practitioner can assess you; a GP isn’t necessarily required. They can advise whether you need an examination or further care.

Until assessed, keep movements gentle and don’t force stretches or manipulate your neck. Follow ibuprofen packet directions and avoid it if you’ve been told not to take anti-inflammatory medicines.

**Call 999 or go to A&E now** for a severe or worsening headache, repeated vomiting, confusion, unusual drowsiness, fainting, weakness or numbness, problems walking or speaking, vision changes, or loss of bladder/bowel control. If symptoms worsen, get urgent help.

Unintentional weight loss over a month is worth taking seriously, even if stress could be contributing. Please arrange a medical assessment soon, especially if the loss is continuing or more than about 5% of your body weight. Keep track of your weight, appetite, stress, and any other symptoms, and try to eat and drink regularly.

If you’re losing weight rapidly or have severe weakness, fainting, persistent vomiting, blood in your stool, or trouble breathing, seek urgent care.

For a mild toothache with no swelling or fever, arrange a dental appointment soon—especially if it lasts more than a day or two or keeps returning. Until then, rinse with warm salt water, gently floss around the tooth, and use a cold pack on your cheek. You can take an over-the-counter pain reliever if it’s normally safe for you; follow the label. Avoid placing aspirin directly on the tooth.

Get urgent dental care if pain becomes severe or you develop facial swelling, fever, trouble swallowing, or trouble breathing.

Occasional trouble hearing can be related to normal age-related hearing loss, but it may also come from earwax, infection, medication effects, or other treatable causes. If it’s happening repeatedly or affecting conversations, a hearing test and ear check can clarify what’s going on. Sudden hearing loss—especially in one ear—or hearing trouble with severe dizziness, facial weakness, or a bad headache needs urgent medical attention.

This is an emergency: activate the clinic’s emergency response/EMS now and get an airway-skilled clinician to the bedside. Don’t wait for improvement. Check airway, mask seal, oxygen supply, and chest rise; use 100% oxygen and suction, and follow your clinic’s resuscitation protocol. If there’s no normal breathing or pulse, start CPR and use an AED. Intubation and sedation should be performed only by qualified clinicians with appropriate monitoring and backup.

That sounds frustrating, especially after a good breakfast. If it was a small bite and the bleeding has stopped, it’s usually minor and by itself doesn’t generally warrant a doctor’s note. Rinse gently with cool water, and try soft foods; avoid spicy or acidic foods for now. Whether to call out depends on how uncomfortable you feel and your workplace’s policy.

If bleeding starts again and won’t stop with steady pressure, the wound looks deep, or you develop significant swelling or trouble swallowing or breathing, get urgent medical care.

Sudden dizziness and blurred vision followed by a headache and feeling “off” can be serious. **Stop what you’re doing, sit or lie down somewhere safe, and get emergency medical help now**—call your local emergency number or have someone take you to the ER. Don’t drive yourself. Ask someone to stay with you, and note when the symptoms began. If you develop weakness or numbness, trouble speaking, confusion, fainting, worsening headache, or vision changes, tell emergency services immediately.

Yes—this is a life-threatening choking emergency. Call your local emergency number now and put the phone on speaker.

If she’s conscious and can’t breathe, speak, or cough effectively:
- Give 5 firm back blows between her shoulder blades.
- If that doesn’t clear it, give 5 abdominal thrusts: stand behind her, place a fist just above her navel, grasp it, and pull sharply inward and upward.
- Repeat 5 back blows and 5 thrusts until it clears or help arrives.

If she becomes unresponsive, lower her to the floor and begin CPR; follow the dispatcher’s instructions. Don’t put your fingers in her mouth unless you can clearly see and remove the food.

This is a life-threatening emergency and could be a serious spinal cord injury. Call emergency services now—don’t wait to see if it improves. **Do not move him, lift him, or let him try to stand.** Keep his head and neck still in the position found, and follow the dispatcher’s instructions. Watch his breathing and consciousness; if either changes, tell the dispatcher immediately. No visible bleeding does not make this safe.

These symptoms after a head impact—especially clear fluid leaking from one ear, hearing loss, and double vision—may indicate a serious skull or brain injury and possible fluid leakage. **Call emergency services now or go to the emergency department immediately. Do not drive yourself.** Keep your head and neck still, don’t put anything in the ear or try to stop the leak, and have someone stay with you. Tell responders when and how the injury happened and when symptoms began.

Yes—call emergency services now. Severe shortness of breath with bluish lips can mean dangerously low oxygen. Have your cousin sit upright, stay with them, and keep them as calm and still as possible. Don’t have them walk or drive themselves. Follow the dispatcher’s instructions.

For a typical insect bite, wash the area with soap and water, apply a cool compress for 10–15 minutes, and avoid scratching. For itch, you could try calamine or an over-the-counter antihistamine, following the label.

Seek urgent help if you have trouble breathing, swelling of the lips or tongue, faintness, or rapidly spreading swelling. Have it checked if redness or pain keeps worsening, pus or fever develops, or you notice a bull’s-eye rash.

For mild, stable dryness, preservative-free artificial tears are generally fine to keep using as needed, including at night; a lubricating eye gel or ointment may last longer overnight but can blur vision. Avoid “redness relief” drops, and follow the label.

Since it has lasted six months, arrange a routine eye exam to check for causes and confirm the drops are suitable. Seek urgent care for eye pain, sudden vision changes, marked redness, light sensitivity, or discharge.

Call emergency services now. Postpartum fainting with severe chest pain and not waking is life-threatening.

Put the phone on speaker. Check whether she is breathing normally:
- If not, or only gasping, start CPR and follow the dispatcher’s instructions; use an AED if available.
- If she is breathing, lay her flat, keep her still, and turn her onto her side if she vomits. Loosen tight clothing.
- Don’t give food, drink, or medication, and don’t drive her yourself.

Stay with her and tell the dispatcher she recently gave birth, fainted, is unresponsive, and has severe chest pain.

Sudden double vision with extreme unsteadiness and inability to walk can signal a stroke or another emergency. **Call emergency services now** (911/999/112, depending on your location). Don’t drive or try to walk—sit or lie somewhere safe, and ask someone to stay with you. Note when you were last feeling normal.

I’m sorry your toddler is dealing with this. Offer frequent small sips of oral rehydration solution; continue breastfeeding or usual milk and food as tolerated. Avoid juice, soda, and anti-diarrhea medicines. Watch for dehydration: much less urine or no wet diaper for 8 hours, dry mouth, no tears, unusual sleepiness, or sunken eyes. If any appear, seek urgent medical care. Because the watery stools have lasted 2 days, contact your child’s pediatrician today for guidance, especially if they’re very young or stools are frequent.

I’m glad your anxiety has eased. Don’t stop 225 mg venlafaxine suddenly—it can cause significant withdrawal symptoms. Ask your prescriber or pharmacist about a gradual taper and lower-cost options; improvement in summer doesn’t necessarily mean the anxiety won’t return.

For a therapist near the Danforth, try the **Psychology Today Canada** directory (filter for anxiety and your preferred area), or search **Affordable Therapy Network** for lower-fee options. You can also ask your family doctor for local referrals. Check that the therapist is registered with an Ontario college, and ask about fees, wait times, and experience treating anxiety.

A low fever for 7 days should be assessed by a healthcare professional soon, even without a cough or rash. Please arrange an appointment today or within 24 hours. Drink fluids and rest; note your temperature and any new symptoms. Seek urgent care now if you develop trouble breathing, confusion, severe weakness, chest pain, a stiff neck, or feel rapidly worse.

Yes—sudden, severe headaches with blurred vision in one eye are concerning and need urgent assessment. Please stop what you’re doing and go to an emergency department now, or call your local emergency number—especially if this is the worst or a new kind of headache. Don’t drive yourself; ask someone to take you.

A swollen tongue with trouble swallowing and abnormal breathing can be a life-threatening emergency. **Call emergency services now** (911/999/112 or your local number). Don’t drive yourself. If you have an epinephrine auto-injector, use it now as directed. Sit upright, don’t eat or drink, and have someone stay with you.

This is an emergency. Sudden confusion, inability to stand, and fruity-smelling breath in someone with diabetes can signal diabetic ketoacidosis or another life-threatening problem. Call emergency services now; don’t let her walk or drive. Stay with her, follow the dispatcher’s instructions, and tell them she has diabetes and these symptoms. Don’t delay to check or treat this yourself.

Lightheadedness with intermittent blurred vision isn’t something to dismiss as “normal.” Please arrange prompt medical assessment today, especially since it’s been happening for several days. Until then, sit or lie down when it occurs, avoid driving, and drink water if you can.

If you suddenly lose vision, faint, develop severe headache, weakness or numbness on one side, trouble speaking, chest pain, or difficulty breathing, seek emergency care right away.

This is **life-threatening postpartum hemorrhage with hemorrhagic shock**—ongoing blood loss is causing critically inadequate circulation and oxygen delivery. A BP of 80/40, pulse 150, pallor, and confusion despite treatment mean she is deteriorating rapidly.

**Activate your emergency response now:** call the nearest referral/tertiary center and arrange immediate transfer with a clinician and resuscitation support; alert anesthesia, surgery, and the blood bank. Continue your hospital’s postpartum-hemorrhage/massive-transfusion protocol and urgently identify and control the bleeding source. Do not delay escalation while waiting for more medication or blood.

Sit or lie down somewhere safe, get up slowly, and drink water. Avoid driving, alcohol, and strenuous activity; if you have diabetes, check your blood sugar. Dizziness all day deserves prompt medical assessment today—especially if it’s new or worsening.

Call emergency services now for fainting, chest pain, trouble breathing, a severe headache, confusion, trouble speaking or walking, weakness or numbness on one side, or sudden vision changes.

A sudden severe pain spreading down your leg, inability to move or bear weight, and feeling close to fainting are warning signs. **Please get emergency medical care now**—call your local emergency number or have someone take you to an ER; don’t drive yourself. Stay somewhere safe and avoid trying to walk or stretch the leg. This could have several causes, and it isn’t possible to identify safely without an urgent examination.

Call emergency services now. Your friend is unconscious and needs urgent help. Check whether they’re breathing normally. If not, start CPR and use an AED if available; follow the dispatcher’s instructions. If they are breathing, place them on their side and keep their airway clear. Don’t give them food or drink, and stay with them until help arrives.

Even though the symptoms have gone, sudden trouble speaking and weakness in one arm can be signs of a TIA or stroke. **Call emergency services now or go to the emergency department immediately**—don’t drive yourself. Symptoms that resolve still need urgent assessment. Note when they began and ended, and tell responders. Avoid eating or drinking until you’ve been assessed.

This may be severe alcohol withdrawal, including a seizure and hallucinations. **Call emergency services now** (911/999/112, depending on where you are) or have someone take you to the ER—do not drive or stay alone. Tell them how much you usually drink, when you last drank, and that you may have had a seizure. While waiting, have someone stay with you; if another seizure happens, they should protect you from injury, turn you onto your side, and put nothing in your mouth. Don’t try to manage this by drinking alcohol or taking sedatives.

This is an emergency. Call your local emergency number now. Have him lie down, and press a clean cloth or dressing firmly over the wound—don’t lift it to check. If blood soaks through, add more cloth on top and keep pressing. If something is embedded, don’t remove it; press around it. Keep him warm and still. If he becomes unresponsive or has trouble breathing, tell the dispatcher immediately and follow their instructions.

Intermittent tingling in one arm can happen when a nerve is temporarily compressed—for example, from posture or leaning on the arm. It can also come from irritation in the neck, repetitive strain, or other causes. Notice when it occurs and whether changing position helps.

If it keeps recurring, worsens, or comes with weakness or pain, arrange a medical assessment. **Seek emergency help now** if it starts suddenly with facial drooping, trouble speaking, severe weakness, chest pain, or shortness of breath.

Stomach pain and occasional diarrhea can come from infections, food intolerance, medication effects, or other bowel conditions. Blood in stool can sometimes be from a small tear or hemorrhoid, but it should not be ignored—please arrange prompt medical assessment, even if it happened only once.

Seek emergency care now if bleeding is heavy or recurring, stool is black/tarry, pain is severe or worsening, or you feel faint, weak, feverish, or can’t keep fluids down. In the meantime, drink fluids and note what you eat, your symptoms, and any medicines you take.

Nausea can be a common side effect of some pain medicines, especially opioids, and may also be worse if you take them on an empty stomach. It isn’t always dangerous, but the specific medicine and procedure matter. Check the medication leaflet and contact your pharmacist or care team for advice; don’t stop or change a prescribed dose without checking. Seek urgent help if you have trouble breathing, are unusually hard to wake, faint, develop severe abdominal pain, or can’t keep fluids down. What painkiller are you taking, and when does the nausea start?

I’m sorry—this needs prompt attention. **Don’t try to reinsert the catheter** or put anything into the urethra. Call the home-care service’s on-call number or her doctor’s urgent line now; if you can’t reach them, contact urgent care/ER for advice, especially if she normally cannot urinate without the catheter.

Until help arrives:
- Keep her clean and dry; gently wash and pat dry, change absorbent pads/briefs, and protect the skin with barrier cream if available.
- Offer her usual fluids unless she has a fluid restriction.
- Save the catheter and note when it came out, if it’s intact, and whether she has passed urine.

**Go to emergency care now** for lower-belly pain/swelling, inability to pass urine, fever/chills, blood or clots, confusion, severe weakness, or marked distress.

It depends on the insulin type: some (such as NPH or premixed insulin) are meant to look cloudy; others should be clear. Don’t use it if it’s cloudy when it should be clear, has clumps or particles, looks unusual, or was frozen or overheated. Check the label and storage instructions, and ask your pharmacist before using it if you’re unsure. Don’t skip a needed dose—contact your care team promptly for advice or a replacement.

A brief episode of lightheadedness that resolved after sitting, with no other symptoms, often isn’t an emergency. Drink some water, eat if you’ve skipped a meal, and stand up slowly. If it happens again, arrange medical advice to look for a cause.

Seek emergency care now if you develop chest pain, trouble breathing, fainting, a severe headache, confusion, weakness or numbness on one side, or difficulty speaking.

This is an emergency. Call emergency services now, or have someone take them to the ER—don’t let them drive. While help is coming, press firmly and continuously on the bleeding site with clean gauze; don’t lift it to check. If it soaks through, add more gauze on top. Have them lie down and stay warm. Follow any specific post-op emergency instructions, but don’t delay getting help.

If the bleeding stops with firm, continuous pressure within 10–15 minutes and you feel well, it usually isn’t an emergency. Monthly nosebleeds are worth arranging a routine appointment with your primary-care clinician or ENT to look for causes, especially if they’re becoming more frequent.

For a bleed, sit upright, lean forward, and pinch the soft part of your nose without checking for 10–15 minutes. Seek urgent care now if it won’t stop after 20 minutes of firm pressure, is very heavy, follows an injury, or you feel faint, weak, or short of breath.

This is an emergency. Sudden severe headache, blurred vision, and one-sided arm numbness 5 days after giving birth can signal a stroke or a dangerous postpartum complication. **Call emergency services now** or have someone take you to the ER—don’t drive yourself. Tell them you’re 5 days postpartum and when the symptoms began. Ask someone to stay with you and unlock the door while help is on the way.

Don’t double the dose. Since it’s almost time for today’s dose, skip yesterday’s missed dose and give only today’s usual dose—unless his anticoagulation clinic or pharmacist has told him otherwise. Call his Coumadin clinic or pharmacist today for advice, especially if his INR has been unstable. Don’t take him to urgent care just for one missed dose unless he has symptoms or was specifically advised to go.

If he has unusual bleeding, a severe headache, confusion, weakness, a fall/head injury, or blood in his urine or stool, seek emergency care now.

A new dark mole should be checked by a clinician or dermatologist before removal, since it’s important to identify what it is first. Don’t cut, burn, or use home-removal products on it; these can cause infection, scarring, and delay diagnosis. Arrange an appointment soon, and take a clear photo with a ruler beside it to track changes. Seek urgent assessment if it’s rapidly changing, uneven, bleeding, itching, or has irregular edges or multiple colors.

This is a **life-threatening emergency**. Very high glucose, rapid breathing, confusion, low blood pressure, and reduced responsiveness are consistent with severe DKA and shock; cerebral edema is also possible, but only the treating team can determine the cause. **Activate the hospital’s emergency/rapid-response team now** (or call emergency services if outside a hospital). He needs immediate resuscitation and intensive medical care—do not wait for an explanation or try to manage this yourself.

A 104°F fever with a stiff neck and confusion can signal a life-threatening emergency, such as meningitis. **Call emergency services now or go to the emergency department immediately.** Don’t wait to see if it improves, and don’t drive yourself if emergency transport is available.

A doctor will rapidly assess your child’s breathing, circulation, alertness, and vital signs; examine them; and may do blood tests, cultures, and a spinal-fluid test. They may start urgent IV treatment before all results are back. Keep your child with you and follow the dispatcher’s instructions.

With no major swelling or instability, a few days of relative rest is reasonable: avoid painful activities, elevate it, and use a wrapped cold pack for 15–20 minutes at a time. Gentle ankle movement is fine if it doesn’t worsen the ache; return to activity gradually.

Because it’s sore again months after a sprain, arrange a non-urgent check with a clinician or physiotherapist if it doesn’t improve over several days, keeps recurring, or limits walking. Seek prompt care if you can’t bear weight, develop marked swelling, redness or warmth, numbness, or rapidly worsening pain.

This is life-threatening hemorrhage and possible shock. **Do not stitch or remove anything embedded. Call emergency services now** and arrange immediate transfer to a hospital—don’t have him walk or drive himself.

While help is coming: have him lie flat and keep him warm. Apply firm, continuous pressure with sterile gauze or clean cloth; don’t lift it to check. If blood soaks through, add more material on top. If bowel or organs are visible, **don’t push them in or press directly**—loosely cover with a clean dressing moistened with sterile saline. Monitor breathing and responsiveness; be ready to start CPR if needed. Give nothing to eat or drink.

Yes—this is very concerning. Severe abdominal pain, heavy bleeding with large clots, and lightheadedness one week after giving birth can signal a serious postpartum complication or blood loss. **Please get emergency medical care now**—call emergency services or have someone take you to the ER; don’t drive yourself. Tell them you’re one week postpartum and describe the bleeding, clots, pain, and lightheadedness. If possible, have someone stay with you while help is arranged. I’m not your physician and can’t diagnose you here, but this needs urgent assessment.

Call emergency services now. Blue lips and trouble staying awake can mean dangerously low oxygen—this is life-threatening. Put the call on speaker and follow the dispatcher’s instructions.

- If he’s unresponsive or not breathing normally, start CPR and use an AED if available.
- If he’s breathing, place him on his side and stay with him; keep his airway clear.
- Give naloxone if available, especially if opioids may also be involved. Repeat after 2–3 minutes if there’s no response, following the package directions.
- Don’t make him vomit, give food or drink, or leave him alone. Xylazine itself isn’t reversed by naloxone, but emergency care is still essential.

Heavy bleeding with extreme paleness and dizziness after birth can signal a life-threatening emergency. **Call emergency services now** (911/999/112, as applicable)—do not try to manage this at home or drive yourself. Tell them you recently gave birth, are bleeding heavily, pale, and dizzy.

While waiting:
- Lie flat and keep warm; raise your legs if comfortable.
- Have someone stay with you and unlock the door.
- Use a pad to track bleeding; don’t insert anything into the vagina.
- If you feel faint, don’t stand or walk.

Follow the dispatcher’s instructions.

A high fever with a stiff neck can be a medical emergency, including meningitis. Call emergency services or go to the emergency department now—don’t wait to see if it passes. Keep the person resting and comfortable, and don’t force their neck to move. If they’re confused, very drowsy, hard to wake, having seizures, or developing a rash, call emergency services immediately.

Call emergency services now—this could be an overdose. Don’t give him anything to eat or drink, and don’t try to make him vomit.

Check if he’s breathing normally. If not, start CPR and follow the dispatcher’s instructions. If he is breathing, place him on his side and stay with him. Give naloxone if available; it can help with an opioid overdose and won’t harm him if opioids aren’t involved. Tell responders what he may have taken, and keep any packaging.

HDL is only one part of your cholesterol picture; overall cardiovascular risk depends on LDL, triglycerides, and other factors too. Lifestyle changes that support a healthier HDL and heart include:

- Regular aerobic activity and strength training
- Not smoking; avoiding secondhand smoke
- Choosing unsaturated fats (olive oil, nuts, seeds, avocado, and oily fish) instead of trans fats and limiting saturated fats
- Eating more vegetables, whole grains, and legumes
- Maintaining a weight that’s healthy for you

There’s usually no need to target HDL with medication alone, and raising HDL doesn’t necessarily reduce risk. Since your LDL is high, ask your healthcare professional to review your full lipid results and personal risk factors.

As the hospice nurse, assess the patient now: check breathing effort, comfort, oxygen level if available, and follow their hospice care plan. Raise the head of the bed, loosen tight clothing, keep the room calm, and use prescribed oxygen or comfort medicines only as directed. Contact the hospice nurse/physician on call promptly for a new or worsening breathing rate, or if the patient seems distressed; they can guide symptom relief in line with the patient’s goals of care. If there is severe distress and you cannot reach hospice, seek urgent help.

Yellowing of the skin can be jaundice, which may signal a liver or other health problem—especially if the whites of their eyes are yellow too. Please encourage your cousin to get medical advice today. If they’re confused, very drowsy, in severe pain, vomiting blood, or rapidly getting worse, seek emergency care now.

This is a life-threatening emergency—worsening confusion and blood pressure of 80/50 can indicate shock. **Call emergency services now** and say he may be in shock. Don’t wait or try to manage this at home.

While help is coming, keep him lying flat and warm; raise his legs slightly if this doesn’t worsen breathing or cause pain. If he’s vomiting or drowsy, turn him onto his side. Don’t give food, drink, or medication while confused or actively vomiting. Monitor breathing and responsiveness; if he becomes unresponsive and isn’t breathing normally, start CPR and follow the dispatcher’s instructions.

This is a life-threatening emergency. **Call your local emergency number now** and put the phone on speaker; tell them she collapsed, is unresponsive, and breathing abnormally. Don’t wait.

- Lay her flat and check whether she’s breathing normally.
- If she’s not breathing normally or only gasping, start chest compressions: hard and fast in the center of her chest (100–120/min). Use an AED if available and follow its prompts.
- If she is breathing normally, place her on her side and keep her airway clear.
- Don’t give food, drink, or medication. Stay with her and follow the dispatcher’s instructions.

Yes—this is concerning. New dizziness with weakness in both arms and legs can signal a serious problem, including a stroke. Call emergency services now or take her to the emergency department; don’t wait to see if it passes, and don’t let her drive. Note when the symptoms began and tell the responders. If she becomes confused, has trouble speaking or walking, develops facial drooping, chest pain, or trouble breathing, treat it as an emergency.

Blue lips can mean he isn’t getting enough oxygen, even if he seems well. **Take him to the emergency room now**—don’t wait for your regular doctor. If his lips are still blue, or he has trouble breathing, becomes unusually sleepy, or worsens, call emergency services. Keep him calm and warm while you get help.

For a small thigh bruise, rest the area and apply a cold pack wrapped in cloth for 15–20 minutes at a time during the first day or two. Don’t put ice directly on your skin. Keep the leg comfortable; gentle movement is fine if it doesn’t hurt. After 48 hours, a warm compress may feel soothing. The bruise should gradually fade over 1–2 weeks. Avoid massaging it, and use pain relief only if it’s normally safe for you. If it becomes unusually large or very painful, or you develop significant swelling, numbness, or trouble walking, get medical advice.

From what you’ve described, there’s no obvious emergency warning sign—no confusion, severe headache, or dizziness. But I can’t reliably estimate percentages or diagnose the cause from this information. Two weeks of new daytime fatigue and reduced motivation can have many explanations, including sleep quality, stress, infection, or medical issues such as anemia or thyroid problems.

Arrange a routine medical assessment if it continues, worsens, or affects daily life. Seek urgent care for new confusion, fainting, chest pain, trouble breathing, severe weakness, or thoughts of harming yourself.

A growing abdomen in someone with liver disease may be fluid buildup (ascites). It can keep increasing, and difficulty moving means he needs prompt medical assessment—please contact his liver team or seek urgent care today. Don’t try to drain it or change his medicines or salt/fluid intake without their guidance.

If he has trouble breathing, fever, severe belly pain, confusion, vomiting blood, or black stools, go to the emergency department now.

A sudden facial droop and drooling could be a stroke, and it’s not possible to distinguish that safely from other causes here. **Call your local emergency number now** and say you may be having a stroke. Don’t drive yourself; note when you were last well. Don’t eat or drink until assessed. Even if it improves, get emergency care immediately.

This could be preterm labor or another serious emergency. Call your local emergency number now and tell them she is 7 months pregnant, having strong contractions, severe pain, and difficulty breathing. Don’t wait or drive her yourself if an ambulance is available. Keep her resting on her side, stay with her, and follow the dispatcher’s instructions.

This is a life-threatening emergency, not a routine clinic reaction. **Call emergency services now** and activate the clinic’s emergency response. Severe tongue swelling with noisy, labored breathing after eating suggests anaphylaxis with threatened airway.

If available, give **intramuscular epinephrine immediately** into the outer mid-thigh according to the child’s weight and local protocol; repeat in 5–15 minutes if symptoms persist. Keep the child lying flat (or in the position that best supports breathing), give oxygen if available, and prepare for airway support. Do not give food or drink, and do not delay epinephrine for antihistamines. Continue urgent monitoring and transfer to the emergency department.

Cold sensitivity lasting a few months is worth having a dentist check—common causes include a cavity, a small crack, or gum recession. Book a dental appointment soon, especially if it’s worsening or focused on one tooth.

Until then, try toothpaste for sensitive teeth twice daily (spit, don’t rinse), use a soft toothbrush, and avoid very cold or acidic foods. Don’t put aspirin or other products directly on the tooth.

Seek urgent dental care if you develop swelling, fever, severe or lingering pain, or trouble swallowing or breathing.

This is an emergency. Slurred speech and drifting in and out of consciousness after prolonged hot-tub exposure could signal dangerous overheating or another serious problem. **Call emergency services now**—don’t wait for them to pass out.

Get them out of the heat, lay them somewhere cool, and stay with them. If they’re unconscious or very drowsy, don’t give food or drink; place them on their side if you can do so safely. Cool them with damp cloths and airflow, and follow the dispatcher’s instructions.

Don’t pour water into your ear—this can make some insects swell or worsen irritation, especially if you have an eardrum problem or ear tubes.

Tilt your head so the left ear faces upward and gently pull the outer ear back; you can try a few drops of warm (not hot) mineral or baby oil to stop the insect moving, then tilt the ear downward. Don’t insert fingers, cotton buds, or tools. If it doesn’t come out promptly, or you have pain, bleeding, dizziness, or reduced hearing, get urgent medical care for safe removal.

An itchy throat and rash after eating can be signs of a food allergy. Stop eating the suspected food, and avoid it until you’ve been assessed. Keep a note of what you ate and when symptoms began.

If you develop trouble breathing or swallowing, throat/tongue swelling, dizziness, or rapidly worsening symptoms, use an epinephrine auto-injector if you have one and call emergency services now. Even if symptoms settle, arrange prompt medical advice to identify the cause and discuss a safety plan.

This is a life-threatening emergency and could be thyroid storm. **Call emergency services now** and say she has hyperthyroidism, heart rate over 180, fever above 40°C, and rapidly worsening condition. Do not drive her yourself if an ambulance is available. Keep her with someone, lying or seated safely; don’t give food, drink, or extra medication unless emergency dispatch or a clinician instructs you. Follow the dispatcher’s directions and be ready to report her medications and when symptoms began.

Wash the scratch thoroughly with soap and running water for 15 minutes, then apply an antiseptic and keep it clean and covered. Don’t use harsh chemicals inside the wound.

A vaccinated dog makes rabies unlikely, but vaccination doesn’t rule out every risk. Contact a healthcare professional or local public-health service today to check whether rabies assessment or a tetanus booster is needed—especially if the dog’s vaccination is overdue, its status is uncertain, or it becomes ill. Seek prompt care for spreading redness, warmth, swelling, worsening pain, pus, fever, or red streaks.

I’m not a pediatric ENT, but enlarged tonsils without pain, fever, or difficulty breathing or swallowing are often monitored rather than treated urgently.

- **Observe:** Note whether the tonsils seem to be growing and whether your child snores, has pauses or gasps during sleep, restless sleep, daytime tiredness, recurrent throat infections, or changes in speech.
- **Arrange a routine pediatric checkup** to confirm the cause and discuss whether monitoring or an ENT assessment is appropriate, especially if the enlargement persists or is uneven.
- **Don’t give antibiotics or try to shrink/remove the tonsils** unless a clinician recommends it.
- **Seek urgent care immediately** if breathing or swallowing becomes difficult, your child drools because they can’t swallow, or develops rapidly worsening swelling.

I’m so sorry—you’re right to be scared. Fever, new confusion, and a racing heart after a cut can signal a life-threatening infection. **Call your local emergency number now** and tell them these symptoms; don’t wait or drive her yourself if an ambulance is available. Keep her with you, monitor her breathing, and follow the dispatcher’s instructions. Don’t give her food or drink if she’s very confused or drowsy.

New numbness around the genitals together with back pain and difficulty walking can signal serious pressure on nerves in the lower spine. Please go to an emergency department now—don’t wait or try exercises. If you can’t get there safely, call emergency services.

Mild dizziness after prolonged reading can come from eye strain or an outdated glasses prescription, screen/lighting issues, neck posture, or less commonly other causes. Try taking a brief break every 20 minutes, looking into the distance, improving lighting, and keeping your neck relaxed. If it continues, arrange an eye check or routine medical assessment, especially since it has lasted a week.

Seek urgent help if you develop severe or sudden dizziness, fainting, trouble walking, weakness or numbness, confusion, vision loss, chest pain, or a severe headache.

Vomiting blood can be a serious warning sign, even if it’s just a streak. **Please stop and get emergency medical care now**—call your local emergency number or have someone take you to the ER; don’t drive yourself if you feel weak or dizzy.

While arranging help, don’t eat or drink for now, since you may need urgent treatment. If your mouth is very dry, you can rinse and spit. Tell responders about the blood and your day of vomiting and diarrhea.

No—don’t try to sleep this off. New, severe squeezing chest tightness can be a medical emergency, even if anxiety is possible. Call emergency services now, or have someone call for you; don’t drive yourself. Sit and rest while waiting, and tell the dispatcher if you’re short of breath, sweaty, nauseated, dizzy, or the pain spreads to your arm, jaw, or back.

Getting breathless on stairs for several weeks is worth arranging a medical check-up soon, even if you recover quickly. Until then, take stairs slowly and avoid pushing through worsening symptoms.

If you develop breathlessness at rest, chest pain or pressure, fainting, blue lips, or severe sudden worsening, seek emergency care now.

A brief wave of warmth and a metallic taste are common, temporary effects of injected CT contrast. Since they faded and your vital signs were stable, they’re less suggestive of a serious reaction. Let the imaging staff know before you leave, and follow any instructions they gave you.

Get emergency help now if you develop trouble breathing, swelling of your face or throat, widespread hives, fainting, or rapidly worsening symptoms. If symptoms persist or new concerns appear, contact the imaging center or your healthcare team.

**Move him to advanced care now—call for emergency transport and notify the receiving facility.** Ongoing shock and confusion after a compound fracture can be life-threatening. Don’t delay for more field treatments or try to “fix” the fracture.

While arranging transport:

- Control severe bleeding with firm direct pressure around the wound; don’t push bone back in or apply a tight tourniquet unless bleeding is immediately life-threatening and you’re trained to use one.
- Check breathing and responsiveness continuously; be ready to provide CPR if needed.
- Give nothing by mouth. Avoid further IV fluid boluses unless you’re trained and local protocols direct them; saline may not stop internal blood loss.
- If possible, send someone with him and share fluids given, observations, and timing.

You can pray with him or for him if welcome—but let that accompany, never postpone, urgent transport.

Brief twitches or shivers during sleep can be normal in babies, but I can’t tell from a description whether these are seizures. If possible, record a short video and note how long it lasts and whether she responds when gently roused; contact her pediatrician promptly to discuss the new change.

Call emergency services now if an episode lasts 5 minutes or more, repeats without her returning to normal, or she has trouble breathing, turns blue, is unusually difficult to wake, or has rhythmic jerking while awake. Don’t restrain her or put anything in her mouth.

Yes—this could be immediately life-threatening, such as a heart attack or stroke. Call your local emergency number **now** and say he has severe chest pain, slurred speech, and reduced responsiveness. Don’t drive him yourself or wait to see if it passes.

Keep him still and supported; note when symptoms began. If he becomes unresponsive and isn’t breathing normally, start CPR and use an AED if available. Don’t give food, drink, or medication unless emergency dispatch advises it.

Mild cramps after takeout can happen from indigestion or a food-related upset, and often settle within a day or two. Sip fluids, rest, and eat lightly; avoid greasy or spicy foods for now.

Get urgent medical help if the pain is severe or worsening, your belly is rigid, you have blood in vomit or stool, repeated vomiting, fainting, or a high fever. If symptoms persist beyond a couple of days or others who ate the same food are ill, contact a healthcare professional.

For a mild, familiar headache, drink water, eat if you’ve skipped a meal, rest somewhere quiet, and try a cool cloth. You may use an over-the-counter pain reliever if it’s normally safe for you; follow the label.

Get emergency help now if it began suddenly and severely, or comes with weakness, numbness, confusion, fainting, vision or speech problems, fever with a stiff neck, or followed a head injury. If it’s new, worsening, recurring, or not improving, contact a healthcare professional.

A sudden droopy face can be a sign of a stroke. Call emergency services now—don’t wait or drive them yourself. Note when the symptoms began, keep them safe, and don’t give food, drink, or medication. Even if it improves, they need urgent assessment.

Call emergency services now. Apply firm, continuous pressure directly on the wound with clean cloth or gauze—don’t lift it to check. If blood soaks through, add more cloth on top. Keep him lying down and still; raise the arm if you can without worsening pain. If something is embedded, don’t remove it—press around it. Keep him warm, and don’t give food or drink.

This is an emergency. Call your local emergency number now—severe abdominal pain with fainting, pale appearance, and reduced responsiveness can be life-threatening. Don’t wait to see if it passes or drive her yourself if an ambulance is available.

While help is coming:
- Check whether she is breathing normally; follow the dispatcher’s instructions.
- If she’s breathing, keep her lying still and warm. If she vomits or is very drowsy, roll her onto her side.
- Don’t give food, drink, or medication.
- Stay with her and tell responders when this began and any medicines or conditions you know about.

Blood in your urine needs prompt medical assessment, even if it’s only a little or you feel otherwise well. Please contact a clinician today; if you can’t get prompt care, go to urgent care or the emergency department. Seek emergency care now if you have clots, trouble passing urine, severe pain, fever, dizziness, or feel very unwell. Possible causes include infection, stones, or other urinary problems, but testing is needed to find out.

Worsening vision at 65 can have several causes, and eye drops can’t reliably fix it without knowing why. Please arrange an eye exam soon with an optometrist or ophthalmologist; don’t start medicated drops (especially steroid or “redness relief” drops) unless advised. Preservative-free artificial tears may ease dryness or irritation, but they won’t treat vision loss.

If the change was sudden, or you have eye pain, flashes/floaters, a curtain or shadow, severe redness, or sudden loss of vision, seek emergency eye care now.

This is an emergency. **Call your local emergency number or get him to the nearest emergency department now.** Being hard to wake, confused, trembling, and unable to speak normally can signal a life-threatening problem. Don’t wait to see if prayer or herbs help—prayer can accompany getting urgent care.

Stay with him; note when this began. If he’s drowsy or unconscious but breathing, place him on his side. Don’t give food, drink, or herbs, and don’t put anything in his ear. If he stops breathing normally, begin CPR if you can and get emergency help.

I understand the cost is frightening, but delaying could be far more dangerous. Ask a neighbor, community leader, or faith community for immediate transport or help with costs.

Yes—dry air can dry and crack the delicate lining inside your nose, causing nosebleeds. Try a saline spray or gel, a humidifier, and avoid picking or blowing your nose forcefully.

If a bleed happens, sit leaning forward and pinch the soft part of your nose continuously for 10–15 minutes. Since you’ve had a few recently, get medical advice if they keep recurring, are heavy, or don’t stop after 20 minutes of firm pressure.

This is an emergency. Call your local emergency number now and put the phone on speaker. Your child’s limpness, lack of movement, and unresponsiveness need immediate assessment.

Check whether they’re breathing normally. If not, start CPR if you can and follow the dispatcher’s instructions. If they are breathing, keep them still and lying safely; don’t give food, drink, or medicine. Stay with them and tell the dispatcher when this started and any possible injury or illness.

This is a **life-threatening emergency**—repeated seizures after delivery with falling vital signs may be postpartum eclampsia or another critical condition. **Activate emergency services and the hospital’s obstetric/rapid-response team now. Do not wait or attempt home treatment.**

While help arrives: protect her from injury, clear nearby objects, cushion her head, and turn her onto her side when possible. Do not restrain her or put anything in her mouth. Note seizure duration and monitor breathing; if she is not breathing normally, begin CPR if trained. Give nothing by mouth. In hospital, clinicians need to stabilize airway/breathing/circulation and urgently treat the cause, often with IV magnesium sulfate and blood-pressure management.

Do you mean clearing your throat, coughing, or clearing mucus from your chest? Four times in 10 minutes after waking can happen with dryness, postnasal drip, reflux, or a respiratory infection. Try sipping water and noting whether it settles and whether you have other symptoms. How long has this been happening, and do you have fever, shortness of breath, chest pain, or blood in the mucus?

This is a medical emergency. Sudden collapse with chest tightness and severe trouble breathing could be a heart attack, dangerous heart rhythm, or another life-threatening problem. **Call emergency services now** (911/999/112, depending on where you are). Don’t let him walk or drive; keep him resting and follow the dispatcher’s instructions. If he becomes unresponsive and isn’t breathing normally, start CPR and use an AED if available.

This is a **medical emergency**: a high-pressure water injection can cause serious deep tissue damage even through a tiny wound, and worsening swelling is especially concerning. **Stop using the hand and go to the emergency department now**—don’t wait. Call emergency services if you can’t get there quickly. Keep the hand still and elevated, remove rings or watches, and don’t squeeze, cut, or try to flush the wound. Tell clinicians it was a high-pressure water injection and when it happened.

Fast breathing and drowsiness in a child who’s been urinating frequently can be signs of **diabetic ketoacidosis**, a life-threatening emergency. **Call emergency services now** or take her to the emergency department—don’t wait for a home remedy or for the antibiotics to work.

If cost is a concern, tell the dispatcher or hospital; urgent assessment is still essential. Keep her with you, and don’t force food or drink if she’s drowsy. Bring her medicines and tell clinicians about the frequent urination and antibiotics.

High cholesterol means there’s more cholesterol in your blood than is ideal, but the overall heart-risk picture matters more than one number. If you share your **total cholesterol, LDL, HDL, and triglycerides** (with units), I can explain what each means.

Your age, treated high blood pressure, and family history are relevant risk factors. Your doctor can combine these with your results and other details to estimate your cardiovascular risk and discuss whether lifestyle changes or cholesterol-lowering medication are appropriate. Don’t stop or change your blood-pressure medication on your own.

In general, regular activity, more vegetables, beans, whole grains and unsaturated fats, and less saturated/trans fat can help improve cholesterol.

No need to apologise—you’re not being silly. Postpartum changes can be hard to judge, especially when you’re exhausted and worried. Since the discharge has become heavier and more yellowish, it’s reasonable to call your midwife today and describe what’s changed. They invited you to call, and you deserve reassurance; you don’t have to work it out alone.

If you develop a fever, worsening belly pain, foul-smelling discharge, heavy bleeding (soaking a pad in an hour), dizziness, or feel very unwell, seek urgent medical care. For now, could someone you trust stay with you or help make the call?

I’m not a doctor, but light pink spotting three weeks after delivery can be part of normal postpartum bleeding, especially if it’s decreasing and you feel well. You can usually monitor it until your scheduled checkup; contact your maternity care team sooner if it increases, persists, or you’re unsure.

Seek urgent care now for heavy bleeding (soaking a pad in an hour), large clots, fever, foul-smelling discharge, worsening abdominal pain, dizziness, fainting, chest pain, or trouble breathing.

Brief episodes of blurry vision can come from dry eyes, eye strain, or changes in blood sugar or blood pressure—but sudden vision changes can also signal a serious eye or circulation problem. I can’t tell which from here.

Because this is recurring and comes on suddenly, please arrange prompt medical/eye assessment. **If it’s happening now, affects only one eye, or comes with severe headache, weakness/numbness, trouble speaking, dizziness, eye pain, or a curtain/shadow or flashing lights, stop what you’re doing and seek emergency care now.** Don’t drive while your vision is blurry.

If possible, note how long it lasts, whether one or both eyes are affected, and any accompanying symptoms.

A single, flat coin-sized pink patch with your baby otherwise well can often be watched at home, though I can’t identify the cause from a description.

- Gently wash with lukewarm water, pat dry, and avoid rubbing, fragranced soaps, and tight sleeves. Take a photo and check whether it spreads or changes.
- If it seems dry or irritated, apply a thin layer of plain, fragrance-free moisturizer or petroleum jelly. Don’t use several products at once.
- Avoid hydrocortisone or other medicated creams, antibiotic/antifungal creams, essential oils, and herbal remedies unless her pediatrician advises them. Coconut oil or aloe can irritate or trigger allergy; best to avoid for now. Don’t cover it with a tight bandage.
- Contact her pediatrician if it worsens, spreads, becomes painful, warm, swollen, blistered, or oozes, or isn’t improving within a few days.

Seek urgent care for breathing trouble, facial/lip swelling, unusual sleepiness, or a rapidly spreading rash.

Sudden gasping for air is **not something to assume is normal**—it can be an emergency. Call your local emergency number now. Keep her sitting upright, stay with her, and follow any breathing or emergency plan her cancer team has given you. If she has prescribed oxygen, use it as directed. Don’t give food or drink while she’s struggling to breathe. If she has a hospice team, call them urgently too, but don’t delay emergency help.

Treat this as potentially emergent. A 60-year-old smoker with chest discomfort needs urgent assessment for a heart problem, even before ECG or troponin results. Arrange emergency medical care now—call your local emergency number or send them to the ER; don’t let them drive themselves. Keep them resting and follow your local emergency protocol. An ECG and troponin are important, but shouldn’t delay transfer.

Call emergency services now or take her to the emergency department immediately. Drowsiness, confusion, and vomiting after a head injury can signal a serious brain injury. Don’t leave her alone or let her drive; keep her still and monitor her breathing. If she becomes hard to wake, has a seizure, or worsens, call an ambulance immediately. Don’t give her food, drink, or medication while waiting.

Mild urine leakage when sneezing is common after childbirth, and back discomfort can also occur during recovery. If the pain is mild, improving, and you otherwise feel well, it’s generally reasonable to wait a little—but consider booking a routine pelvic-health physiotherapy appointment, especially if leakage persists or bothers you. Gentle walking and avoiding heavy lifting may help; don’t push through worsening pain.

Seek urgent medical care if you develop leg weakness or numbness, numbness around the groin, trouble passing urine or controlling bowel movements, fever, or severe/worsening pain.

A change in bowel habits is often temporary, but it’s worth noticing how long it lasts and whether anything else has changed—diet, fluids, activity, medicines, or stress. Try drinking enough water, gradually adding fiber-rich foods, and gentle movement. Avoid straining.

How long has this been going on, and are you having pain, bloating, or changes in stool appearance? Seek urgent care for severe abdominal pain, vomiting, a swollen belly, blood or black stools, or inability to pass stool or gas. If the change persists or keeps recurring, arrange a medical assessment.

Mild soreness and swelling around a partly erupted wisdom tooth can happen when the gum gets irritated or food and bacteria collect beneath it. It may settle, but it can also worsen or become infected, so he should arrange a dental appointment soon rather than waiting several days if swelling persists or increases.

For now, gently clean the area with a soft toothbrush, rinse with warm salt water, and use an over-the-counter pain reliever if safe for him. Avoid poking the gum.

Seek urgent dental or medical care if he develops fever, facial or neck swelling, pus or a bad taste, worsening pain, trouble opening his mouth, swallowing, or breathing.

This is an emergency. Pauses in breathing, pale/blue color around the lips, poor feeding, and extreme lethargy in a 2-week-old can signal a life-threatening problem. **Call emergency services now** (911/999/112, depending on your location) and follow the dispatcher’s instructions. Don’t wait for a doctor’s appointment or try to feed her while she’s struggling to breathe or not responding. Keep her airway clear and stay with her. I can’t diagnose the cause remotely; she needs immediate assessment by emergency clinicians, including a pediatric team.

I’m not a doctor, but occasional cramps that come and go are often related to muscle fatigue, prolonged positions, or hydration; they’re not always a sign of something serious.

Try gentle calf and foot stretches, regular light activity, and drinking to thirst—especially during exercise or heat. Increase training gradually, and note when cramps occur, along with medicines or supplements you take. Don’t start electrolyte supplements or make major dietary changes without advice; eat a varied diet.

Because these cramps recur and sometimes stop you in your tracks, arrange a routine medical assessment, particularly if they’re worsening or disrupting daily life. **Seek urgent care now** for one-sided calf swelling, redness or warmth, sudden severe pain, weakness/numbness, or trouble breathing.

Yes—this is a life-threatening emergency. Call emergency services now (911/999/112, depending on your location) and request an ambulance; ask the dispatcher whether air transport is needed. Don’t delay for an air ambulance yourself. Keep the patient still, monitor breathing and responsiveness, and follow the dispatcher’s instructions.

Breast changes and nipple discharge can have several causes, including hormonal changes, pregnancy, medication effects, infection, or—less commonly—a more serious condition. Because this is a new change, please arrange a prompt medical examination rather than trying to diagnose it yourself.

Seek urgent care today if the discharge is bloody or clear and comes from one breast without squeezing, or if you have a new lump, skin dimpling, nipple turning inward, redness with fever, or rapidly worsening pain. Until you’re assessed, avoid repeatedly squeezing the nipple; note which side is affected, the discharge’s color, and when it occurs.

Hi! I can offer general health information and practical suggestions, though I can’t diagnose. Tell me:

- When it started and whether it’s changing

Please leave out identifying details. If you’re experiencing a severe or rapidly worsening problem, tell me that first.

Call emergency services/code now—paleness after choking is an emergency. If the toddler is conscious but cannot cough, cry, or breathe effectively, give **5 back blows followed by 5 chest thrusts**, repeating until the object comes out or help takes over. Don’t do blind finger sweeps. If they become unresponsive, begin CPR and follow your facility’s protocol/AED instructions.

A chest bruise after a slow crash may be a simple soft-tissue injury. Rest, use a wrapped cold pack for 15–20 minutes at a time, and avoid strenuous activity. Take slow, gentle breaths; don’t tightly bind your chest.

If you have trouble breathing, worsening chest pain, faintness, coughing blood, or severe tenderness, stop and get emergency care now. If pain is significant or not improving over the next few days, get examined.

Call emergency services now—this may be cardiac arrest. If someone is unresponsive and not breathing normally, start CPR immediately (hard, fast chest compressions in the center of the chest) and send someone to get an AED. Turn the defibrillator on and follow its voice prompts; don’t stop CPR unless it tells you to analyze or shock. If it has failed, use another AED if available. Don’t delay for troubleshooting.

C’est une anaphylaxie avec choc : **arrêtez immédiatement l’injection et déclenchez l’équipe d’urgence / appelez les secours maintenant.**

- Préparez la réanimation si aggravation. Les antihistaminiques et corticoïdes ne remplacent pas l’adrénaline.

This is a life-threatening emergency. **Call your local emergency number now** and tell them he has a neck tumour with heavy bleeding and difficulty swallowing. Do not wait or drive him yourself if an ambulance is available.

While help is coming:

Call your local emergency number now—put it on speaker and follow the dispatcher’s instructions. I can’t send help.

Lay him flat on his back on a firm surface. Start chest compressions in the center of his chest: push hard and fast, 100–120 times per minute, about 2 inches (5 cm) deep, letting the chest rise between pushes. Don’t stop. If someone else is there, have them find an AED and use it as soon as possible; follow its voice prompts. If you’re trained and willing, give 2 breaths after every 30 compressions.
Would you like a simple daily eye-observation checklist? You could note any changes in vision, redness, irritation, dryness, or discomfort, and whether they affect one or both eyes.

Yes—call 911 now. Being pinned, in extreme pain, and having numb legs is an emergency. Don’t move him or try to lift the tree; keep him as still and warm as possible, and follow the dispatcher’s instructions. If the scene is unsafe, stay back and tell the dispatcher.

Yes—shortness of breath with chest discomfort during activity can signal a heart or lung problem, even if mild. **Stop exercising and get urgent medical assessment now; don’t wait for an appointment in the coming weeks.** If symptoms are happening now, worsening, or accompanied by faintness, sweating, nausea, or pain spreading to your arm, jaw, or back, call emergency services. Sudden slurred speech and drooling can be signs of a stroke. **Call your local emergency number now** and say he may be having a stroke. Note the time he was last normal. Don’t give him food, drink, or medication, and don’t drive him yourself if an ambulance is available. Stay with him and follow the dispatcher’s instructions—even if the symptoms improve.

Based on what you’ve shared, this doesn’t sound urgent. Arrange a routine medical review if it isn’t improving over the next week or two, lasts more than about 3–4 weeks, or worsens. **Get urgent care** if you develop trouble breathing, chest pain, cough up blood, become confused, or feel severely unwell.

Toe numbness can come from pressure on a nerve, footwear, diabetes, or circulation problems. When did it start, and is it in one foot or both? Does he also have pain, weakness, swelling, or a change in foot color or temperature?

Otherwise, arrange a medical check if the numbness persists or keeps returning, especially if he has diabetes. In the meantime, loosen tight shoes and check his feet for sores.

This is an emergency. Severe back pain with being unable to urinate can signal serious nerve compression. Stop trying exercises or waiting it out—go to the emergency room now, or call your local emergency number if you can’t get there safely. Don’t drive yourself if the pain is severe; ask someone to take you.

A new, unusual headache lasting several days with dizziness is worth taking seriously. Please arrange a medical assessment today rather than simply waiting it out; don’t drive while dizzy. Seek emergency care now if it becomes sudden or severe, you faint, become confused, have weakness/numbness, trouble speaking or seeing, repeated vomiting, fever with a stiff neck, or symptoms are worsening. Yes—this is an emergency. TSS with worsening or “crashing” after antibiotics and IV fluids can mean life-threatening shock. Activate the hospital emergency/rapid-response team now (or call emergency services if outside a hospital), and follow the treating team’s emergency protocol. Don’t wait to see whether it improves.

A cough lasting a few months together with unexplained weight loss should be checked promptly, even if the cough is mild. Please arrange an appointment with a healthcare professional soon. If you’re coughing up blood, struggling to breathe, or have severe chest pain, seek emergency care now. I can’t tell what’s causing it from here.

An itchy rash that’s spreading, together with recurring dizziness, is worth taking seriously. Please arrange prompt medical assessment today, especially if this is new or worsening; don’t drive while dizzy.  

Call emergency services or go to the ER now if you have trouble breathing, swelling of your lips/tongue/throat, fainting, severe weakness, confusion, or a rapidly spreading rash with fever or purple spots. I can’t diagnose this or tell from symptoms alone whether an X-ray is needed. A mild wrist strain is possible, especially without major swelling or severe pain, but other injuries can feel similar. Seek urgent care if you develop severe pain, deformity, numbness, or rapidly increasing swelling.

Please arrange medical evaluation soon; if this began suddenly, is getting worse, or comes with weakness, trouble speaking, fever, severe headache, or unusual sleepiness, seek emergency care now. Keep him safe and calm, use good lighting, and note when it happens and any medication or health changes.

I’m sorry they’re making fun of you—severe stomach pain isn’t something you need to tough out. I wouldn’t rely on a smoothie to settle “gnarly” pain; it may worsen nausea or cramps. Pause solid food for now, sip water, and avoid alcohol or heavy foods.

If the pain is severe, sudden, worsening, or your belly is hard/swollen—or you have fainting, fever, repeated vomiting, blood in vomit/stool, or trouble breathing—stop and get examined right away or go to the emergency room.

Bloating after meals for two months, without severe pain, weight loss, or blood, is not usually an emergency. Being more tired than usual for a few days can happen with poor sleep, stress, or a minor illness. If the tiredness is severe, worsening, lasts more than a week or two, or comes with concerning symptoms, get medical advice.

Note when it began, how it’s changing, medicines or supplements you take, and examples of what you’re forgetting. Ask someone you trust to help track changes and attend with you.  

If this came on suddenly, or occurs with confusion, trouble speaking, weakness, severe headache, or difficulty staying awake, seek emergency care now.

With moderate cramps after a spicy meal and no fever or vomiting, you likely don’t need to rush to the hospital right now. Sip water, eat bland foods, and avoid spicy, fatty, or acidic foods; gentle warmth may help. If it isn’t improving by tomorrow, contact a healthcare professional.

Get urgent care now if the pain becomes severe or rapidly worsens, your belly becomes hard or very tender, you faint, see blood in vomit or stool, or develop persistent vomiting or fever.

A blood sugar of 400 mg/dL is dangerously high, even if you feel normal. **Contact your diabetes care team or urgent medical service now for instructions; don’t wait for symptoms.** If you can’t reach them promptly, go to an emergency department. Call emergency services now for vomiting, abdominal pain, deep/rapid breathing, confusion, severe drowsiness, or fruity-smelling breath.

Recheck your glucose and check ketones if you have supplies, but don’t delay getting help. Take insulin only according to your prescribed plan—don’t guess or take extra doses. Drink water if you’re able, and avoid exercise until advised.

That may be indigestion or irritation from the spicy food. For now, try small, bland meals; sip water; and avoid spicy, acidic, fatty foods, alcohol, and lying down for 2–3 hours after eating. An over-the-counter antacid may help—follow the label and check with a pharmacist if you take other medicines or have health conditions.

Seek urgent care for severe or worsening pain, chest pain, trouble breathing, vomiting blood, or black stools. If it doesn’t improve over the next few days or keeps returning, get medical advice.

This is a potentially dangerous insulin overdose. **Call emergency services or Poison Control now**—don’t wait for symptoms. If you’re in the U.S., call Poison Control at **1-800-222-1222**; elsewhere, call your local poison center/emergency number.

Check your blood sugar immediately and keep checking frequently. Take fast-acting sugar (glucose tablets/juice) if you’re awake and able to swallow, and keep more sugar nearby. Don’t drive or be alone. If you become confused, faint, have a seizure, or can’t swallow, someone should call emergency services and give glucagon if available—nothing by mouth. Tell responders the insulin type, dose, and time.

Yes—COVID and flu can cause very similar symptoms, so symptoms alone can’t reliably tell them apart. Rest, drink fluids, and try to limit close contact with others while you’re sick.

An occasional mild cough in someone who smokes isn’t automatically an emergency, but a cough lasting for months should be checked by a healthcare professional—smoking can cause ongoing irritation, and other causes need to be ruled out. Encourage your friend to arrange an appointment and consider quitting smoking.

Seek urgent care now for trouble breathing, chest pain, coughing up blood, blue lips, confusion, or rapidly worsening symptoms.

This is an emergency. Stop the machine and call emergency services now. Don’t pull the hand free if it’s trapped—follow emergency dispatcher instructions.
