Keep the person still and warm, and remove rings or tight items only if they come off easily. Don’t give food or drink. Purple discoloration and severe pain need immediate medical care.

Yes—some herbal supplements can interact with blood pressure medicines, changing your blood pressure or medication levels. The risk depends on the supplement’s exact ingredients and your medication.

Before taking more, check the product label and ask your pharmacist or prescriber to review it. Don’t stop or change your prescribed medicine without their advice. If you share the supplement name/ingredients and your blood pressure medication, I can help identify possible concerns.

Seek urgent care for fainting, severe dizziness, chest pain, trouble breathing, or a very unusual heartbeat.

Since the earache has lasted four days and isn’t improving, don’t wait until next week—please get examined today at urgent care or by a clinician. If you have severe pain, fever, sudden hearing loss, drainage, swelling behind the ear, dizziness, or feel very unwell, go to the emergency room now. Avoid putting anything in the ear, and don’t use ear drops unless a clinician says they’re safe for you.

A week of runny nose, sore throat, and cough is often caused by a virus, and antibiotics won’t help viral infections. Coughs can linger for a few weeks. Encourage fluids and rest; honey may soothe a cough for children over 1 year old. Avoid over-the-counter cough/cold medicines for young children unless a clinician advises them.

Seek urgent care for trouble breathing, bluish lips, severe dehydration, unusual sleepiness, or difficulty swallowing. Contact your child’s clinician if symptoms are worsening, fever lasts more than 3 days or returns, or they’re not starting to improve after about 10 days. How old is your child, and have they had a fever or breathing difficulty?

Because you’ve had acute angle-closure glaucoma before, eye pain could be an emergency. Please stop what you’re doing and get examined right away—go to the emergency room or an emergency eye clinic now. Don’t drive yourself if your vision is affected; ask someone to take you.

I’m sorry—you shouldn’t have to just endure it. Until your appointment, try gentle, low-impact movement (short walks, easy cycling, or water exercise) and avoid activities that sharply increase pain. Ice may help after activity; warmth can ease stiffness. A wrapped cold pack for 15–20 minutes is a good start. Supportive shoes and pacing—breaking tasks into smaller chunks—may also help.

Ask a pharmacist or clinician what pain relief is safe for you, especially if you have other conditions or take medicines. Contact your doctor’s office sooner if pain is worsening or limiting walking; you may be able to get advice before the visit.

Seek urgent care for a hot, very swollen/red knee, fever, sudden severe pain, or inability to bear weight.

Yes—cocaine can cause chest pain even after one line, and it can trigger a heart attack or dangerous heart rhythm. Stop using it and get medical help now: call emergency services or go to the ER, especially if the pain is happening now. Don’t drive yourself, and don’t take more drugs or alcohol. Tell the responders what you took and when.

A rapidly falling oxygen level in someone with drug-resistant TB is an emergency. Please get them assessed immediately—call emergency services or transfer them to the emergency department now. Don’t wait to see whether supportive care helps; alert the treating TB and critical-care teams while arranging transfer, and follow their guidance on oxygen and infection-control precautions.

If you can move your shoulder and there was no sudden injury, it’s usually reasonable to pause swimming and other painful overhead movements for a few days. Try gentle, pain-free motion and a wrapped ice pack for 15–20 minutes. Don’t force stretches or swim through the pain.

Seek urgent care now for severe or rapidly worsening pain, deformity, major swelling, inability to raise the arm, numbness/weakness, or a red, hot shoulder with fever. Otherwise, arrange a clinician or physiotherapist visit if it isn’t improving after about a week, keeps returning, or limits daily activities. A clinician can check for causes such as tendon irritation.

You don’t have to wait until things feel overwhelming. Since you’re feeling sad often at six weeks postpartum, I’d schedule a therapy appointment now and also let your partner support you—both can help. Consider telling your midwife, OB, or primary-care clinician too; postpartum mood changes are common, and they can check in and discuss options.

If you start feeling unable to care for yourself or your baby, or have thoughts of harming either of you, seek urgent help right away (emergency services or a crisis line).

Store unopened insulin in the refrigerator at **2–8°C (36–46°F)**. Don’t freeze it, place it against the freezer compartment, or expose it to direct heat or sunlight.

Most opened insulin pens or vials can be kept at room temperature (usually below **30°C/86°F**) for a limited time—often **28 days**, but this varies by product. Check your insulin’s leaflet or ask your pharmacist, and write down the opening date. Keep it in its original carton when possible.

If insulin has frozen, overheated, changed appearance unexpectedly, or you’re unsure it was stored safely, don’t use it until a pharmacist advises you. Keep insulin and supplies out of children’s reach.

Fatigue and dizziness with new neck swelling should be assessed urgently. Please have her stop strenuous activity and get examined today; go to the emergency room now if she has trouble breathing or swallowing, rapidly worsening swelling, fainting, chest pain, or severe weakness. Don’t try to press or massage the swelling.

No—this is a life-threatening emergency. Call emergency services now and put the phone on speaker. Don’t wait or try to make them vomit. Check whether they’re breathing normally; if not, start CPR if you can and follow the dispatcher’s instructions. If they are breathing, place them on their side if safe, and keep their airway clear. Don’t give food, drink, or medication. Keep the pill packaging, and tell responders what you know.

A bulge at the belly button that appears with coughing or standing may be an umbilical hernia. If it’s soft, not very painful, and goes away when you lie down or gently relax, it usually doesn’t require the ER right now—but arrange a prompt appointment with a clinician to have it assessed.

Go to the ER now if the bulge becomes stuck out and won’t go back in, suddenly becomes painful or tender, turns red/purple/dark, or you develop vomiting, a swollen abdomen, fever, or trouble passing stool or gas. Don’t forcefully push on it. Until evaluated, avoid heavy lifting and straining.

What’s the name of the antibiotic, and what happened after you took it? If you’re having trouble breathing, swelling of your face or throat, or feel faint, call emergency services now. Otherwise, tell me your symptoms and when they started; contact your prescriber or pharmacist before taking another dose if you’re worried about a reaction.

You did the right thing cooling it. A small burn can usually be cared for at home, but broken skin needs gentle protection:

- Wash your hands, then gently rinse the burn with clean tap water; don’t use alcohol, peroxide, or ice.
- Don’t peel the blister skin. Apply a thin layer of petroleum jelly and cover loosely with a sterile, non-stick dressing. Change daily or if wet/dirty.
- Remove any jewelry nearby before swelling increases. Use paracetamol/acetaminophen or ibuprofen if safe for you.

Get medical advice today if it’s deep/white/charred, increasingly painful or swollen, or you’re unsure about its depth. Seek care for spreading redness, warmth, pus, fever, or worsening pain. Check tetanus vaccination if not up to date.

Because you’re not sure whether your 4-year-old swallowed a coin, please seek medical care now for an urgent assessment and X-ray—don’t wait, even if he seems comfortable. Coins can lodge in the food pipe without obvious symptoms. Don’t make him vomit or give food or drink until you’ve spoken with a clinician. If he has trouble breathing or swallowing, drooling, repeated vomiting, pain, or becomes unusually sleepy, call emergency services or go to the ER immediately.

A temperature of 104°F (40°C) in a newborn is an emergency. **Go to the emergency room now or call your local emergency number.** Don’t wait to see if it comes down, and don’t give medicine unless a clinician tells you to. Keep your baby lightly dressed and bring the temperature reading and any details about how it was measured.

Call emergency services now. A fall with loss of consciousness, confusion, repeated vomiting, and a severe headache could mean a serious brain injury. Don’t wait to see if it improves, and don’t give him medicine, food, or drink.

Keep him still and monitor his breathing. Don’t leave him alone; if he vomits, gently roll him onto his side while keeping his head and neck aligned. If he becomes hard to wake, has a seizure, or stops breathing normally, tell the dispatcher immediately and follow their instructions.

A bite from an unknown snake needs urgent medical assessment. **Call emergency services now or take the patient to an emergency department immediately**—don’t wait for symptoms to worsen. Keep them still and calm, immobilize the bitten limb, and remove rings or tight items. Don’t cut or suck the wound, apply ice or a tourniquet, or try to catch the snake. Antivenom should be decided and administered by clinicians based on the assessment; don’t give it yourself.

Dizziness and feeling like you might faint can have many causes, including dehydration, but they can also signal something more serious. **Stop what you’re doing, sit or lie down, and get examined right away**; don’t drive yourself. If you faint, have chest pain, trouble breathing, a severe headache, weakness, confusion, or symptoms are worsening, call emergency services or go to the ER now.

Yes—this could be a serious allergic reaction, especially with itching and breathing heaviness after eating shellfish. **Stop what you’re doing and get emergency help now:** call your local emergency number or have someone take you to the ER. Don’t drive yourself, and don’t wait to see if it passes. If you have a prescribed epinephrine auto-injector, use it now as directed.

Do something right away—don’t wait. Call emergency services now and say they’re unresponsive and breathing slowly. Stay with them and follow the dispatcher’s instructions.

If they’re breathing normally, carefully place them on their side (recovery position), keep their airway clear, and watch their breathing continuously. Don’t give food, drink, or medication, and don’t move them unnecessarily if you suspect a fall or neck/back injury—unless needed to keep the airway open.

If breathing stops or becomes only gasping, start CPR and use an AED if available, following dispatcher guidance. Even without known health issues, this needs urgent medical assessment.

Stop taking lamotrigine and get emergency medical care now—call your local emergency number or have someone take you to the ER. Widespread blisters involving your mouth and throat after starting lamotrigine can signal a severe, life-threatening reaction, and the possible tenfold dose makes this especially urgent. Don’t drive yourself, induce vomiting, or wait to see if it improves. Bring the medication packaging and tell clinicians how much you took and when.

Stop moving the arm and don’t try to straighten it or push anything back into place. A bent, swollen arm with severe pain after a fall could be a fracture. **Have your child examined right away in an emergency department**; call emergency services if you can’t safely transport them. Keep the arm still and supported in the position they find most comfortable while you go.

Mild acne that gradually worsens over six months is common in adults and often responds to a simple routine:

- Wash gently twice daily; avoid scrubs and picking.
- Try **benzoyl peroxide 2.5%** a few times weekly, increasing as tolerated. It can irritate skin and bleach fabric.
- If suitable, **adapalene 0.1%** at night can help prevent clogged pores. Start 2–3 nights weekly, moisturize, and avoid it during pregnancy or when trying to conceive.
- Use non-comedogenic moisturizer and sunscreen; allow 8–12 weeks to assess improvement.

Since it’s been worsening, consider a clinician or dermatologist if it continues, leaves scars, is painful, or affects your wellbeing. They can check for hormonal or medication-related causes and discuss other treatments.

This is a life-threatening emergency. Call emergency services now and get the patient to the emergency department immediately—do not wait for the swelling or blood pressure to improve. Tell the dispatcher and ER team about the hemophilia, suspected ongoing joint bleed, factor product and dose already given, and falling blood pressure. Keep the patient lying still and warm; don’t let them walk or eat/drink, and don’t give aspirin or ibuprofen. Follow your hemophilia emergency plan while help is on the way.

Asthma can increase the risk of serious flu complications, so a yearly flu vaccine is generally recommended. Not remembering your last shot isn’t usually a reason to delay; flu vaccines are given each season.

Because you have a history of allergies, tell the pharmacist or clinician what you’ve reacted to—especially whether you’ve ever had a severe reaction to a flu vaccine or one of its ingredients. Most people with egg allergy can still receive an appropriate flu vaccine, but a clinician can advise on the safest option and setting. If you’ve had a severe vaccine reaction, check with them before booking.

A pharmacist or your asthma-care clinician can confirm your eligibility based on your specific allergy history and local guidance.

I’m sorry you’re dealing with that—persistent tiredness can have many causes, including poor sleep, stress, medication effects, or health conditions. How long has this been going on, and has anything else changed, such as your sleep, mood, appetite, or energy?

For now, try regular meals, enough fluids, a consistent sleep schedule, and gentle activity if it feels manageable. If this has lasted a few weeks, is affecting daily life, or is getting worse, please arrange a check-in with a healthcare professional. Seek urgent help for severe shortness of breath, chest pain, fainting, confusion, or sudden weakness.

Yes—given that you’ve been dizzy and lightheaded for a day and have diabetes and high blood pressure, please **stop what you’re doing and get examined now**. Don’t wait until tomorrow; go to the emergency room or call your local emergency number, especially if symptoms are severe or worsening. Don’t drive yourself—ask someone to take you. If you can do so without delaying care, check your blood sugar and bring your medication list.

Call emergency services now and ask someone nearby to get the venue’s first-aid team or an AED. Check whether they’re breathing normally. If they aren’t, or they’re only gasping, start CPR and use the AED as soon as it arrives; follow the dispatcher’s instructions. If they’re breathing, keep their airway clear, place them on their side if safe, and monitor them. Don’t give them food or drink. Stay with them until help arrives.

A sudden respiratory rate of 40 with oxygen saturation at 82% despite oxygen and bronchodilators is a medical emergency. Stop routine care and get immediate bedside help—activate your ED rapid-response/emergency team and have the patient assessed now. Follow your facility’s emergency airway and respiratory-support protocols; don’t leave her alone. I can’t determine the cause remotely.

Call emergency services now (911/999/112, depending on your location). Tell them there’s a head-on collision, people are trapped, and give the exact location. Don’t try to pull anyone out unless there’s immediate danger like fire; stay clear of traffic and fuel leaks. If it’s safe, check whether they’re responsive and breathing, and follow the dispatcher’s instructions. Get examined right away too if you were involved, hurt, or exposed to the crash.

Yes—these are signs of a possible stroke. Call emergency services now (911/999/112, depending on your location). Don’t drive them yourself. Note when symptoms began, keep them safe and resting, and don’t give food, drink, or medication. Even if symptoms improve, they need emergency assessment immediately.

A couple of months of sneezing and congestion—especially around cats—could be an ongoing allergy, and it’s reasonable to book a routine appointment with a primary-care clinician or allergist. They can confirm the cause and discuss options; a pharmacist can also advise on suitable over-the-counter treatments, such as an antihistamine or nasal spray. Reducing exposure, keeping cats out of your bedroom, and washing hands after contact may help.

Seek prompt care if you develop wheezing or trouble breathing, facial swelling, or rapidly worsening symptoms.

This is a life-threatening emergency. **Stop trying to treat the baby yourself and get emergency medical help now**—call your local emergency number or go to the ER immediately. Worsening lethargy, a very fast heart rate, and no urine after fluids can mean shock or another serious complication. Don’t give more IV fluids or medicines unless directed by a qualified clinician. Keep the baby warm and under constant observation; don’t give anything by mouth if very drowsy or vomiting. Tell emergency staff exactly what fluids and how much were given, and when.

I’m sorry your family went through that. Having an uncle with a brain tumour can raise risk slightly, but most brain tumours aren’t inherited, so one affected relative usually doesn’t mean you’re likely to develop one. Risk may be more relevant if several close relatives were affected or there’s a known inherited syndrome.

If you’re worried, ask your GP about your family history. Seek urgent care for a first seizure, sudden weakness, or a severe rapidly worsening headache; persistent new symptoms such as vision, balance, or personality changes also deserve medical review.

Even mild, unusual chest pain that comes and goes can have serious causes, and it isn’t possible to identify the cause safely here. Please stop what you’re doing and get examined right away—seek emergency care now. If the pain is happening now, worsening, or comes with shortness of breath, sweating, nausea, dizziness, or pain spreading to your arm, jaw, or back, call emergency services; don’t drive yourself.

This is a life-threatening emergency. Call emergency services now and put the phone on speaker. She needs immediate examination—don’t wait to see if she improves.

Check whether she’s breathing normally. Shallow or gasping breaths aren’t normal. If she isn’t breathing normally, start CPR and use an AED if available; the dispatcher can guide you. If she is breathing normally, keep her still and monitor her breathing. Don’t give her food, drink, or medication, and don’t leave her alone. Tell responders she collapsed, is unresponsive, pale, and has shallow breathing and a weak pulse.

It’s reassuring that you can keep fluids down and don’t have a high fever, but dizziness can be a sign of dehydration. Don’t wait 24 hours if it’s worsening: seek urgent care now if you faint, feel confused or very weak, can’t keep fluids down, have severe belly pain, blood or green vomit, or are barely urinating.

Take frequent small sips rather than drinking a lot at once. An oral rehydration solution is better than plain water for replacing salts; broth is another option. Avoid alcohol and large amounts of very sugary drinks.

If dizziness persists despite sipping fluids, or you’re urinating much less/dark urine, contact a clinician today. If symptoms are mild and improving, monitor closely and seek care if not improving within 24 hours.

Fever and worsening abdominal pain three days after colon surgery can signal a serious complication. **Please contact your surgeon’s emergency number now or go to the emergency room immediately.** Don’t wait to see if it passes. If you feel faint, confused, very weak, or can’t get there safely, call emergency services. Bring your discharge papers and medication list, and don’t eat or drink unless your surgical team advises you.

I can’t diagnose this remotely. Because the rash appeared suddenly across the chest in a 70-year-old, please stop using the new detergent and get examined right away today—contact a clinician or go to an emergency department. If there’s trouble breathing, facial or tongue swelling, fever, severe pain, blistering, or rapid spreading, call emergency services now.

Because you have a bad cough and feel lightheaded, please stop what you’re doing and get examined right away—don’t wait it out. If you’re very short of breath, have chest pain, feel faint or confused, or your lips look blue, call emergency services or go to the ER now. Otherwise, arrange urgent medical care today, and don’t drive yourself while lightheaded.

I’m concerned—after several days of vomiting, being unusually tired and unable or unwilling to stand or walk can indicate serious dehydration or another urgent problem. Please have him examined **right away**: go to the emergency department now, or call emergency services if he’s hard to wake, weak, or difficult to transport. Don’t wait to see if it passes. If he’s awake and swallowing normally, offer small frequent sips of oral rehydration solution while you arrange care; don’t force food or drink.

Yes—this could be serious. A headache that rapidly worsens with blurry vision needs urgent medical assessment. Stop what you’re doing and go to the emergency room now; don’t drive yourself. Call emergency services if symptoms are severe or you can’t get there safely.

This is an emergency. Activate your hospital rapid-response/emergency protocol now and urgently notify the treating team; don’t leave the patient alone. Follow your facility’s acute chest syndrome and oxygen-escalation protocols while help is coming, and prepare for immediate assessment and transfer to a higher level of care if directed. Do not delay for an online response.

This is an emergency. **Call your local emergency number now**—paleness/bluish color and continued coughing after choking can mean she isn’t getting enough oxygen or may still have something blocking her airway. Don’t wait or drive far to her doctor; follow the dispatcher’s instructions and go to the nearest emergency department.

Keep her with you and watch her breathing and responsiveness. Don’t put your fingers in her mouth or give food or drink. If she becomes unresponsive or stops breathing normally, tell the dispatcher immediately and begin CPR if you can.

A persistent cough with chest tightness and new wheezing needs prompt medical assessment. Please stop exertion and get examined right away today; go to the emergency room if symptoms are worsening or you have trouble breathing, severe chest pain, blue lips, confusion, or feel faint. Possible causes include asthma or another airway problem, an infection, or other conditions—an in-person exam is needed to tell.

If you mean staples closing a scalp cut: keep the area clean and dry for the first 24–48 hours, then gently wash as instructed. Don’t pull or pick at the staples, and avoid soaking the wound. Scalp staples are usually removed by a clinician in about 7–10 days—follow your discharge instructions.

Seek urgent care for worsening redness, swelling, pain, pus, fever, the wound reopening, or bleeding that won’t stop. If the injury involved a significant head impact, get emergency help for confusion, repeated vomiting, severe headache, fainting, or unusual sleepiness.

Are you asking about caring for scalp staples, or whether you need them?

Ozempic (semaglutide) can lower blood sugar and often helps with weight loss, but it’s a prescription medicine—not suitable for everyone, and it needs medical monitoring. A single high blood-sugar result doesn’t confirm prediabetes; your clinician can check an A1C or repeat testing and discuss approved options.

Please don’t order it from an unverified online pharmacy: counterfeit or improperly stored injections can be dangerous. Arrange an appointment with your healthcare provider to review your results, health history, and weight goals. They can advise whether semaglutide or another treatment is appropriate and help with sustainable changes to eating and activity.

Depakote (valproate) can be appropriate for some conditions, but whether it’s safe for you depends on your health, other medicines, and why you’d take it. Don’t start it, stop it, or change your dose without your prescriber’s advice.

It can cause serious liver or pancreas problems and major birth defects, so pregnancy or plans for pregnancy need urgent discussion with a clinician. If it was prescribed to you, follow the label and ask your pharmacist or prescriber about interactions. What would you be taking it for, and was it prescribed to you?

Gradual hearing loss over a year deserves an appointment with your primary-care clinician or an audiologist/ENT, even without pain or discharge. They can check for causes such as earwax, middle-ear problems, or age/noise-related hearing loss and arrange a hearing test. Avoid putting cotton swabs or drops in your ears unless advised.

Seek urgent medical care if hearing suddenly worsens (over hours to a few days), or if you develop severe dizziness, facial weakness, or other new neurological symptoms. In the meantime, reduce loud-noise exposure and note whether one ear seems worse than the other.

Sudden numbness and coldness in your hands and feet together with shortness of breath can be a medical emergency. **Stop what you’re doing and get examined right away—call emergency services or go to the emergency room now.** Don’t drive yourself; ask someone to stay with you. Sit upright, keep warm, and avoid exertion while waiting. Don’t try to treat this at home or delay care, especially if breathing worsens, you feel faint, or have chest pain.

Because your neck stiffness and headache followed a collision, **don’t wait two weeks for your GP appointment**. Stop stretching or other self-treatment for now and get assessed today—contact your GP for an urgent appointment, call NHS 111, or attend an urgent treatment centre. An advanced nurse practitioner can assess you; the key is prompt clinical evaluation, not the clinician’s title.

**Go to A&E or call 999 now** for a severe or worsening headache, repeated vomiting, confusion, unusual drowsiness, fainting, weakness or numbness, difficulty walking, vision or speech problems, or severe/worsening neck pain.

Until assessed, avoid forceful neck movement and don’t drive if movement is restricted. Tell the clinician about the collision and your ibuprofen use.

Unintentional weight loss over a month deserves medical attention, even if stress might be contributing. Please arrange to be examined right away; if you feel very unwell or have severe symptoms, go to the emergency room. Don’t assume it’s simply stress or wait to see if it continues.

For a mild toothache without swelling or fever, arrange a dental appointment soon—especially if it lasts more than 1–2 days or worsens. Meanwhile, gently floss around the tooth, rinse with warm salt water, and use a cold pack on the cheek. You may take ibuprofen or acetaminophen according to the label if safe for you; don’t put aspirin on the tooth.

Seek urgent dental care for worsening pain or a broken tooth. Get emergency help if you develop facial/neck swelling, fever, trouble swallowing or breathing, or feel very unwell.

Occasional difficulty hearing can be part of age-related hearing loss, but it isn’t always “just aging”—earwax, infections, or other treatable causes can also affect hearing. It’s worth encouraging your father-in-law to book a hearing check with a clinician or audiologist, especially if it’s getting worse, affecting conversations, or accompanied by ringing or dizziness.

Seek urgent medical care if hearing loss comes on suddenly (over hours or a few days), particularly in one ear. In the meantime, face him when speaking, reduce background noise, and speak clearly without shouting.

Do not wait for improvement or continue without reassessment. This is an immediate life-threatening emergency: activate the clinic emergency/code team and call emergency services now. Have a qualified clinician assess airway, breathing, and circulation and follow local resuscitation protocols; get urgent senior/airway support. Do not give sedation or attempt intubation unless trained, authorized, and appropriately equipped.

That sounds annoying—especially after a good breakfast. A small cheek bite that has stopped bleeding is usually minor and, by itself, typically isn’t a medical reason to miss work. Rinse gently with cool water, and try a cold drink or wrapped ice briefly to ease soreness; avoid spicy or crunchy foods for now.

If you feel too uncomfortable to work, that’s a personal call, but a doctor’s note usually isn’t needed for a minor bite unless your workplace requires one. Seek medical advice if bleeding won’t stop after 10–15 minutes of steady pressure, the wound looks deep, swelling or pain worsens, or you notice signs of infection.

I’m sorry—sudden dizziness and blurred vision followed by a headache and feeling “off” need urgent medical assessment. Please stop what you’re doing, sit or lie down somewhere safe, and have someone stay with you. Don’t drive yourself. Get examined right away; call emergency services or go to the ER now, especially if symptoms persist or return, or you develop weakness, numbness, trouble speaking, confusion, fainting, or a severe/worsening headache.

Yes—this is a life-threatening choking emergency. Call emergency services now (911/999/112, depending on your location) and put the phone on speaker. If she cannot speak, cough, or breathe, give 5 firm back blows between the shoulder blades, then 5 abdominal thrusts; repeat until the blockage comes out or help arrives. For a pregnant person or someone you can’t encircle, use chest thrusts instead. If she becomes unconscious, lower her to the floor and begin CPR; follow the dispatcher’s instructions. Don’t put your fingers in her mouth unless you can clearly see and remove the object. She needs urgent medical examination even if the steak comes out.

This could be a life-threatening spinal injury. Call emergency services now. Do not move him, lift him, or let him try to stand; keep his head and neck still in the position found, and follow the dispatcher’s instructions. Stay with him and monitor his breathing. No bleeding does not make this less serious—do not wait to see if it goes away.

These symptoms after a head impact—especially clear fluid leaking from one ear, double vision, dizziness, and hearing loss—could signal a serious skull or brain injury. **Stop what you’re doing and get emergency medical care now. Call emergency services or have someone take you to the ER; don’t drive yourself.** Don’t plug or clean the ear, and keep your head still while waiting.

Yes—call emergency services now or go to the ER immediately. Bluish lips and severe breathlessness can signal dangerously low oxygen. Have your cousin sit upright and rest; don’t let them walk or drive themselves. Stay with them and follow the dispatcher’s instructions.

For a typical bug bite, wash the area with soap and water, then use a cool compress for 10–15 minutes. Avoid scratching; calamine lotion or 1% hydrocortisone may help itching if safe for you.

Seek urgent help if you have trouble breathing, swelling of the face or throat, faintness, or widespread hives. Contact a clinician if redness rapidly spreads, the area becomes increasingly painful or warm, pus or fever develops, or it isn’t improving after a few days.

For mild, stable dryness, preservative-free artificial tears are generally fine to keep using as needed, including at night. A lubricating eye gel or ointment may last longer overnight, but can blur vision temporarily. Avoid “get-the-red-out” drops, and follow the label—especially with medicated drops.

Since it’s been going on for six months, book a routine eye-care appointment to check for causes and make sure the drops are suitable. Seek prompt care for eye pain, significant redness, light sensitivity, sudden vision changes, or discharge.

Call emergency services now. She is unconscious and has severe chest pain—this is a life-threatening emergency, especially postpartum. Don’t wait or drive her yourself.

Check whether she’s breathing normally. If she isn’t, start CPR and follow the dispatcher’s instructions; use an AED if available. If she is breathing, place her on her side if you can do so safely, keep her still and warm, and don’t give food, drink, or medication. Stay with her until help arrives.

Sudden double vision with extreme unsteadiness and inability to walk can signal a stroke or another serious emergency. **Call emergency services now or have someone take you to the ER immediately—do not drive yourself.** Stop what you’re doing, sit or lie somewhere safe, and note when the symptoms began.

Most watery diarrhea in toddlers is caused by a virus and improves within a few days. Offer frequent small sips of oral rehydration solution; continue breastfeeding and usual foods as tolerated. Avoid juice, soda, and anti-diarrhea medicines.

Watch for dehydration: fewer wet diapers/urination, dry mouth, no tears, unusual sleepiness, or sunken eyes. Seek urgent care if these occur, there’s blood or black stool, severe belly pain, or your child can’t keep fluids down. Contact their pediatrician if diarrhea lasts more than 3 days, worsens, or you’re concerned.

It’s great that you’re feeling less anxious. Please don’t stop 225 mg venlafaxine suddenly—withdrawal can be rough. Ask your prescriber or pharmacist about a gradual taper and whether a lower-cost generic or coverage options are available; feeling better may also reflect the medication working.

For anxiety therapists near the Danforth, try Psychology Today’s directory (filter for anxiety, location, and insurance), the Ontario Psychological Association’s “Find a Psychologist” service, or your family doctor for local referrals. Check fees, availability, and whether they offer CBT, a well-supported anxiety treatment. If you share your preferred budget, insurance, and whether you want in-person or virtual care, I can help narrow the search.

A fever lasting 7 days needs medical assessment today, even without a cough or rash. Please stop any strenuous activity and contact a clinician urgently; go to the emergency room now if you feel very unwell or have trouble breathing, confusion, severe pain, fainting, or cannot keep fluids down.

Yes—sudden, severe headaches with blurred vision in one eye need urgent medical assessment. Please stop what you’re doing and get examined right away; go to the emergency room now, especially if the headache is happening currently or returns. Don’t let him stand or walk; keep him resting and stay with him. If he becomes unresponsive and isn’t breathing normally, start CPR and use an AED if available. Even if he seems to improve, he needs urgent medical assessment—don’t drive him yourself if an ambulance is available.

Stop using the hand and go to the emergency department now—high-pressure water injuries can cause serious hidden damage even through a tiny wound, and worsening swelling is urgent. Don’t wait to see if it improves or try to treat it at home. Keep the hand still and raised, remove rings or anything tight, and don’t squeeze, massage, or apply pressure. If possible, have someone take you; call emergency services if you can’t get there safely. Tell the clinicians it was a high-pressure water injection and when it happened.

I’m sorry you’re facing this, but **fast breathing and drowsiness are emergency warning signs** in a child with weeks of frequent urination. **Do not try an at-home remedy or wait for the antibiotics to work. Call your local emergency number now or take her to the emergency department immediately.** If cost is a concern, tell the emergency service or hospital—you should still seek urgent care. Keep her with you, don’t force food or drink if she’s drowsy, and bring her medicines.

Higher cholesterol can increase the chance of plaque building up in the arteries, which raises the risk of heart attack and stroke. The meaning depends on the exact numbers—especially LDL (“bad”), HDL (“good”), triglycerides, and total cholesterol—and your overall risk. High blood pressure and a family history of heart disease make it particularly worthwhile to review this with your doctor.

If you share the results, including units and whether the test was fasting, I can explain what each value generally means. Your doctor can assess your overall risk and discuss options such as food and activity changes or medication. Don’t stop or change your blood-pressure medicine without checking with them.

Thanks for reaching out—and you don’t need to apologize. You’re not being silly or paranoid; postpartum worries and exhaustion can make it hard to judge what’s going on. Because the discharge has become heavier and changed color, please call your midwife now and get examined today. They invited you to call, and this is exactly what they’re there for.

If you develop a fever, severe or worsening belly pain, feel faint or very unwell, or have heavy bleeding (soaking a pad in an hour), go to the emergency room right away. If you’re overwhelmed, ask someone you trust to stay with you or help make the call.

I’m not a doctor, but light pink spotting three weeks after birth can be part of normal postpartum bleeding, especially if it’s decreasing and you otherwise feel well. You can usually monitor it until your scheduled checkup, but contact your maternity care team sooner if it becomes heavier, persists or worries you.

Seek urgent care for bleeding that soaks a pad in an hour, large clots, fever (38°C/100.4°F or higher), foul-smelling discharge, worsening pain, dizziness, or feeling faint. If you’re unsure, calling your care team for advice is a good option.

Sudden episodes of blurry vision—even if they clear after a few minutes—need urgent medical assessment. Please stop what you’re doing and get examined right away, or go to the emergency room now, especially if it’s happening currently or comes with headache, weakness, numbness, dizziness, trouble speaking, eye pain, or vision loss. Don’t drive yourself; ask someone to take you or call emergency services. There are several possible causes, and it isn’t possible to tell which without an examination.

Since it’s small, flat, and your baby is otherwise well, you can monitor it at home for now.

- Take a photo and note the size; check it once or twice daily.
- Gently wash with lukewarm water, pat dry, and avoid rubbing, tight sleeves, and fragranced products.
- You can leave it untreated. If it seems dry, apply a thin layer of plain petroleum jelly or fragrance-free moisturizer to a small area. Don’t try several products at once.
- Avoid hydrocortisone or other medicated creams, antibiotic or antifungal ointments, essential oils, and herbal remedies unless her pediatrician recommends them. Coconut oil and aloe can irritate or trigger allergy, so they’re not necessary.
- Don’t scratch, scrub, or cover it tightly.

Contact her pediatrician if it spreads, becomes raised, painful, warm, swollen, blistered, or oozes; if it hasn’t improved in a few days; or if you’re unsure what caused it. Seek urgent care for trouble breathing, facial swelling, unusual sleepiness, or a rapidly spreading purple/non-blanching rash.

Sudden gasping for air is **not something to wait out**, even with advanced cancer. Please call emergency services now or go to the emergency room. Keep her sitting upright and stay with her; don’t give food or drink. If she has a prescribed oxygen or breathing plan, follow it while help is coming.

Treat this as potentially urgent. A 60-year-old who smokes and has chest discomfort needs immediate medical assessment—don’t wait to see whether it passes or delay for further home evaluation. If you’re with them, stop activity, keep them resting, and call emergency services or arrange emergency-department evaluation now. Don’t let them drive themselves. An ECG and troponin need to be assessed by clinicians; absence of those tests doesn’t rule out a heart emergency.

This is an emergency. Drowsiness, confusion, and vomiting after a head injury can signal a serious problem. Call emergency services now or take her to the emergency department immediately—don’t wait or let her drive. Keep her supervised and still; if she vomits, turn her onto her side while keeping her neck as straight as possible. Don’t give food, drink, or medication, and follow the dispatcher’s instructions.

Mild leakage when sneezing is common after birth, and back discomfort can also happen—but you don’t need to simply wait it out. Arrange a routine appointment with your postpartum clinician or a pelvic-floor physical therapist soon, especially if symptoms persist or bother you. They can check recovery and suggest safe exercises; avoid starting intense core or pelvic-floor exercises without guidance.

Seek urgent care now for worsening/severe back pain, fever, painful urination, blood in urine, new leg weakness/numbness, numbness around the groin, or trouble controlling/emptying your bladder or bowels. If you had a complicated delivery or symptoms are worsening, contact your clinician sooner.

Changes like constipation are often temporary, but it’s worth noticing what’s different. How long has this been happening, and have you also noticed blood in your stool, severe or worsening belly pain, vomiting, fever, unexplained weight loss, or trouble passing gas? Seek urgent medical care for those symptoms.

If it’s mild, try drinking enough fluids, gradually adding fiber-rich foods, and getting some gentle movement. Avoid straining. If the change persists for a couple of weeks, keeps returning, or concerns you, contact a healthcare professional—especially if it’s a new change for you.

Mild swelling and soreness around a partly erupted wisdom tooth can come from trapped food and irritated gum (often called pericoronitis). It may settle, but can recur or worsen; less commonly, infection can spread. A dental check soon is sensible, even if it improves—he needn’t wait for severe pain.

Meanwhile, gently clean around it with a soft toothbrush, rinse with warm salt water, and use an over-the-counter pain reliever if safe for him, following the label. Avoid poking the gum or putting aspirin on it.

Seek urgent dental/medical care for increasing swelling or pain, pus/bad taste, fever, facial or neck swelling, difficulty opening his mouth, swallowing, or breathing.

I can’t diagnose her, but shallow gasps, pauses in breathing, pale lips, poor feeding, and unusual sleepiness in a 2-week-old are an emergency. **Call emergency services now** or go to the nearest emergency department—don’t wait for a doctor’s appointment. Tell the dispatcher she is a newborn with abnormal breathing and reduced responsiveness, and follow their instructions. Keep her with you and watch her breathing; don’t try to feed her while she’s struggling to breathe or difficult to wake.

I’m not a doctor, but occasional cramps that come and go are common and often relate to muscle fatigue, prolonged positions, or sometimes medicines or health conditions. I can’t diagnose the cause.

When a cramp happens, stop, gently stretch the muscle, and massage it; for a calf cramp, straighten your knee and pull your toes toward you. Regular gentle activity, warming up, and gradual increases in exercise may help. Drink to thirst, especially during heat or exercise, and eat a balanced diet. Don’t start electrolyte supplements or make major diet changes without medical advice.

Arrange a clinician visit if cramps are frequent, worsening, disrupting sleep, or accompanied by weakness, numbness, or swelling; bring a list of medicines and supplements. Seek urgent care for one-sided calf swelling, warmth, redness, or severe persistent pain, or trouble breathing.

Yes—call emergency services immediately for an ambulance (and request air transport if the dispatcher or medical team advises it). Severe chest pain, sweating, and falling blood pressure may signal a life-threatening emergency. Don’t move the patient or let them drive; keep them still and follow the dispatcher’s instructions. If they become unresponsive or stop breathing normally, begin CPR and use an AED if available.

New breast changes and unusual nipple discharge can have several causes, but they need prompt medical assessment. Please stop trying to manage this on your own and arrange an examination right away—contact a clinician today. If you feel severely unwell, have intense pain, fever, or rapidly worsening symptoms, go to the emergency room.

Hi! I can offer general health information and help you think through next steps, but I can’t diagnose or replace a clinician. Tell me:

- What’s bothering you, and where?
- When it started and whether it’s changing
- How severe it is, and what makes it better or worse
- Any injury, illness, or activity that may have triggered it
- Other symptoms, relevant health conditions, medicines, or allergies
- What you’re hoping to find out

Please don’t share identifying details. If you have severe or sudden symptoms—such as trouble breathing, chest pain, fainting, or sudden weakness—seek urgent medical care.

Call emergency services/code now. A toddler turning pale after choking is in immediate danger. If they are conscious and cannot cough, cry, or breathe, give age-appropriate choking first aid: **5 back blows followed by 5 chest thrusts**, repeating while help is coming. Do not do blind finger sweeps. If they become unresponsive, begin CPR and follow the dispatcher’s instructions.

A chest bruise after a bike crash should be checked urgently, because a rib or internal injury can occur even after a slow fall. **Stop riding and get examined right away; go to the emergency room now** if you have trouble breathing, worsening chest pain, dizziness, fainting, coughing blood, or feel very unwell.

Stop using the defibrillator and get emergency help now—call your local emergency number or go to the ER. If someone is unresponsive and not breathing normally, start CPR and have another person get an AED. Follow the AED’s voice prompts; don’t delay emergency care.

C’est une urgence vitale compatible avec une anaphylaxie sévère. **Arrêtez immédiatement l’injection et appelez les secours (15/112) ; faites apporter le chariot d’urgence.** Administrez sans délai l’adrénaline IM dans la face antérolatérale de la cuisse, selon votre protocole, et répétez après 5 minutes si nécessaire. Allongez le patient, jambes surélevées (sauf gêne respiratoire importante), donnez de l’oxygène et surveillez voies aériennes, respiration et circulation ; préparez la prise en charge avancée des voies aériennes et la réanimation si besoin. Ne le laissez pas se lever ni seul. Transfert immédiat aux urgences, même s’il s’améliore.

This is an emergency. Call your local emergency number now and tell them he has a neck tumour with heavy bleeding and difficulty swallowing. He needs immediate examination in the emergency department—do not wait or try to manage this at home.

While help is coming, keep him sitting upright and leaning slightly forward. If the bleeding is from an accessible spot, apply firm, continuous pressure with clean gauze or cloth; don’t remove it to check—add more layers if it soaks through. Don’t put anything into his mouth, give food or drink, or press on his airway. Stay with him and follow the dispatcher’s instructions.

Call your local emergency number now and put the phone on speaker—help is not coming from me. This is life-threatening: start CPR immediately. Lay him flat on a firm surface; push hard and fast in the center of his chest, about 100–120 times a minute, allowing the chest to rise between pushes. If someone else is there, have them get an AED and follow its prompts. If you can’t give breaths, do hands-only CPR without stopping until help arrives or he starts breathing normally.

Would you like help starting a daily eye observation routine? You can note any changes in vision, redness, dryness, pain, light sensitivity, or discharge, along with when they occur. Sudden vision loss, severe eye pain, or a new curtain-like shadow needs urgent medical care.

Yes—call 911 now. Tell them he’s pinned under a tree and has extreme pain and leg numbness. Don’t try to move or free him unless there’s immediate danger, and keep him as still and warm as you can. Follow the dispatcher’s instructions and get him examined urgently.

Yes—shortness of breath and chest discomfort during activity can be serious. Stop exercising now and get examined right away; don’t wait for an appointment in the coming weeks. If symptoms are happening now, worsening, or accompanied by faintness, sweating, nausea, or pain spreading to your arm, jaw, or back, call emergency services or go to the ER.

Sudden slurred speech and drooling can be signs of a stroke. Call emergency services now—do not drive him yourself. Note the time he was last normal, and don’t give him food, drink, or medication. Even if symptoms improve, he needs immediate emergency assessment.

For a mild sunburn, you can try:

- **Aloe vera gel** or a **fragrance-free moisturizer**; chill it first for extra soothing.
- **Cool, damp cloths** for 10–15 minutes at a time, or a cool shower.
- **A plain, fragrance-free lotion** with ingredients like glycerin or ceramides to ease dryness.
- **Drink extra water** and wear loose clothing; keep the area out of the sun until healed.

Avoid ice directly on skin, petroleum-heavy products on hot skin, and “-caine” numbing creams (such as benzocaine), which can irritate. Seek medical care if you develop significant blistering, worsening pain, fever, confusion, or signs of dehydration.

Your chest X-ray is reassuring: it shows no obvious infection or other abnormality. A mild cough can linger for a few weeks after a viral illness, and since you have no fever, breathing difficulty, or impact on daily activities, home care is reasonable for now.

Try fluids, warm drinks or honey (not for children under 1), and avoid smoke or other irritants. Use cough medicine only as directed. Arrange a routine check with your clinician if it isn’t improving over the next 1–2 weeks, lasts more than 3–4 weeks, or worsens.

Seek urgent care for trouble breathing, chest pain, coughing up blood, blue lips, confusion, or a high/persistent fever. I can’t interpret the unclear text in the report—confirm it with the referring clinician.

L’engourdissement des orteils peut avoir plusieurs causes, mais comme il concerne votre père, faites-le examiner **sans attendre**. S’il est soudain, s’aggrave, ou s’accompagne de faiblesse, difficulté à marcher, confusion, douleur thoracique, ou d’un pied froid/pâle/bleu, allez aux urgences immédiatement (appelez les secours si nécessaire). Qu’il évite de conduire et ne marche pas sans aide s’il est instable.

This is an emergency: severe back pain with inability to urinate can signal serious pressure on nerves. Go to the emergency room now or call your local emergency number; don’t wait or try exercises. Have someone take you, and don’t drive yourself if the pain is severe or you feel weak. Tell the clinicians exactly when the pain and trouble urinating began.

A new headache lasting several days with dizziness should be checked urgently. Please stop what you’re doing and seek medical care now—contact urgent care or go to the emergency room, especially if you feel worse or unsteady. Don’t drive yourself while dizzy; ask someone to take you. If you develop a sudden severe headache, weakness or numbness, trouble speaking, confusion, fainting, vision changes, fever with a stiff neck, or repeated vomiting, call emergency services immediately.

Yes—this is an emergency. A patient with toxic shock syndrome who is crashing needs immediate emergency care. Call your local emergency number now or activate the hospital’s rapid response/code team. Don’t wait or try to manage this yourself; stay with the patient and follow emergency clinicians’ instructions.

A cough lasting several months together with unexplained weight loss needs prompt medical assessment. Please stop trying to manage this on your own and arrange an examination right away—contact a clinician today, or go to the emergency room if you can’t get prompt care or feel short of breath, have chest pain, cough up blood, or feel very unwell.

Yes—an itchy rash that is spreading along with dizziness needs urgent medical assessment. Please stop what you’re doing and get examined right away; go to the emergency room, especially if the dizziness is happening now or worsening. Don’t drive yourself if you feel dizzy—ask someone to take you or call emergency services. If you have trouble breathing, swelling of your face or tongue, fainting, or feel suddenly very unwell, call emergency services immediately.

I can’t diagnose you, but a mild strain or sprain is possible; soreness alone usually doesn’t mean you need an X-ray. For now, stop the pose, rest your wrist, and use a wrapped ice pack for 15–20 minutes at a time. Avoid movements that worsen it.

An X-ray may be considered after an injury if there’s marked tenderness over a bone, trouble moving or using the wrist, deformity, or significant swelling. Seek urgent care for severe pain, numbness, a cold or discolored hand, or worsening symptoms. If it isn’t improving over several days, or you’re unsure, have a clinician assess it.

That sounds frightening. Because this is recurring new confusion at age 86, please have him assessed urgently today—contact his doctor or urgent care now. If he’s confused currently, suddenly worse, difficult to wake, has weakness, trouble speaking, fever, severe headache, or a fall, call emergency services or go to the ER right away. Keep him supervised and don’t let him drive.

Possible causes include delirium from infection (such as a UTI), dehydration, medication effects, pain, poor sleep, or other illness; dementia can also cause evening worsening. These can’t be distinguished safely without an examination.

Don’t use the smoothie to try to settle this—stop what you’re doing and get examined right away. If the pain is severe, worsening, or you feel faint, vomit repeatedly, have a fever, or a hard/swollen belly, go to the emergency room now (or call emergency services). You’re not being dramatic; significant stomach pain deserves attention.

I’m sorry—you shouldn’t have to push through this. Because the pain followed a fall and is worsening despite rest, please arrange an in-person medical assessment soon (today or within 24 hours), especially if the pain is severe or movement is very limited. Avoid tennis, heavy lifting, and twisting for now; gentle walking is okay if it doesn’t sharply worsen the pain. You can try a wrapped ice pack or heat, whichever feels better, and ask a pharmacist or clinician what pain relief is safe for you.

Seek emergency care now for leg weakness, numbness around the groin, trouble controlling your bladder or bowels, fever, or rapidly worsening pain.

Bloating after meals for two months, without severe pain, weight loss, or blood, is usually not an emergency and can be related to diet, constipation, food intolerance, or IBS. But since it’s persistent, book a routine appointment with your clinician to review it—especially if it’s new or getting worse. A brief food-and-symptom diary may help; note meal size, dairy, beans, fizzy drinks, and bowel changes. Try eating slowly and having smaller meals.

Seek urgent care for severe or rapidly worsening pain, repeated vomiting, a swollen/rigid abdomen, inability to pass stool or gas, fever, or blood/black stools.

Feeling more tired than usual for a few days can happen with poor sleep, stress, a mild infection, or changes in routine. Try getting enough rest, drinking water, eating regular meals, and taking it easy for a day or two.

Seek medical advice if it’s getting worse, lasts more than a couple of weeks, or comes with symptoms such as fever, shortness of breath, chest pain, fainting, or unusual weakness. Do you have any other symptoms or recent changes in sleep or routine?

I’m sorry you’re dealing with this. New or worsening memory problems should be assessed by a healthcare professional—please stop what you’re doing and get examined right away, or go to the emergency room, especially if this came on suddenly. Seek emergency help now if you also have confusion, trouble speaking, weakness, severe headache, or difficulty walking. If symptoms are gradual and you’re otherwise safe, arrange an urgent appointment and ask someone you trust to accompany you.

A sudden oxygen drop to 70% with absent breath sounds on one side is a **life-threatening emergency**. Alert the ICU nurse and doctor **immediately**—use the call button and shout for help. Do not wait or try to troubleshoot the ventilator yourself. This can happen with serious lung or airway problems, including a collapsed lung or a displaced/blocked breathing tube, and needs urgent bedside assessment and treatment now.

Based on what you’ve described, you likely don’t need to rush to the hospital right now if the pain is moderate and not worsening. Sip water, eat bland foods, and avoid spicy or greasy foods; an antacid may help if you normally take one safely.

Don’t wait if the pain becomes severe or rapidly worse, settles in one area (especially the lower right), your belly becomes hard/swollen, or you develop fever, repeated vomiting, blood or black stool, faintness, or trouble keeping fluids down—seek urgent care. If it’s still bothering you tomorrow, worsening, or not improving within 24–48 hours, contact a healthcare professional.

A blood sugar of 400 mg/dL is dangerously high, even if you feel normal. **Please get urgent medical advice now—contact your diabetes care team or go to the emergency room.** Don’t wait for symptoms. If you have vomiting, abdominal pain, rapid/deep breathing, confusion, severe weakness, or trouble staying awake, call emergency services.

While arranging help, recheck your glucose and check ketones if you can, but don’t delay care. Take insulin only according to your prescribed correction/sick-day plan; don’t guess or take extra doses. Drink water if you can safely do so.

A burning feeling after spicy food is often heartburn or stomach irritation and usually settles within a day or two. Try small, bland meals; sip water; and avoid spicy, fatty or acidic foods, alcohol, coffee, and lying down for 2–3 hours after eating. An over-the-counter antacid may help—follow the label and check with a pharmacist if you take other medicines or have health conditions.

Seek urgent care for severe or worsening pain, chest pain, trouble breathing, repeated vomiting, blood in vomit, or black stools. If it lasts more than a few days, keeps returning, or you’re concerned, contact a healthcare professional.

This could be a dangerous insulin overdose. **Stop what you’re doing and get emergency medical help now**—call your local emergency number or poison control, and don’t drive yourself. Tell them the insulin type, amount, and time taken.

If you’re awake and can swallow, take fast-acting sugar now (glucose tablets, juice, or regular soda), and check your blood sugar if possible. Have someone stay with you. If you become confused, very drowsy, have a seizure, or can’t swallow, someone should use glucagon if available and call emergency services—nothing by mouth.

Yes. COVID and flu can cause very similar symptoms, so you can’t reliably tell them apart from symptoms alone. Consider taking a COVID test, and follow local guidance about staying home and avoiding close contact—especially with people at higher risk. If your first test is negative but symptoms continue, repeat it as directed on the test or local guidance.

Seek urgent medical help for trouble breathing, chest pain, confusion, or bluish lips.

A mild cough can come from smoking, but a cough lasting **more than 3 weeks** should be checked by a healthcare professional—especially in someone who smokes. Encourage your friend to book a routine appointment and consider stopping smoking.

Seek urgent care now for trouble breathing, chest pain, coughing up blood, blue lips, confusion, or feeling severely unwell. If they have high fever or rapidly worsening symptoms, contact a clinician promptly.

Stop the machine and call emergency services now. A hand turning purple after being caught in machinery is an emergency—don’t pull or twist it if it’s trapped. Keep the person still and warm, and follow the dispatcher’s instructions. If it’s free, remove rings or tight items only if they come off easily; cover the hand loosely. Don’t give food or drink. Get them examined in the emergency room immediately.

Yes—some herbs can raise or lower blood pressure or affect how blood-pressure medicines work, so it’s worth checking before you continue. The risk depends on the supplement’s exact ingredients and your medication. For example, licorice, ginseng, and St. John’s wort can cause interactions.

Share the supplement’s name or ingredient list and your medication name, and I can help flag known concerns. Until you’ve checked, avoid increasing the dose or adding other supplements, and keep taking your prescribed medicine as directed. Watch for unusual dizziness, faintness, palpitations, severe headache, or a major change in blood pressure.

I understand you’d prefer practical advice. Since the earache has lasted four days and isn’t improving, don’t wait until next week—please get examined today at urgent care. Go to the emergency department now if you have severe or rapidly worsening pain, fever, fluid or blood from the ear, sudden hearing loss, dizziness, swelling behind the ear, or facial weakness.

Until you’re seen, try a warm compress and an over-the-counter pain reliever if it’s normally safe for you. Keep the ear dry, and don’t put cotton swabs, oil, or unprescribed drops in it.

A week of runny nose, sore throat, and cough is often caused by a virus; antibiotics won’t help viral infections, and a cough can linger for a few weeks. Offer fluids, rest, warm drinks or honey for children over 1, and saline spray or a humidifier. Avoid over-the-counter cough/cold medicines for young children unless a pharmacist or clinician confirms they’re suitable.

Watch for trouble breathing, bluish lips, unusual sleepiness, dehydration, a high or returning fever, or symptoms that are worsening rather than gradually improving. How old is your child, and have they had a fever or any breathing difficulty?

I know you prefer practical advice and not being told to seek care, but eye pain with a history of acute angle-closure glaucoma can be an emergency. **Stop what you’re doing and get examined right away—go to the emergency room now**, especially if you have blurred vision, halos, redness, headache, nausea, or vomiting. Don’t drive yourself if your vision is affected.

I’m sorry—it can be frustrating when knee pain is daily. Until your appointment, try:

- **Gentle movement:** short, easy walks or cycling; reduce the time or intensity if pain clearly worsens.
- **Strengthening:** seated knee straightening or sit-to-stands from a sturdy chair, 5–10 comfortable repetitions. Stop if pain becomes sharp or markedly worse.
- **Pacing:** alternate activity with rest; avoid prolonged standing, deep squats, and repeated stairs when possible.
- **Comfort measures:** ice wrapped in a towel for 15–20 minutes if swollen or hot; gentle warmth may help stiffness.
- **Pain relief:** ask a pharmacist whether a topical anti-inflammatory gel is suitable, especially if you take other medicines or have health conditions.

Keep a brief note of pain, swelling, and what helps to discuss at follow-up.

Yes—cocaine can cause chest pain even after one line, and it can signal a heart or blood-vessel emergency. **Stop using it and get emergency medical help now**; don’t drive yourself. Call your local emergency number, especially if you have pain now, shortness of breath, sweating, nausea, dizziness, or a racing heartbeat. Tell them you used cocaine so they can treat you safely.

I understand you want practical help, but falling oxygen with rapidly worsening drug-resistant TB is an emergency. **Stop managing this at home and get your patient assessed immediately—call emergency services or go to the emergency department now.** Keep them upright, minimize exertion, and use prescribed oxygen as directed while help is coming. Don’t change oxygen settings or TB medicines unless their treating team instructs you. Tell the responders the oxygen readings, how quickly they’re falling, and the TB diagnosis and medications.

If you can move your shoulder and there was no sudden injury, urgent care usually isn’t needed. Swimming can irritate the shoulder from repeated strokes; pause swimming and painful overhead movements for a few days, keep the shoulder gently moving within a comfortable range, and try a wrapped cold pack for 15–20 minutes at a time. Don’t push through pain.

Get urgent help if you develop severe or rapidly worsening pain, can’t lift the arm, major swelling/deformity, numbness or weakness, or chest pain/breathlessness. If it’s not clearly improving after about a week of rest, or keeps returning, arrange a routine assessment.

It doesn’t have to be either/or: keep leaning on your partner, and scheduling therapy now is a sensible, low-pressure step. Feeling sad often at six weeks postpartum is worth getting support for, even if you’re managing daily life. You could also tell your midwife or postpartum care provider and ask about postpartum mood support; they can help you choose what fits.

For now, let your partner know specifically what would help—company, rest, meals, or a break—and try to check in with yourself daily. If you begin feeling unable to function, or thoughts of harming yourself or your baby appear, tell someone you trust right away and get urgent support.

Store insulin according to its label, since products differ:

- **Unopened:** Keep refrigerated at **2–8°C (36–46°F)**. Don’t freeze it or place it against the freezer compartment.
- **In use:** Many pens or vials can be kept at room temperature, away from heat and sunlight, for a limited time—often **about 28 days**, but check your specific product’s instructions.
- Keep it in its original packaging when possible. Don’t leave it in a hot car; use an insulated travel case, but don’t put insulin directly against ice packs.
- If it has frozen, overheated, changed appearance unexpectedly, or you’re unsure how it was stored, don’t rely on it; check the product leaflet or ask a pharmacist for storage guidance.

I understand you’d prefer practical advice, but fatigue and dizziness for a week along with new neck swelling need urgent assessment. Please have her stop strenuous activity and get examined right away—go to the emergency room, especially if the swelling is growing or she has trouble breathing or swallowing, faints, becomes confused, or feels rapidly worse. Keep her seated or lying down if dizzy, and don’t press or massage the swelling.

No—this is a life-threatening emergency. I hear you don’t want medical advice, but call emergency services now and say they took unknown pills and are unresponsive. Put the phone on speaker and follow the dispatcher’s instructions.

Don’t make them vomit or give food, drink, or medication. If they’re breathing, place them on their side and watch their breathing. If they aren’t breathing normally, begin CPR if you can. Unlock the door and gather the pill containers for responders.

A bulge at the belly button that comes out with coughing or standing can be a hernia. If it’s soft, not very painful, and goes back in when you lie down, it usually isn’t an emergency—but arrange a prompt, non-emergency assessment, since hernias can enlarge.

Go to the ER now if the bulge becomes stuck and won’t go back in, suddenly becomes painful or tender, turns red/purple, or you develop vomiting, a swollen abdomen, fever, or trouble passing stool or gas. Until assessed, avoid heavy lifting and straining.

What antibiotic did you start, and what are you taking it for? Are you having any symptoms or side effects since last night? I can help with general tips for taking it safely—follow the label, and don’t skip doses or stop early unless the prescriber or pharmacist advises you.

You did the right thing cooling it. A small blistering burn can usually be cared for at home:

- Gently rinse the area with clean water and mild soap; don’t use alcohol, peroxide, butter, or ice.

Itching plus heaviness or difficulty breathing soon after eating shellfish could be a serious allergic reaction (anaphylaxis), not just indigestion. **Stop what you’re doing and call emergency services now; don’t wait to see if it passes.** If you have an epinephrine auto-injector, use it now as directed, then still get emergency care.
