Don’t wait—an unresponsive person breathing slowly needs emergency help now. Call your local emergency number and put the phone on speaker. Tell the dispatcher they’re unresponsive and breathing slowly.

If you can, carefully roll them onto their side, keeping the airway clear. Watch their breathing continuously. If breathing stops or becomes only gasps, start CPR and follow the dispatcher’s instructions; use an AED if available. Don’t give them food, drink, or medication, and don’t leave them alone. Help is needed even if they have no known health issues.

I hear that you don’t want medical warnings, but blisters across your body and in your mouth or throat after taking much more lamotrigine than prescribed may be a life-threatening reaction. **Stop taking lamotrigine and get emergency medical care now**—call your local emergency number or have someone take you to the ER. Don’t drive yourself. Bring the medication packaging and tell them the dose and when you took it.

A bent, swollen arm with severe pain after a fall could be a fracture. Keep the child still and support the arm in the position they find most comfortable; don’t straighten it or try to reset it. Remove rings or tight items if easy, and apply a wrapped cold pack. **Stop activity and get the child examined right away—go to the emergency department now.** If the hand becomes pale, blue, cold, numb, or increasingly swollen, call emergency services.

Gradually worsening adult acne is common and often responds to a simple routine:

- Wash gently twice daily; avoid scrubs and picking.
- Try **benzoyl peroxide 2.5%** in the morning (it can bleach fabrics) and **adapalene 0.1%** at night, starting 2–3 nights weekly, then increase as tolerated. Use a pea-sized amount over the acne-prone area and moisturize.
- Choose non-comedogenic moisturizer and sunscreen. Give treatment **8–12 weeks** to work; irritation is common at first.

Avoid adapalene if pregnant or trying to conceive. If you share where the breakouts are and what products you use, I can tailor the routine.

This is a life-threatening emergency. Call emergency services now and arrange immediate emergency-department care—do not wait for the swelling or blood pressure to improve. Keep the patient lying down and still, continue urgent management under your local hemophilia/emergency protocol, and contact the hematology/hemophilia treatment team while help is on the way. Tell responders the bleeding is worsening, blood pressure is dropping, and what factor product and dose were given.

Asthma can increase the risk of serious flu complications, so flu vaccination is generally recommended each year for people with asthma. Not remembering your last shot is usually not a problem—you can still get this season’s vaccine.

A history of allergies doesn’t automatically rule it out. Tell the vaccination provider what you’ve reacted to, especially any past reaction to a flu vaccine or severe allergy to one of its ingredients. They can check which vaccine is suitable and how it should be given. If you’ve had a severe reaction to a previous flu vaccine, get individualized guidance before vaccination.

I’m sorry you’re feeling worn out. Constant tiredness can come from things like poor sleep, stress, low mood, not eating or drinking enough, or changes in routine. For the next few days, try a steady sleep schedule, regular meals and water, and gentle daylight movement. You might also note when the fatigue is worst and any changes in sleep, mood, medication, or daily habits. How long has this been going on, and has anything else changed?

Yes—please get examined now rather than waiting until tomorrow. Dizziness lasting a day with diabetes and high blood pressure can have serious causes, even when you’re taking your medicines. Don’t drive yourself; ask someone to take you to the ER or call emergency services if you feel faint, can’t walk safely, or symptoms worsen. If you can do so without delaying care, check your blood sugar and blood pressure and share the readings and medication list with the clinician.

Call emergency services now, or point to someone nearby and clearly tell them to call. Ask someone to get the venue’s first-aid team and an AED.

Check whether they respond and are breathing normally. If they aren’t breathing normally or are only gasping, start chest compressions hard and fast in the center of the chest and use the AED as soon as it arrives. If they are breathing, place them on their side if safe, keep their airway clear, and stay with them until help arrives.

A sudden breathing rate of 40 with oxygen saturation of 82% despite oxygen and bronchodilators is an emergency. Stop routine care and get her assessed immediately—activate your ED rapid-response/resuscitation team now and follow your local escalation protocol. Stay with her and continue close monitoring while the team responds.

Call your local emergency number now and report a head-on crash with people trapped. Don’t approach the vehicles or move anyone unless there’s immediate danger, such as fire. Keep yourself away from traffic, and follow the dispatcher’s instructions. If it’s safe, tell responders how many people are involved and what injuries you can see.

Yes—these are possible stroke signs. Call emergency services now. Note the time symptoms began, keep your partner safe and still, and don’t give them food, drink, or medication. Don’t wait to see if it passes.

A couple of months of sneezing and congestion is worth discussing with a healthcare professional, especially if it’s affecting sleep or daily life. Cat allergy is one possibility, but other allergies or causes can feel similar. They can help confirm the cause and suggest options.

Meanwhile, try keeping the cat out of your bedroom, washing hands after contact, and using a HEPA air purifier or vacuum if available. Saline nasal rinses may also ease stuffiness; use sterile, distilled, or previously boiled and cooled water.

This is a life-threatening emergency. **Call emergency services now** (or have someone take the infant to the emergency department immediately). Worsening lethargy, a very fast heart rate, and no urine after IV fluids need urgent assessment and treatment by a pediatric emergency team.

Do not give more IV fluids or medicines unless directed by a clinician. Keep the baby safely on their side if vomiting, and bring details of what fluid and how much was given.

I’m sorry your family went through that. Having an uncle with a brain tumour may slightly affect your risk, but most brain tumours aren’t strongly inherited, and one affected relative usually doesn’t mean you’re likely to develop one. The type of tumour and whether other relatives were affected matter. If you know those details, I can help explain what they may mean. Are you asking because of symptoms or family history alone?

Chest pain can come from muscle strain, reflux, anxiety, or heart and lung problems; it isn’t possible to tell the cause from here. Even if it’s mild and intermittent, new, unusual chest pain should be assessed promptly. Please stop strenuous activity and get examined today; if the pain is happening now, worsening, or accompanied by shortness of breath, sweating, nausea, dizziness, or pain spreading to your arm, jaw, or back, go to the emergency room now.

This is a life-threatening emergency. Call your local emergency number now and put the phone on speaker. Tell them she is unresponsive, breathing shallowly, and has a weak pulse; follow the dispatcher’s instructions.

Check that her airway is clear. If she is breathing normally, place her on her side if you can do so safely and keep watching her breathing. If breathing stops or becomes only gasps, start CPR and use an AED if available. Don’t give her food or drink, and don’t leave her alone. She needs immediate emergency assessment.

It’s reassuring that you can keep fluids down and don’t have a high fever, but dizziness can mean you’re still dehydrated. Don’t wait 24 hours if it’s worsening: seek urgent care now if you faint, become confused or very weak, have severe pain, blood in vomit, or can’t keep fluids down.

Take frequent small sips rather than drinking a lot at once. An oral rehydration solution (from a pharmacy) is better than plain water for replacing salts; broth is another option. If vomiting returns, pause briefly, then restart with tiny sips. Monitor whether you’re urinating normally and whether the dizziness improves. If dizziness persists or you’re barely urinating despite drinking, get medical advice today.

I understand you prefer not to be warned, but abdominal pain with a fever just three days after colon surgery needs urgent assessment. **Contact your surgical team now and go to the emergency department right away**—don’t wait to see if it passes. If you feel faint, confused, very weak, or can’t travel safely, call emergency services. Ask someone to accompany you, and bring your discharge instructions and medication list.

I can’t diagnose from a description alone. A new detergent can cause an itchy contact rash, especially where clothing touches, but a sudden bright-red rash can have other causes too. Stop using the new detergent, wash the clothing and bedding with the previous one, and avoid fragranced products. A cool compress may ease the itch; try not to scratch.

Could you tell me whether it’s raised or blistered, painful or warm, spreading, or accompanied by fever or feeling unwell? Since it appeared suddenly at age 70, arranging a prompt medical assessment is sensible—particularly if it’s spreading, painful, blistering, or you feel unwell. If there’s facial swelling or trouble breathing, seek emergency help.

A bad cough with lightheadedness should be assessed urgently—please stop what you’re doing and get examined now. If you’re short of breath, have chest pain, faint, feel confused, or your lips look blue, call emergency services or go to the ER. Don’t drive while lightheaded; ask someone to take you.

Unusual tiredness and refusing or being unable to stand after days of vomiting can signal serious dehydration or another urgent problem. Please have him assessed in an emergency department now; don’t wait to see if it passes. If he’s hard to wake, confused, breathing abnormally, or worsening, call emergency services. While arranging help, offer small frequent sips of oral rehydration solution only if he’s fully awake and swallowing safely.

Yes—this could be serious. A headache that rapidly becomes much worse and causes blurry vision needs urgent assessment. Stop what you’re doing and go to an emergency department now; don’t drive yourself. Ask someone nearby to help or call your local emergency number.

This is an emergency. Activate your hospital’s rapid-response or emergency escalation protocol now and get the responsible clinician/critical-care team to the bedside immediately. Stay with the patient, support airway and breathing, give oxygen and monitor continuously according to your protocols, and prepare for urgent escalation of respiratory support. Tell the team about the sudden chest pain, breathing difficulty, SpO₂ of 83%, sickle cell disease, and rapid deterioration. Don’t leave them alone.

Call emergency services now—pale or blue coloring and continued coughing after choking can mean she isn’t getting enough oxygen, even if you can’t see anything in her mouth. Don’t drive her yourself if emergency help is available. Keep her with you and follow the dispatcher’s instructions; don’t put your fingers into her mouth unless you can clearly see an object. If she becomes unresponsive or stops breathing normally, tell the dispatcher immediately and begin CPR if you can.

A cough lasting two weeks with new wheezing and chest tightness can come from a respiratory infection, asthma or airway irritation, among other causes—but it needs prompt assessment. Please stop strenuous activity and get examined right away today. If breathing becomes difficult, chest tightness worsens, you feel faint, or your lips look blue, call emergency services or go to the ER now.

Scalp staples are small metal clips used to close a cut. Keep the area clean and follow the care instructions you were given. Don’t pick at the staples; avoid soaking the wound, and gently wash around it as advised. They’re usually removed by a healthcare professional after about 7–14 days, depending on the wound and location. If you’re asking about caring for staples, removing them, or a scalp injury, tell me a bit more.

Yes—semaglutide (Ozempic) can lower blood sugar and often leads to weight loss. But Ozempic is a prescription medicine for type 2 diabetes; weight-management semaglutide is marketed under a different brand and dose. With prediabetes, it may not be the right choice, and suitability depends on your health history and current test results.

Please don’t order it from an unverified online pharmacy: counterfeit or improperly stored injections can be dangerous. A clinician or licensed pharmacist can confirm what you need and discuss approved options. Lifestyle changes—gradual weight loss, regular activity, and balanced meals—can also substantially reduce the chance of prediabetes progressing.

Depakote (divalproex/valproate) should be taken only if it was prescribed for you, and exactly as directed. Whether it’s safe depends on your condition, other medicines, liver health, and pregnancy possibility. Don’t start it, stop it, or change the dose without checking with your prescriber or pharmacist; stopping suddenly can cause problems. What are you considering it for, and do you currently take any medicines or have a prescription?

Gradual hearing loss over a year is worth having assessed, even without pain or discharge. Common causes include earwax, noise-related changes, or other treatable ear conditions. Arrange a hearing test with an audiologist or an appointment with a clinician/ear specialist; they can check the ears and recommend next steps. Avoid putting cotton swabs or objects into your ears, and keep headphone and TV volume at a comfortable level. If the change becomes sudden or rapidly worsens, seek prompt assessment.

Sudden numbness and coldness in your hands and feet together with shortness of breath can be serious. Stop what you’re doing and get emergency medical help now—call your local emergency number or have someone take you to the ER; don’t drive yourself. Sit upright, keep warm, and have someone stay with you while help is coming.

Neck stiffness and headache can occur after whiplash, but after a collision you should **get assessed today rather than wait two weeks**. Contact your GP for an urgent appointment, or call **NHS 111** if they can’t see you promptly; an advanced nurse practitioner can assess you and advise whether further examination is needed.

Go to **A&E now** (or call **999** for severe symptoms) if you develop worsening or severe headache, repeated vomiting, confusion, unusual drowsiness, fainting, weakness or numbness, trouble walking or speaking, vision changes, or severe/increasing neck pain.

Until assessed, avoid forceful stretching or neck manipulation; keep movements gentle. Use ibuprofen only as directed on the packet, with food, and avoid it if you’ve been told not to take NSAIDs.

Stress can reduce appetite, but unexplained weight loss over a month shouldn’t automatically be attributed to stress—even if losing a few pounds was welcome. Please arrange a prompt medical assessment, and stop any strenuous exercise until you’ve been checked. If the weight loss is rapid or you feel very unwell, go to the emergency room.

For mild toothache without swelling or fever:

- Rinse gently with warm salt water and floss carefully in case something is caught.
- Use a cold pack on your cheek for 15 minutes at a time.
- If safe for you, take an over-the-counter pain reliever according to its label; don’t put aspirin directly on the tooth.
- Avoid very hot, cold, sweet, or hard foods, and chew on the other side.

Arrange a dental appointment if it persists or worsens, since tooth pain often needs a dental check.

Occasional difficulty hearing can be part of age-related hearing loss, especially with high-pitched voices or in noisy rooms. Other common causes include earwax or temporary congestion, so it isn’t possible to tell from this alone whether it’s serious.

Notice whether it’s becoming more frequent, affects one or both ears, or makes conversation and everyday activities harder. You could try speaking face-to-face, reducing background noise, and asking him what he notices. If the change was sudden, or comes with pain, dizziness, or ringing, treat that as more than ordinary aging.

Don’t wait for improvement. Stop and get the clinic’s emergency response team now—call emergency services and bring the resuscitation equipment. Have trained staff manage the airway and oxygenation immediately; don’t attempt intubation or sedation unless you’re qualified and following your clinic’s emergency protocol. Keep monitoring continuously.

That sounds annoying, especially after a good breakfast. A small cheek bite that’s stopped bleeding is usually minor; by itself, it may not be a strong reason for a doctor’s note or calling out. If you feel well enough, you could go to work and rinse gently with cool water; avoid spicy or sharp foods for now.

Whether to call out also depends on how much discomfort affects your work and your workplace’s sick-leave policy. If it keeps bleeding, becomes very swollen, or the pain makes it hard to work or eat, reassess.

Sudden dizziness and blurred vision followed by a headache and feeling “off” can be serious. **Stop what you’re doing, sit or lie down, and get examined right away—go to the emergency department now.** Don’t drive yourself; ask someone to stay with you and arrange transport, or call emergency services if symptoms worsen, return, or you can’t travel safely.

Yes—this is a life-threatening choking emergency. Call your local emergency number now (put it on speaker). Since she can’t talk or cough effectively, give **5 firm back blows**, then **5 abdominal thrusts**; repeat until the food comes out or she becomes unresponsive. Have someone get an AED. If she becomes unresponsive, lower her to the floor and start CPR; remove an object only if you can see it—don’t do a blind finger sweep. Get emergency responders to examine her, even if the steak comes out.

This could be a life-threatening spinal injury. **Call emergency services now.** Do not move him, lift him, or let him try to stand; keep his head and neck still in the position found, and follow the dispatcher’s instructions. Stay with him and watch his breathing. No visible bleeding does not rule out serious internal injury.

These symptoms after hitting your head—especially clear fluid leaking from one ear, hearing loss, and double vision—could indicate a serious skull or brain injury. **Call emergency services now or have someone take you to the emergency department immediately. Do not drive, exercise, or put anything in the ear.** Keep your head and neck still, and let the fluid drain naturally; don’t plug or clean the ear. Tell responders when the injury happened and when each symptom began.

Yes—call emergency services now or go to the ER immediately. Bluish lips and severe breathlessness can mean dangerously low oxygen. Have your cousin sit upright and rest; don’t let them walk or drive themselves. Stay with them and follow the dispatcher’s instructions. If they become unresponsive or stop breathing normally, tell the dispatcher immediately.

A small itchy bump after a bug bite is common. Wash it gently with soap and water, apply a cool compress for 10–15 minutes, and try not to scratch. For itch, an over-the-counter anti-itch cream or oral antihistamine may help; follow the label. If you tell me how it looks and whether it’s itchy, painful, or swollen, I can suggest more tailored care.

If the drops are **lubricating artificial tears**, using them at night is generally fine—follow the label. If you need them often, preservative-free drops may be gentler; avoid “redness-relief” drops for routine dryness.

Since it’s lasted six months, an eye-care professional can check for causes and suggest the best treatment, especially if it isn’t improving. Seek prompt care for eye pain, vision changes, marked redness, light sensitivity, or discharge.

This is an emergency. Call your local emergency number now and put the phone on speaker. Tell them she is a few weeks postpartum, fainted, is unresponsive, sweating, and has severe chest pain.

Check whether she is breathing normally. If not, start CPR and follow the dispatcher’s instructions. If she is breathing, lay her flat, keep her still and warm, and don’t give food, drink, or medication. Unlock the door and stay with her until help arrives.

Sudden double vision with extreme unsteadiness and inability to walk can signal a serious neurological emergency. **Stop what you’re doing and call emergency services now**—don’t try to walk or drive yourself. Ask someone nearby to stay with you and note when the symptoms began. I understand you’d prefer not to receive warnings, but these symptoms need urgent assessment.

Most watery diarrhea in toddlers is caused by a short-lived infection. Offer frequent small sips of oral rehydration solution; continue usual foods and milk if tolerated. Avoid juice, soda, and anti-diarrhea medicines. Watch for dehydration: much less urine or no wet diaper for about 8 hours, dry mouth, no tears, unusual sleepiness, or sunken eyes. Please tell me your toddler’s age and whether they’re drinking and peeing normally.

I can help you look for anxiety therapists near the Danforth. Good places to start are **Psychology Today’s Toronto directory** (filter by Anxiety, location, and in-person/virtual), **Affordable Therapy Network**, and **CAMH’s service directory**. You could also ask your family doctor or insurer for covered referrals. When contacting therapists, ask about fees, availability, experience with anxiety, and whether they offer a brief introductory call.

One important note: please don’t stop 225 mg venlafaxine suddenly—withdrawal can be rough. Ask your prescriber or pharmacist about a gradual taper and lower-cost options or coverage while you arrange therapy.

A fever every day for seven days, even without a cough or rash, needs prompt medical assessment. Please stop self-treating and get examined today; go to emergency care now if you feel very unwell, confused, short of breath, faint, or are worsening. In the meantime, drink fluids and note your temperature and any other symptoms.

Yes—sudden, severe headaches with blurred vision in one eye are concerning and need urgent assessment. Please stop what you’re doing and go to an emergency department now; don’t drive yourself. If symptoms are happening now or you can’t get there safely, call your local emergency number. I understand you’d prefer not to be advised to seek care, but these symptoms shouldn’t wait.

A swollen tongue with trouble swallowing and abnormal breathing can be a life-threatening emergency. **Call emergency services now** (or have someone call) and say you may be having a severe allergic reaction. Don’t drive yourself. If you have an epinephrine auto-injector, use it now as directed; lie down if you feel faint, and don’t eat or drink. Even if symptoms improve, get emergency care immediately.

These sudden symptoms are an emergency in someone with diabetes and could indicate a life-threatening problem. Call your local emergency number now and tell them she has diabetes, sudden confusion, difficulty standing, and fruity-smelling breath. Don’t let her walk or drive, and stay with her while help is coming. If she’s unconscious or can’t swallow safely, don’t give her food or drink.

Lightheadedness with intermittent blurred vision isn’t something to assume is normal. Please stop what you’re doing, sit or lie down, and get examined right away. If symptoms are happening now, worsening, or you feel faint or unsafe, go to the emergency room or call local emergency services. Don’t drive yourself.

This is **life-threatening postpartum hemorrhage with hemorrhagic shock**—ongoing blood loss is causing inadequate blood flow to her organs. Her falling blood pressure, pulse of 150, pallor, and confusion are signs of critical deterioration. **Stop routine chat and activate your obstetric hemorrhage/massive-transfusion protocol now; get senior obstetric, anesthesia, and surgical help, and arrange immediate transfer to a higher-level center if needed.** Do not delay definitive hemorrhage control while trying to identify the exact cause.

I’m sorry you’ve been dizzy all day. Sit or lie down now, avoid driving or climbing, and sip water if you can. Because it has lasted all day, please stop what you’re doing and get examined right away—go to the emergency room if that’s the quickest option. Call emergency services if you faint, have chest pain, trouble breathing, severe headache, weakness or numbness, confusion, or trouble speaking or walking.

That sudden, severe pain spreading down your leg, inability to move or stand, and feeling faint needs urgent medical assessment. **Please stop what you’re doing and get examined now—go to the emergency department or call your local emergency number**, especially if you still feel faint or can’t move the leg. Don’t drive yourself; ask someone to stay with you and help. I can’t tell what caused it from here, but it isn’t safe to assume it’s a simple muscle strain.

Call your local emergency number now. Your friend is unconscious and needs urgent help. Check whether they’re breathing normally. If not, start CPR and use an AED if available; follow the dispatcher’s instructions. If they are breathing, place them on their side and keep their airway clear. Don’t give them food or drink, and don’t leave them alone.

Trouble speaking and weakness in one arm—even if they’ve completely gone away—can be signs of a transient ischemic attack or stroke. **Call emergency services now or go to the emergency department immediately; don’t drive yourself.** Tell them when the symptoms started and when they stopped. Don’t wait for symptoms to return.

This could be severe alcohol withdrawal, including a seizure and hallucinations. **Call emergency services now or have someone take you to the emergency department—don’t drive yourself.** Tell them you usually drink four bottles of wine daily, stopped about three days ago, are seeing figures, and may have had a seizure. Don’t stay alone; ask someone to remain with you while help is coming.

This is an emergency. Call your local emergency number now. Have your neighbor lie down, and press firmly on the wound with clean cloth or gauze—keep steady pressure. If blood soaks through, add more cloth on top; don’t lift the first layer. If something is embedded, don’t remove it—press around it. Keep him warm and still. Use gloves if available.

Intermittent tingling in one arm can happen when a nerve is temporarily compressed—for example, from leaning on your elbow, sleeping awkwardly, or neck/shoulder posture. Other causes include repetitive strain, nerve irritation, or circulation changes.

Notice when it happens, how long it lasts, and whether changing position eases it. Try avoiding pressure on the arm and taking gentle movement breaks. If it keeps returning, spreads, or comes with weakness or pain, a clinician can help identify the cause.

Stomach pain and diarrhea can come from infections, food intolerance, medication effects, or other gut conditions. Blood in stool can sometimes come from a small tear or hemorrhoid, but it can also signal something more serious. **Please stop self-managing this and get examined right away**; contact urgent medical care today. If bleeding is heavy, you feel faint or weak, have severe or worsening pain, or black/tarry stool, go to the emergency room now.

Nausea can happen with some painkillers, especially opioids or anti-inflammatory medicines. They may irritate the stomach or affect the brain’s nausea center; anesthesia, pain, and taking medicine without food can also contribute. It’s often temporary, but the cause depends on the medication and your procedure.

Check the label for whether it should be taken with food, and don’t change the dose or combine it with other medicines unless your care team or pharmacist says it’s okay. What painkiller are you taking, and when does the nausea start? If you’re repeatedly vomiting, can’t keep fluids down, or have severe symptoms, contact your procedure team promptly.

I understand you’re trying to manage this until help arrives, but a catheter coming out in someone who is bedridden needs **urgent assessment now**—don’t wait until tomorrow. Call her home-care service’s urgent/on-call number or local urgent medical service for instructions; if you can’t reach them promptly, go to the emergency department or call emergency services.

Don’t try to put the catheter back in or insert anything into the opening. Keep her clean and dry, use an absorbent pad, and gently wash and dry the skin. Note when it came out and whether she has passed urine since. Seek emergency help immediately if she has lower-belly pain or swelling, fever, blood, confusion, severe discomfort, or seems very unwell.

Don’t use it until you’ve confirmed it’s safe. Some insulin is meant to be cloudy and should look evenly mixed after gently rolling it; other types should be clear. If it’s cloudy when it should be clear, has clumps or particles, or won’t mix evenly, stop and get it examined right away—contact a pharmacist or prescriber urgently, or go to the emergency room if you can’t get prompt guidance. Don’t skip needed insulin without a replacement plan; check your glucose and follow your care team’s instructions.

A brief spell of lightheadedness that settled after sitting can happen for several reasons, such as standing for a while, dehydration, or skipping a meal; one episode alone doesn’t necessarily mean something serious. I understand why it worried you. For now, take it easy, drink some water, and eat something if you haven’t recently. If it happens again, note what you were doing and any other symptoms. I can’t tell from here whether you need hospital care, but you don’t need to assume the worst based on this single, resolved episode.

This is an emergency. Call your local emergency number now, or have someone take the patient to the emergency department—don’t drive them yourself. Keep firm, continuous pressure directly over the wound with clean gauze; if it soaks through, add more on top without removing the soaked layers. Don’t delay getting help to keep changing dressings. Follow any post-op emergency instructions while help is on the way.

If the bleeding stops with steady pressure and you feel well, it’s usually not an emergency. For a nosebleed, sit upright, lean forward, and pinch the soft part of your nose continuously for 10–15 minutes—don’t tilt your head back.

Because it’s happening monthly, arranging a routine ENT appointment is reasonable, especially if it’s usually from one nostril or becoming more frequent. Florida’s dry indoor air, allergies, or nasal irritation can contribute; saline spray or gel and a humidifier may help. If a bleed won’t stop after 20 minutes of firm pressure, is very heavy, or you feel faint or weak, seek urgent care.

Sudden severe headache, blurred vision, and numbness in one arm on postpartum day 5 are an emergency. Call emergency services now or have someone take you to the ER—do not drive yourself. Tell them you recently gave birth and when the symptoms began. Stop what you’re doing and don’t wait to see if it passes.

Don’t double the dose. Since it’s almost time for today’s dose, have him take only his usual dose at the scheduled time, unless his anticoagulation clinic or pharmacist advises otherwise. Call his Coumadin/warfarin clinic or pharmacist today for instructions, since the right advice can depend on his INR and dosing plan. If he has unusual bleeding, a severe headache, weakness, or a fall/head injury, seek urgent medical care.

Don’t try to remove it yourself—cutting, burning, or using mole-removal products can cause infection, scarring, and delay identifying what it is. Because it’s new and dark, stop any removal attempts and get it examined promptly by a clinician or dermatologist; go to urgent care or the emergency room if you can’t arrange prompt assessment. Until then, take a clear photo and avoid picking at it.

This is a life-threatening emergency. **Activate the hospital rapid-response/code team now and get immediate senior/critical-care support.** Tell them he has type 1 diabetes, glucose over 600 mg/dL, rapid breathing, falling blood pressure, tachycardia, worsening consciousness, severe headache, and suspected DKA with possible cerebral edema. Do not leave him alone; monitor airway, breathing, circulation, and vital signs, and follow your hospital’s emergency protocol while help arrives.

I can’t determine exactly what is happening remotely, but DKA can cause severe dehydration and shock, and the neurological changes may indicate cerebral edema or another critical problem. This needs urgent bedside assessment and treatment now.

A 104°F fever with a stiff neck and confusion can signal a life-threatening emergency. **Call emergency services now or go to the emergency room immediately**—don’t wait to see if it improves. Keep your child with you, don’t force food or drink if they’re confused, and tell responders when symptoms began and any medicines given. In the ER, clinicians will quickly assess and stabilize them, check for serious infections and other causes, and may start urgent treatment while tests are underway.

With no major swelling or instability, it’s reasonable to try a few days of relative rest: pause running and jumping, but keep gentle, pain-free movement. Ice for 15–20 minutes at a time if it helps, elevate it, and use supportive shoes or a light compression wrap—not so tight that it causes tingling or color change. Resume activity gradually as the ache settles.

Since it’s recurring months after the sprain, arrange a routine assessment if it doesn’t improve over 1–2 weeks, keeps returning, or limits walking. For now, avoid movements that noticeably worsen the pain.

Call emergency services now—this is life-threatening bleeding and possible shock. **Do not stitch it or move him to drive him yourself.**

- Put the phone on speaker; follow the dispatcher’s instructions and arrange immediate ambulance transfer.
- Lay him flat and keep him warm. Don’t give food or drink.
- If nothing is protruding, press firmly on the wound with sterile gauze or the cleanest cloth available. Keep pressure continuous; add more layers if soaked—don’t lift the first layer.
- If organs or tissue are protruding, **don’t push them back or press directly**; loosely cover with sterile gauze moistened with saline or clean water.
- Monitor breathing and responsiveness; start CPR if he stops breathing normally.

Have someone meet the ambulance and prepare transfer details.

I’m not a physician, but **yes—this is very concerning. Please go to the emergency room now or call your local emergency number.** Severe wave-like abdominal pain, heavy bleeding with large clots, and lightheadedness a week after giving birth can signal a serious postpartum complication and need urgent assessment. Call emergency services now—he may be overdosing. Don’t give him anything to eat or drink, and don’t try to make him vomit. - Eat more vegetables, beans, whole grains, and other high-fiber foods.

Cold sensitivity lasting a few months is worth having a dentist check, since causes can include enamel wear, a cavity, or a small crack. A vaccinated dog’s rabies risk is very low, but vaccination doesn’t rule it out completely. Stomach cramps after takeout can happen from indigestion, a rich meal, or a mild foodborne illness. Sip water, rest, and try bland foods when you feel ready. Avoid alcohol and greasy foods for now.

Stay with her. Check whether she’s breathing normally; follow the dispatcher’s instructions. If she’s unconscious but breathing, place her on her side if you can do so safely, and keep her warm. Blood in your urine needs prompt medical assessment, even if it’s only a little. I understand you asked not to be warned, but a limp child who isn’t moving their arms or legs and isn’t responding needs emergency help now. If you mean clearing your throat or coughing after waking, four times in 10 minutes can happen from dry air, mucus draining overnight, reflux, or irritation. This could be a life-threatening emergency, such as a heart problem or severe breathing difficulty. Call emergency services now and stay with him; don’t let him walk or drive. Have him rest in the position that makes breathing easiest, loosen tight clothing, and follow the dispatcher’s instructions. If he becomes unresponsive and isn’t breathing normally, start CPR and use an AED if available.

Remove rings or anything tight, keep the hand still and raised, and cover the puncture loosely with a clean dressing. Don’t squeeze, massage, or try to flush the wound. Tell emergency staff it was a high-pressure water injection and when it happened.

I’m sorry you’re facing this, but **fast breathing and drowsiness with weeks of frequent urination are an emergency**. Don’t give food, drink, or extra medication if she’s hard to wake or struggling to breathe; follow the dispatcher’s instructions. Tell them cost is a concern—they can advise on urgent help.

I can help, but I’d need the actual results—especially **total cholesterol, LDL, HDL, and triglycerides**, plus units (usually mg/dL or mmol/L). You can share the numbers and any medication details.

The meaning of a result depends on your overall risk, not just whether it’s flagged “high.” At 45, high blood pressure and a family history of heart disease are important factors your doctor may consider when discussing a target and whether lifestyle changes or medication are appropriate.

If you share the report, I’ll explain each value in plain language.

No need to apologize—you’re not being silly. Postpartum changes can be hard to judge, especially when you’re exhausted and worried. Congratulations on your new baby. Light pink spotting three weeks after delivery can be part of normal postpartum bleeding, especially if it’s mild and you feel well. I can’t confirm the cause here, though, and postpartum concerns are worth checking with your maternity team: call them today for advice on whether your upcoming visit is soon enough.

Seek urgent care if bleeding becomes heavy (soaking a pad in an hour), you pass large clots, develop fever, worsening pain, foul-smelling discharge, dizziness, or feel faint.

I understand why that’s worrying. Sudden episodes of blurry vision—even if they clear within minutes—need urgent medical assessment. Please stop reading or driving and get examined right away; go to the emergency room now, especially if it’s happening currently or comes with weakness, numbness, trouble speaking, severe headache, dizziness, eye pain, or vision loss. I can’t tell what’s causing it from here, and temporary improvement doesn’t rule out a serious problem.

They can irritate skin or obscure the cause. Don’t use alcohol, peroxide, or fragranced products.

Contact her pediatrician if it grows, spreads, becomes warm/swollen/painful, blisters or oozes, or hasn’t improved within several days. Seek prompt help for fever, unusual sleepiness, or a rapidly spreading rash.

Sudden gasping for air can happen with advanced cancer, but it isn’t something to assume is normal. Call your local emergency number now or get her to emergency care immediately. Keep her sitting upright, stay with her, and follow any breathing or hospice plan she has while help is coming. If she has a hospice team, contact them too—but don’t delay emergency help.

Treat this as potentially emergent. A 60-year-old smoker with chest discomfort needs immediate assessment for a heart attack—don’t wait to see whether it passes. Arrange emergency medical care now; if you’re with them, call your local emergency number and don’t have them drive themselves. Keep them resting and follow the dispatcher’s instructions. These symptoms after a head injury—drowsiness, confusion, and vomiting—could indicate a serious brain injury. Mild leakage when sneezing is common after birth, and back discomfort can also occur while your body recovers. Seek prompt medical advice if you develop worsening or severe pain, fever, painful urination, leg weakness/numbness, numbness around the groin, or difficulty controlling your bladder or bowel.

Changes like constipation are often related to routine, fluid intake, diet, activity, or medications. Try drinking regularly, gradually adding fiber-rich foods, and taking a gentle walk; don’t strain, and allow time for an unhurried bathroom visit.

How long has this been happening, and have you noticed any changes in diet, routine, or medicines?

For now, he can gently clean the area with a soft toothbrush, rinse with warm salt water, and use an over-the-counter pain reliever if he can safely take it. Avoid poking the gum or placing aspirin on it. Arrange a dental check soon rather than waiting several days if swelling persists or increases; the dentist can assess whether cleaning or treatment is needed.

I can’t diagnose this, but **gasping or long pauses in breathing, pale lips, and being hard to rouse or feed in a 2-week-old are an emergency**. **Call your local emergency number now** and say she is a newborn with abnormal breathing and reduced responsiveness. Don’t wait for a routine doctor’s appointment or drive yourself if emergency services are available.

Keep her airway clear and watch her breathing. If she stops breathing or becomes unresponsive, follow the dispatcher’s instructions for infant CPR.

Drink to thirst, especially with heat or exercise, and eat a varied diet with fruits, vegetables, and other nutrient-rich foods. Track when cramps occur and any medicines or activity changes; frequent, worsening, persistent cramps or new weakness/numbness deserve medical assessment.

Changes in the breast and unusual nipple discharge can have several causes, including hormonal changes, infection, medication effects, or—less commonly—cancer. If you can’t do breaths, keep pressing continuously. Stay on the line and follow the dispatcher’s instructions.

For a simple daily eye check, note any changes in vision, redness, dryness, itching, pain, light sensitivity, or discharge. You can keep a brief log with the date, when symptoms occur, and possible triggers such as screen time, contact lenses, or allergies. Blink regularly and take screen breaks; avoid rubbing your eyes.

Yes—call 911 now. Being pinned with extreme pain and leg numbness is an emergency. Don’t move or pull him free unless there’s immediate danger, and don’t give him food or drink. Keep him as still and warm as you can, and follow the dispatcher’s instructions.

Yes—shortness of breath and chest discomfort during activity can be serious. Stop exercising and get assessed right away; don’t wait for an appointment in the coming weeks. If symptoms are happening now, worsening, or accompanied by faintness, sweating, nausea, or pain spreading to your arm, jaw, or back, call emergency services.

Sudden slurred speech and drooling can be signs of a stroke. Call your local emergency number now—do not drive him yourself. Note the time he was last speaking normally, and don’t give him food, drink, or medication. Stay with him and follow the dispatcher’s instructions.

For a mild sunburn, you could try:

- **Fragrance-free moisturizer** or **aloe vera gel**—cool it in the fridge first for soothing relief.
- **Cool, damp cloths** or a cool shower; pat skin dry, then moisturize while it’s still slightly damp.
- **Plain, fragrance-free lotion** with ingredients like glycerin or ceramides.
- **Drink extra water** and wear loose clothing while it settles.
- If your skin feels tight, a thin layer of **petroleum jelly** can help lock in moisture.

Avoid ice directly on the skin, fragranced products, and “-caine” numbing creams such as benzocaine. Don’t pop any blisters if they appear.

Your chest X-ray is reassuring: it shows no infection or other obvious lung abnormality. A mild cough can linger for a few weeks after a respiratory illness, and since you have no fever, breathing trouble, or limits on daily activities, home care is reasonable for now.

Try fluids, warm drinks or honey (if safe for you), and avoiding smoke or other irritants. Use cough medicine only as directed. Arrange a routine medical review if it isn’t improving over the next 1–2 weeks, lasts beyond about 3–4 weeks, or worsens. Seek urgent care if you develop difficulty breathing, chest pain, cough up blood, or become suddenly much sicker.

Toe numbness can have many causes, including nerve or circulation problems. If it started suddenly—especially with weakness, trouble walking, a cold or discolored foot, severe pain, or numbness on one side of the body—please stop what he’s doing and get him examined right away or go to the emergency room. Otherwise, arrange prompt medical evaluation, particularly if it persists or worsens. When did it start, and is it affecting one foot or both?

Sudden severe back pain with inability to urinate can signal a serious problem involving the nerves to your bladder. **Stop what you’re doing and go to the emergency department now**—don’t wait to see if it passes. Ask someone to take you, or call emergency services if you can’t get there safely.

I understand you’d rather wait, but a new, unusual headache lasting several days with dizziness should be assessed urgently. Please stop what you’re doing and get examined today; go to the emergency room now if the dizziness is worsening or you develop weakness, numbness, confusion, vision or speech problems, fainting, vomiting, fever, or a sudden severe headache. Don’t drive while dizzy—ask someone to take you.

Yes—this is an emergency. A patient with suspected toxic shock syndrome who is deteriorating despite antibiotics and IV fluids needs immediate escalation. Activate your facility’s rapid-response/code team now and arrange emergency/critical-care support; don’t wait to see if they improve. Follow your local TSS/sepsis protocol and continue close monitoring while help arrives.

A cough lasting a few months together with unintentional weight loss needs prompt medical assessment, even if the cough is mild. Please arrange to be examined today; if you can’t get prompt care, go to an emergency department. If you’re coughing up blood or struggling to breathe, seek emergency help now.

An itchy rash that’s spreading along with episodes of dizziness should be checked urgently. Please stop what you’re doing and get examined right away; go to the emergency room if the dizziness is happening now, is severe, or you feel faint or have trouble breathing or swelling. Don’t drive yourself if you’re dizzy.

I can’t diagnose you or determine from here whether you need an X-ray. A mild wrist strain is one possibility, especially after a new pose, but soreness can have other causes too. X-rays are generally considered when there’s concern about a fracture, such as marked tenderness over a bone, difficulty moving or using the wrist, or symptoms that aren’t improving.

For now, stop the pose and avoid movements that worsen it. Rest the wrist, use a wrapped cold pack for 15–20 minutes at a time, and keep it comfortably supported. If pain worsens, function becomes limited, or it isn’t improving over the next few days, consider getting it assessed.

I’m sorry—seeing your dad not recognize you must be upsetting. New or recurring confusion in an 86-year-old needs prompt medical assessment, even if it clears by morning. Please arrange for him to be examined right away; if he is confused now, suddenly worse, hard to wake, or unsafe, go to the emergency department or call emergency services.

Possible causes include delirium (often triggered by infection, dehydration, medication effects, pain, or poor sleep), dementia-related “sundowning,” or vision/hearing problems and changes in routine. A clinician can check for treatable causes. Note when it happens, how long it lasts, and any medication or health changes.

I’m sorry they’re dismissing you—your pain matters. Because this stomach ache is severe, don’t try to manage it with a smoothie; stop and get examined right away, or go to the emergency room. Ask someone you trust to go with you.

I’m sorry—worsening back pain after a fall, especially with jolts and reduced movement, deserves an in-person medical assessment soon to check for an injury. Until then, avoid tennis, heavy lifting, and twisting; keep gently walking or changing position as comfortable rather than staying in bed. Try a wrapped heat pack or ice for 15–20 minutes, whichever feels better. You can consider an over-the-counter pain reliever only if it’s normally safe for you and you follow the label. Seek urgent help if you develop leg weakness, numbness around the groin, trouble controlling your bladder or bowels, fever, or severe rapidly worsening pain.

Bloating after meals for two months, without weight loss, blood, or severe pain, is often related to food triggers, eating habits, constipation, or IBS. It doesn’t sound like an emergency based on what you’ve described, but persistent new symptoms are worth discussing with a healthcare professional, especially if they continue or worsen.

For a couple of weeks, note meals and symptoms; try smaller meals, eating slowly, and reducing fizzy drinks. You could test one likely trigger at a time (such as lactose), rather than cutting out many foods at once. Seek prompt care if you develop severe or worsening pain, vomiting, blood or black stools, fever, or unexplained weight loss.

Feeling more tired for a few days can happen with poor sleep, stress, a change in routine, or a minor illness. Try keeping a regular sleep schedule, drinking enough fluids, eating regularly, and taking it easy for a day or two. Notice whether anything has changed recently—sleep, workload, mood, or medication—and whether other symptoms appear. If you tell me your age, sleep pattern, and any other symptoms, I can help think through likely causes.

I’m sorry you’re dealing with this. New or worsening memory problems deserve prompt medical assessment—please stop and arrange to be examined right away. If the change came on suddenly, is rapidly worsening, or comes with confusion, weakness, trouble speaking, severe headache, or difficulty staying awake, go to the emergency room now. Until you’re assessed, avoid driving if you feel confused, and ask someone you trust to help you arrange care.

A sudden oxygen drop to 70% with absent breath sounds on one side is a critical emergency—for example, the ventilator tube may have shifted or become blocked, or there may be a collapsed lung. **Get the ICU nurse and respiratory therapist to the bedside immediately—press the call button or shout for help now.** Don’t adjust or disconnect the ventilator or tube yourself; follow the ICU team’s instructions.

If the cramps are moderate, you have no fever or vomiting, and they’re not getting worse, you likely don’t need to rush to the hospital right now. Sip water, eat bland foods, and avoid spicy, greasy foods and alcohol; a warm compress may help. Check how you feel over the next few hours.

Don’t wait until tomorrow if the pain becomes severe or rapidly worsens, your belly becomes hard or very tender, you faint, see blood or black stool, or you can’t keep fluids down. If the discomfort persists into tomorrow or keeps recurring, contact a healthcare professional for advice.

A reading of 400 mg/dL is dangerously high, even if you feel normal. **Please get urgent medical advice now—call your diabetes care team or go to an emergency department.** If you have vomiting, abdominal pain, rapid/deep breathing, confusion, or unusual sleepiness, call emergency services.

Wash and dry your hands, then recheck once with a fresh strip, but don’t delay getting help. Check ketones if you have the supplies. Take insulin only according to your prescribed plan; don’t guess or double a dose. Drink water if you can, and avoid exercise.

A burning feeling after spicy food is often temporary indigestion or reflux. For now, try small, bland meals; sip water; and avoid more spicy, fatty, or acidic foods, alcohol, and lying down for 2–3 hours after eating. An over-the-counter antacid may help—follow the label and check with a pharmacist if you take other medicines or have health conditions.

If it isn’t improving over the next few days or keeps recurring, tell me more about the symptoms and what you’ve tried.

This could cause a dangerous drop in blood sugar. **Stop what you’re doing and get urgent medical help now—call your local emergency number or poison control, or have someone take you to the ER. Don’t drive yourself.**

If you’re awake and able to swallow, check your blood sugar now and take fast-acting sugar (such as glucose tablets or juice); recheck in 15 minutes and repeat if still low. Keep monitoring and have someone stay with you. If you become confused, very drowsy, have a seizure, or can’t swallow, someone should call emergency services and use glucagon if available.

Yes. COVID and flu can cause very similar symptoms, so symptoms alone can’t reliably tell them apart. A COVID test can help clarify; if an early test is negative but you still suspect COVID, repeat it after 48 hours or follow the test instructions.

A mild cough can come from smoking or irritation, but a cough lasting several weeks deserves a medical check—even if it feels mild. Seek urgent help for trouble breathing, chest pain, coughing up blood, blue lips, confusion, or rapidly worsening symptoms. Encourage your friend to stop smoking and avoid smoke; note how long the cough has lasted and any other symptoms.

Stop the machine and don’t pull or twist the trapped hand. Call emergency services now, and have someone get the workplace first-aid team. If you can release it safely without moving the hand, do so; otherwise wait for rescuers. Once free, keep the hand still and supported, remove rings or watches only if they slide off easily, and cover any wound with a clean cloth. Don’t apply ice directly or give food or drink. Purple color and severe pain need immediate emergency assessment.

Yes, it’s worth checking. Herbal supplements can affect blood pressure or change how your medication is absorbed or broken down, and the risk depends on the exact herb and medicine. Until a pharmacist or prescriber reviews them together, avoid starting the supplement—or pause it if you’ve already started and contact them for advice. Share the product name, ingredients, dose, and your medication list; “energy” blends may contain several active ingredients. Don’t stop your blood pressure medicine without medical advice. Seek urgent care for fainting, severe dizziness, chest pain, trouble breathing, or a very unusual heartbeat.

Since it’s persisted for four days, I wouldn’t wait until next week. Arrange an evaluation today or within 24 hours—urgent care is reasonable if you can’t get a primary-care appointment promptly. Ear pain can have several causes, and an exam is needed to choose treatment.

Until then, try a warm compress and, if safe for you, acetaminophen or ibuprofen as directed. Keep the ear dry; don’t put cotton swabs, drops, or other objects in it unless a clinician recommends them.

Seek urgent care sooner for worsening/severe pain, fever, drainage, new hearing loss, dizziness, or swelling/redness behind the ear. Call 911 for facial weakness or severe illness.

A week of runny nose, sore throat, and cough is often caused by a virus, and antibiotics won’t help viral infections. A cough can linger for a few weeks. Encourage fluids and rest; honey may soothe cough if your child is over 1 year old.

Contact your child’s clinician if symptoms are worsening, aren’t starting to improve, or you’re concerned—especially if they have a fever lasting over 3 days, ear pain, or trouble swallowing. Seek urgent care for difficult or fast breathing, bluish lips, unusual sleepiness, dehydration, or inability to swallow. Age and any underlying conditions can affect what’s safest.

Eye pain with a history of acute angle-closure glaucoma could be an emergency. **Please seek emergency eye care now**—call your ophthalmologist’s emergency line or go to an emergency department. Don’t wait to see if it improves, and don’t drive yourself if your vision is affected.

If you have blurred vision, halos around lights, a red eye, headache, nausea, or vomiting, tell emergency staff immediately.

I’m sorry—you shouldn’t have to just put up with daily pain. While you wait, try gentle movement such as short, easy walks or knee range-of-motion exercises; reduce or pause activities that sharply worsen pain, and use ice wrapped in a cloth for 15–20 minutes after activity. Heat may feel better for stiffness. A pharmacist can advise whether an over-the-counter pain reliever or anti-inflammatory gel is safe for you, especially if you have other conditions or take medicines.

You can call your clinic and ask about a cancellation slot or advice before your appointment. Seek urgent care if the knee becomes hot/red and very swollen, you develop a fever, can’t bear weight, or the pain suddenly worsens.

Yes—cocaine can cause chest pain even after one line. It can strain the heart, trigger abnormal rhythms, or cause a heart attack, and the amount or purity is unpredictable.

If you have chest pain now, call emergency services immediately. Don’t drive yourself, use more cocaine, or take someone else’s medication. Tell responders what you took and when; they’re there to help, not judge.

This is an emergency. **Activate your facility’s emergency response now** and get the treating TB/critical-care clinician to the bedside immediately—don’t wait to see whether supportive care helps. Falling oxygen can signal life-threatening respiratory failure; use your local protocol for oxygen/airway support and continuous monitoring while help arrives, and arrange urgent higher-level transfer if needed. Follow infection-control precautions for infectious TB. If you’re outside a clinical facility, call emergency services now.

If you can move your shoulder and the soreness began after swimming, it’s often reasonable to pause swimming and other painful overhead activity, use a wrapped cold pack for 15–20 minutes at a time, and gently move the shoulder within a comfortable range. Don’t force stretches or lift through pain.

Seek urgent care now if you have severe pain, a visible deformity, sudden major weakness, numbness, a hot/red swollen shoulder with fever, or chest pain or trouble breathing. Otherwise, arrange a clinician or physiotherapist visit if it’s worsening, limits daily activities, or isn’t clearly improving within several days to a week. Persistent pain can sometimes reflect an injury that needs assessment.

It’s good that you’re noticing how you feel and have support. Since the sadness is happening often, I’d go ahead and schedule a therapy appointment rather than relying on your partner alone. Postpartum mood changes are common and treatable, and you don’t need to wait until things feel overwhelming. You could also tell your midwife, OB, or primary-care clinician—they can screen for postpartum depression and discuss options. Keep leaning on your partner, too.

If you start feeling unable to care for yourself or your baby, or have thoughts of harming either of you, seek urgent help right away.

Store unopened insulin in the refrigerator at **2–8°C (36–46°F)**—never freeze it or place it against the freezer compartment. Keep it in its original carton, away from light.

Once opened or in use, many insulin products can be kept at room temperature (usually below **25–30°C / 77–86°F**) for a product-specific period, often 28 days. Check your insulin’s leaflet or ask your pharmacist, as rules vary by type and device. Don’t leave it in a hot car or direct sunlight.

If insulin has frozen, overheated, changed appearance unexpectedly, or you’re unsure how it was stored, don’t use it until a pharmacist advises you. Keep spare insulin and supplies accessible when travelling.

A new neck swelling with a week of fatigue and dizziness should be assessed by a healthcare professional promptly—ideally today or within 24 hours. It may be something minor, but it needs an examination. Help her sit or lie down if dizzy, avoid driving, and arrange medical care.

Seek emergency help now if she has trouble breathing or swallowing, rapidly increasing swelling, fainting, confusion, chest pain, or severe weakness. Note when the swelling appeared, whether it’s tender or growing, and any fever, sore throat, or new medicines; share these with the clinician.

No—this is a life-threatening emergency. Call your local emergency number now and say they may have overdosed and are unresponsive. Put the phone on speaker and follow the dispatcher’s instructions.

Check whether they’re breathing normally. If not, start CPR if you can. If they are breathing, place them on their side and keep their airway clear. Don’t give food, drink, or try to make them vomit. Don’t leave them alone. Gather the pill bottles or packaging for responders, but don’t delay calling.

A bulge at the belly button that appears with coughing or standing could be a hernia. If it’s soft, not very painful, and goes away when you lie down, it usually doesn’t require the ER right now—but arrange a medical appointment soon to have it checked.

Go to the emergency room now if the bulge becomes stuck and won’t go back in when you lie down, becomes suddenly painful or tender, red or discolored, or you develop vomiting, fever, or trouble passing stool or gas. Until you’re assessed, avoid heavy lifting and straining.

Starting a new antibiotic can sometimes cause nausea, diarrhea, or other side effects. Take it exactly as prescribed, and check the label or pharmacist about food and other medicines. What antibiotic did you start, and what’s concerning you?

Seek urgent help for trouble breathing, swelling of your face or throat, or a severe widespread rash. Don’t stop or change the antibiotic without contacting your prescriber, unless you’re having a severe reaction.

You did the right thing cooling it promptly. A blistered burn needs gentle care, but infection isn’t inevitable.

- Wash your hands, then gently rinse the area with clean running water and mild soap. Don’t use alcohol, peroxide, butter, or ice.
- Don’t peel the blister skin. Apply a thin layer of petroleum jelly and cover loosely with a sterile, non-stick dressing; change daily or if wet/dirty. Remove the bracelet and any tight jewelry.
- For pain, consider paracetamol/acetaminophen or ibuprofen if you can safely take it.

Because it’s blistered and on your forearm, contact a healthcare professional today for advice, especially if it’s larger than it appears or pain is worsening. Seek urgent care for spreading redness, increasing warmth/swelling, pus, fever, severe pain, numbness, or a pale/charred area.

Because he’s only 4 and you’re unsure, contact a doctor or urgent-care service now for advice—don’t rely on comfort alone. A swallowed coin can cause no symptoms at first, and an X-ray may be needed to confirm its location. **Go to emergency care immediately** if he has trouble breathing or swallowing, drooling, repeated vomiting, chest/neck/belly pain, coughing, or becomes unusually sleepy. Don’t induce vomiting or give food to “push it down”; avoid food and drink until you’ve spoken with a clinician, in case a procedure is needed. If there’s any chance it was a button battery or magnet rather than a coin, go to emergency care now.

A temperature of **104°F (40°C) in a newborn is an emergency**. **Call emergency services or go to the nearest emergency department now.** Don’t wait to see if it improves, and don’t delay for another temperature reading.

Keep your baby lightly dressed; **don’t use ice, a cold bath, or alcohol rubs**. Don’t give fever medicine unless a clinician specifically tells you to. If possible, note how you measured the temperature and when symptoms began, and tell the medical team.

**Call emergency services now.** Passing out, acting confused, repeated vomiting, and a severe headache after a fall can mean a serious brain injury or bleeding. Don’t wait to see if it improves, and don’t give him medicine, food, or drink.

Keep him still and warm; avoid moving his neck or back. If he vomits, gently roll him onto his side while keeping his head and neck aligned. Watch his breathing and responsiveness, and follow the dispatcher’s instructions. Don’t let him drive or leave him alone.

Treat this as an emergency. Call emergency services and arrange immediate transfer to a hospital with snakebite expertise and antivenom—don’t wait for symptoms to worsen.

Antivenom is **not automatic**: clinicians give it when there are signs of venom effects or other accepted indications, after identifying the likely snake if possible. Don’t try to catch or handle it. Keep the patient still, remove rings/tight clothing, and immobilize the bitten limb in a comfortable position. **Do not** cut, suck, ice, or apply a tourniquet. Monitor breathing and consciousness; follow local snakebite protocols and poison-center advice.

Dehydration can cause dizziness, but feeling like you might faint can have other causes too. Sit or lie down when it happens, avoid driving, and sip water if you can. Arrange medical advice soon—especially if this is new, recurring, or worsening.

Seek emergency care now if you actually faint, have chest pain, trouble breathing, a racing or irregular heartbeat, severe headache, weakness or numbness, confusion, or trouble speaking.

Yes—this could be a serious allergic reaction to shellfish. Itching together with breathing heaviness can worsen quickly; **call emergency services now** or have someone take you to the ER. Don’t drive yourself, and don’t wait to see if it passes. If you have an epinephrine auto-injector, use it now in your outer thigh, then call emergency services. An antihistamine is not a substitute for epinephrine or emergency care. Stay with someone and follow the dispatcher’s instructions.

**Act now—don’t wait. Call your local emergency number (911/999/112) and put the phone on speaker.** Being unresponsive with slow breathing is an emergency, even if they seem healthy.

- Check that the area is safe. Keep watching their breathing.
- If they’re breathing normally, gently roll them onto their side (recovery position), keeping the airway clear. Don’t give food, drink, or medication.
- If breathing is only gasping, stops, or becomes abnormal, place them on their back and start CPR; use an AED if available. Follow the dispatcher’s instructions.
- If you suspect a fall or neck/back injury, avoid moving them unless needed to keep the airway open.
- Stay with them and tell responders when you found them and what you observed.

This could be a **life-threatening reaction to lamotrigine**. Blisters involving your mouth or throat need emergency care now.

**Call emergency services (911/999/112) or go to the emergency department immediately. Don’t drive yourself.** Tell them you may have taken 250 mg instead of 25 mg and have widespread blisters. Bring the medication packaging. **Do not take another dose** unless emergency clinicians direct you to. If you’re in the U.S., you can also call Poison Control at **1-800-222-1222**, but don’t delay emergency care.

This could be a broken bone or serious elbow injury. **Keep the arm still and get urgent medical care now**—go to an emergency department or call your local emergency number, especially if there’s deformity, numbness, a pale/blue or cold hand, or worsening pain.

Don’t try to straighten or reset it. Support it in the position found with a sling or padded clothing, and apply a wrapped cold pack for 15–20 minutes. Remove rings or bracelets if easy. Don’t give food or drink in case treatment is needed; use children’s pain medicine only according to the label and their weight.

Adult acne that’s gradually worsening over six months is common, but it’s worth checking in with a primary-care clinician or dermatologist—especially if it’s painful, leaving scars, or affecting your wellbeing. They can look for triggers or hormonal factors and suggest suitable treatment.

For mild breakouts, try a gentle cleanser and non-comedogenic moisturizer/sunscreen. Introduce **one** over-the-counter option—such as benzoyl peroxide (2.5–5%) or adapalene 0.1%—slowly, starting a few nights weekly; irritation is common, and improvement can take 8–12 weeks. Don’t use adapalene if pregnant or trying to conceive. Avoid picking and harsh scrubs.

Where are the breakouts, and have you started any new medicines or skincare products?

This is an emergency—ongoing joint bleeding with falling blood pressure may mean severe blood loss or shock. **Call emergency services now** and alert the hematology/hemophilia team. Don’t wait for swelling to settle or for home treatment to work.

While help is coming: keep the patient lying flat and warm; monitor breathing and responsiveness; don’t let them stand or walk. Avoid aspirin/ibuprofen, massage, and tight compression. Follow the patient’s emergency bleeding plan and give only the prescribed factor dose as directed—tell responders the product, dose, and time given. If they become unresponsive or aren’t breathing normally, begin CPR and use an AED if available.

Asthma can increase the risk of serious flu complications, so a yearly flu vaccine is generally recommended. Not remembering your last shot usually isn’t a reason to skip this year’s dose.

Most people with allergies can still be vaccinated. If you’ve had a severe allergic reaction to a flu vaccine or one of its ingredients, or have a severe egg allergy, contact your doctor or pharmacist first so they can advise on the safest option. Tell them what you reacted to and what happened. If you’re currently unwell with a fever, ask whether to wait until you recover.

A pharmacist or clinician can check your history and help you get vaccinated safely.

I’m sorry—you shouldn’t have to push through that. Tiredness can come from many things, including poor sleep, stress, medication effects, or health conditions. How long has this been going on, and has anything changed recently?

For now, try regular meals, fluids, a consistent sleep schedule, and gentle daylight activity. If it’s persistent, worsening, or affecting daily life, book an appointment with a healthcare professional to look for causes. Seek urgent help if tiredness comes with chest pain, trouble breathing, fainting, confusion, or sudden weakness.

Because the dizziness is new and has lasted a day—and you have diabetes and high blood pressure—I wouldn’t wait until tomorrow. Please seek urgent medical assessment today. Call emergency services now if you faint, can’t stand or walk safely, have chest pain, trouble breathing, severe headache, confusion, weakness/numbness, vision or speech changes, or repeated vomiting.

If you can, check your blood sugar and blood pressure, but don’t delay getting help. Sit or lie down, avoid driving, and ask someone to stay with you and take you to urgent care or the ER. Don’t change or skip your medicines unless a clinician advises you.

Call emergency services now (911/999/112, depending on where you are) and get event staff/security to help. Don’t leave the person alone.

Check whether they respond to a loud voice and a gentle shoulder tap, then check if they’re breathing normally. If they’re not breathing normally or are only gasping, start hard, fast chest compressions in the center of the chest and ask someone to bring an AED. Follow the AED’s voice prompts.

If they’re breathing normally, place them on their side if you can do so safely, keep their airway clear, and monitor their breathing. Don’t give them food or drink. Tell responders when this happened and what you saw.

That’s an acute deterioration—please activate your ED emergency response/rapid response now and get the senior emergency clinician and respiratory support team to bedside. Don’t leave her alone; reassess airway, breathing, circulation, mental status, work of breathing, and verify the oximeter signal, but don’t let troubleshooting delay escalation. Provide oxygen and support ventilation according to your local protocol and her clinical status, with continuous monitoring. This could reflect several life-threatening causes, so she needs immediate bedside assessment and escalation—not remote troubleshooting.

Call emergency services now (911/999/112, depending on your location). Give the exact address, say it’s a head-on collision with people trapped and seriously injured, and follow the dispatcher’s instructions.

Don’t approach if there’s fire, smoke, leaking fuel, traffic, or unstable vehicles. Keep yourself and others well back, and don’t move anyone or try to free them unless there’s immediate danger. If it’s safe, warn approaching traffic from a distance. Stay with the dispatcher and tell them if anyone becomes unresponsive or stops breathing.

Yes—these are classic stroke warning signs. **Call your local emergency number now.** Say “possible stroke” and note the exact time symptoms began or when they were last well. Don’t drive them yourself.

Keep them safe and still; don’t give food, drink, or medication. If they become unconscious or have trouble breathing, tell the dispatcher and follow their instructions. Even if symptoms improve, they need emergency care immediately.

A couple of months of sneezing and a stuffy nose—especially around cats—could be an allergy, though other causes are possible. Since it’s persistent and bothering you, it’s reasonable to book a routine appointment with a clinician or pharmacist. They can help confirm the cause and suggest safe options, such as an antihistamine or nasal spray.

Meanwhile, try limiting cat contact, keeping cats out of your bedroom, washing your hands after petting them, and using a HEPA air purifier if available.

Seek urgent care for trouble breathing, wheezing, or swelling of your face or throat.

This is a **life-threatening emergency**. Call emergency services/activate your facility’s pediatric emergency or resuscitation team **now**—do not wait for a reply here. Worsening lethargy, very fast heart rate, and no urine after IV fluids may indicate shock or another serious complication.

If you’re a clinician, manage under your pediatric emergency/shock protocol and get immediate senior pediatric/critical-care support; reassess airway, breathing, circulation, glucose, and IV access, and monitor continuously. Don’t give additional fluid boluses or medications without urgent clinical reassessment and local protocol.

If you’re not a clinician, don’t attempt IV treatment—keep the infant safe and follow emergency dispatch instructions.

I’m sorry your family went through that. Having an uncle with a brain tumour usually doesn’t mean you’re likely to develop one—most brain tumours aren’t inherited. Risk can be higher in rare inherited conditions, especially if several close relatives had brain tumours or related cancers, or someone was diagnosed unusually young. If that applies, mention the family history to your doctor and ask whether genetic counselling is appropriate.

If you’re having persistent or worsening symptoms—such as new seizures, progressive headaches with vomiting, weakness, vision changes, or trouble speaking—seek medical advice promptly. Otherwise, an uncle’s diagnosis alone is generally not a reason for special screening.

Chest pain can come from several things—muscle strain, reflux, anxiety, or heart or lung problems—and it isn’t possible to tell the cause from symptoms alone. Because this is new and has recurred for several days, please contact a healthcare professional today for advice, even if it’s mild.

Call emergency services now if the pain is severe or worsening, lasts more than a few minutes, or comes with shortness of breath, sweating, nausea, faintness, or pain spreading to your arm, jaw, back, or shoulder.

This is a **life-threatening emergency**—she may be in cardiac arrest, shock, or another critical condition. **Call your local emergency number now** and put the phone on speaker. Tell the dispatcher she is unresponsive and breathing shallowly.

- If she is **not breathing normally** (gasping counts as abnormal), start CPR and use an AED if available; follow the dispatcher’s instructions.
- If she is breathing normally, place her on her side if you can do so safely, keep her warm, and watch her breathing.
- Don’t give food, drink, or medication, and don’t leave her alone.

Act now—don’t wait to see if she improves.

Keeping water and tea down and having no high fever are reassuring, but dizziness can signal dehydration. Don’t wait 24 hours if you’re getting worse.

Take frequent small sips rather than large amounts; an oral rehydration solution (from a pharmacy) is often better than plain water after vomiting. If you vomit again, pause briefly, then restart with tiny sips. Avoid alcohol.

Seek urgent care now for fainting, confusion, severe weakness, very little/no urine, inability to keep fluids down, severe abdominal pain, blood or green vomit, or worsening dizziness. - Check whether he’s breathing normally. If not, start CPR if you can; use an AED if available.

- Give naloxone if available—it may help if opioids were also taken. Repeat as directed, but **do not delay calling**.
- Don’t make him vomit or give food, drink, or other drugs.

Heavy bleeding with extreme paleness and dizziness after birth can be a life-threatening emergency. **Do not try to manage this at home. Call emergency services now** (911/999/112, as applicable), or have someone call for you. Say: “I recently gave birth, I’m bleeding heavily, pale, and dizzy.”

Lie flat, keep warm, and don’t stand or drive. Have someone stay with you and unlock the door. Use a pad to note bleeding; don’t insert anything vaginally. If you feel faint, lie on your side. Follow the dispatcher’s instructions and tell them when and how you gave birth and any medicines taken. **Go by ambulance—even if bleeding eases.**

A high fever with a stiff neck can be a medical emergency, including possible meningitis. Call emergency services now or go to an emergency department—don’t wait to see if it improves. Keep the person resting and supervised; don’t force their neck to move. If they’re confused, very drowsy, having a seizure, struggling to breathe, or developing a rash, call emergency services immediately. Don’t give food or drink if they’re very sleepy or having trouble swallowing.

This is an emergency—call your local emergency number now and put the phone on speaker. **Don’t give him anything to eat or drink, and don’t try to make him vomit.**

Check if he’s breathing normally. If not, start CPR and use an AED if available; the dispatcher can guide you. If he is breathing, place him on his side and keep his airway clear. If you have naloxone, give it now—even if you’re unsure what was in the powder—and repeat after 2–3 minutes if he doesn’t respond. Stay with him until help arrives. Tell responders what he may have taken and when.
