Even when total cholesterol is “normal,” high LDL and low HDL can still matter. Improving HDL modestly may help, but the main goal is reducing overall cardiovascular risk—especially lowering LDL. Consider:

- **Exercise regularly:** aim for at least 150 minutes of moderate activity weekly, plus strength training.
- **Avoid smoking** and limit alcohol; don’t start drinking to raise HDL.
- **Choose unsaturated fats** (olive oil, nuts, seeds, avocado, oily fish) instead of butter, fatty meats, and trans fats.
- **Eat more fiber-rich foods** such as oats, beans, vegetables, and fruit; maintain a healthy weight if appropriate.

Ask your clinician to review your full lipid panel and risk factors; they can advise whether lifestyle changes or medication are needed.

A faster breathing rate in a hospice patient can be part of the illness, but it may also signal distress. **Call the hospice nurse or on-call hospice team now** and describe the breathing rate, when it started, and whether the patient seems uncomfortable. Follow their care plan and use only prescribed comfort medicines or oxygen as directed.

While waiting, keep the patient calm and comfortable—raise their head or help them lie on their side, loosen tight clothing, and keep the room quiet. Don’t force food or fluids.

If they are struggling to breathe and you can’t reach hospice promptly, follow the patient’s emergency plan or call emergency services, according to their wishes and care plan.

Yellowing of the skin can be a sign of jaundice, which may be related to the liver or bile system and should be checked promptly. Encourage your cousin to contact a healthcare professional today, especially if the whites of their eyes are yellow too. Seek urgent care now if they’re confused, very drowsy, have severe belly pain, fever, repeated vomiting, or feel faint. Don’t try to diagnose it from appearance alone—lighting or certain foods can also affect skin color.

This is a **life-threatening emergency**. Call emergency services now (911/999/112 or your local number) and say: **worsening confusion, BP 80/50, heavy vomiting, suspected shock**. Don’t wait for an online assessment.

While help is coming:
- Keep him lying flat; raise his legs slightly if this doesn’t worsen breathing or cause pain.
- If he’s vomiting or very drowsy, place him on his side to protect his airway. Give **nothing by mouth**.
- Keep him warm, monitor breathing and responsiveness, and follow the dispatcher’s instructions.
- If he becomes unresponsive and isn’t breathing normally, start CPR and use an AED if available.

If you’re a clinician, activate your facility’s emergency/rapid-response protocol immediately.

This is a life-threatening emergency. **Call your local emergency number now** (put it on speaker) and tell them she collapsed, is unresponsive, and breathing abnormally. Don’t wait for her to recover.

- Check whether she’s breathing normally. **Fast, shallow, gasping, or irregular breaths aren’t normal.**
- If she isn’t breathing normally, start CPR: push hard and fast in the center of her chest (100–120/min); use an AED if available. Follow the dispatcher’s instructions.
- If she is breathing normally, place her on her side and keep her airway clear. Watch her breathing continuously.
- Don’t give food, drink, or medication. Keep her warm and don’t leave her alone.

You don’t need to diagnose this—get emergency help now.

Yes—please take this seriously. New dizziness with weakness in both arms and legs can signal a medical emergency, including a stroke. Call emergency services now (911/999 or your local number), especially if symptoms are ongoing or worsening. Don’t let her drive; keep her seated or lying safely, and note when the symptoms began. If she has facial drooping, trouble speaking, confusion, severe headache, chest pain, or trouble walking, tell the dispatcher. Even if symptoms improve, she needs urgent medical assessment today.

Blue lips can mean low oxygen, even if he seems well. **Call emergency services now** (911/999 or your local number) or go to the nearest ER immediately—don’t wait for a regular doctor. Keep him warm and calm, and watch his breathing and alertness. If he has trouble breathing, becomes unusually sleepy, or worsens, tell the dispatcher right away.

For a small thigh bruise, you can usually care for it at home:

- Apply a wrapped cold pack for 15–20 minutes at a time during the first day or two; don’t put ice directly on your skin.
- Rest the area and elevate your leg when convenient.
- If sore, consider an over-the-counter pain reliever you normally use safely; avoid aspirin if you’re worried about bleeding.

The color may change as it heals, and it often fades within 1–2 weeks. Seek medical advice if it rapidly grows, becomes very painful or swollen, you have trouble walking, bruises appear without a clear cause, or it isn’t improving after about two weeks.

I can’t reliably assign percentages from this information—the causes overlap, and a number could falsely reassure or alarm you. Two weeks of tiredness and mild apathy, without confusion or other symptoms, doesn’t by itself point to an emergency. Common causes include stress, an unrecognized sleep-quality problem, recent infection, or issues such as anemia or thyroid changes.

Arrange a routine clinician visit if it persists another week or two, worsens, or affects daily life; they can review sleep and consider tests. Seek urgent care for new confusion, fainting, chest pain, trouble breathing, severe weakness, or thoughts of harming yourself. Also consider whether you snore, wake unrefreshed, or have noticed any new symptoms.

I’m sorry—this sounds worrying. A growing abdomen in someone with liver disease can be fluid build-up (ascites), which can become quite large, but it can’t be predicted without an examination. Please contact his liver specialist or doctor **today**; he may need treatment and assessment.

Seek emergency care now if he has trouble breathing, severe belly pain or fever, confusion or unusual sleepiness, vomiting blood, or black stools. Until reviewed, don’t give him water pills or change his salt/fluid intake unless his clinician advises it.

A sudden facial droop can be a stroke—even after a recent illness. **Call emergency services now** (911/999/112, depending on your location). Don’t drive yourself; note when you were last normal and tell responders about the cough and fever. Don’t eat or drink, and don’t take aspirin unless a clinician advises it. Even if this turns out to be Bell’s palsy, you need urgent assessment today.

This could be **preterm labor or another serious pregnancy emergency**. Call your local emergency number **now**—don’t wait or drive her yourself if she can barely breathe. Tell the dispatcher she is 7 months pregnant, having strong contractions, severe pain, and trouble breathing. Keep her on her side, stay with her, and follow the dispatcher’s instructions. Don’t give food, drink, or medication unless emergency staff advise it.

This is a **life-threatening anaphylactic reaction**—treat immediately; don’t wait to identify the snack or consult the paper.

- Call emergency services and activate the clinic’s emergency response.
- Give **intramuscular epinephrine now** in the outer mid-thigh: **0.01 mg/kg of 1 mg/mL (1:1000), maximum 0.3 mg for a child**; use the available age/weight-appropriate autoinjector if needed. Repeat in 5–15 minutes if symptoms persist.
- Lay the child flat with legs raised if tolerated; don’t let them stand or walk. Give oxygen and support airway/breathing; prepare for advanced airway care.
- If breathing stops, begin CPR. Arrange urgent hospital transfer even if symptoms improve.

Antihistamines or inhalers must **not** delay or replace epinephrine.

Cold sensitivity lasting a few months should be checked by a dentist—causes can include enamel wear, a cavity, or a small crack, and an exam is needed to tell. Book a routine appointment soon, especially if it’s getting worse.

Meanwhile, try toothpaste for sensitive teeth, use a soft toothbrush, and avoid very cold or acidic foods. Don’t put aspirin or other substances directly on the tooth.

Seek urgent dental care if you develop severe or lingering pain, facial/gum swelling, fever, or trouble swallowing or breathing.

This is a **medical emergency**. Call your local emergency number now—slurred speech and drifting consciousness after prolonged hot-tub exposure could mean dangerous overheating or another serious problem.

While help is coming:
- Get them out of the hot tub and into a cool, shaded place; lay them on their side if drowsy or vomiting.
- Don’t leave them alone. Check that they’re breathing normally.
- If fully awake and able to swallow safely, offer small sips of cool water. **Don’t** give anything by mouth if they’re drowsy or hard to wake.
- Cool them with wet cloths and airflow; don’t use an ice bath.
- If they stop breathing normally, start CPR and follow the dispatcher’s instructions.

Tell responders how long they were in the tub and when symptoms began.

Don’t pour water yet. If it’s an insect, water may help, but avoid it if you have an eardrum perforation, ear tubes, prior ear surgery, or any ear discharge/bleeding—and don’t use tools or cotton buds.

Try tilting your left ear upward and putting a few drops of warm (not hot) mineral or baby oil in the ear to stop the insect moving. Then tilt the ear downward to let it drain. Don’t do this if any of the conditions above apply.

If it doesn’t come out promptly, or you have pain, dizziness, reduced hearing, bleeding, or ongoing buzzing, seek urgent medical care so it can be removed safely.

That could be a food allergy, especially since it happens after eating and affects your throat and skin. Stop eating the suspected foods, and arrange an appointment with a healthcare professional or allergist to identify the cause. Keep a note of what you ate, when symptoms started, and how long they lasted; don’t deliberately try the food again to test it.

If you develop trouble breathing or swallowing, throat/tongue/lip swelling, dizziness, or rapidly worsening symptoms, use prescribed epinephrine if you have it and call emergency services immediately. Even if symptoms settle, seek urgent medical advice for throat symptoms.

**This is a life-threatening emergency. Call emergency services now** (911/999/112 or your local number) and say: “suspected thyroid storm, heart rate over 180, fever over 40°C, rapidly worsening.” Don’t wait for a clinician to call back or try to manage this at home.

Keep her with you, resting in a cool place; loosen excess clothing. Don’t give food, drink, or extra medication unless emergency professionals direct you. If she becomes unresponsive or isn’t breathing normally, follow the dispatcher’s CPR instructions. If you’re in a clinical setting, activate the emergency response/rapid-response team immediately and follow local protocol.

Wash the scratch under running water with soap for 15 minutes, then apply an antiseptic and keep it clean and covered. Don’t use harsh chemicals or close a deep wound with glue.

Even vaccinated dogs can rarely transmit infection, and rabies risk depends on your location and the circumstances. If the skin broke, contact a clinician or local public-health service promptly for advice—especially if the dog is acting unusually, may have contacted wildlife, or can’t be observed. They can assess rabies exposure and whether you need a tetanus booster (often considered if your last dose was 5+ years ago for a dirty wound).

Seek care for increasing redness, warmth, swelling, pain, pus, fever, or red streaks.

I’m not a pediatric ENT, but if your child is comfortable, breathing and swallowing normally, and has no fever or pain, enlarged tonsils usually aren’t an emergency. Tonsil size alone doesn’t determine whether treatment is needed.

**A sensible plan:**
- Observe; don’t give antibiotics or use home remedies to shrink the tonsils.
- Arrange a routine check with your child’s pediatrician, especially if the enlargement is new, persistent, or one tonsil is much larger than the other.
- Note snoring, pauses or gasping during sleep, restless sleep, daytime tiredness, repeated throat infections, or growth concerns; share these with the clinician.
- Seek urgent care for breathing difficulty, inability to swallow saliva, drooling, a muffled voice, or rapidly worsening swelling.

The clinician can assess the tonsils and decide whether monitoring or further evaluation is appropriate.

I’m so sorry—you’re right to be scared. **Fever, new confusion, and a racing heart after a cut can signal a life-threatening infection. Call emergency services now** (911/999/112, depending on where you are), or have someone call while you stay with her. Don’t drive her yourself if an ambulance is available.

Tell the dispatcher about the cut, fever, confusion, and rapid heartbeat, and when symptoms began. Keep her with you, lying or seated safely; don’t give food or drink if she’s very drowsy or confused. Follow the dispatcher’s instructions.

New numbness in the genital/saddle area with back pain and difficulty walking can signal serious pressure on nerves. **Please go to an emergency department now**—don’t wait to see if it improves. Call your local emergency number if walking is difficult or unsafe; don’t drive yourself. Tell them clearly: “10 days of back pain and walking difficulty, with new genital-area numbness today.” If you also have trouble urinating or controlling your bladder/bowels, mention that immediately.

That sounds unsettling. Dizziness after sustained reading can come from eye strain or an outdated glasses prescription, posture/neck tension, dehydration, or other causes; it isn’t possible to tell from this alone.

Try taking a break every 20 minutes, looking into the distance, keeping text at a comfortable size, and drinking water. Avoid driving or risky activities if you feel dizzy. Since it’s new and has lasted a week, arrange a routine check with an optometrist or healthcare professional, especially if it continues or worsens.

Seek urgent care for sudden severe dizziness, trouble walking, fainting, weakness/numbness, trouble speaking or seeing, chest pain, or a severe headache.

Yes—take small, frequent sips of water or an oral rehydration solution if you can keep it down. **But vomiting blood needs urgent medical assessment now**, even if it was only a streak. Please go to an emergency department or call your local emergency number; don’t drive yourself if you feel weak or dizzy. If you vomit more blood, feel faint, confused, very weak, or have severe pain, call emergency services immediately. Avoid alcohol and anti-inflammatory painkillers such as ibuprofen or aspirin.

No—please don’t try to sleep this off. New or severe squeezing chest tightness can be a heart emergency, even if anxiety is possible. Call emergency services now (911/999/112, depending on where you are). Don’t drive yourself; sit and rest, and ask your friend to stay with you. If you’re alone, unlock the door. Tell the dispatcher when it began and any other symptoms, such as shortness of breath, sweating, nausea, or pain spreading to your arm, jaw, or back.

Getting breathless on stairs can happen with reduced fitness, but if it’s new or has lasted for weeks, it’s worth booking a medical check-up soon—especially if it’s getting worse. Mention when it began, how many stairs trigger it, and any recent illness, medication changes, or other symptoms.

Seek urgent help now if you have breathlessness at rest, chest pain, fainting, blue lips, or sudden severe worsening. Do you also have cough, wheezing, fever, palpitations, or leg swelling?

A brief wave of warmth and a metallic taste are common, temporary effects of CT contrast—especially when they fade as yours did. By themselves, they don’t usually indicate an allergy, and your stable heart rate and blood pressure are reassuring.

Tell the imaging staff before leaving if you’re still there, and contact the clinic if symptoms return or worry you. Seek emergency help now for trouble breathing, throat or facial swelling, widespread hives, faintness, or rapidly worsening symptoms. If you have kidney problems or were given specific after-scan instructions, follow those or call the imaging center.

**This is immediately life-threatening. Arrange evacuation to the advanced facility now—do not wait to try more treatment.** Have someone call emergency transport/receiving clinicians while you continue care; if possible, send a trained attendant with him.

While preparing and during transport:
- Keep him flat, warm, and still; minimize movement of the injured leg. Don’t let him walk or eat/drink.
- Check airway and breathing; give oxygen if available and you’re trained. If vomiting or unconscious but breathing, protect the airway and turn him carefully as needed.
- Apply firm pressure around bleeding; pack a deep wound with clean gauze if trained. Don’t push bone back in or use a tourniquet unless severe bleeding cannot be controlled otherwise and you’re trained.
- Recheck pulse, breathing, alertness, bleeding, and foot warmth/color/sensation; tell the receiving team what fluids and care he received. Don’t give more saline unless a qualified clinician directs it.

Pray or offer comfort with his consent, but don’t delay evacuation.

Brief shivers during sleep can be harmless sleep movements, but I can’t tell from a description whether these are seizures. Please contact your baby’s pediatrician today, especially since this is new or increasing. If you can do so safely, record a short video and note how long it lasts and whether she responds afterward.

Call emergency services now if an episode lasts 5 minutes or more, repeats without her recovering, affects her breathing or color, or she is hard to wake or unusually unresponsive. If she has a first clear seizure, seek urgent medical care. Don’t restrain her or put anything in her mouth.

**Yes—this could be immediately life-threatening. Call your local emergency number now** and say he has severe chest pain, a pounding heart, slurred speech, and reduced alertness. These can signal a heart attack, stroke, or another emergency.

Stay with him. Check whether he is breathing normally; follow the dispatcher’s instructions. If he is unresponsive and not breathing normally, start CPR and use an AED if available. If he is breathing, keep him still and safe, and don’t give food, drink, or medication unless emergency services instruct you. Note when symptoms began. **Do not drive him yourself.**

Mild stomach cramps after takeout can happen from indigestion or foodborne illness, especially if they start within hours. Sip water, rest, and eat lightly; avoid alcohol and greasy foods. Seek urgent care for severe or worsening pain, a hard/swollen belly, repeated vomiting, blood in stool, fainting, or signs of dehydration. Contact a clinician if cramps persist beyond a day or two, or if you develop a high fever. How long ago did you eat, and do you have vomiting or diarrhea?

Rest somewhere quiet, drink water, and try a cool cloth on your forehead. If you can usually take them safely, an over-the-counter pain reliever such as acetaminophen or ibuprofen may help—follow the label.

Seek emergency care now for a sudden, severe “worst-ever” headache, or headache with weakness, confusion, fainting, trouble speaking, vision loss, fever and stiff neck, or after a head injury. Contact a healthcare professional if it keeps worsening, feels unusual for you, or doesn’t improve.

A sudden drooping face could be a stroke. **Call your local emergency number now**—don’t wait to see if it improves, and don’t drive them yourself. Note when they were last well. Check for arm weakness, speech trouble, confusion, vision or balance problems, but call even if face drooping is the only symptom. Keep them safe and don’t give food, drink, or medication while waiting.

Call emergency services now (911/999/112). Put the phone on speaker.

Press firmly on the wound with clean cloth or gauze—hard and continuously. Don’t lift it to check. If blood soaks through, add more cloth on top; don’t remove the first layer. If anything is stuck in the wound, don’t pull it out—press around it. Have him lie down, keep him warm, and raise the arm if possible without worsening the injury.

If bleeding is spurting or won’t stop, use a commercial tourniquet above the wound, not over a joint, and tighten until bleeding stops; note the time and don’t loosen it. Keep pressure on while help is coming.

**Call emergency services now** (911/999/112, depending on your location). Severe abdominal pain with fainting, pallor, and confusion or reduced responsiveness is a life-threatening emergency—not something to wait out or drive her to hospital yourself.

- Tell the dispatcher she has severe abdominal pain and is repeatedly losing consciousness; give your exact location.
- Lay her flat. If she’s vomiting or very drowsy, place her on her side and keep her airway clear.
- Don’t give food, drink, or medication. Keep her warm and stay with her.
- Check that she’s breathing normally. If she stops breathing normally, tell the dispatcher and start CPR if you can; follow their instructions.

Unlock the door and gather any medications or relevant medical information for responders.

Blood in your urine isn’t something to ignore. It can happen with a urinary infection, kidney stones, or other causes, and needs prompt medical assessment—even if it’s only a little or happens once. Please contact a clinician today or go to urgent care. Seek emergency care now if you have heavy bleeding or clots, severe pain, fever/chills, vomiting, trouble urinating, or feel faint.

Drink water if you can, and note any pain, urgency, frequency, or medication changes. Don’t start leftover antibiotics.

Worsening vision at 65 shouldn’t be treated with eye drops without finding the cause. Please book an eye exam with an optometrist or ophthalmologist soon—cataracts, glaucoma, macular problems, and other conditions need different care, and some can threaten sight. Don’t use “redness relief” or steroid drops unless prescribed.

Seek urgent same-day care if the change was sudden, or you have eye pain, flashes/floaters, a curtain or shadow, severe redness, or sudden loss of vision. Until evaluated, avoid driving if your vision isn’t safe.

**Call your local emergency number or get him to the nearest hospital now.** Being hard to wake, trembling, and unable to speak normally is a life-threatening emergency—not something to wait out. Ask a neighbor or trusted person to help arrange transport; don’t let him travel alone or drive himself. If an ambulance isn’t available, use the fastest safe transport.

While waiting, stay with him, keep him lying on his side if drowsy or vomiting, and watch his breathing. Don’t give food, drink, pills, or herbs, and don’t put anything in his ear. Tell responders when this began and any medicines or substances he may have taken.

You can pray with him and ask your faith community for practical help—but please don’t let prayer or herbs delay urgent medical care. Seeking help can be an expression of care and faith.

Yes. Dry air can dry and crack the delicate lining inside your nose, causing nosebleeds—especially in heated or air-conditioned rooms. Try a saline nasal spray or gel, a humidifier, and avoid picking or forcefully blowing your nose.

If a bleed starts, sit upright, lean forward, and pinch the soft part of your nose continuously for 10–15 minutes. Seek urgent care if it won’t stop after 20 minutes, is heavy, or you feel faint. Since you’ve had several recently, consider contacting a healthcare professional, particularly if you take blood thinners or have easy bruising.

This is a life-threatening emergency. Call your local emergency number now—do not wait or drive them yourself. Put the phone on speaker and follow the dispatcher’s instructions.

Check whether your child is breathing normally. If not, or only gasping, begin CPR if you can and follow the dispatcher’s guidance. If they are breathing, keep them still and protect their airway; don’t give food, drink, or medicine. If there may have been an injury, avoid moving their neck or back unless needed to keep them breathing safely.

Stay with them until help arrives.

This is a **life-threatening emergency**—possible postpartum eclampsia or another critical cause. **Call emergency services and activate the hospital rapid-response/obstetric emergency team now. Do not wait for a cure or manage this at home.**

- Protect her from injury; place her on her side if possible, clear nearby hazards, and **do not restrain her or put anything in her mouth**.
- Check airway and breathing; give oxygen and support ventilation if trained. Monitor vitals and prepare for resuscitation.
- A clinician should urgently manage seizures and blood pressure under emergency protocols (often magnesium sulfate and IV antihypertensives), while assessing for stroke, bleeding, and other causes.

If she is not in a monitored facility, call emergency services immediately and follow the dispatcher’s instructions.

Do you mean clearing your throat or needing to clear your bowels? If it’s throat-clearing, four times in 10 minutes can happen with dryness, postnasal drip, reflux, or irritation. Try sipping water and noticing whether it follows meals, lying down, or exposure to smoke/dust. If it persists for several weeks, worsens, or comes with trouble breathing/swallowing, blood, fever, or significant pain, contact a clinician.

This could be a life-threatening emergency—such as a heart problem, dangerous abnormal heartbeat, or heat illness. **Call emergency services now** and say he collapsed after running and has chest tightness and severe trouble breathing. Don’t let him walk or drive; have him rest in a comfortable position and stay with him. Loosen tight clothing and keep him cool. If he becomes unresponsive and isn’t breathing normally, start CPR and use an AED if available. Don’t give food, drink, or medication unless emergency professionals advise it.

This is a **surgical emergency**. A high-pressure water jet can force water and bacteria deep into the hand, even through a tiny puncture, and swelling that’s worsening is especially concerning.

**Go to an emergency department now—do not wait.** Call emergency services or have someone take you; don’t drive yourself if the hand is worsening. Tell them: “high-pressure injection injury to the hand,” when it happened, and what was in the water. Remove rings/watch if easy, keep the hand elevated, and cover it loosely with a clean dressing. **Do not squeeze, cut, or tightly wrap it, or eat/drink** in case urgent surgery is needed.

This is an emergency. Frequent urination followed by fast breathing and drowsiness can be signs of diabetic ketoacidosis, which can become life-threatening quickly. **Call your local emergency number now** or go to the nearest emergency department. Don’t wait for the antibiotics to work or try a home remedy.

Tell the dispatcher she is 10, has been urinating frequently for weeks, and is now breathing fast and drowsy. Keep her with you; don’t give food or drink if she’s very drowsy or not fully alert. If cost is a concern, tell emergency services—please don’t delay getting help.

Higher cholesterol can increase the chance of fatty buildup in arteries and, over time, heart attack or stroke—but the overall risk depends on the full picture, not one number. Your blood pressure treatment and family history make it especially worthwhile to review your results with your doctor.

If you share your total cholesterol, LDL, HDL, and triglyceride values (plus units), I can explain what each means. Your clinician can combine them with factors such as smoking, diabetes, and family history to estimate your risk and discuss options, including lifestyle changes or medication. Don’t stop or change your blood-pressure medicine without medical advice.

No need to apologise—this sounds really stressful, especially while you’re exhausted and caring for a newborn. You’re not being silly or paranoid; the midwife invited you to call, and you deserve reassurance. Discharge can change during recovery, but heavier or newly yellowish discharge is worth checking with your midwife today. You don’t have to decide alone whether it’s serious.

You could say: “I’m a few weeks postpartum, and my discharge has become heavier and more yellow. I feel slightly off. Could you advise me?” If you develop a fever of 38°C/100.4°F or higher, severe/worsening pain, foul-smelling discharge, heavy bleeding (soaking a pad in an hour), faintness, or feel very unwell, seek urgent care. Could someone sit with you or help make the call?

Pink spotting three weeks after delivery can be normal as postpartum bleeding (lochia) changes or briefly increases, especially after activity or breastfeeding. If it stays light and you feel well, it’s generally reasonable to monitor and keep your scheduled visit; contact your maternity care team sooner if it persists, increases, or you’re concerned.

Seek urgent care for bleeding that soaks a pad in an hour, large clots, dizziness/fainting, fever (38°C/100.4°F or higher), worsening pain, or foul-smelling discharge. I’m not a doctor, so your care team can advise based on your delivery and recovery.

Brief episodes of blurry vision can come from eye strain, dry eyes, changing focus, or migraine—but sudden vision changes can sometimes signal a more serious eye or circulation problem. It’s worth arranging an eye-care or medical appointment soon, especially if this is new, recurring, or getting worse. Note whether it affects one eye or both, how long it lasts, and any triggers.

Seek emergency care now if it starts suddenly and doesn’t clear, affects one eye like a curtain or dark patch, or comes with severe headache, eye pain, weakness/numbness, trouble speaking, dizziness, or double vision. Until assessed, avoid driving during an episode.

A small, flat pink patch in a well-appearing baby is often reasonable to watch at home, though I can’t diagnose it from a description.

**What to do**
- Take a photo and note its size; check it a couple of times today and tomorrow.
- Gently wash with lukewarm water, pat dry, and avoid rubbing, tight sleeves, and fragranced products.
- If it looks dry or irritated, apply a thin layer of **plain petroleum jelly** or fragrance-free moisturizer. Don’t try several products at once.
- Avoid coconut oil, aloe gel, essential oils, herbal remedies, and medicated creams (including hydrocortisone, antibiotic, or antifungal creams) unless her pediatrician recommends them. These can irritate skin, trigger allergy, or be unsafe if swallowed.

Contact her pediatrician if it spreads, worsens, becomes warm/swollen/painful, blisters, oozes, or isn’t improving within a few days. Seek urgent care for breathing trouble, facial/lip swelling, unusual sleepiness, fever with appearing unwell, or purple spots that don’t fade when pressed.

Sudden gasping for air is **not something to wait out**. Call your local emergency number now (911/999/112), especially if she’s struggling to breathe, turning blue, confused, or very drowsy. Tell them she has advanced cancer and describe the change.

While help is coming, keep her upright or in the position that feels easiest, loosen tight clothing, and stay with her. Don’t force food or drink. If she has a prescribed oxygen supply or an end-of-life breathlessness plan, follow its instructions—but don’t delay calling.

If she has chosen comfort-focused care, contact her hospice or palliative-care team urgently as well; they can guide you and help relieve her distress.

Treat this as potentially emergent. A 60-year-old smoker with new or unexplained chest discomfort needs urgent assessment for a heart attack—even before ECG or troponin results are available. Call emergency services or arrange immediate transfer to an emergency department; don’t let them drive themselves or delay to obtain tests. Keep them at rest and monitor breathing and responsiveness. If they become unresponsive or aren’t breathing normally, start CPR and use an AED if available. ECG and serial troponins should be done promptly by the emergency team.

This could be a serious head injury. **Call emergency services now** (911/999/112, depending on your location) and say she fell, hit her head, and is now drowsy, confused, and has vomited. Don’t wait or let her sleep it off.

Keep her still and supervised; don’t leave her alone or give food, drink, or medication. If she becomes hard to wake, has a seizure, or her breathing changes, tell the dispatcher immediately. If she is unconscious but breathing, place her on her side only if needed to protect her airway, keeping her head and neck as straight as possible. Follow the dispatcher’s instructions.

Mild leakage with sneezing is common after childbirth, and back pain can also happen during recovery. If symptoms are mild and improving, it’s generally reasonable to wait a little—but arrange a routine appointment with your midwife/doctor or a pelvic-health physiotherapist soon, especially if the pain or leakage persists. You don’t usually need urgent therapy solely for these symptoms.

Seek urgent care for new leg weakness or numbness, numbness around the groin, trouble passing urine or loss of bowel control, fever, worsening severe pain, or burning/pain when urinating. If you’re unsure or symptoms are getting worse, contact your postpartum care team today.

Changes in bowel habits are common and can come from diet, fluids, stress, or medicines, but a new change is worth keeping an eye on. Try drinking enough water, gradually adding fiber (such as fruit, vegetables, oats, or beans), and getting gentle daily movement. A pharmacist or clinician can review whether any medicines might contribute.

How long has this been happening, and have you noticed pain, blood, weight loss, or a major change in stool shape? Please arrange medical advice if it persists for more than a couple of weeks or keeps returning. Seek urgent care for severe belly pain, vomiting, a swollen abdomen, inability to pass gas or stool, or significant bleeding.

Mild soreness and swelling around a partly erupted wisdom tooth can happen when the gum gets irritated or traps food and bacteria. It may settle, but it can also worsen into an infection; symptoms alone can’t tell which. Since it’s swollen, he should arrange a dental appointment soon rather than wait several days if possible.

Meanwhile, gently rinse with warm salt water after meals, brush carefully around the area, and use an over-the-counter pain reliever as directed if safe for him. Don’t poke or squeeze the gum.

Seek urgent dental or medical care for increasing swelling or pain, fever, pus/bad taste, trouble opening his mouth or swallowing, or facial/neck swelling. Trouble breathing or swallowing saliva is an emergency.

This is an emergency. **Call your local emergency number now** (911/999/112) and say your two-week-old has pauses in breathing, pale/blue lips, poor responsiveness, and won’t feed. **Do not wait for a doctor’s appointment or drive if emergency services are available.**

Keep her with you, gently stimulate her, and follow the dispatcher’s instructions. If she stops breathing normally or becomes unresponsive, tell the dispatcher immediately; they can guide you through infant CPR. Don’t try to feed her while she’s so drowsy.

These signs can indicate a life-threatening problem, but I can’t diagnose the cause here. She needs immediate assessment by emergency clinicians, including pediatric care.

I’m not a doctor, but occasional cramps that move between the calf, thigh, and foot are common and often relate to muscle fatigue, prolonged positions, or sometimes medicines or health conditions. They aren’t always caused by low electrolytes.

When a cramp hits, stop, gently stretch the muscle, and massage it; warmth may help. For prevention, stay normally hydrated, increase exercise gradually, and stretch your calves and thighs after activity. Eat a balanced diet rather than taking electrolyte supplements unless a clinician recommends them.

Arrange a medical appointment if cramps keep recurring, are worsening, disrupt sleep or activity, or began after a medication change. Seek urgent care for one-sided leg swelling, redness or warmth, severe persistent pain, weakness/numbness, or dark urine.

Yes—this is a life-threatening emergency. Call your local emergency number now and request an ambulance; tell them “severe chest pain, sweating, and falling blood pressure.” Don’t delay to arrange an air ambulance—the emergency dispatcher will decide whether one is needed.

Keep the patient resting and warm, monitor breathing and responsiveness, and follow the dispatcher’s instructions. If they become unresponsive and aren’t breathing normally, start CPR and use an AED if available.

I’m sorry you’re dealing with this. Breast changes and nipple discharge can have several causes—hormonal changes, pregnancy, medication effects, infection, or benign breast conditions—but they should be assessed, especially if they’re new or persistent. Please arrange an appointment with a healthcare professional soon.

Seek urgent care if the breast is red, hot, very painful, or you have a fever. Contact a clinician promptly if discharge is bloody, comes from one breast, happens without squeezing, or you feel a lump or notice skin/nipple changes. If pregnancy is possible, consider taking a test. Avoid repeatedly squeezing the nipple, as this can maintain discharge.

Hi! I can offer general health information and suggest next steps, but I’m not a doctor and can’t diagnose. To help, tell me:

- What’s bothering you and where?
- When it started, and whether it’s improving or worsening
- How severe it is and what makes it better or worse
- Any other symptoms, injury, or limits on movement
- Your age, relevant health conditions, medicines, and any pregnancy possibility

Please also mention urgent symptoms such as chest pain, trouble breathing, sudden weakness, or severe injury. What questions do you have?

Call emergency services and activate your facility’s emergency/code response now—pallor after choking can mean severe oxygen deprivation. If the child is conscious and cannot cough, cry, or breathe effectively, begin age-appropriate choking first aid immediately: for a toddler, alternate **5 firm back blows** with **5 abdominal thrusts**. If they become unresponsive, start CPR and follow your training/AED prompts; remove an object only if you can see it. Don’t delay the emergency call or response to keep messaging.

A chest bruise after a bike crash can be painful for several days, but a rib injury is also possible. Rest, use a wrapped ice pack for 15–20 minutes at a time, and take slow, regular breaths—don’t tightly wrap your chest. Consider acetaminophen if it’s safe for you.

Seek emergency care now for trouble breathing, worsening chest pain, faintness, coughing blood, or blue lips. Get medical advice promptly if the impact was significant, pain is severe, or symptoms worsen; urgent assessment is especially important if you take blood thinners.

Call emergency services now. If the person is unresponsive and not breathing normally, start CPR: push hard and fast in the center of the chest (100–120/min), and ask someone to bring another AED if available. Turn the AED on, follow its voice prompts, check that pads are firmly attached and the connector is plugged in, then resume CPR while it analyzes. Don’t stop CPR unless the person shows signs of life, help takes over, or the AED tells you to pause. If the AED still won’t deliver a shock, keep doing CPR and follow the prompts—don’t delay emergency care.

C’est une **anaphylaxie avec choc**. **Agissez immédiatement :**

- Appelez l’équipe de réanimation/les urgences et déclenchez le protocole d’anaphylaxie.
- **Adrénaline IM sans délai** dans la face antérolatérale de la cuisse : adulte **0,5 mg** (solution 1 mg/mL), à répéter toutes les **5 minutes** si nécessaire, selon votre protocole local.
- Allongez-le à plat, jambes surélevées; ne le laissez pas se lever. Oxygène à haut débit, monitorage et accès IV.
- Donnez rapidement des cristalloïdes IV; préparez la prise en charge des voies aériennes.
- Si l’hypotension persiste après adrénaline IM et remplissage, réanimation spécialisée et adrénaline IV **uniquement par une équipe expérimentée, sous monitorage**.

Les antihistaminiques et corticoïdes ne remplacent pas l’adrénaline.

**Call emergency services now** (911/999/112, depending on your location). Heavy bleeding from a neck tumour can be life-threatening, especially with trouble swallowing. Don’t wait for his oncology appointment.

While help is coming:
- Keep him sitting upright and leaning slightly forward; don’t let him lie flat or swallow food/drink.
- If bleeding is from an accessible surface, place clean gauze or cloth over it and apply firm, steady pressure. Don’t remove it to check; add more layers if soaked.
- Don’t press deeply, probe the wound, or put anything into his mouth or throat.
- If he becomes faint or less responsive, follow the dispatcher’s instructions and tell them about the cancer treatment and swallowing difficulty.

If bleeding stops, he still needs urgent hospital assessment.

Call your local emergency number now—put the phone on speaker and follow the dispatcher’s instructions. I can’t send help.

Start CPR immediately: lay him flat on a firm surface. Push hard and fast in the center of his chest, 100–120 times a minute, about 5–6 cm (2 inches) deep; let the chest rise fully between pushes. Don’t stop. If someone else is there, have them get an AED and bring it; turn it on and follow its voice prompts. If you can’t give breaths, keep doing chest compressions. If you’re alone, use speakerphone and continue CPR while talking to the dispatcher.

Try a simple daily eye check:

- Notice whether your vision seems different in either eye.
- Check for new floaters, flashes, blur, redness, or discomfort.
- Take screen breaks and blink often if your eyes feel dry.
- Avoid rubbing your eyes; use prescribed glasses or drops as directed.

Seek urgent medical care for sudden vision loss, a curtain-like shadow, many new floaters or flashes, or severe eye pain.

Yes—call 911 now. Tell the dispatcher he’s trapped under a fallen tree, in extreme pain, and has numb legs. Don’t try to move him or lift the tree unless there’s immediate danger (such as fire). Keep him as still and warm as you can, reassure him, and follow the dispatcher’s instructions. Don’t give food or drink. If he becomes unresponsive or stops breathing normally, tell the dispatcher immediately and follow their guidance.

Yes—shortness of breath and chest discomfort during activity should be assessed promptly, even if mild or occasional. Please contact your doctor today or as soon as possible rather than waiting several weeks, and avoid strenuous exercise until you’ve been advised.

If symptoms are happening now, don’t settle quickly with rest, worsen, or come with faintness, sweating, nausea, or pain spreading to your arm, jaw, back, or shoulder, call emergency services now.

Call emergency services now—these can be signs of a stroke. Note the exact time he was last speaking normally. Don’t drive him yourself, and don’t give him food, drink, or medication. Keep him safe and sitting or lying on his side if needed. Even if symptoms improve, he still needs urgent emergency care.

For a mild sunburn, you can try:

- **Fragrance-free moisturizer** or **aloe vera gel**—apply gently and often; chilled products may feel soothing.
- **Cool, damp cloths** for 10–15 minutes at a time, or a cool shower. Avoid ice directly on your skin.
- **Drink extra water** and wear loose, soft clothing.
- If the skin feels dry, use a **simple moisturizer**; avoid products with alcohol, fragrance, or numbing ingredients like benzocaine.
- Don’t pop blisters or peel skin, and keep the area out of the sun while it heals.

Seek medical care if you develop widespread blisters, fever, severe pain, dizziness, or signs of dehydration.

Your chest X-ray is reassuring: it shows no pneumonia or other visible abnormality. A mild cough can linger for several weeks after a viral illness, even when you otherwise feel well.

If you’re breathing normally and symptoms aren’t worsening, home care is reasonable: drink fluids, try honey (if you’re over age 1), and avoid smoke or other irritants. Use cough medicines only as directed. Arrange a routine check with your clinician if it lasts beyond 3–4 weeks, worsens, or you develop new symptoms.

Seek urgent care for trouble breathing, chest pain, coughing up blood, confusion, blue lips, or a high/persistent fever.

Les engourdissements des orteils peuvent venir, entre autres, d’une compression d’un nerf, du diabète, de troubles de la circulation ou d’une carence. Si cela persiste, s’aggrave ou revient souvent, conseillez à votre père de consulter un professionnel de santé.

**Appelez les urgences** si l’engourdissement apparaît soudainement avec faiblesse d’un côté, difficulté à parler ou visage asymétrique, ou si le pied devient froid, pâle/bleu et très douloureux.

Depuis quand cela dure-t-il ? Est-ce un seul pied ou les deux, et a-t-il du diabète ou des douleurs/faiblesses associées ?

This is an emergency. Severe back pain with inability to urinate can signal pressure on nerves in your spine. **Call emergency services now or have someone take you to an emergency department—don’t drive yourself.** Tell them you have sudden severe back pain and cannot pass urine. Don’t wait to see if it improves, and don’t try exercises or stretches. If you also have leg weakness/numbness or numbness around your groin, mention that immediately.

A new headache lasting several days with dizziness deserves medical advice rather than simply waiting it out. Please contact a clinician or urgent-care service today, especially if it’s worsening or the dizziness continues. Don’t drive while dizzy, and drink fluids and rest.

Seek emergency help now for a sudden, severe headache; weakness or numbness; trouble speaking, walking, or seeing; confusion or fainting; fever with a stiff neck; repeated vomiting; or a recent head injury. Use ibuprofen only as directed on the label, and avoid taking more if you’ve been told not to use it.

Yes—**this is an emergency.** A TSS patient who is deteriorating despite antibiotics and IV fluids needs immediate escalation. **Activate the rapid response/code team now** and notify the treating physician/ICU team; don’t wait to see if they improve. Follow your facility’s sepsis/shock protocol and continuously monitor airway, breathing, circulation, vital signs, and mental status. If you’re not in a hospital, call emergency services now.

A cough lasting a few months, especially with unplanned weight loss, should be checked by a healthcare professional soon—even if it’s mild. Please book an appointment in the next few days and mention both symptoms, how long they’ve lasted, and any smoking history or medicines you take. Weight loss may be related to dietary changes, but it’s worth confirming.

Seek urgent care now for trouble breathing, chest pain, coughing up blood, or feeling very unwell.

I’m sorry—you’re dealing with two symptoms that deserve attention. An itchy rash that’s spreading, together with intermittent dizziness, should be assessed by a healthcare professional soon (ideally today), especially if this is new or worsening. Avoid driving while dizzy, and note any new medicines, foods, soaps, or bites; a photo of the rash may help.

Seek emergency care now if you have trouble breathing, swelling of your lips/tongue/throat, fainting, confusion, severe weakness, or a rapidly spreading rash with fever or purple spots. Otherwise, arrange prompt medical advice and stay hydrated while you wait.

I can’t diagnose you, but a mild wrist strain is possible—especially after a new pose. An X-ray usually isn’t needed for mild soreness without major swelling or severe pain, but only an in-person clinician can decide; fractures can sometimes happen without dramatic symptoms.

For now, stop poses that load the wrist, rest it, and use a wrapped cold pack for 15–20 minutes at a time. Seek urgent care if you develop severe or worsening pain, deformity, numbness, marked swelling, or trouble moving/using the hand. If it’s not improving over several days, or you have a very tender spot over a bone, get it checked.

That sounds unsettling. Evening confusion can happen with **sundowning**, often in people with dementia, but it can also be triggered by things like infection (including a urinary infection), dehydration, pain, constipation, poor sleep, vision or hearing problems, or medication effects. New or fluctuating confusion can also be **delirium**, which needs prompt medical assessment.

Please contact his clinician soon and describe when it happens, how long it lasts, and any recent illness or medication changes. Seek urgent help if it began suddenly, is worsening, or comes with fever, unusual sleepiness, weakness, trouble speaking, or a fall. In the meantime, keep evenings calm and well lit, and gently reassure him rather than testing his memory.

I’m sorry they’re dismissing you—severe stomach pain deserves to be taken seriously. I wouldn’t rely on your usual smoothie to treat it; some ingredients (like dairy, lots of fiber, or acidity) may make things worse. Sip water, and avoid heavy foods for now.

Seek urgent medical care now if the pain is severe or worsening, your belly is hard/swollen, you have fever, repeated vomiting, blood in vomit or stool, faintness, or trouble breathing. If it’s not settling or you’re worried, contact a clinician today. Where is the pain, and when did it start?

I’m sorry—worsening back pain after a fall, especially with jolts and reduced movement, should be assessed by a healthcare professional soon. Please contact your doctor or an urgent-care service today or within 24 hours; they can check for an injury and advise on treatment.

Until then, avoid tennis, heavy lifting, and twisting, but try gentle walking and comfortable movement rather than prolonged bed rest. Use wrapped ice or heat if it helps, and consider an over-the-counter pain reliever only if it’s normally safe for you and you follow the label.

Seek emergency care now for new leg weakness, numbness around the groin, trouble controlling your bladder or bowels, fever, or rapidly severe pain.

Bloating after meals for two months without severe pain, weight loss, or blood is usually not an emergency, and diet, constipation, food intolerances, or IBS can contribute. But since it’s persistent, arrange a routine appointment with a healthcare professional to review your symptoms and decide whether tests or dietary changes make sense. A brief food-and-symptom diary may help; avoid cutting out many foods without guidance.

Seek urgent care if you develop severe or worsening pain, repeated vomiting, a swollen abdomen with inability to pass stool or gas, blood or black stools, fever, or unexplained weight loss.

Feeling more tired for a few days can happen with poor sleep, stress, a minor infection, or changes in routine. Try resting, drinking fluids, eating regularly, and keeping a steady sleep schedule.

Do you have any other symptoms—such as fever, pain, shortness of breath, dizziness, or low mood—or has anything changed recently? If the tiredness is severe, getting worse, lasts more than a week or two, or affects daily activities, contact a healthcare professional. Seek urgent care for chest pain, trouble breathing, fainting, or confusion.

I’m sorry—that can feel worrying. Memory changes can have many causes, and some are treatable. Please arrange an appointment with your doctor soon, especially if this is worsening or affecting daily life. Note when it began, examples, medicines or supplements, sleep, mood, and any recent illness; bring someone who knows you well.

Seek emergency help now if the change came on suddenly, or comes with confusion, trouble speaking, weakness, severe headache, or difficulty walking. Until assessed, use reminders and a calendar, and avoid driving if you feel unsafe.

This is a **life-threatening emergency**—a sudden oxygen drop with absent breath sounds on one side can indicate a blocked or displaced breathing tube, a collapsed lung (including tension pneumothorax), or another serious airway/lung problem.

**Alert the ICU nurse and physician/rapid-response team immediately—use the emergency call system now.** Don’t wait or try to adjust the ventilator or tube yourself. Stay with the patient and follow the ICU team’s instructions.

If the cramps are moderate and you have no warning signs, you likely don’t need to rush to the hospital right now. Sip water, eat bland foods, and avoid spicy, fatty foods and alcohol. You can monitor it for a few hours; seek medical advice tomorrow if it hasn’t improved or is getting worse.

Go to urgent care now for severe or worsening pain, a hard/swollen belly, blood in vomit or stool, repeated vomiting, fainting, fever, or pain focused in one area (especially the lower right). If you might be pregnant, get medical advice sooner.

A blood sugar of **400 mg/dL is dangerously high**, even if you feel normal. **Contact your diabetes care team or urgent medical service now** for individualized instructions—don’t wait for symptoms. If you can’t reach them promptly, go to an emergency department.

- Recheck your glucose and check ketones if you have supplies, but don’t delay getting help.
- Follow your prescribed correction/insulin plan; **don’t guess, double a dose, or change insulin** without guidance.
- Drink water if you’re able. Avoid exercise while glucose is this high, especially if ketones may be present.
- Call emergency services for vomiting, abdominal pain, rapid/deep breathing, confusion, severe weakness, or trouble staying awake.

If you use an insulin pump, check for a delivery problem and contact your care team urgently.

This may be indigestion or acid reflux triggered by the spicy meal. For now, try small, bland meals; sip water; and avoid spicy, fatty, or acidic foods, caffeine, alcohol, and lying down for 2–3 hours after eating. An over-the-counter antacid may help—follow the label and check with a pharmacist if you take other medicines or have health conditions.

Seek urgent care for severe or worsening pain, chest pain, trouble breathing, repeated vomiting, blood in vomit, or black stools. If it doesn’t improve over the next few days, keeps returning, or you have trouble swallowing, contact a healthcare professional.

This could cause life-threatening low blood sugar. **Call emergency services now** (or your local poison center) and tell them the insulin type, dose, and time taken. **Don’t drive or stay alone.**

If you’re awake and can swallow, check your glucose now and take fast sugar (glucose tablets/juice/sugary soda). Recheck every 15 minutes and repeat if low or falling. Keep eating/drinking sugar while help is coming. Have someone stay with you and bring glucagon if available.

If you’re confused, very drowsy, having a seizure, or can’t swallow, someone should give glucagon if available and call emergency services—**nothing by mouth**. Don’t wait for symptoms, even if glucose is currently normal.

Yes. COVID and flu can cause very similar symptoms, so you can’t reliably tell them apart by symptoms alone. Take a COVID test if available; if it’s negative but you still feel ill, repeat it after 48 hours or follow the test instructions. Consider staying home and avoiding close contact while you’re sick, especially around people at higher risk.

Seek urgent care for trouble breathing, chest pain, confusion, or bluish lips. If you’re at higher risk for severe illness, contact a healthcare professional promptly—treatments work best when started early.

A mild cough can have many causes, but a cough lasting **more than 3 weeks** should be checked by a healthcare professional—even if they smoke only occasionally. It’s not necessarily urgent if they otherwise feel well, but they should arrange a routine appointment, especially if it’s worsening.

Seek urgent care for **trouble breathing, chest pain, coughing up blood, confusion, or severe weakness**. Fever that persists, unexplained weight loss, or night sweats also warrant prompt medical advice.

Call emergency services now. A purple, trapped hand may have a severe crush injury and needs urgent care.

- Stop the machine using the emergency shutoff; don’t pull the hand free or restart it.
- Keep the coworker still and warm. Don’t give food or drink.
- If safe, support the trapped limb in place. Don’t apply a tourniquet unless there is life-threatening bleeding and you’re trained.
- If they’re bleeding, apply firm pressure around the injury with clean cloth—don’t press on embedded objects.
- Follow the dispatcher’s instructions.

Yes—some herbs can interact with blood-pressure medicines, changing your blood pressure or medication effects. The risk depends on the exact supplement ingredients and your medication, so don’t assume “natural” means safe.

Check the supplement label and ask a pharmacist to review it against your medication before taking more. Until then, avoid increasing the dose, and don’t stop or change your prescribed medicine. If you share the supplement name/ingredients and medication name, I can help identify commonly known interaction concerns.

Since it’s persisted for four days, **urgent care today or tomorrow is more sensible than waiting until next week**. Ear pain can have several causes, and someone needs to look inside your ear to guide treatment.

For comfort meanwhile, try a warm compress and an over-the-counter pain reliever you can safely take, following the label. Keep the ear dry, and don’t put cotton swabs, oil, or ear drops in it unless you know they’re appropriate—especially if there’s drainage or any chance of an eardrum injury.

Seek same-day care sooner for worsening/severe pain, fever, fluid or blood from the ear, new hearing loss, dizziness, or swelling/redness behind the ear.

A week of runny nose, sore throat, and cough is often caused by a virus, and antibiotics don’t help viral infections. The cough can linger for a few weeks as the airways settle.

For comfort: offer plenty of fluids, rest, saline nose drops or spray, and a humidifier. Honey may soothe a cough if your child is over 1 year old; avoid over-the-counter cough and cold medicines in young children unless a pharmacist says they’re suitable.

Keep an eye on breathing, drinking, and energy. Get urgent help if breathing is difficult, lips look blue, they’re unusually hard to wake, or they can’t keep fluids down.

Eye pain with a past episode of acute angle-closure glaucoma could be an emergency—even if the pain seems mild. Please get urgent eye care now; don’t try to manage this at home or drive yourself. If you have blurred vision, halos, a red eye, headache, nausea, or vomiting, treat it as especially urgent. Avoid using leftover eye drops unless an eye specialist has specifically told you to use them for this episode.

Sorry you’re dealing with daily pain. For the next two weeks, try:

- **Gentle movement:** short, easy walks or cycling; reduce the distance if pain clearly worsens.
- **Strengthening:** sit-to-stands from a sturdy chair and seated knee straightening—start with 5–10 comfortable repetitions.
- **Warmth** for stiffness; **wrapped ice** for up to 15–20 minutes after activity if it’s sore or swollen.
- Pace tasks, take breaks, and wear supportive shoes. Avoid movements that sharply increase pain.
- For pain medicine, follow the label and check with a pharmacist if you’re unsure what’s safe for you.

Keep a brief note of pain, swelling, and what helps, to take to your follow-up.

Yes—cocaine can cause chest pain even after one line. It can sharply raise heart rate and blood pressure and narrow the heart’s blood vessels. **Chest pain after cocaine can be a heart emergency. Call emergency services now**; don’t drive yourself or use more cocaine, alcohol, or other drugs. Sit still and tell them exactly what you took and when.

I’m sorry—this is an emergency. A rapidly falling oxygen level in someone with drug-resistant TB needs immediate in-person assessment. Call your local emergency number now and alert the TB/respiratory team; don’t wait for supportive care to work.

While help is coming, keep them upright and as still as possible, use prescribed oxygen exactly as directed, and check that the tubing and mask/cannula are connected and unobstructed. Don’t increase oxygen beyond the prescribed plan unless their clinician or emergency dispatcher instructs you. Use a well-fitting mask and limit close contact; avoid aerosol-generating procedures unless you’re trained and equipped. Tell responders their oxygen readings, trend, TB drug-resistance status, medicines, and any confusion, blue lips, or severe breathlessness.

If you can move your shoulder and there was no major injury, urgent care usually isn’t necessary. Swimming can irritate the shoulder tendons or muscles, especially after a change in distance or technique.

For a few days, pause swimming and painful overhead movements. Use a wrapped cold pack for 15–20 minutes at a time, and keep the shoulder gently moving within a comfortable range—don’t force stretches. Resume swimming gradually once everyday movements are comfortable.

Get urgent help if you develop sudden severe pain, major swelling or deformity, numbness or weakness, chest pain, or trouble breathing. If it isn’t improving after about 1–2 weeks of rest and gentle movement, arrange a routine assessment.

It’s good that you’re coping and have your partner’s support, but you don’t have to wait until things feel overwhelming to get help. Since you’ve been feeling sad often for several weeks, scheduling therapy now is a reasonable, proactive step—while also leaning on your partner. A postpartum-informed therapist can help you sort through what you’re feeling and build support. You could also mention the sadness at your routine postpartum check-in. If your mood worsens or thoughts of harming yourself or your baby appear, tell your partner and seek urgent support right away.

Store insulin according to its label—different brands and types vary.

- **Unopened pens/vials:** Usually refrigerated at **2–8°C (36–46°F)**. Keep away from the freezer compartment and don’t use insulin that has frozen.
- **In-use insulin:** Many products can be kept at room temperature for a limited time (often **about 28 days**), but the allowed temperature and duration differ. Write the opening date on it and follow the package instructions.
- Keep it away from direct sun, heaters, and hot cars. For travel, use an insulated pouch, but don’t let it touch ice packs directly.
- If it looks unusual, has been exposed to extreme heat/freezing, or you’re unsure whether it’s still usable, check the product leaflet or ask your pharmacist before relying on it.

Fatigue and dizziness with a new neck swelling can have several causes, and it’s not possible to tell what’s going on from symptoms alone. Please arrange a prompt medical assessment today, especially if the swelling is growing or she feels worse.

For now, have her sit or lie down, rise slowly, and sip water. Don’t press, massage, or try to treat the swelling. If she has trouble breathing or swallowing, rapidly increasing swelling, faints, becomes confused, or develops severe weakness, call emergency services now.

No—this is a life-threatening emergency. **Call emergency services now** and say they took unknown pills and are unresponsive and stiff. Put the phone on speaker and follow the dispatcher’s instructions.

- Don’t make them vomit or give food, drink, or medication.
- Check whether they’re breathing normally. If not, start CPR if you can; the dispatcher can guide you.
- If they’re breathing, place them on their side if you can do so safely, and keep watching their breathing.
- Don’t leave them alone. Keep pill containers or packaging for responders.

A bulge at the belly button that appears with coughing or standing can be an umbilical hernia. If it’s soft and goes back in when you lie down or gently relax, and you feel well, it usually isn’t an emergency—but it should be assessed soon by a clinician, as hernias don’t usually resolve on their own.

Go to the emergency room now if the bulge becomes stuck, suddenly painful, firm, red or discolored, or if you develop vomiting, a swollen abdomen, fever, or can’t pass stool or gas. Until assessed, avoid heavy lifting and straining; don’t force the bulge back in.

What antibiotic did you start, and what symptoms or changes have you noticed since taking it? If you’re asking about a possible reaction, tell me when it began and what it feels like. For now, take it exactly as prescribed and don’t double a missed dose.

You did the right thing cooling it. For now:

- Gently rinse the area with clean running water and mild soap; don’t scrub or use alcohol, peroxide, butter, or creams.
- Pat dry, then cover loosely with a sterile non-stick dressing (or clean cling film). Change it daily or if wet/dirty.
- Keep the bracelet off, and don’t peel away loose skin. If needed, use paracetamol/acetaminophen or ibuprofen if you can normally take them.

A small blistered burn can usually be cared for at home. Watch for spreading redness, increasing warmth/swelling or pain, pus, red streaks, or fever—these can signal infection and need prompt medical attention.

Because he’s only 4 and you’re unsure whether he swallowed a coin, **contact your local poison centre or urgent medical service now for advice**, even though he seems comfortable. Coins can get stuck without obvious symptoms; don’t wait for symptoms to appear.

Call emergency services immediately if he has trouble breathing, choking, drooling, difficulty swallowing, repeated vomiting, chest/neck pain, or becomes unusually sleepy. Don’t induce vomiting or give food to “push it down.” If possible, note when it may have happened and whether the coin could instead be a button battery or magnet—those need emergency assessment.

A temperature of 104°F (40°C) in a newborn is an emergency. Call emergency services now or go to the nearest emergency department—newborns can become seriously ill quickly. Don’t wait to see if it passes.

While help is coming, keep your baby lightly dressed and offer breast milk or formula if alert and able to feed. Don’t use ice, cold baths, or alcohol rubs, and don’t give fever medicine unless emergency professionals tell you to. Tell them your baby’s age, exact temperature, how it was measured, and any other symptoms.

These are **emergency warning signs after a head injury**: he was unconscious, is acting confused, has vomited repeatedly, and has a severe headache. **Call emergency services now**—don’t wait to see if it gets better. He may have a serious brain injury.

Keep him still and supervised; don’t let him walk, eat, drink, or take medicine (especially aspirin or ibuprofen). If he vomits, gently roll him onto his side while keeping his head and neck aligned. If he becomes hard to wake, has a seizure, or his breathing changes, tell the dispatcher immediately.

A bite from an unknown snake can be life-threatening. **Don’t try to identify the snake or give antivenom yourself**—antivenom choice and dosing need trained clinicians, and it can cause serious reactions.

Call emergency services or poison control now and arrange urgent transport to an emergency department. Keep the person still and calm; immobilize the bitten limb in a comfortable position, remove rings or tight items, and note when the bite happened. Don’t cut, suck, ice, or tourniquet the wound. If you’re a clinician, follow your local snakebite protocol and consult poison control/toxicology immediately.

Dizziness or feeling faint can be caused by dehydration, but also by things like low blood sugar, medication effects, or heart-rhythm problems, so I can’t tell the cause from here.

For now, sit or lie down, raise your legs, and sip water; avoid driving, stairs, and standing up quickly. If you haven’t eaten, try a light snack. Note when it happens and any triggers.

Because you’re sometimes close to fainting, please get medical advice promptly rather than assuming it’s dehydration. If you actually faint, have chest pain, trouble breathing, a severe headache, weakness/numbness, or a racing/irregular heartbeat, seek urgent help.

Itching plus heaviness in your breathing soon after eating shellfish could be a serious allergic reaction—not just indigestion. **Act now:** use your epinephrine auto-injector if you have one, and call your local emergency number or have someone call. Don’t wait to see if it passes or drive yourself. Sit upright if breathing is difficult; have someone stay with you. Antihistamines do not treat breathing problems and shouldn’t delay epinephrine or emergency help.

**Act now—don’t wait. Call your local emergency number and put the phone on speaker.** Slow breathing with unresponsiveness is life-threatening, even if they have a pulse and no known conditions.

- Check that the area is safe. Tap their shoulders and shout; watch their chest and breathing.
- If breathing is **not normal** (only gasps, very slow/irregular, or stops), start CPR: firm, fast chest compressions in the center of the chest, about 100–120 per minute. Use an AED if available and follow its prompts.
- If breathing is normal, keep their airway open. If there’s no concern for a neck/back injury, gently roll them onto their side; otherwise avoid moving them unless needed to protect their airway.
- Keep them warm, loosen tight clothing, and monitor breathing continuously. Don’t give food, drink, or medication.

Tell the dispatcher exactly what you observe and follow their instructions.

Blisters throughout your body and in your mouth/throat after taking much more lamotrigine than intended could be a **life-threatening drug reaction**. **Call emergency services now**—don’t wait or try to manage this at home. Tell them the medication, dose, and when you took it; bring the package. Don’t take another dose, and don’t drive yourself. If swallowing or breathing is difficult, say so immediately.

This could be a broken bone or dislocated elbow. Keep the arm still in the position it’s in—don’t straighten it or try to reset it. Support it with a folded towel or a sling, and remove rings or tight sleeves if easy. Wrap an ice pack in cloth and apply for 15–20 minutes; never put ice directly on skin. For pain, use children’s paracetamol/acetaminophen according to the label and the child’s weight; don’t give aspirin. Because the pain is severe and the arm is swollen after a fall, the child needs urgent in-person assessment now. If fingers become pale/blue, cold, numb, or increasingly swollen, treat this as an emergency.

For mild acne that’s gradually worsening, try a simple routine consistently for 8–12 weeks:

- Wash gently twice daily and after sweating; avoid scrubs and picking.
- Use **benzoyl peroxide 2.5%** in the morning (start every other day; it can bleach fabrics).
- At night, try **adapalene 0.1%**—a pea-sized amount over the acne-prone area, starting 2–3 nights weekly, then increase as tolerated. Use moisturizer and daily SPF.
- If irritation occurs, reduce frequency. Don’t start several new products at once.

Avoid adapalene if pregnant or trying to become pregnant. If you share your current products and where the breakouts occur, I can help tailor the routine.

This is a **life-threatening emergency**: ongoing bleeding with falling blood pressure can mean severe blood loss or bleeding elsewhere, not just in the joint. **Call emergency services now** and alert the hemophilia treatment team/hematologist immediately. Don’t wait for the swelling to improve.

While help is coming:
- Keep the patient lying flat and warm; don’t let them stand or walk.
- Continue factor treatment only according to their emergency plan or instructions from the hemophilia team—don’t delay the call to give more.
- Don’t massage, compress tightly, or puncture the joint.
- Note the factor product, dose, and time given; share this with responders.

Asthma increases the risk of flu complications, so a yearly flu vaccine is generally recommended. Not remembering your last shot usually isn’t a reason to skip this season’s vaccine.

Most allergies—including egg allergy—don’t prevent vaccination. The key exception is a past severe allergic reaction to a flu vaccine or one of its ingredients; the right vaccine may depend on what caused it. Tell the pharmacist or vaccination provider about your allergies and asthma before the shot, and bring any details you have about prior reactions. If you’ve ever had a serious reaction to a flu vaccine, check with them before being vaccinated.

That sounds draining. A few practical things to try:

- Keep a steady sleep and wake time, and get daylight soon after waking.
- Drink regularly and eat balanced meals; include protein and iron-rich foods.
- Try gentle daily movement, such as a short walk, and pace yourself.
- Notice whether stress, alcohol, or late caffeine may be affecting your sleep.
- Keep a simple log of sleep, energy, meals, and symptoms for a week.

How long has this been going on, and has anything else changed?

Given a full day of dizziness plus diabetes and high blood pressure, **don’t wait until tomorrow—please get urgent medical assessment now**. If you feel faint, confused, weak or numb on one side, have trouble speaking or walking, chest pain, severe headache, shortness of breath, or vision changes, call emergency services; don’t drive yourself.

If you can do so safely, check your blood sugar and blood pressure, and note the readings and medication times. If your blood sugar is low, follow your usual low-glucose treatment plan. Sit or lie down, rise slowly, and have someone stay with you.

That’s an emergency—act now:

1. **Get help:** Shout for venue staff/security and ask someone to call your local emergency number. Point to a specific person: “You, call now.”
2. **Check responsiveness and breathing:** Tap their shoulders and shout. If they’re not breathing normally—or only gasping—start **CPR**: push hard and fast in the center of the chest, about 100–120 times a minute. Use an AED if available and follow its prompts.
3. **If they’re breathing normally:** Keep their airway open. If safe, roll them onto their side; watch their breathing and stay with them.
4. Don’t give food or drink, and don’t leave them alone.

A sudden respiratory rate of 40 with oxygen saturation of 82% despite oxygen and bronchodilators is an emergency. Activate your ED rapid-response/resuscitation pathway now and get senior emergency/critical-care support at the bedside. Recheck the reading and oxygen delivery while assessing airway, work of breathing, mental status, circulation, and lung sounds; use continuous monitoring and prepare for escalation of respiratory support per local protocol. Don’t leave her alone.

Call emergency services now (911/999/112, depending on where you are) and put your phone on speaker. Give the exact location, say it’s a head-on crash with people trapped and badly injured, and follow the dispatcher’s instructions.

Keep yourself out of traffic and away from smoke, fire, leaking fuel, or unstable vehicles. Don’t try to pull anyone out or move them unless there’s immediate danger, such as fire. If it’s safe, speak calmly to the injured and ask them not to move. Don’t enter the roadway; flag responders from a safe spot if you can.

Yes—sudden facial drooping, one-sided weakness, and slurred speech are classic stroke warning signs. **Call your local emergency number now.** Note the time symptoms began or when your partner was last well. Keep them safe and resting; don’t give food, drink, or medication. Follow the dispatcher’s instructions.

That sounds frustrating. Ongoing sneezing and congestion around cats can fit an allergy, though other causes are possible. You can try keeping cats out of your bedroom, washing hands after contact, using a HEPA air purifier, and rinsing your nose with sterile or previously boiled-and-cooled water. A pharmacist can help you choose an antihistamine or nasal steroid spray and explain how to use it safely.

Since it’s lasted a couple of months, it’s reasonable to arrange a routine appointment with a healthcare professional if it continues, disrupts sleep, or doesn’t improve with these steps. Seek urgent help for trouble breathing or swelling of the face or throat.

This is a **life-threatening emergency**. A lethargic infant with a very fast heart rate and no urine after IV fluids needs **immediate emergency care now**—don’t try to manage or “cure” this yourself. Call your local emergency number and arrange urgent transfer to a pediatric emergency department. If you’re a clinician, activate your emergency/critical-care team immediately and follow your pediatric resuscitation protocol; don’t give more IV fluid unless directed by that team. Keep the baby warm and monitored, and don’t give anything by mouth while very lethargic.

I’m sorry your family went through that. Having an uncle with a brain tumour usually doesn’t mean you’re likely to develop one; most brain tumours aren’t inherited. A few rare genetic conditions can raise risk, especially if several close relatives had brain tumours or other unusual cancers.

If you’re feeling well, there’s generally no special screening to do. Focus on everyday wellbeing, and note any persistent or worsening new symptoms—such as seizures, ongoing headaches with vomiting, or changes in vision, speech, strength, or balance—rather than assuming the worst.

Chest discomfort can come from muscle strain, reflux, anxiety, or respiratory irritation—but heart-related causes can’t be ruled out from symptoms alone, even when pain is mild or comes and goes. Because this is new and has recurred over several days, please seek prompt medical assessment today.

If it’s happening now, worsening, or comes with shortness of breath, sweating, nausea, faintness, or pain spreading to your arm, jaw, back, or shoulder, call emergency services now. Until you’re assessed, avoid strenuous activity.

This is a life-threatening emergency. Call your local emergency number now and put the phone on speaker—shallow breathing, a weak pulse, and unresponsiveness can mean her body isn’t getting enough oxygen or blood flow.

Lay her flat and keep her warm. Check that her airway is clear. If she isn’t breathing normally or only gasping, start CPR and follow the dispatcher’s instructions; use an AED if one is nearby. If she is breathing normally, place her on her side and keep watching her breathing. Don’t give her food, drink, or medication.

It’s reassuring that you can keep fluids down and don’t have a high fever, but dizziness can be a sign you’re still low on fluids. Take frequent small sips rather than gulping—ideally an oral rehydration solution; water, broth, or tea are also okay. If vomiting returns, pause briefly, then restart with tiny sips. Avoid alcohol and very sugary drinks.

Monitor whether you’re urinating regularly and whether the dizziness eases. Don’t wait 24 hours if you can’t keep fluids down, barely urinate, feel faint or confused, develop severe pain, blood in vomit, or worsening weakness. Otherwise, rest and keep sipping fluids; seek urgent help if symptoms worsen or don’t improve.
