Check that she’s breathing normally. If she isn’t, or you’re unsure, begin CPR and follow the dispatcher’s instructions; use an AED if available. If she is breathing, place her on her side if you can do so safely, keep her warm, and watch her breathing. Don’t give her food, drink, or medication, and don’t leave her alone.

Keeping water down is reassuring, and small, frequent sips are better than drinking a lot at once. An oral rehydration solution (from a pharmacy) can replace salts; follow its directions. Avoid alcohol and large amounts of very sugary drinks. Watch for urinating much less or very dark urine.

Because you’re dizzy after vomiting, don’t wait 24 hours if it worsens or you can’t keep fluids down. Seek urgent medical care now for fainting, confusion, severe weakness, severe abdominal pain, blood or green vomit, or very little/no urine. If dizziness persists despite sipping fluids, get assessed promptly. A high fever isn’t required for dehydration to be serious.

Fever with abdominal pain just three days after colon surgery can signal a serious complication. **Please contact your surgeon’s emergency/on-call team now or go to the emergency department.** Don’t wait to see if it passes. If you feel faint, confused, very weak, have trouble breathing, worsening/severe pain, or can’t reach your surgical team promptly, call emergency services. Have someone else take you, and follow your discharge instructions while arranging urgent care.

A new detergent could cause an itchy contact rash, but a rash that appears suddenly across the chest can’t be diagnosed from a description alone. Stop using the new detergent, gently rinse the area, avoid scratching, and use a cool compress. Don’t apply new creams or scented products for now.

Because you’re 70 and this appeared overnight, please get examined promptly to check for infection or another cause. Seek emergency care now if you have trouble breathing, face or throat swelling, fever, severe pain, rapidly spreading redness, blisters, or feel very unwell.

A bad cough with lightheadedness can sometimes signal a problem that needs prompt attention. Please get examined today; if you’re fainting, struggling to breathe, have chest pain, blue lips, confusion, or cough up blood, go to the emergency room now. Sit or lie down, avoid driving, and sip fluids while arranging help.

Being unusually tired and unable or unwilling to stand after days of vomiting is a danger sign. It could mean severe dehydration or another serious problem. **Please take him to an emergency department now or call emergency services.** Don’t wait to see if it passes.

While arranging help, if he’s awake and swallowing normally, offer tiny frequent sips of oral rehydration solution. Don’t force food or drink, and don’t give medicines unless a clinician advises. If he’s hard to wake, confused, breathing abnormally, or worsening, call emergency services immediately.

Yes—this could be serious. A headache that rapidly becomes much worse along with blurry vision needs urgent assessment. Stop what you’re doing and go to the emergency room now, or call your local emergency number. Don’t drive yourself; ask someone to stay with you and take you.

This is an emergency. Activate your rapid response/code team now and follow your unit’s acute chest syndrome protocol—don’t wait. Stay with the patient, alert the provider and charge nurse immediately, support oxygenation per protocol, and prepare for urgent escalation of care. A saturation of 83% with new chest pain and breathing difficulty needs immediate in-person assessment.

Call your local emergency number now—paleness and bluish color after choking can mean she isn’t getting enough oxygen. Don’t wait or drive a long distance to her doctor.

If she’s coughing strongly and breathing, keep her upright and let her cough; don’t put fingers in her mouth or give food or drink. If she can’t breathe, cry, or cough effectively, start age-appropriate choking first aid (back blows and abdominal thrusts) and follow the emergency dispatcher’s instructions. If she becomes unresponsive or stops breathing normally, begin CPR if you can. Keep her with you and monitor her breathing until help arrives.

A cough lasting two weeks with new wheezing and chest tightness can happen with a lingering infection, asthma or airway irritation, or other lung problems. Because the wheezing is new and you’re feeling chest tightness, please get examined promptly today so your breathing can be checked.

If you’re struggling to breathe, the tightness is severe or worsening, your lips look bluish, you feel faint or confused, or you have chest pain, seek emergency care now. Until assessed, rest, avoid smoke and strenuous activity, and use any prescribed inhaler only as directed.

If you mean staples closing a scalp wound: keep the area clean and follow the discharge instructions. Don’t pick at the staples; avoid soaking the wound, and ask the clinic that placed them when they should be removed (often around 7–10 days). Seek urgent care now if bleeding won’t stop, the wound opens, or you develop worsening headache, vomiting, confusion, unusual sleepiness, weakness, or fever.

Ozempic (semaglutide) can lower blood sugar and often helps with weight loss, but it’s a prescription medicine—not suitable for everyone, and the right dose and product matter. Unregulated online sellers may supply counterfeit or unsafe medication. It can also cause nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, and, rarely, serious complications.

A “prediabetes” result alone doesn’t establish diabetes or mean Ozempic is the right choice. Please don’t order it without a qualified clinician confirming your results, checking risks, and prescribing from a legitimate pharmacy. In the meantime, gradual weight loss, regular activity, and balanced meals can reduce diabetes risk.

Depakote (valproate) can be appropriate for some conditions, but whether it’s safe for you depends on your diagnosis, other medicines, and health history. Take it only if it was prescribed to you, and follow the prescriber’s directions—don’t start, stop, or change the dose on your own. It can cause serious liver or pancreas problems and has major risks during pregnancy. What are you considering it for, and was it prescribed to you?

Gradual hearing loss over a year is worth getting assessed, even without pain or discharge. An ear exam and hearing test can check for treatable causes such as earwax and identify whether hearing aids or other care might help. Please arrange an appointment with a clinician or hearing specialist; avoid putting cotton swabs or objects in your ears, and use ear protection around loud sounds. Seek urgent care if hearing suddenly worsens, especially in one ear, or comes with severe dizziness, facial weakness, or other new neurological symptoms.

Sudden numbness and coldness in your hands and feet along with shortness of breath can be an emergency. **Stop what you’re doing and call emergency services now** (or have someone call); don’t drive yourself. Sit upright, stay warm, and loosen tight clothing while you wait. If you’re alone, unlock the door and keep your phone nearby. Do not try to treat this only at home.

Persistent neck stiffness and headache two days after a collision should be assessed sooner than your appointment in two weeks. Contact your GP practice for same-day triage, or call NHS 111; an advanced nurse practitioner can assess you and arrange further care if needed. Don’t force stretches or movements—keep activity gentle and use pain relief only as directed, checking with a pharmacist if you’re unsure ibuprofen is suitable for you.

**Seek emergency care now** for a worsening/severe headache, repeated vomiting, confusion, unusual drowsiness, fainting, weakness or numbness, trouble walking or speaking, vision changes, or severe neck pain.

Whiplash symptoms can evolve over several days, so getting prompt advice is sensible even without tingling.

Unintentional weight loss over a month is worth taking seriously, even if stress may be contributing. Please arrange a medical assessment soon rather than assuming the cause; a clinician can check for common causes and advise what to do. Seek urgent care now if you’re fainting, very weak or confused, unable to keep fluids down, or have severe pain, blood in your vomit or stool, or trouble breathing.

For now, note your weight change, appetite, stress, and any other symptoms, and try regular meals and fluids. Do you know roughly how much weight you’ve lost, and have you noticed any other changes?

For a mild toothache lasting 3 days, arrange a dental appointment soon—cavities and other causes need treatment even without swelling or fever. Meanwhile, gently floss around the tooth, rinse with warm salt water, avoid very hot, cold, or sugary foods, and use an over-the-counter pain reliever as directed if it’s safe for you. Don’t put aspirin directly on the tooth.

Seek urgent care if you develop facial or neck swelling, fever, pus, trouble swallowing or breathing, or rapidly worsening pain.

Occasional difficulty hearing can be part of age-related hearing loss, but it may also come from earwax, infection, or other treatable causes. Notice whether it’s getting worse, affects both ears, or makes conversation/TV difficult; background noise can make hearing harder. Try speaking face-to-face, clearly, and reduce background noise—don’t shout.

A sudden hearing loss (especially in one ear), severe ear pain, dizziness, or weakness/numbness needs urgent assessment. Otherwise, a hearing test can clarify what’s going on and whether simple measures or hearing aids may help.

This is a life-threatening emergency. Stop routine care and activate the clinic’s emergency response now; call emergency services. Do not wait for improvement. Have a trained airway clinician manage the airway immediately, with continuous monitoring and resuscitation per local protocol. Check the bag, mask seal, oxygen source, and airway position while help arrives.

That sounds annoying, but a small cheek bite that has stopped bleeding usually isn’t a reason by itself to call out. Rinse gently with cool water, and try cold water or an ice chip; avoid spicy, acidic, or crunchy foods for a bit. If you feel well enough, you can likely go to work—whether to call out is more about how you feel and your workplace’s rules than needing a doctor’s note.

If bleeding starts again and won’t stop after 10–15 minutes of steady pressure, or you develop major swelling or trouble breathing or swallowing, get urgent care.

Sudden dizziness with blurred vision, followed by a headache and feeling “off,” can be a warning sign of a serious problem. **Please stop what you’re doing, sit or lie down somewhere safe, and get emergency medical help now.** Call your local emergency number or ask someone nearby to call and stay with you. Don’t drive yourself.

Yes—this is a life-threatening choking emergency. Call emergency services now (speakerphone if possible).

If she’s conscious and cannot breathe, speak, or cough effectively:
- Give **5 firm back blows** between the shoulder blades.
- Then **5 abdominal thrusts**: stand behind her, make a fist just above her navel, grasp it, and pull sharply inward and upward.
- Repeat until the steak comes out or she becomes unresponsive.

If she becomes unresponsive, lower her to the floor and begin CPR; follow the dispatcher’s instructions. Don’t put your fingers in her mouth unless you can clearly see and remove the food.

This is a life-threatening emergency and could be a serious spinal cord injury. Call emergency services now—don’t wait to see if it passes. Keep your friend still in the position found; do not lift, turn, or move them, and don’t let them try to stand. Keep their head and neck aligned and steady, and follow the dispatcher’s instructions. If they stop breathing normally, tell the dispatcher immediately and follow their CPR guidance. No bleeding does not rule out a severe injury.

These symptoms after a head injury—especially clear fluid from one ear, hearing loss, dizziness, and double vision—could indicate a serious skull or brain injury. **Stop moving around and get emergency medical help now; call your local emergency number.** Don’t drive, put anything in the ear, or try to stop the fluid. Keep your head and neck still, and have someone stay with you while help is coming.

Yes—bluish lips and severe breathlessness with minimal activity are emergency warning signs. Call emergency services now or go to the ER; don’t wait to see if it passes. Keep your cousin sitting upright and resting, and don’t let them walk or drive themselves. If they become unresponsive or stop breathing normally, follow the dispatcher’s instructions.

Wash the bite gently with soap and water, then use a cool, damp cloth for 10–15 minutes to ease itching or swelling. Try not to scratch; an over-the-counter anti-itch cream or oral antihistamine may help—follow the label.

Seek emergency care now if you have trouble breathing, swelling of your lips or tongue, faintness, or rapidly spreading hives. Get prompt medical advice if redness is rapidly expanding, the area becomes increasingly hot or painful, pus appears, or you develop a fever.

For mild dryness, preservative-free artificial tears can usually be used as needed, including at night; a lubricating eye gel or ointment may last longer overnight but can blur vision temporarily. Follow the product label, and avoid “redness-relief” drops for routine dryness.

Since it has lasted six months, arrange an eye-care assessment to check the cause and make sure the drops are suitable. Seek urgent care if there’s eye pain, sudden vision change, marked redness, light sensitivity, or discharge.

Call emergency services now. This is life-threatening—especially just weeks after childbirth. Put the phone on speaker and follow the dispatcher’s instructions.

Check whether she is breathing normally. If she is not breathing normally or only gasping, start CPR: push hard and fast in the center of her chest (100–120 times a minute) and use an AED if available. If she is breathing, lay her flat, keep her still and warm, and turn her onto her side if she vomits. Don’t give food, drink, or medication. Stay with her until help arrives.

Sudden double vision with extreme unsteadiness and inability to walk can signal a medical emergency, such as a stroke. **Call emergency services now** (911/999/112 or your local number); don’t drive yourself. Ask someone nearby to stay with you, and note when you were last feeling normal.

Most toddler diarrhea is short-lived. Offer frequent small sips of oral rehydration solution; continue usual foods and milk, and avoid juice, soda, and anti-diarrhea medicines. Watch for dehydration: much less urine/no wet diaper for 8 hours, dry mouth, no tears, unusual sleepiness, or sunken eyes. If any appear, seek urgent medical care. Also get prompt advice if there’s blood or black stool, severe belly pain, or your child can’t keep fluids down. If watery stools continue beyond a few days or worsen, contact their pediatric clinician.

I’m glad you’re feeling better. **Don’t stop venlafaxine suddenly**—at 225 mg, abrupt stopping can cause significant withdrawal symptoms and anxiety may return. Ask your prescriber or pharmacist about a gradual taper and lower-cost options; in Canada, ask about generics and whether your coverage can help.

For anxiety therapists around the Danforth, try the **Psychology Today Canada therapist directory** (filter for Toronto, anxiety, and your preferred approach such as CBT), or **Affordable Therapy Network**. Check fees, waitlists, and whether they offer virtual sessions. A family health team or community health centre may also have lower-cost counselling.

A low fever lasting 7 days should be assessed by a healthcare professional, even without cough or rash. Please arrange prompt medical advice today. Seek emergency care now if you have trouble breathing, confusion, severe headache or stiff neck, chest pain, fainting, severe weakness, or can’t keep fluids down. Meanwhile, rest, drink fluids, and note your temperature and any new symptoms.

Yes—sudden, severe headaches with blurred vision in one eye are warning signs. Please stop what you’re doing and get emergency medical care now; don’t drive yourself. This can have serious causes, and it needs urgent assessment even if the symptoms ease.

This may be a severe allergic reaction or another emergency. **Call emergency services now** (911/999/112, depending on your location). Don’t drive yourself. If you have an epinephrine auto-injector, use it now as directed; lie down with legs raised unless that makes breathing harder. Don’t eat or drink, and stay with someone while help is coming.

This is an emergency. Sudden confusion, inability to stand, and fruity-smelling breath in someone with diabetes can signal diabetic ketoacidosis or another life-threatening problem. Call emergency services now—don’t let her walk or drive, and don’t leave her alone. If she’s unconscious or struggling to breathe, tell the dispatcher immediately. Follow their instructions; don’t give food or drink if she’s very drowsy or confused.

Dizziness with episodes of blurred vision isn’t something to assume is normal, especially when it’s been recurring for days. Please stop what you’re doing, sit or lie down, and don’t drive. Because these symptoms can sometimes signal a serious problem, get examined urgently today. If the blurring is happening now, you faint, develop weakness or numbness, trouble speaking, severe headache, chest pain, or trouble walking, call emergency services or go to the ER now.

This is **life-threatening postpartum hemorrhage with hemorrhagic shock**—ongoing blood loss is causing critically inadequate circulation to her organs. A blood pressure of 80/40, pulse 150, pallor, and confusion despite treatment indicate rapid deterioration. The exact bleeding source can’t be determined remotely.

**Activate your obstetric hemorrhage protocol and emergency transfer/escalation now.** Get senior obstetric, anesthesia, and surgical support; urgently arrange blood products and transport to a higher-level center while continuing resuscitation and rapidly identifying the source (uterine atony, trauma, retained tissue, or coagulopathy). Don’t delay escalation for an online assessment.

Dizziness all day can happen with dehydration, not eating enough, illness, or other causes. Sit or lie down, get up slowly, sip water, and avoid driving, heights, or machinery. If you can, have a light snack and ask someone to check on you.

Because it’s lasted all day, please get medical advice today. Call emergency services now for fainting, chest pain, trouble breathing, severe headache, confusion, weakness or numbness, trouble speaking, or difficulty walking.

That sudden, severe pain spreading down your leg, inability to move or stand, and feeling faint are **danger signs**. Please get emergency medical help now—call your local emergency number or have someone take you to an emergency department. Don’t drive yourself or try to walk it off; lie somewhere safe and ask someone to stay with you. I can’t diagnose the cause here, but this needs urgent assessment.

This is an emergency. Call emergency services now (911/999/112, depending on your location). Put your friend on their back, check whether they’re breathing normally, and follow the dispatcher’s instructions. If they aren’t breathing normally, start CPR and use an AED if available. If they are breathing, place them on their side and keep watching their breathing. Don’t give them food or drink.

Trouble speaking and weakness in one arm—even if they’ve completely resolved—can be signs of a stroke or transient ischemic attack. **Call emergency services now or have someone take you to an emergency department immediately. Don’t drive yourself.** Note when the symptoms started and when they stopped, and tell responders. Don’t wait to see if they return.

These are signs of a **life-threatening alcohol withdrawal seizure and hallucinations**. **Call emergency services now** or have someone take you to the emergency department—don’t drive yourself. Tell them you usually drink four bottles of wine daily, stopped three days ago, and may have had a seizure.

Stay with another person, move away from stairs or sharp objects, and don’t try to manage this with alcohol, sedatives, or sleeping pills. If another seizure happens, they should protect your head, turn you on your side, and put nothing in your mouth.

Call emergency services now. Have him lie down and keep him still. Press firmly on the wound with clean cloth or gauze—don’t lift it to check. If blood soaks through, add more layers on top and keep pressing. If an object is embedded, don’t remove it; press around it. Keep him warm, and don’t give food or drink. If he becomes faint or unresponsive, tell the dispatcher immediately and follow their instructions.

Intermittent arm tingling can happen when a nerve is briefly compressed—such as from leaning on your arm, sleeping on it, or neck/shoulder posture. It can also relate to repetitive use or other health conditions.

Try changing position, avoiding pressure on the arm, and taking gentle movement breaks. Notice when it happens and whether it comes with neck pain, weakness, or numbness.

If it starts suddenly with weakness, facial drooping, trouble speaking, chest pain, or shortness of breath, stop and seek emergency care now. If it keeps recurring or worsens, get it checked.

Stomach pain and occasional diarrhea can come from infections, food intolerance, medication effects, or other bowel conditions. Blood can sometimes be from a small tear or hemorrhoid, but it can also signal something more serious. Because you’ve had abdominal pain and blood in your stool, please get examined promptly; if bleeding returns or is heavy, pain becomes severe, or you feel faint, go to the emergency room now. Meanwhile, drink fluids and note when symptoms occur, what you’ve eaten, and any medicines you take.

Nausea can be a common side effect of some pain medicines, especially opioids, and may be worse if you take them on an empty stomach. It isn’t always dangerous, but follow your discharge instructions and don’t take extra doses or mix it with alcohol or sedatives. If the medication permits, taking it with a small snack may help; check the label or ask a pharmacist about your specific medicine.

Get urgent help if you have trouble breathing, become very hard to wake, faint, develop facial/throat swelling, or can’t keep fluids down. What painkiller are you taking, and when does the nausea start?

I’m sorry—that’s stressful. **Don’t try to put the catheter back in or insert anything into her urethra.** Call the home-care service’s on-call number now and ask for an urgent nurse visit; if unavailable, contact her clinician’s after-hours line for instructions. A catheter that came out may need prompt replacement, especially if she normally cannot urinate.

Meanwhile, keep her clean and dry: use a clean absorbent pad, gently wash and pat dry, change wet bedding/clothes, and protect skin with barrier cream. Offer fluids as usual unless she has a fluid restriction. Note when it came out and how much she urinates.

**Get urgent medical help now** if she cannot pass urine, has a painful/swollen lower belly, fever or chills, blood/clots, severe pain, confusion, or becomes very unwell.

Don’t use it until you’ve checked the label and confirmed with a pharmacist or your diabetes care team. Some insulins are meant to look cloudy and should become evenly milky after gently rolling; others should be clear. **Discard it** if it’s normally clear but looks cloudy, has clumps or particles, changed color, or won’t mix evenly. Use an unopened, properly stored replacement if available. If you can’t get a safe dose, contact your care team or pharmacist promptly—don’t guess or skip insulin, especially if you have type 1 diabetes.

A brief episode that passed after sitting can happen from dehydration, heat, or standing for a while, but I can’t tell the cause from here. If you’re now feeling normal, rest, drink water, and stand up slowly. Don’t drive if lightheadedness returns.

Seek emergency care now if you faint, have chest pain, trouble breathing, a racing or irregular heartbeat, severe headache, weakness/numbness, confusion, or trouble speaking. If it happens again, persists, or you’re still concerned, get prompt medical advice.

This is an emergency. **Call emergency services now**—don’t wait for it to stop. Keep the patient lying down and still. Apply firm, continuous pressure directly over the bleeding with clean gauze or cloth; don’t lift it to check. If it soaks through, add more layers on top. Follow the surgical team’s emergency instructions while help is coming.

Nosebleeds once a month that stop with steady pressure are usually not an emergency. Sit upright, lean forward, and pinch the soft part of your nose continuously for 10–15 minutes; avoid tilting your head back. If they keep recurring, arranging a routine ENT visit is reasonable—especially if they’re becoming more frequent or you take blood thinners.

Get urgent care now if bleeding won’t stop after 20 minutes of firm pressure, is very heavy, follows a significant injury, or you feel faint, weak, or short of breath.

Sudden severe headache, blurred vision, and numbness in one arm on day 5 postpartum are emergency warning signs, including possible stroke or postpartum preeclampsia. **Call emergency services now**—don’t drive yourself or wait to see if it passes. Tell them you’re 5 days postpartum and describe all three symptoms. Have someone stay with you and unlock the door; don’t take aspirin or other medication unless emergency professionals advise it.

Don’t double the dose. Since it’s almost time for today’s dose, **skip yesterday’s missed dose and take today’s dose at the usual time**, unless his anticoagulation clinic or pharmacist has given him a different plan. Contact his anticoagulation clinic or pharmacist today for guidance, and let them know the missed dose; don’t change the schedule on your own.

If he has unusual bleeding, a fall or head injury, severe headache, weakness, confusion, chest pain, or trouble breathing, get emergency care now.

Don’t try to remove it yourself—cutting, burning, or using mole-removal products can cause infection, scarring, or hide a serious skin problem. Because it’s new and dark, have it examined promptly by a healthcare professional or dermatologist before considering removal. Seek urgent care if it’s rapidly changing, irregular, bleeding, painful, or growing. In the meantime, take a clear photo with a ruler beside it and protect it from sun.

This is a **life-threatening emergency**. In a person with type 1 diabetes, extreme hyperglycemia, rapid breathing, confusion, and worsening responsiveness strongly suggest severe DKA; falling blood pressure and a very fast heart rate may indicate shock. The severe headache and declining consciousness raise concern for cerebral edema or another brain emergency.

**Activate the hospital emergency/critical-care team now** and follow your facility’s emergency protocol. Do not leave him alone or give anything by mouth. He needs immediate in-person assessment and treatment; I can’t determine exactly what is happening remotely.

A 104°F fever with a stiff neck and confusion is an emergency. Call emergency services now or go to the ER—don’t wait or try to manage this at home. These symptoms can signal a serious infection that needs immediate assessment and treatment. Keep your child with you, note when symptoms began and any medicines given, and don’t force food or drink if they’re confused.

With no major swelling or instability, it’s reasonable to try a few days of relative rest: avoid running, jumping, and anything that worsens the ache, but keep gentle, comfortable movement. Ice wrapped in a cloth for 15–20 minutes can help; supportive shoes and light compression may also be useful. Resume activity gradually as it improves.

Because the ache has returned months after the sprain, arrange a non-urgent assessment if it doesn’t clearly improve within several days, keeps recurring, or limits walking. Seek urgent care if you suddenly can’t bear weight, develop marked swelling or deformity, numbness, a hot/red ankle, or severe worsening pain.

**Call emergency services now—this is life-threatening. Do not stitch it or send him away by himself.**

- Put him flat, keep him warm, and don’t give food or drink.
- Apply firm, continuous pressure with sterile gauze or a clean cloth. If blood soaks through, add more on top; don’t lift the first layer.
- If anything is embedded or tissue is protruding, **don’t press on it or push it back in**—cover loosely with sterile dressing.
- Keep monitoring breathing and responsiveness; be ready to start CPR if needed.
- Arrange immediate emergency transfer and follow the dispatcher’s instructions.

Yes—this is very concerning. Severe wave-like abdominal pain, heavy bleeding with large clots, and lightheadedness one week after giving birth can signal a serious postpartum emergency. **Call emergency services now or have someone take you to the emergency department. Do not drive yourself.** Don’t wait to see if rest or iron helps. If possible, have someone stay with you and tell responders you gave birth about a week ago and describe the bleeding, clots, pain, and lightheadedness. I’m not a physician, but you need urgent in-person assessment now.

Call emergency services now—blue lips and difficulty staying awake can mean dangerously low oxygen. Don’t leave him alone or let him “sleep it off.”

- Check whether he responds and is breathing normally.
- If he isn’t breathing normally, start CPR and use an AED if available; follow the dispatcher’s instructions.
- If he is breathing, place him on his side and keep his airway clear.
- Give naloxone if available, as xylazine may be mixed with opioids. It won’t reverse xylazine, but can help if opioids are involved. Give another dose after 2–3 minutes if there’s no response.
- Don’t give food, drink, or other drugs. Tell responders what he may have taken.

Heavy bleeding with marked paleness and dizziness after birth can mean severe blood loss. **Call emergency services now** (or have someone call) and say you may have postpartum hemorrhage. Do not try to manage this at home or drive yourself.

While waiting:
- Lie flat, preferably with legs raised; keep warm.
- Have someone stay with you and unlock the door.
- Use a pad to track bleeding; don’t insert anything into the vagina.
- If you feel faint, don’t stand or walk. Follow the dispatcher’s instructions.

Even if you’ve asked not to be sent to hospital, these symptoms need immediate emergency assessment.

A high fever with a stiff neck can signal meningitis, which is an emergency. Call emergency services or go to the emergency department now—don’t wait to see if it improves. Keep the person resting and comfortable, don’t force their neck to move, and follow the dispatcher’s instructions. If they’re confused, hard to wake, having a seizure, or developing a rash, tell emergency services immediately.

This is an emergency—call your local emergency number now, even if you’re unsure what he took. **Don’t give him anything to eat or drink, and don’t try to make him vomit.**

If you have naloxone, give it now; repeat in 2–3 minutes if there’s no response. Check his breathing. If he’s breathing, place him on his side and stay with him. If he isn’t breathing normally, start CPR/rescue breathing if you can, and follow the dispatcher’s instructions. Tell responders what he may have taken and when.

A normal total cholesterol can still hide an unfavorable balance. To support a healthier HDL profile:

- Do regular aerobic activity—aim for about 150 minutes weekly, building up gradually.
- If you smoke, quitting can help raise HDL.
- Choose unsaturated fats (olive oil, nuts, seeds, avocado, and oily fish) instead of trans fats and excess saturated fat.
- If you’re above your comfortable weight, gradual weight loss may help.
- Don’t start drinking alcohol to raise HDL; it can cause other harms.

HDL is only one part of risk—LDL and your overall health matter more than trying to raise HDL alone. Discuss your full results and risk factors with a healthcare professional.

Tell the hospice nurse or on-call hospice team **now**—faster breathing can be a change they can help assess and ease. Keep the patient calm and comfortable, raise their upper body or help them lie on their side, loosen tight clothing, and use any oxygen or comfort medicines **only as prescribed in the hospice plan**. Don’t force food or fluids.

If breathing is suddenly severe, the patient is struggling, turning blue/gray, or hard to wake, call the hospice emergency number immediately; if the hospice team can’t be reached, call emergency services.

Yellow skin can be a sign of jaundice, sometimes linked to a liver or bile-duct problem. Please tell your cousin to get urgent medical assessment today—especially if their eyes are yellow, urine is dark, stools are pale, or they have pain, fever, vomiting, or confusion. If they’re confused, very drowsy, or severely unwell, go to the emergency room now.

This is a life-threatening emergency: worsening confusion and blood pressure of 80/50 after heavy vomiting may indicate shock. **Call emergency services now** and say you suspect shock; don’t wait or try to manage this at home.

While help is coming, keep him lying flat and warm. If he vomits or is drowsy, turn him onto his side; give nothing by mouth if confused or not fully alert. Monitor breathing and responsiveness, and follow the dispatcher’s instructions.

This is an emergency. **Call your local emergency number now** and put the phone on speaker—don’t wait or try to manage this alone. Tell them she collapsed, is unresponsive, breathing rapidly and shallowly, and is pale and sweaty.

Check whether she’s breathing normally. If she isn’t, or you’re unsure, start CPR and follow the dispatcher’s instructions; use an AED if one is nearby. If she is breathing, lay her flat, keep her warm, and watch her breathing. Don’t give her food, drink, or medicine, and don’t leave her alone.

Yes—new dizziness with weakness in both arms and legs can signal a serious problem, including a stroke. Please call emergency services or go to the emergency department now; don’t let her drive or wait to see if it passes. Note when the symptoms began and any changes, and keep her seated or lying safely while help is arranged.

Blue lips can mean your son isn’t getting enough oxygen, even if he seems fine. **Take him to the emergency room now**—don’t wait for a regular appointment. Call emergency services if the blue color persists, he has trouble breathing, becomes unusually sleepy, or worsens. Keep him calm and warm while you get help.

For a small thigh bruise, you can:

- Apply a cold pack wrapped in cloth for 15–20 minutes at a time during the first day; don’t put ice directly on skin.
- Rest the area and elevate your leg when comfortable.
- After 24–48 hours, gentle warmth may help. Avoid hard massage.
- For pain, consider acetaminophen if it’s safe for you; follow the label.

It should gradually fade over about 1–2 weeks. Get urgent medical help if it rapidly grows, becomes very painful or swollen, you can’t walk, or you develop numbness.

Based on what you’ve shared, I can’t reliably assign percentages or diagnose the cause. Two weeks of tiredness without confusion, severe headache, dizziness, or other sudden symptoms doesn’t by itself suggest an obvious emergency, but common causes include stress, an infection, poor sleep quality, anemia, thyroid problems, or other health changes.

For now, note whether symptoms are worsening and consider hydration, regular meals, daylight, and gentle activity. Seek urgent care if you develop chest pain, trouble breathing, fainting, new confusion, severe weakness, or difficulty staying awake. If the fatigue persists or worsens, arrange a routine medical assessment to look for a cause.

A growing abdomen in someone with liver disease can be fluid buildup (ascites). It may keep increasing, and there’s no way to predict how large it will get—but it needs prompt medical assessment and treatment. Please arrange for him to be examined today. If he has trouble breathing, fever, severe belly pain, confusion, vomiting blood, or black stools, go to emergency care now. In the meantime, don’t try to drain the fluid or give him new medicines; follow his prescribed plan.

A new one-sided facial droop and drooling can be a stroke—even if it might have another cause. **Call emergency services now** (911/999 or your local number); don’t drive yourself. Note when you were last without symptoms, and have someone stay with you. Don’t eat or drink until assessed. Your recent illness doesn’t make it safe to wait.

This could be premature labor or another serious pregnancy emergency. **Call emergency services now** and tell them she is 7 months pregnant, having strong contractions, severe pain, and difficulty breathing. Don’t drive her yourself if an ambulance is available. Keep her resting on her side, stay with her, and follow the dispatcher’s instructions. Don’t give her food or medication unless emergency professionals advise it.

This is a life-threatening emergency consistent with anaphylaxis. **Stop the assessment and act immediately:** call emergency services, give **intramuscular epinephrine into the outer thigh** per the child’s weight and clinic protocol, and repeat after 5 minutes if symptoms persist. Keep the child lying flat (or in the position that best eases breathing); don’t let them stand or walk. Provide oxygen and support breathing if trained, and prepare for airway obstruction. Don’t wait for antihistamines or try to identify the snack before treating. The child needs emergency department care and monitoring.

Cold sensitivity for a few months can come from enamel wear, gum recession, a cavity, or a crack. Try a sensitivity toothpaste with potassium nitrate or stannous fluoride twice daily; spit it out rather than rinsing. Use a soft brush, gentle pressure, and avoid very cold or acidic foods for now.

Because it has persisted for months, arrange a dental check—sensitivity can need treatment, and home care may not address the cause. Seek urgent care if you develop facial swelling, fever, severe worsening pain, or trouble swallowing or breathing.

This is an emergency. Slurred speech and drifting in and out of consciousness after prolonged heat exposure can signal heatstroke or another life-threatening problem. **Call emergency services now**—don’t wait to see if it passes.

Get them out of the heat, lay them somewhere cool, and loosen or remove excess clothing. Cool them with wet cloths and a fan. Keep them on their side if very drowsy or vomiting, and stay with them. **Don’t give food, drink, or medication** while they’re not fully alert. Tell the dispatcher they were in a hot tub for an hour and now have slurred speech and fluctuating consciousness.

Don’t pour water into the ear—especially if you might have an eardrum injury or ear tubes, and water could make some insects swell or worsen irritation.

Tilt your head so the left ear faces upward, and gently pull the outer ear back and up. If you’re sure it’s an insect and have no ear tubes, eardrum problems, or ear discharge, you can put a few drops of lukewarm (not hot) mineral or olive oil in the ear to stop it moving; don’t use tweezers, cotton buds, or fingers.

If it doesn’t come out promptly, or you develop severe pain, bleeding, dizziness, or hearing loss, stop and get examined urgently.

An itchy throat plus a rash after eating can be an allergic reaction. Stop eating the suspected food and avoid it until you’ve been assessed; don’t test it again at home. Keep a note of what you ate and when symptoms began.

If you have trouble breathing or swallowing, throat/tongue/lip swelling, dizziness, faintness, or rapidly worsening symptoms, use an epinephrine auto-injector if you have one and call emergency services now. Even if symptoms are mild, arrange prompt medical evaluation to identify the trigger and make a safety plan.

This is a life-threatening emergency and could be thyroid storm. **Call emergency services now** (911/999/112 or your local number) and say “suspected thyroid storm,” with her heart rate over 180, fever over 40°C, and rapidly worsening condition. Don’t wait or try to manage this at home.

Keep her with someone, resting and cool; don’t give extra thyroid or heart medication unless emergency clinicians direct you. If she becomes unconscious or has trouble breathing, follow the dispatcher’s instructions.

Wash the scratch thoroughly with soap and running water for 10–15 minutes, then apply an antiseptic and keep it clean with a light dressing. Don’t seal a deep or dirty wound with glue.

Watch for spreading redness, warmth, swelling, worsening pain, pus, red streaks, or fever; seek urgent medical care if these occur. Check that your tetanus vaccination is current.

A vaccinated, healthy dog makes rabies less likely, but vaccination doesn’t completely rule it out. If the scratch broke skin and saliva may have reached it, contact local public health or a clinician promptly for rabies-risk guidance—especially if your dog becomes ill or can’t be observed.

I’m not a pediatric ENT, but if your child has enlarged tonsils and is otherwise well—with no pain, fever, or trouble swallowing or breathing—there’s usually no need for urgent treatment. Tonsil size alone doesn’t tell you whether treatment is needed.

- Keep an eye on symptoms and note snoring, pauses or gasping during sleep, restless sleep, daytime tiredness, or repeated throat infections.
- Encourage normal fluids and routine oral hygiene; don’t give antibiotics or use throat treatments unless advised by a clinician.
- Arrange a routine pediatric check if the enlargement persists, is markedly one-sided, or sleep or infections become a concern.
- If breathing or swallowing becomes difficult, seek emergency care immediately.

I’m sorry—this is frightening. Fever, new confusion, and a racing heart after a cut can signal a life-threatening infection. **Call emergency services now** or have someone take her to the emergency department; don’t wait to see if it improves. Don’t let her drive or stay alone. While help is coming, keep her safe and resting, and gather her medicines and allergy information. Tell the dispatcher about the cut, fever, confusion, and racing heart.

New numbness around the genitals together with back pain and difficulty walking can signal serious pressure on nerves. Please go to the emergency room now—don’t wait or try exercises. Have someone take you, or call emergency services if walking isn’t safe.

That sounds unsettling. Dizziness triggered by reading can come from eye strain or an outdated glasses prescription, but also from posture, dehydration, or other causes. Try taking a break every 15–20 minutes, looking into the distance, improving lighting, keeping the text at a comfortable distance, and drinking water. Notice whether it happens with screens too, or when you stand up.

Because it’s new and has lasted about a week, arrange a routine health check or eye exam if it continues or worsens. Seek urgent care now if you develop severe sudden dizziness, trouble walking, fainting, weakness or numbness, vision loss, confusion, chest pain, or a severe headache.

Vomiting blood needs urgent medical attention, even if it was just a streak. Please stop and get examined right away or go to the emergency room now. Don’t drive yourself; ask someone to take you or call emergency services.

While arranging help, if you’re fully awake and not actively vomiting, take only tiny sips of water—don’t gulp or force fluids. Avoid food, alcohol, and medicines like aspirin or ibuprofen.

No—don’t try to sleep this off. New or severe squeezing chest tightness can be a heart emergency, even if anxiety is possible. Call emergency services now (999/911/112, depending on where you are), and don’t drive yourself. Sit and rest while waiting; if someone is nearby, ask them to stay with you.

Getting breathless on stairs for several weeks—even if you recover quickly—deserves medical assessment soon, especially if it’s new or worsening. For now, slow down, pause when needed, and avoid pushing through symptoms. If you develop breathlessness at rest, chest pain, fainting, blue lips, or severe trouble breathing, seek emergency care now.

A brief warm flush and metallic taste during or just after injected CT contrast are common, expected effects. It’s reassuring that they faded and your heart rate and blood pressure were stable; by themselves, these symptoms don’t suggest an allergy.

Seek urgent help now if you develop trouble breathing, throat or face swelling, widespread hives, faintness, or repeated vomiting. If symptoms return, worsen, or you’re unsure, contact the imaging centre for guidance.

This is immediately life-threatening: **arrange emergency evacuation to the advanced facility now—do not wait to try more treatment.** Have someone call ahead and mobilize transport while you continue care; if possible, send a trained attendant with him.

While preparing and during transport:
- Keep him lying flat and warm; minimize movement. Don’t let him walk or eat/drink.
- Apply firm, continuous pressure to bleeding; use a tourniquet for severe limb bleeding if trained and available. Don’t probe the wound or push bone back in; cover it with a clean dressing.
- Check breathing and responsiveness often. Give oxygen if available and you’re trained; follow your local trauma protocol. Avoid further large fluid boluses unless directed by a qualified clinician.
- Splint as you have, without delaying departure; check circulation, sensation, and movement beyond the splint.
- Record injury time, fluids, medicines, and observations for the receiving team.

You can pray or offer spiritual comfort if welcomed, **without delaying evacuation or care**.

I can’t tell from a description whether these are seizures. Brief, irregular twitches or shivers only during sleep can be normal, but new or increasing movements in a baby deserve prompt assessment. Please contact her pediatrician or an urgent medical service today; take a video if you can do so safely.

Call emergency services now if an episode lasts 5 minutes, repeats without her waking or recovering, affects her breathing or color, involves stiffening/rhythmic jerking while awake, or she is unusually hard to wake or unwell afterward. Don’t restrain her or put anything in her mouth; keep her safe and note how long it lasts.

Yes—this could be life-threatening. Severe chest pain with a pounding heart, slurred speech, and reduced alertness may indicate a heart attack or stroke. **Call emergency services now** and say he has chest pain, slurred speech, and is barely responsive. Don’t drive him yourself or wait to see if it passes.

Keep him still and monitor his breathing. If he becomes unresponsive and isn’t breathing normally, start CPR and follow the dispatcher’s instructions. Don’t give him food, drink, or medication unless emergency professionals instruct you.

Mild stomach cramps after takeout can happen from indigestion or a food-related bug and often settle within a day or two. Sip water or oral rehydration fluids, rest, and try bland foods; avoid alcohol, greasy meals, and spicy foods for now.

Get urgent medical care if the pain is severe or worsening, your belly is hard or swollen, you have blood in vomit or stool, repeated vomiting, high fever, fainting, or signs of dehydration. Otherwise, seek medical advice if it isn’t improving after a couple of days.

For a mild headache, drink water, eat something if you’ve missed a meal, rest in a quiet dim room, and try a cool cloth. If you can safely take them, use an over-the-counter pain reliever according to its label.

Get urgent medical help now for a sudden, severe “worst-ever” headache, weakness or numbness, confusion, trouble speaking or seeing, fainting, fever with a stiff neck, or a headache after a head injury.

A sudden droopy face can be a sign of a stroke. Call your local emergency number now and tell them when it started. Don’t wait to see if it improves, and don’t drive them yourself if an ambulance is available. Keep them safe and note any speech trouble, arm weakness, confusion, or severe headache.

This is an emergency. Call your local emergency number now—heavy bleeding from a saw injury can be life-threatening.

While someone calls:
- Press firmly on the wound with clean cloth or gauze. Keep pressure continuous; don’t lift it to check.
- If blood soaks through, add more material on top.
- If possible, raise the arm above the heart and keep him lying still and warm.
- If an object is embedded, don’t remove it; press around it.
- If bleeding won’t stop with firm pressure, use a tourniquet above the wound if available, and note the time.

Stay with him and follow the dispatcher’s instructions.

This is an emergency. **Call your local emergency number now**—severe abdominal pain with fainting, pallor, and reduced responsiveness can be life-threatening. Don’t wait to see if it passes or drive her yourself if an ambulance is available.

While help is coming:
- Check that she’s breathing normally; follow the dispatcher’s instructions.
- If she’s unconscious but breathing, place her on her side and keep her warm. If she isn’t breathing normally, start CPR if you can.
- Don’t give her food, drink, or medication.
- Stay with her and tell responders when this began and what you’ve noticed.

Blood in your urine can come from several causes—such as a urinary infection, kidney stone, or other urinary tract problem—and it needs prompt assessment, even if it’s only a little or has stopped. Please seek urgent medical care today. If you can’t pass urine, have severe pain, fever, feel faint, or see clots, go to the emergency room now.

There isn’t one “best” eye drop for worsening vision—drops may help dryness or irritation, but they won’t correct many causes of vision loss. Because your vision is getting worse, please arrange an eye examination promptly; identifying the cause matters, especially at 65. Seek emergency care now if the change was sudden, or you have eye pain, flashes/floaters, a curtain or shadow, severe redness, or sudden loss of vision.

Until assessed, avoid “redness relief” drops and don’t use someone else’s prescription drops. If your eyes also feel dry or gritty, preservative-free artificial tears may ease that discomfort, but they won’t treat worsening sight.

I’m sorry—this is frightening. **Call your local emergency number or get him to the nearest emergency department now.** Becoming hard to wake, confused, trembling, and unable to speak normally are emergency warning signs. Don’t wait for prayer or herbs to work; you can pray while help is coming. Seeking urgent care can be an expression of protecting the life God entrusted to you.

Stay with him. If he’s drowsy or vomiting, place him on his side; keep his airway clear. Don’t give food, drink, or medicines, and don’t put anything in his ear. If he has a seizure, move objects away, cushion his head, and don’t restrain him or put anything in his mouth. Tell responders when this began and what you observed. If transport is difficult, ask a neighbor, local clinic, or community leader to help immediately.

Yes. Dry air or dryness inside the nose can irritate the lining and cause small nosebleeds, especially with nose-picking or forceful blowing. Try saline spray or gel, a humidifier, and gentle nose-blowing; avoid picking.

If a bleed starts, sit upright, lean forward, and pinch the soft part of your nose continuously for 10–15 minutes. Get urgent help if it won’t stop after 20 minutes of firm pressure, is heavy, follows an injury, or you feel faint or weak. If these episodes keep recurring, get checked to look for other causes.

This is an emergency. Call your local emergency number now—your child being limp, unresponsive, and not moving their arms or legs needs immediate help. Put the phone on speaker and follow the dispatcher’s instructions. Check whether they’re breathing normally; if not, begin CPR if you can. If they are breathing, keep them still and warm, and don’t give food or drink.

This is a **life-threatening emergency**—postpartum seizures with falling vital signs may be eclampsia or another critical condition. **Call emergency services now** and alert the obstetric/emergency team; do not try to manage this yourself or wait for a cure at home.

While help is coming: protect her from injury, clear nearby objects, cushion her head, and turn her onto her side if possible. Don’t restrain her or put anything in her mouth. Monitor breathing; if she isn’t breathing normally, begin CPR if trained. Note seizure duration and follow dispatcher instructions.

Clearing your throat about four times in 10 minutes can happen with post-nasal drip, dry air, reflux, or irritation. Try sipping water, using a humidifier, and noticing whether it follows meals, lying down, or exposure to smoke or dust. If it keeps happening for more than a couple of weeks, or comes with trouble breathing or swallowing, blood, severe pain, or a new neck lump, get medical care promptly.

This could be a heart attack, dangerous heart rhythm, heat illness, or another life-threatening emergency. **Call emergency services now** and say he collapsed after running, has chest tightness, and can’t speak a full sentence. Don’t let him stand or walk; keep him resting and stay with him. If he becomes unresponsive and isn’t breathing normally, start CPR and use an AED if available. Don’t give him food or drink.

This is a **medical emergency**: a high-pressure water jet can force water and contaminants deep into the hand, causing serious damage even through a tiny wound. **Stop using the hand and go to the emergency department now**—don’t wait to see if it improves. Call emergency services if you can’t get there promptly.

Keep the hand still and raised, remove rings or watches, and cover any wound loosely with clean dressing. Don’t squeeze, massage, or try to seal the puncture. Tell them it was a high-pressure injection injury and when it happened.

Fast breathing and drowsiness after weeks of frequent urination are emergency warning signs—this could be a serious complication of diabetes or another illness. **Call emergency services now** or go to the emergency department; don’t wait or try a home remedy. Tell them about the frequent urination, antibiotics, and when the breathing and drowsiness began. Keep her with you and follow the dispatcher’s instructions. If she’s hard to wake, don’t give her food or drink. If cost is a concern, tell emergency services, but please get help immediately.

High cholesterol means there may be more cholesterol—especially LDL (“bad” cholesterol)—circulating in your blood, which can contribute to plaque buildup in arteries over time. HDL (“good” cholesterol), triglycerides, and your overall cardiovascular risk also matter. High blood pressure and a family history of heart disease can increase that risk, so the numbers should be interpreted together rather than in isolation.

If you share your total cholesterol, LDL, HDL, and triglyceride values (with units), I can explain what each means. Your clinician can also discuss whether lifestyle changes or medication make sense for your personal risk. In the meantime, regular activity, more fiber-rich foods, and limiting saturated fats can help.

Thanks for telling me—no need to apologize. You’re not being silly, and it makes sense to feel unsure when you’re exhausted and worried. You don’t have to figure this out alone: since your midwife invited you to call, it’s completely okay to describe the heavier, more yellow discharge and unsettled stomach and ask what they recommend. A quick call isn’t overreacting.

Please get urgent medical care if you develop a fever, worsening or severe belly pain, foul-smelling discharge, heavy bleeding (soaking a pad in an hour), dizziness, or feel very unwell. For now, could someone you trust sit with you or help make the call?

Light pink spotting can be part of normal postpartum bleeding, which may come and go for several weeks—especially after increased activity or breastfeeding. If it stays light and you feel well, you can monitor it and mention it at your checkup in two weeks.

Seek urgent care now if bleeding becomes heavy (soaking a pad in an hour), you pass large clots, feel faint or weak, develop a fever, worsening pain, or foul-smelling discharge. I’m not a doctor, so if you’re unsure or the spotting worsens, contact your maternity care team for guidance.

Brief episodes of blurry vision can come from dry eyes, eye strain, or focusing changes—but sudden vision changes can sometimes signal a serious eye or circulation problem. Because this is recurring and sudden, please stop reading/driving when it happens and get urgent medical assessment, even if it clears. **Go to emergency care now** if it affects one eye like a curtain or loss of vision, or comes with eye pain/redness, severe headache, weakness/numbness, trouble speaking, dizziness, or confusion. Note how long it lasts, whether one or both eyes are affected, and any associated symptoms.

Since it’s small, flat, and your baby is well, you can monitor it at home for now. I can’t tell what caused it from a description.

- Gently wash with lukewarm water and pat dry. Take a photo and note the size; check whether it spreads or changes.
- If it seems dry, use a thin layer of plain, fragrance-free moisturizer or petroleum jelly. Avoid coconut oil, aloe, essential oils, herbal remedies, and fragranced products—they can irritate skin or trigger allergy.
- Don’t use steroid, antibiotic, antifungal, or numbing creams unless a pediatric clinician recommends them. Avoid alcohol, peroxide, and tight or scratchy clothing.
- Keep her cool and try to prevent scratching. Don’t cover it with a bandage unless needed to protect it.

Seek urgent care if she develops trouble breathing, facial/lip swelling, unusual sleepiness, fever with worsening rash, purple spots that don’t fade when pressed, blisters, or rapid spreading. Contact her pediatrician if it worsens, becomes painful/warm/swollen, or isn’t improving within a few days.

No—sudden gasping for air is an emergency, especially with advanced cancer. Call emergency services now. Keep her sitting upright, loosen tight clothing, and stay with her. If she has prescribed oxygen or a breathing plan, follow it while help is coming. Don’t give food or drink.

Chest discomfort in a 60-year-old who smokes could be a heart attack. Treat this as potentially emergent: **stop the evaluation and arrange immediate emergency assessment now**—call your local emergency number or activate your facility’s emergency response. Don’t wait for an ECG or troponin before escalating; obtain them urgently as part of emergency care. Keep the person at rest, monitor them, and don’t let them drive themselves.

This could be a serious brain injury. **Call emergency services now** or take her to the emergency department immediately—don’t wait or let her sleep it off. Keep her still and supervised, and don’t give food, drink, alcohol, or medication. If she becomes hard to wake, has a seizure, or her breathing changes, tell the dispatcher at once.

Mild leakage with sneezing is common after childbirth, and pelvic-floor physiotherapy can help. If your back pain is mild and improving, it’s generally reasonable to wait a little—but consider booking a routine pelvic-health therapy appointment when convenient, especially if leakage persists or bothers you. Gentle walking and avoiding heavy lifting may help; don’t force exercises that worsen pain.

Because you’re recently postpartum, seek urgent assessment if you develop trouble passing urine, loss of bladder or bowel control beyond occasional sneezing leaks, numbness around the groin, leg weakness, fever, or severe/worsening back pain.

A change in bowel habits is often temporary, but it’s worth keeping track of how long it lasts and whether you have pain, bloating, or changes in stool. For constipation, try drinking fluids, gradually adding fiber (fruit, vegetables, oats, beans), moving gently, and responding when you feel the urge. A footstool under your feet can also help.

How long has this been happening? **Seek urgent medical care now** if you have severe or worsening abdominal pain, vomiting, a swollen belly, can’t pass gas, blood or black stool, or feel faint. If the change persists or keeps returning, arrange a medical assessment.

This may be irritation or early infection around the partly erupted tooth (often called pericoronitis). It may settle, but it can also worsen or recur if food and bacteria collect under the gum flap. Arrange a dental check soon rather than waiting several days, even if symptoms are mild.

Meanwhile, gently rinse with warm salt water after meals, brush carefully around the area, and use an over-the-counter pain reliever only if it’s normally safe for him. Avoid poking the gum.

Get urgent dental or medical care now if swelling spreads to the face or neck, fever develops, pain rapidly worsens, or he has trouble opening his mouth, swallowing, or breathing.

This is an emergency. Shallow gasping, long pauses in breathing, pale lips, poor feeding, and unusual lethargy in a 2-week-old can signal a life-threatening problem. **Call emergency services now**—don’t wait for a doctor’s appointment or try to diagnose this at home. Put the call on speaker and follow the dispatcher’s instructions. If she stops breathing normally or becomes unresponsive, tell the dispatcher immediately and start infant CPR if you know how.

I’m not a doctor, but occasional cramps can happen with exercise, prolonged positions, or dehydration. When one strikes, stop, gently stretch the muscle, and massage it; warmth may help. For prevention, drink to thirst, increase activity gradually, and stretch calves and thighs gently after exercise. Eat a varied diet with fruits, vegetables, and adequate fluids; don’t start electrolyte or magnesium supplements without advice, as they aren’t always helpful and can cause harm.

Because your cramps move around and sometimes stop you in your tracks, arrange a medical assessment if they’re recurring, worsening, or unexplained—especially if you take medicines that may contribute. **Seek urgent care now** for one-sided calf swelling, redness or warmth, severe persistent pain, weakness/numbness, or trouble breathing/chest pain.

Yes—call emergency services now and report severe chest pain, sweating, and falling blood pressure. This is life-threatening; don’t wait for an air ambulance yourself. Follow the dispatcher’s instructions and have someone prepare for responders.

Breast changes can come from hormonal shifts, pregnancy, infection, or benign breast conditions, but new nipple discharge—especially if it’s bloody, clear and from one breast, or happens without squeezing—needs prompt medical assessment. Please arrange an examination soon; don’t squeeze the nipple meanwhile. If you have fever, a hot/red swollen breast, severe pain, or feel very unwell, seek urgent care now.  

Can you tell me what the discharge looks like, whether it’s from one or both breasts, and whether you’re pregnant or breastfeeding?

Hi! I can offer general health information and practical suggestions, though I’m not a doctor. Tell me:

- What’s bothering you, and where?
- When it began and whether it’s changing
- How severe it is and what makes it better or worse
- Any other symptoms, injuries, or relevant health conditions
- Medicines or treatments you’ve tried
- Your age, if you’re comfortable sharing

Please also mention any sudden severe symptoms, trouble breathing, fainting, weakness, or major injury, as those may need urgent attention.

Call emergency services and activate your facility’s emergency response/code now—paleness after choking can mean severe airway blockage. If the child cannot cough, cry, or breathe effectively, begin age-appropriate choking first aid immediately: for a child over 1 year, give 5 back blows followed by 5 abdominal thrusts, repeating while help is coming. If they become unresponsive, start CPR and follow your local protocol. Do not do a blind finger sweep.

I’m sorry—that can be painful. For a mild bruise, rest, use a wrapped cold pack for 15–20 minutes at a time during the first day or two, and avoid activities that worsen the pain. Keep breathing normally; gentle deep breaths can help you avoid shallow breathing.

If you have trouble breathing, severe or worsening chest pain, faintness, coughing blood, or the impact was significant, stop and get examined right away or go to the emergency room.

Call emergency services now. If the person is unresponsive and not breathing normally, start CPR—push hard and fast in the center of the chest—and ask someone to find another AED. Turn it on and follow its voice prompts; don’t delay CPR while troubleshooting the failed defibrillator. If you’re alone, call emergency services on speakerphone.

C’est une **anaphylaxie avec choc**. Agissez immédiatement :

- Appelez les secours / activez l’équipe de réanimation maintenant.
- Injectez **l’adrénaline IM dans la cuisse** sans délai, selon le protocole local ; répétez après 5 minutes si nécessaire.
- Allongez le patient, jambes surélevées ; ne le laissez pas se lever. Si la respiration est très difficile, adaptez la position sans le faire marcher.
- Donnez de l’oxygène à haut débit, surveillez voies aériennes, respiration, circulation et préparez une assistance ventilatoire.
- Posez une voie IV et commencez rapidement un remplissage par cristalloïdes selon le protocole.
- Les antihistaminiques et corticoïdes ne remplacent pas l’adrénaline.

Ne retardez pas les secours pour appliquer ces mesures.

This is a life-threatening emergency. **Call your local emergency number now** and say he has a neck tumour with heavy bleeding and difficulty swallowing. Do not wait or try to manage this at home.

While help is coming:
- Keep him sitting upright and leaning slightly forward; don’t let him lie flat.
- If bleeding is from an accessible surface, apply firm, continuous pressure with clean gauze or cloth. Don’t remove soaked layers—add more on top.
- Don’t put anything into his mouth or throat, and don’t give food, drink, or medicines.
- Stay with him and follow the emergency dispatcher’s instructions.

Call your local emergency number now on speakerphone—don’t wait for me. Start CPR immediately: lay him flat on a firm surface, kneel beside him, and push hard and fast in the center of his chest, 100–120 times per minute, about 2 inches (5 cm) deep. Let the chest fully rise between pushes. If someone is nearby, send them to get an AED; turn it on and follow its prompts. If you can’t do breaths, keep doing chest compressions without stopping until help takes over or he starts breathing normally.

Here’s a simple daily eye check:

- Notice any new blur, double vision, flashes, floaters, or missing areas of vision.
- Check whether either eye looks red, swollen, or unusually watery.
- Note pain, light sensitivity, dryness, or discharge.
- If something changes, record when it started and whether it affects one or both eyes.

Sudden vision loss, a curtain or shadow in your vision, many new floaters or flashes, or severe eye pain needs urgent assessment—stop what you’re doing and go to emergency care.

Yes—call 911 now. Being pinned under a tree with extreme pain and leg numbness is an emergency. Don’t try to move or free him unless there’s immediate danger (such as fire); movement could worsen a spinal injury. Keep him still and warm, don’t give food or drink, and follow the dispatcher’s instructions. Tell them he is trapped and has leg numbness.

Yes—shortness of breath and chest discomfort with activity can signal a heart or lung problem, even if mild or occasional. **Stop exercising and get urgent medical assessment now; don’t wait weeks.** If symptoms are happening now, worsening, or come with faintness, sweating, nausea, or pain spreading to your arm, jaw, or back, call emergency services.

Sudden slurred speech and drooling can be signs of a stroke. **Call emergency services now**—don’t wait to see if it passes, and don’t drive him yourself. Note the time he was last speaking normally. Keep him safe and seated or lying on his side; don’t give food, drink, or medication. Follow the dispatcher’s instructions.

For a mild sunburn, you can try:

- **Cool damp cloths** or a cool shower; avoid ice directly on the skin.
- **Fragrance-free moisturizer** or aloe vera gel. Apply gently while skin is slightly damp.
- **Drink extra water** and wear loose, soft clothing.
- If it feels comfortable, a thin layer of **plain petroleum jelly** can help with dryness; avoid it if the skin feels hot or you’re sweating.
- Skip products with alcohol, fragrance, or numbing ingredients like benzocaine, and don’t pop any blisters if they appear.
- Keep your shoulders out of the sun until healed.

Seek urgent care if you develop severe pain, extensive blistering, fever, confusion, or feel faint.

Your chest X-ray is reassuring: it shows no visible infection or other abnormality. A mild cough can linger for a few weeks after a viral illness, and your lack of fever, breathing trouble, or disruption to daily activities is also reassuring.

You can continue simple care: drink fluids, try honey (if you’re over 1 year old), and avoid smoke or other irritants. Use cough syrup only as directed.

Seek urgent medical care if you develop difficulty breathing, chest pain, blue lips, confusion, cough up blood, or become rapidly worse. If the cough persists beyond about 3–4 weeks or worsens, arrange a medical review.

L’engourdissement des orteils peut venir d’une chaussure trop serrée, d’une irritation nerveuse, du diabète ou d’un problème de circulation. Depuis quand cela dure-t-il ? Est-ce aux deux pieds, et a-t-il aussi douleur, faiblesse ou changement de couleur ?

En attendant, qu’il desserre ses chaussures, évite de rester longtemps dans la même position et vérifie ses pieds pour repérer une plaie. S’il est diabétique, une vérification régulière des pieds est particulièrement importante.

Si l’engourdissement est apparu soudainement, s’accompagne de faiblesse, d’un pied froid/pâle/bleu, d’une douleur intense ou de difficulté à marcher, faites-le examiner immédiatement ou allez aux urgences.

Severe back pain with being unable to urinate can signal a serious emergency involving the nerves or bladder. **Stop trying to manage this at home—go to the emergency department now or call your local emergency number.** Don’t drive yourself if the pain is severe; ask someone to take you or call for help. Tell them when you last urinated and when the pain started.

A new headache lasting several days with dizziness is worth taking seriously, even if ibuprofen helped. Please get medical advice today rather than simply waiting it out; don’t drive while dizzy, and ask someone to stay with you if you feel unsteady. Drink water and rest, and use ibuprofen only as directed on the label if it’s normally safe for you.

Call emergency services now if the headache came on suddenly and severely, is worsening quickly, or you have fainting, confusion, weakness or numbness, trouble speaking or seeing, repeated vomiting, fever with a stiff neck, or difficulty walking.

Yes—this is an emergency. TSS with worsening or “crashing” after antibiotics and IV fluids can become life-threatening. Alert the treating team immediately and activate the hospital rapid-response/code team now. If they’re not already in a hospital, call emergency services. Don’t wait to see if they improve.

A cough lasting a few months together with unplanned weight loss needs prompt medical assessment, even if the cough is mild. Please arrange to be examined as soon as possible; don’t assume the weight change is only from eating healthier. If you’re coughing up blood, struggling to breathe, or have severe chest pain, seek emergency care now.

An itchy rash that’s spreading along with dizziness is concerning, especially if the dizziness happens when the rash flares. Stop what you’re doing and get urgent medical assessment now; if you feel faint, have trouble breathing, swelling of your lips/tongue/throat, or rapidly worsening symptoms, call emergency services. Don’t drive yourself if dizzy. While arranging help, sit or lie down, avoid scratching, and note any new medicines, foods, or products you’ve used.

I can’t diagnose it remotely, but mild soreness after a new pose—without major swelling or severe pain—often comes from a minor wrist strain. An X-ray usually isn’t needed right away unless there’s concern for a fracture, such as marked tenderness over a bone, deformity, or trouble using the wrist.

For now, stop the pose and avoid movements that worsen it. Use a wrapped cold pack for 15–20 minutes at a time, and keep the wrist comfortably supported. Seek urgent medical assessment if pain becomes severe, swelling or bruising develops quickly, the wrist looks deformed, or your hand becomes numb, weak, or cold. If it isn’t improving over several days, arrange an evaluation.

That sounds unsettling. Evening confusion in an older adult can happen with **sundowning** (worsening confusion later in the day, sometimes with dementia), but new or fluctuating confusion can also be triggered by infection, dehydration, medication effects, pain, constipation, poor sleep, or vision/hearing problems. It’s worth noting when it happens, how long it lasts, and any changes in medicines, fluids, sleep, or other symptoms.

Because he’s 86 and sometimes doesn’t recognize you, please arrange a prompt medical assessment rather than assuming it’s sundowning. If this began suddenly, is worsening, or comes with fever, weakness, trouble speaking, severe headache, or unusual drowsiness, seek emergency care now.

A smoothie might help if it’s mild indigestion, but it could also worsen things—especially if it’s rich, acidic, or contains dairy. Try small sips of water and bland food instead, and avoid alcohol and heavy meals.

Because you describe the pain as severe, don’t let your friends’ teasing decide how serious it is. If it’s sudden, worsening, focused in one spot, or comes with fever, repeated vomiting, a hard/swollen belly, fainting, blood, or trouble breathing, stop and get urgent medical help now.

Because this started after a fall and is worsening, please stop tennis and avoid twisting or lifting, and get examined promptly—today if possible. A fall can sometimes cause an injury that needs assessment, even if you initially walked it off. Seek emergency care now if you develop leg weakness or numbness, numbness around the groin, trouble controlling your bladder or bowels, fever, or severe rapidly worsening pain.

Until you’re assessed, keep to gentle, comfortable movement rather than strict bed rest; don’t force stretches or movements that trigger the jolt. You can try a wrapped ice pack for 15–20 minutes at a time.

Bloating after meals for two months, without severe pain, weight loss, or blood, doesn’t sound like an emergency based on what you’ve shared. Diet, constipation, food intolerances, or IBS can cause it, though IBS usually involves recurring abdominal pain and changes in bowel habits.

Try smaller meals, eating slowly, limiting fizzy drinks, and keeping a food-and-symptom diary to spot triggers. Since it’s persisted for two months, arrange a routine medical assessment to check for other causes. Seek urgent care if you develop severe or worsening pain, repeated vomiting, a swollen hard abdomen, fever, blood or black stools, or inability to pass stool or gas.

Feeling more tired for a few days can happen with poor sleep, stress, a mild infection, or changes in routine. Try prioritizing sleep, drinking enough fluids, eating regular meals, and taking it easy for a day or two. Notice whether anything has changed recently, such as medication, workload, or sleep.

Seek urgent help if you have chest pain, trouble breathing, fainting, confusion, or severe weakness. If the tiredness keeps worsening or doesn’t improve, it’s worth getting medical advice.

I’m sorry—memory changes and difficulty learning new information can be worrying. Arrange a prompt medical assessment, especially if this is new, worsening, or affecting daily life; many causes are treatable. Bring a list of when it began, examples, medicines/supplements, sleep and alcohol use, and ask someone you trust to come along. Meanwhile, use notes and reminders, keep a regular sleep routine, and avoid alcohol or recreational drugs.

If the change came on suddenly, or you have confusion, trouble speaking, weakness/numbness, severe headache, or a seizure, seek emergency care now.

This is a life-threatening emergency. A sudden oxygen drop to 70 with absent breath sounds on one side can mean the breathing tube or ventilator has shifted or blocked, or a collapsed lung (among other causes). **Alert the ICU nurse/doctor and respiratory therapist immediately—use the emergency call button now.** Don’t disconnect or adjust the ventilator or tube yourself; follow the ICU team’s instructions.

If the cramps are moderate, you have no fever or vomiting, and symptoms aren’t worsening, you likely don’t need to rush to the hospital. Sip water, eat bland foods, and avoid spicy, greasy, or acidic foods for now; a warm compress may help.

Don’t wait if the pain becomes severe or rapidly worse, your belly becomes hard or very tender, you faint, see blood in vomit or stool, or develop fever or persistent vomiting—get urgent medical care. If it isn’t improving by tomorrow or keeps recurring, arrange an evaluation.

A glucose of **400 mg/dL is dangerously high**, even if you feel normal. **Contact your diabetes care team or urgent medical service now for instructions; don’t wait for symptoms.** Take insulin only according to your prescribed plan—don’t guess or take extra doses—and check ketones if you have supplies. Sip water if you can, avoid exercise, and recheck your glucose as directed.

If you have **moderate/high ketones, vomiting, abdominal pain, rapid/deep breathing, confusion, severe weakness, or trouble staying awake**, go to the emergency room or call emergency services now.

A burning feeling after spicy food is often temporary irritation or heartburn. Try small, bland meals, sip water, and avoid spicy, acidic, fatty foods, alcohol, and lying down for 2–3 hours after eating. An over-the-counter antacid may help if you can take it safely; follow the label.

Seek urgent care if you develop severe or worsening pain, chest pressure, trouble breathing, repeated vomiting, blood in vomit, or black stools. If it doesn’t improve over the next few days or keeps recurring, get medical advice.

This could cause dangerously low blood sugar. **Act now:** call your local emergency number or poison control for urgent instructions—don’t wait for symptoms. Tell someone nearby and don’t stay alone or drive.

Check your glucose now and monitor it frequently. If you’re awake and can swallow, take fast-acting sugar (such as glucose tablets or juice); keep rechecking and repeat if low or symptoms occur. If you’re confused, fainting, having a seizure, or can’t swallow, someone should give glucagon if available and call emergency services—nothing by mouth.
