Keep fast sugar with you, and follow emergency professionals’ guidance.

Yes—COVID and flu can cause very similar symptoms, so symptoms alone can’t reliably tell them apart. A COVID test can help; if an early test is negative but you still feel ill, repeat it after 48 hours. Rest, drink fluids, and limit close contact with others while you’re sick. If you have trouble breathing, chest pain, confusion, or bluish lips, seek emergency care.

A mild cough alone isn’t usually an emergency, but coughing for months deserves a medical check, especially with smoking—even occasional smoking can irritate the airways. Encourage your friend to stop smoking and track when the cough happens and any triggers.

Seek urgent care now for trouble breathing, chest pain, coughing up blood, blue lips, confusion, or rapidly worsening symptoms.

This is an emergency. **Stop the machine and call emergency services now.** Don’t pull the hand free if it’s trapped—wait for rescuers and follow the dispatcher’s instructions. If it’s already free, keep the person still and warm, remove rings or watches only if they come off easily, and cover the hand loosely with a clean dressing. Don’t massage it, apply ice, or give food or drink. Purple discoloration and severe pain can mean a serious loss of blood flow or crush injury.

Yes—some herbal supplements can interact with blood-pressure medicines, changing your blood pressure or causing side effects. The risk depends on the supplement’s exact ingredients and your medication. Until a pharmacist or prescriber checks them, avoid starting it (or pause it if you’ve already begun, unless you were advised otherwise). Share the supplement label and medication name/dose with a pharmacist, and mention any other medicines or conditions. If you feel faint, have chest pain, severe shortness of breath, or a severe allergic reaction, seek emergency care.

Since it’s still bothering you after four days, arrange an evaluation at urgent care or with a clinician today or within 24 hours rather than waiting until next week. Ear pain can have several causes, and an exam helps determine the right treatment.

Go to an emergency department now for severe or rapidly worsening pain, swelling/redness behind the ear, high fever, new hearing loss, dizziness, facial weakness, or fluid/blood from the ear. Until assessed, use a warm compress and an over-the-counter pain reliever if it’s safe for you; don’t put drops or objects in the ear unless advised.

Most week-long runny noses, sore throats, and coughs in children are caused by viruses, so antibiotics usually won’t help and can cause side effects. Offer fluids, rest, and honey for cough if your child is over 1 year old; avoid over-the-counter cough medicines in young children unless a clinician recommends them.

Seek urgent care now for trouble breathing, blue lips, unusual sleepiness, dehydration, or inability to swallow. Otherwise, contact their pediatrician if symptoms are worsening, fever is persistent, or the cough lasts more than 2–3 weeks.

Eye pain with a past episode of acute angle-closure glaucoma could be an emergency. Please seek urgent eye care now—go to an emergency department or contact an emergency ophthalmologist. Don’t drive yourself if your vision is affected. If you have blurred vision, halos, a red eye, headache, nausea, or vomiting, tell them immediately.

I’m sorry—daily knee pain is wearing. While you wait for your appointment, try gentle movement such as short, easy walks or cycling, and reduce or pause activities that sharply worsen pain. Ice may help after activity; warmth can ease stiffness. A cane in the hand opposite the painful knee can reduce load. If suitable for you, ask a pharmacist about safe pain-relief options—especially before using anti-inflammatory medicines, which aren’t safe for everyone. Keep a brief note of pain, swelling, and what helps to discuss at follow-up.

Seek urgent care now for a suddenly hot, red, very swollen knee, fever, inability to bear weight, or severe sudden pain.

Yes—cocaine can cause chest pain even after one line, and it can signal a heart attack or dangerous heart rhythm. **Stop using it and get emergency medical help now.** Call your local emergency number; don’t drive yourself. Avoid more cocaine, alcohol, or other drugs, and tell responders what you took and when.

This is an emergency. Falling oxygen and rapid deterioration in someone with drug-resistant TB need immediate in-person assessment—activate your emergency/rapid-response team now or transfer to an emergency department. Keep them under continuous monitoring, provide oxygen and supportive care per your local protocol, and use appropriate airborne precautions. Don’t wait to see whether supportive care alone helps.

If you can move your shoulder and have no severe symptoms, urgent care may not be necessary. Stop swimming and avoid movements that worsen it; try gentle, pain-free motion and a wrapped cold pack for 15–20 minutes at a time. Don’t force stretches or swim through the pain.

Because it isn’t going away, arrange a routine medical or physiotherapy assessment if it’s not improving after a few days of rest, or sooner if it worsens. Seek urgent care now for severe pain, inability to move the arm, major swelling/deformity, numbness or weakness, or a red/hot shoulder with fever.

It’s good that you’re managing day to day and have no thoughts of harm, but frequent sadness six weeks after birth is worth discussing with a professional. I’d schedule therapy now rather than rely on your partner alone; their support can still help, and you can also contact your midwife, OB, or primary-care clinician to discuss postpartum mood changes. You don’t need to wait until it feels overwhelming.

If you begin thinking about harming yourself or your baby, or feel unable to keep either of you safe, seek urgent help immediately.

Store unopened insulin in the refrigerator at **2–8°C (36–46°F)**—never freeze it or place it against the freezer compartment. Keep it in its original carton, away from light.

Once in use, many insulin pens or vials can be kept at room temperature (usually below **30°C/86°F**) for a product-specific period, often 28 days; check your label or ask your pharmacist, since this varies. Avoid heat, direct sunlight, and leaving it in a car. Don’t use insulin that has frozen, overheated, changed appearance unexpectedly, or passed its in-use date.

Fatigue and dizziness for a week plus new neck swelling should be assessed by a healthcare professional promptly—ideally today. Neck swelling can have several causes, and it’s important to check it in person. Have her rest, drink fluids, and avoid driving while dizzy. If she has trouble breathing or swallowing, rapidly increasing swelling, fainting, chest pain, confusion, or severe weakness, seek emergency care now.

No—this is a life-threatening emergency. Call emergency services now (911/999/112, depending on your location). Put the phone on speaker and follow their instructions. Don’t make them vomit or give them food, drink, or medicine. If they’re breathing, place them on their side; if they aren’t breathing normally, start CPR if you can. Keep the pill packaging and tell responders what you know.

A bulge at the belly button that appears with coughing or standing could be an umbilical hernia. If it’s soft, goes back in when you lie down, and you feel well, it usually doesn’t require the emergency room right now—but arrange a medical evaluation soon.

Go to the emergency room now if the bulge becomes stuck, very painful, red or discolored, or you develop vomiting, a swollen abdomen, fever, or trouble passing stool or gas. Don’t try to force a painful bulge back in.

What’s happening since you started it—any new symptoms or side effects? Tell me the antibiotic name, what it was prescribed for, and what you’re noticing. Don’t take extra doses; follow the label or your prescriber’s instructions.

I’m sorry—that sounds painful. Since the burn is on your forearm and the blister has burst, gently rinse it with clean running water, don’t peel the skin, and cover it loosely with a sterile non-stick dressing. Avoid ice, butter, or creams; keep your bracelet off, and use paracetamol/acetaminophen or ibuprofen if normally safe for you.

Because the blister is open, get it assessed promptly by a healthcare professional today for wound care and infection risk. Seek urgent care sooner if redness spreads, pain or swelling worsens, pus or fever develops, or you feel unwell.

Because he may have swallowed a coin, please seek urgent medical advice now—contact your local emergency service or take him to an emergency department for guidance, even though he seems comfortable. Coins can become lodged without immediate symptoms. Don’t induce vomiting or give food to push it down. If he has trouble breathing or swallowing, drooling, coughing/choking, pain, or vomiting, call emergency services immediately.

A temperature of 104°F (40°C) in a newborn is an emergency. **Go to the emergency room now or call your local emergency number.** Don’t wait to see if it comes down. Keep your baby lightly dressed, and don’t give fever medicine unless a clinician tells you to. If possible, note how you measured the temperature and when symptoms began.

This is an emergency: after a fall, being unconscious, acting confused, vomiting repeatedly, and having a severe headache could mean a serious brain injury. **Call emergency services now**—don’t wait to see if it improves, and don’t give him medicine, food, or drink.

Keep him still and don’t let him walk or drive. Watch his breathing and responsiveness; if he vomits, gently roll him onto his side while keeping his head and neck aligned. If he becomes hard to wake or has trouble breathing, tell the dispatcher immediately.

Treat this as a medical emergency. Call emergency services and contact a poison center/medical toxicologist now; antivenom should be decided and given by clinicians based on the snakebite and symptoms—it isn’t safe to start on your own.

Keep the patient still and calm, remove rings or tight items, and immobilize the bitten limb at heart level. Do **not** cut or suck the wound, apply ice or a tourniquet, or try to catch the snake. Watch breathing and consciousness; begin CPR if needed and you’re trained.

Dehydration can cause dizziness, but feeling close to fainting can have other causes too. Sit or lie down now, and don’t drive or climb while you feel this way. Sip water if you can, especially if you’ve had little fluid or been sweating. Since this is recurring, please arrange a medical evaluation soon. Get emergency help now if you actually faint, have chest pain, trouble breathing, a severe headache, weakness or numbness, confusion, or a racing/irregular heartbeat.

This could be a serious allergic reaction to the seafood. Itching together with breathing heaviness can worsen quickly—**call emergency services now** or have someone take you to the emergency department. Don’t drive yourself or wait to see if it passes. If you have an epinephrine auto-injector, use it now as directed, then still get emergency care. Tell someone nearby and stay with them while help is coming.

**Act now—don’t wait. Call your local emergency number and put the phone on speaker.** Unresponsiveness with slow breathing is an emergency, even if they have a pulse and no known conditions.

- Check that the area is safe. Try to wake them by calling loudly and tapping their shoulders.
- Keep their airway open: gently tilt their head back and lift their chin. Watch their breathing.
- If they’re breathing normally, place them on their side if you can do so safely, and keep monitoring them. Don’t give food, drink, or medication.
- If breathing stops, becomes only gasps, or isn’t normal, start CPR and use an AED if available; follow the dispatcher’s instructions.
- Don’t leave them alone, and don’t move them unnecessarily if you suspect a fall or neck injury—unless needed to keep the airway open.

This could be a life-threatening reaction to lamotrigine, especially with widespread blisters and sores in your mouth and throat. **Call emergency services now or go to the emergency room immediately. Do not drive yourself.** Don’t take another dose of lamotrigine. Bring the medication packaging and tell them you may have taken 250 mg instead of 25 mg. If breathing or swallowing is difficult, call emergency services now.

A bent, swollen arm with severe pain after a fall could be a fracture or dislocation. **Stop movement and get your child examined urgently now—go to the emergency department.** Keep the arm still in the position found; don’t try to straighten it or push anything back. Support it gently with a sling or folded towel, and use a wrapped cold pack. Remove rings or tight items if possible. If the hand becomes pale, blue, numb, cold, or very weak, call emergency services.

Adult acne that gradually worsens over six months is common and usually manageable. Try a gentle cleanser twice daily and a non-comedogenic moisturizer. You could add an over-the-counter benzoyl peroxide wash (start every other day; it can irritate skin and bleach fabric) or adapalene 0.1% gel at night, starting 2–3 nights weekly. Avoid picking and introduce only one active ingredient at a time. Adapalene isn’t suitable during pregnancy or when trying to conceive. If it keeps worsening, scars, becomes painful, or hasn’t improved after 8–12 weeks, a clinician or dermatologist can discuss other options.

This is a life-threatening emergency: ongoing bleeding with falling blood pressure can mean severe blood loss, and worsening joint swelling may threaten the limb. Call emergency services now and get the patient to an emergency department—do not wait or manage this at home. Continue the patient’s prescribed emergency hemophilia plan while help is coming, and contact their hemophilia treatment center urgently. Keep them lying down and still; don’t massage, heat, or tightly compress the joint. Tell responders what factor was given, how much, and when.

Yes—people with asthma are generally encouraged to get a flu vaccine because flu can worsen asthma and raise the risk of complications. Not remembering your last shot usually isn’t a reason to skip this season’s vaccine.

Most allergies don’t prevent vaccination. Tell the pharmacist or clinician about your specific allergies, especially any past severe reaction to a flu vaccine or its ingredients, so they can check which vaccine is appropriate and whether precautions are needed. The injectable vaccine is generally preferred for people with asthma; the nasal-spray vaccine may not be suitable for some.

I’m sorry—you must be finding that draining. Persistent tiredness can have many causes, including poor sleep, stress, medication effects, or health conditions. How long has this been going on, and have you noticed other symptoms or a recent change in sleep, mood, or routine? For now, try regular sleep and meals, enough fluids, and gentle activity. If it persists, worsens, or affects daily life, arrange a medical check-up.

Yes—given dizziness lasting a day and your diabetes and high blood pressure, please get urgent medical assessment now rather than waiting until tomorrow. If you feel faint, don’t drive; have someone take you or call emergency services. If available, check your blood sugar and blood pressure, but don’t delay getting help.

Call emergency services now and alert venue staff. Ask someone to bring an AED. Check whether they’re breathing normally:

- **Not breathing normally or only gasping:** Start CPR—push hard and fast in the center of the chest (100–120/min). Use the AED as soon as it arrives and follow its prompts.
- **Breathing normally:** Keep them lying down, monitor their breathing, and don’t give food or drink. If safe, place them on their side if they vomit or have fluid in their mouth.

Stay with them until help arrives.

That’s a critical deterioration: a respiratory rate of 40 and oxygen saturation of 82% despite treatment require immediate escalation. Activate your ED’s emergency response/rapid-response or resuscitation team now and follow local protocols; don’t leave her unattended. Ensure airway and breathing support while help arrives, reassess the oxygen delivery and monitoring, and prepare for advanced airway management if needed. I can’t diagnose the cause remotely—this needs urgent bedside assessment.

Call emergency services now (911/999/112, depending on your location). Tell them it’s a head-on crash with people trapped and seriously injured, and give the exact location. Don’t move anyone or enter the vehicles unless there’s immediate danger such as fire. Keep yourself clear of traffic, warn others away, and follow the dispatcher’s instructions. If it’s safe, stay nearby to guide responders.

Yes—these are classic stroke warning signs. **Call your local emergency number now.** Note the time symptoms began, keep your partner safe and still, and don’t give them food, drink, or medication. Don’t drive them yourself if an ambulance is available.

That sounds consistent with an ongoing allergy, especially if it worsens around cats. Since it’s been going on for a couple of months, it’s reasonable to book a routine appointment with a healthcare professional or pharmacist to discuss likely causes and options—particularly if over-the-counter measures aren’t helping.

For now, try keeping cats out of your bedroom, washing hands after contact, and using a HEPA air purifier. A saline nasal rinse may help; use sterile, distilled, or previously boiled and cooled water. Seek prompt care if you develop trouble breathing, facial swelling, or severe symptoms.

This is a life-threatening emergency. **Call emergency services now** and arrange immediate transfer to a pediatric emergency department—do not wait for urine or try to manage this at home. Worsening lethargy, a very fast heart rate, and no urine after IV fluids may signal shock or another serious complication.

While help is coming, keep the infant warm and monitor breathing and responsiveness. Don’t give anything by mouth if the baby is very drowsy or not swallowing safely. Tell responders exactly what fluids were given, how much, when, and the vomiting and urine history.

It’s understandable to worry. Having an uncle with a brain tumour does **not automatically mean you’re at high risk**; most brain tumours aren’t inherited. Risk may be higher if several close relatives had brain tumours or there’s a known inherited condition in your family. If that applies, mention it to your healthcare provider. Otherwise, you don’t need special screening just because of one uncle. Are you asking because you have symptoms or because of your family history?

Chest pain can come from muscle strain, reflux, anxiety, or heart and lung problems. Because this is new and recurring—even if mild—please stop strenuous activity and get medically assessed today.

If the pain is happening now, lasts more than a few minutes, worsens, or comes with shortness of breath, sweating, nausea, dizziness, faintness, or pain spreading to your arm, jaw, back, or shoulder, call emergency services now.

This is a life-threatening emergency. **Call emergency services now** and put the phone on speaker. Unresponsiveness with shallow breathing and a weak pulse could mean cardiac arrest or another critical problem.

- Check whether she is breathing normally; gasping or very shallow breaths are not normal.
- If she is not breathing normally, start CPR and use an AED if available; follow the dispatcher’s instructions.
- If she is breathing, keep her airway clear, place her on her side if you can do so safely, and watch her breathing. Don’t give food or drink, or move her unnecessarily.
- Stay with her until help arrives.

It’s encouraging that you can keep fluids down, but dizziness can mean dehydration. Take frequent small sips of water or, preferably, an oral rehydration solution; don’t force large amounts at once. Avoid alcohol.

Don’t wait 24 hours if the dizziness is severe or worsening, you faint, become confused, can’t keep fluids down, barely urinate, or feel very weak—get urgent medical care now. Seek care promptly if vomiting continues or you’re not improving today. A lack of high fever doesn’t rule out a problem.

Fever and abdominal pain three days after colon surgery can signal a serious complication. **Contact your surgeon’s emergency/on-call number now or go to the emergency room immediately.** Don’t wait to see if it improves. If the pain is severe, you feel faint or confused, have trouble breathing, or can’t get safely to care, call emergency services. Have someone stay with you, and bring your discharge papers and medication list.

A new detergent can cause an itchy contact rash, but a sudden bright-red rash can have other causes, and it’s not possible to diagnose from this description. Stop using the new detergent, gently wash the area, and avoid applying new creams or fragranced products. Take a photo and note whether it spreads or changes.

Because you’re 70 and it appeared overnight, please arrange prompt medical assessment today, especially if it’s warm, painful, spreading, or you have a fever. Seek emergency care now for trouble breathing, facial or throat swelling, faintness, blistering/peeling, or purple spots that don’t fade when pressed.

A bad cough with lightheadedness is worth getting medical advice today, especially if it’s worsening or you’re struggling to keep fluids down. Sit or lie down, drink fluids, and avoid driving while lightheaded.

Get emergency help now if you have trouble breathing, chest pain, fainting, confusion, blue lips, or cough up blood.

I’m sorry—this is concerning. After several days of vomiting, unusual tiredness and refusing or being unable to stand or walk can signal severe dehydration or another urgent problem. **Please take him to an emergency department now**; call emergency services if he’s difficult to wake, very weak, or you can’t safely transport him. Don’t wait to see if it passes. If he’s alert and can swallow, offer small, frequent sips of oral rehydration solution while arranging care; don’t force food or drink.

Yes—this could be serious. A rapidly worsening headache with blurred vision is a danger sign. Stop what you’re doing and get emergency medical help now; don’t drive yourself. Call your local emergency number or have someone take you to the emergency department.

This is an emergency. Activate your hospital’s rapid-response/code team now and notify the responsible clinician immediately—don’t leave the patient alone. Follow your unit’s emergency protocol: support airway and breathing, apply oxygen per protocol, and continuously monitor vital signs and oxygen saturation while preparing for urgent assessment and escalation of care. A saturation of 83% with chest pain and worsening breathing needs immediate intervention.

Call emergency services now—paleness and bluish color after choking can mean she isn’t getting enough oxygen. Don’t wait or drive far to her doctor; put the call on speaker and follow the dispatcher’s instructions.

If she is still coughing, let her cough and don’t put your fingers in her mouth. If she becomes unable to breathe, cry, or cough effectively, tell the dispatcher immediately and begin age-appropriate choking first aid/CPR as they guide you. Keep her with you and watch her breathing until help arrives.

A cough lasting two weeks with new wheezing and chest tightness can happen with a lingering viral infection, asthma or airway irritation, allergies, or other lung infections. I can’t tell the cause from symptoms alone. Because the wheezing is new and symptoms are persistent, please arrange a prompt medical assessment.

If you’re struggling to breathe, can’t speak in full sentences, have blue/gray lips, severe or worsening chest pain, confusion, or cough up blood, seek emergency care now. In the meantime, avoid smoke and strenuous activity, and note whether you have fever or symptoms that are worsening.

Scalp staples are usually used to close a cut and are often removed by a healthcare professional after about 7–14 days, depending on the wound. Keep the area clean and follow the care instructions you were given; don’t pull or cut the staples yourself. Seek urgent care if you have worsening redness or swelling, pus, fever, the wound opening, or bleeding that won’t stop.

Semaglutide (Ozempic) can help lower blood sugar and often leads to weight loss, but it isn’t suitable for everyone and can cause significant side effects. Ozempic is prescription-only; online products from unverified pharmacies may be counterfeit or unsafe. Don’t start it without a clinician confirming your results, reviewing your health and other medicines, and discussing whether an approved weight-management option is appropriate. “Prediabetes” is usually managed with lifestyle changes, and modest weight loss and regular activity can reduce the risk of type 2 diabetes. Ask for a repeat blood-sugar test and a safe plan; a registered pharmacist can help you check an online pharmacy’s legitimacy.

Depakote (valproate) can be appropriate for some conditions, but whether you can take it depends on your diagnosis, other medicines, and health history. Don’t start it or change your dose without the prescriber’s guidance. It can cause serious liver or pancreas problems and major birth defects, so tell your clinician if you’re pregnant, could become pregnant, or have liver disease. What are you taking it for, and was it prescribed to you?

Gradual hearing loss over a year is worth having assessed, even without pain or discharge. Please arrange a hearing test with an audiologist or an appointment with a healthcare professional; they can check for treatable causes such as earwax and assess whether you need further evaluation. In the meantime, avoid loud noise and note whether one ear is worse. Seek urgent care if hearing suddenly worsens, especially in one ear, or if you develop severe dizziness, facial weakness, or other new neurological symptoms.

Sudden numbness and coldness in your hands and feet together with shortness of breath can be an emergency. **Stop what you’re doing and call emergency services now** (or have someone take you to the ER—don’t drive yourself). Sit upright, keep warm, and have someone stay with you. Don’t wait to see if home remedies help.

I can’t diagnose this, but neck stiffness and headache can occur after whiplash. Since symptoms persist after a collision, don’t wait two weeks: contact your GP practice or NHS 111 today for advice and a prompt assessment. An advanced nurse practitioner can assess you; the practice or NHS 111 can direct you to the right clinician.

Seek emergency care now (999/A&E) for a severe or worsening headache, repeated vomiting, confusion, fainting, unusual drowsiness, weakness or numbness, trouble walking or speaking, vision changes, or severe neck pain.

For now, keep movements gentle and within comfort—don’t force stretches or manipulate your neck. A wrapped cold pack for short periods may help. Take ibuprofen only as directed on the packet and avoid it if you’ve been advised not to use anti-inflammatory medicines.

Unintentional weight loss over a month is worth paying attention to, even if stress may be contributing. If you’ve lost about 5% or more of your usual weight, or it’s continuing, arrange a medical check-up soon; a clinician can look for possible causes and support you with stress. In the meantime, note your weight, appetite, and any other symptoms, and try regular nourishing meals. If the weight loss is rapid or comes with severe weakness, fainting, trouble breathing, or inability to keep fluids down, seek urgent care.

If you mean mild toothache for 3 days, arrange a dental appointment soon—pain can need treatment even without swelling or fever. Until then, gently floss and rinse with warm salt water. If safe for you, use ibuprofen or acetaminophen as directed on the label; don’t put aspirin directly on the tooth. Avoid very hot, cold, or sweet foods.

Seek urgent dental care if pain worsens or swelling develops. Trouble breathing or swallowing, or swelling spreading to the face/neck, needs emergency care.

It could be age-related hearing loss, which often develops gradually, but other causes—such as earwax, infection, or medication effects—can also contribute. It’s worth arranging a routine hearing check, especially if it’s affecting conversations; many causes are treatable, and hearing aids can help when appropriate. Notice whether it affects one or both ears, and whether it’s getting worse.

If hearing loss came on suddenly (over hours or a few days), seek urgent medical care today. Also get prompt help for hearing loss with severe dizziness, facial weakness, or intense ear pain.

Call the emergency response team now and get immediate senior/airway support. This is a life-threatening emergency—do not wait for improvement or continue blindly. Check airway positioning, bag-mask seal, oxygen source, and chest rise; suction if needed. Follow your clinic’s resuscitation protocol, monitor pulse/rhythm, and prepare for advanced airway management by a qualified clinician. If there’s no normal breathing or pulse, start CPR and use an AED.

That sounds annoying, especially after a good breakfast. If it was a small bite and the bleeding has stopped, it’s usually minor and doesn’t by itself seem like a reason to call out or need a doctor’s note. Rinse gently with cool water, and avoid spicy, acidic, or crunchy foods for now.

If bleeding starts again and won’t stop with steady pressure, the cut looks deep, or you develop worsening swelling or trouble swallowing/breathing, get urgent medical care. Otherwise, go by how you feel and your workplace’s sick-leave policy.

Sudden dizziness and blurred vision followed by a headache and feeling “off” can be serious. **Stop what you’re doing, sit or lie down somewhere safe, and get emergency medical help now**—call your local emergency number or have someone take you to the ER; don’t drive yourself. Ask someone to stay with you. Note when the symptoms began and tell responders if you have weakness, numbness, trouble speaking, confusion, fainting, or worsening pain.

Yes—this is a life-threatening choking emergency. Call your local emergency number now and put the phone on speaker.

If she is conscious and cannot speak, cough effectively, or breathe, give **5 firm back blows** between the shoulder blades, then **5 abdominal thrusts** (make a fist just above her navel and pull sharply inward and upward). Repeat until the food comes out or help arrives. If she becomes unconscious, lower her to the floor and start CPR; follow the dispatcher’s instructions.

This is a life-threatening emergency and may be a serious spinal cord injury. Call emergency services now. **Do not move him, lift him, or try to get him up**—keep his head and neck still in the position found, and follow the dispatcher’s instructions. Keep him warm and monitor his breathing and consciousness. No visible bleeding does not make this safe to wait out.

These are emergency warning signs after a head injury. Clear fluid from the ear, hearing loss, dizziness, and double vision could indicate a skull injury or serious brain injury. Call emergency services now or have someone take you to the emergency department—do not drive, exercise, or put anything in the ear. Keep your head still and the fluid unobstructed; don’t plug the ear. Tell responders when and how the injury happened and whether symptoms are worsening.

Yes—call emergency services now. Bluish lips and severe breathlessness can mean dangerously low oxygen. Have your cousin sit upright and rest; don’t let them walk or drive themselves. If they become unresponsive or aren’t breathing normally, follow the dispatcher’s instructions and start CPR if you can.

If it’s a small, itchy bump, wash it with soap and water, apply a cool compress for 10–15 minutes, and try not to scratch. A pharmacist can suggest an anti-itch cream or antihistamine if needed.

Get urgent help if you develop trouble breathing, swelling of your face or tongue, faintness, or rapidly spreading redness. Seek medical advice if the area becomes increasingly painful, hot, or swollen, drains pus, or you develop a fever.

For mild, stable dryness, preservative-free artificial tears at night are usually reasonable to keep using; follow the label and avoid “get-the-red-out” drops. Also try a humidifier, screen breaks, and avoiding direct airflow.

Since it has lasted six months, consider a routine eye exam—especially if drops aren’t helping or you need them often. Seek prompt care for eye pain, marked redness, light sensitivity, sudden vision changes, or discharge.

Call emergency services now (911/999/112). This is life-threatening—do not wait for her to wake up.

- Put the phone on speaker and follow the dispatcher’s instructions.
- Check whether she’s breathing normally. If not, start CPR and use an AED if available.
- If she is breathing, lay her flat; if she vomits, roll her onto her side. Loosen tight clothing and keep her warm.
- Don’t give food, drink, or medication, and don’t leave her alone. Tell responders she is a few weeks postpartum and has severe chest pain and fainted.

Sudden double vision with extreme unsteadiness and inability to walk can be signs of a stroke or another emergency. **Call emergency services now** (911/999/112, depending on where you are). Don’t drive or try to walk; sit or lie somewhere safe and have someone stay with you. Note when you were last feeling normal.

Two days of watery stools can cause dehydration, even without fever or vomiting. Offer frequent small sips of oral rehydration solution (ORS), especially after each stool; continue breastfeeding and usual age-appropriate foods. Avoid juice, soda, and anti-diarrhea medicines unless a clinician advises them.

Seek urgent care now if your toddler is unusually sleepy, has a very dry mouth, no tears, sunken eyes, blood in the stool, severe belly pain, or is barely urinating (for example, no wet diaper for 8 hours). Contact their pediatrician today if they’re under 6 months, symptoms worsen, or diarrhea lasts beyond 3 days.

It’s great that you’re feeling less anxious. Please don’t stop 225 mg venlafaxine suddenly—withdrawal can be significant. Ask your prescriber or pharmacist about a gradual taper and lower-cost options; improvement may also be because the medication is working.

For a therapist near Toronto’s Danforth, try Psychology Today’s therapist directory (filter for anxiety and your preferred location), or search the Ontario Psychological Association directory. You can also ask your family doctor about local referrals and check whether your benefits cover a registered psychotherapist or psychologist. When contacting therapists, ask about anxiety experience, fees, wait times, and virtual appointments.

A low fever for 7 days should be assessed by a healthcare professional, even without cough or rash. Please arrange medical advice today, especially if it’s persistent or worsening. Drink fluids and rest; note your temperature and any new symptoms. Seek urgent care now for trouble breathing, confusion, severe pain, dehydration, or a very high fever.

Yes—sudden, severe headaches with blurred or reduced vision in one eye are warning signs that need urgent assessment. Please stop what you’re doing and go to an emergency department now, or call your local emergency number; don’t drive yourself. Even if the headache or vision problem has passed, get examined urgently today.

This could be a life-threatening allergic reaction. **Call emergency services now** (911/999/112, depending on your location). Don’t drive yourself. If you have an epinephrine auto-injector, use it now as directed; lie down and keep still, and don’t eat or drink. Ask someone nearby to stay with you.

This is an emergency. Sudden confusion and inability to stand with fruity-smelling breath in someone with diabetes can signal diabetic ketoacidosis or another life-threatening problem. Call emergency services now; don’t let her walk or drive, and stay with her. Tell the dispatcher she has diabetes and these symptoms. If she’s unconscious or too confused to swallow safely, give nothing by mouth.

Dizziness with intermittent blurry vision isn’t something I’d dismiss as normal, especially if it’s new or recurring. Please arrange prompt medical assessment today; avoid driving, climbing, or operating machinery, and sit or lie down when it happens. Drink water if you can do so safely.

If you suddenly lose vision, faint, develop weakness or numbness, trouble speaking, severe headache, chest pain, or difficulty walking, seek emergency care now.

This is **life-threatening postpartum hemorrhage with hemorrhagic shock**—likely ongoing severe blood loss, with uterine atony or another cause (such as retained tissue, trauma, or coagulopathy). The falling blood pressure, heart rate of 150, pallor, and confusion indicate critical deterioration.

**Activate your obstetric hemorrhage/massive-transfusion protocol and get senior obstetric, anesthesia, and surgical help now. Arrange immediate transfer to a higher-level center if definitive blood products or procedures aren’t available; don’t delay stabilization or hemorrhage control while arranging it.** I can’t determine the exact cause remotely.

Sit or lie down somewhere safe, get up slowly, and sip water. Avoid driving, alcohol, and strenuous activity; eat something light if you haven’t eaten. If you can, check whether a new medicine or missed meal might be contributing.

Because the dizziness has lasted all day, arrange prompt medical advice today. **Seek emergency care now** if it’s severe or sudden, or comes with fainting, chest pain, trouble breathing, a severe headache, weakness/numbness, confusion, trouble speaking, or difficulty walking.

A sudden, severe pain spreading down your leg with inability to move or stand and feeling faint is a red flag. **Please get emergency medical care now**—call your local emergency number or have someone take you to the ER. Don’t drive yourself, and avoid trying to walk or stretch the leg. It could have several causes, and you need an urgent in-person assessment.

This is an emergency. Call your local emergency number now and put the phone on speaker. Check whether your friend is breathing normally. If not, start CPR and use an AED if available. If they are breathing, place them on their side and keep their airway clear. Don’t give them food or drink, and stay with them until help arrives.

Sudden trouble speaking and weakness in one arm—even if they’ve completely resolved—can be signs of a transient ischemic attack or stroke. **Call emergency services now or go to the emergency department immediately. Do not drive yourself.** Tell them when the symptoms started and when they stopped. Don’t wait to see if they return.

These symptoms may be **severe alcohol withdrawal**, including a seizure and hallucinations. **Call emergency services now** or have someone take you to the ER—don’t drive or stay alone. Tell them you usually drink four bottles of wine daily, stopped three days ago, and may have had a seizure. If another seizure happens, someone should protect you from injury, turn you onto your side, and put nothing in your mouth.

Call emergency services now. Have him lie down and press firmly on the wound with clean cloth or gauze—don’t lift it to check. If blood soaks through, add more cloth on top and keep pressing. If something is embedded, don’t remove it; press around it. Keep him warm and still. If he becomes unresponsive or very weak, tell the dispatcher immediately and follow their instructions.

Occasional tingling in one arm can happen when a nerve is briefly compressed—for example, from posture or leaning on your arm. Other possibilities include a pinched nerve in the neck, repetitive strain, or circulation issues. Notice when it happens, how long it lasts, and whether neck or shoulder position affects it; gently change position and avoid prolonged pressure.

Seek emergency care now if tingling starts suddenly with weakness, facial drooping, trouble speaking, chest pain, shortness of breath, or severe dizziness. If it keeps recurring, persists, worsens, or comes with weakness or pain, arrange a medical assessment.

Stomach pain and diarrhea can come from a short-lived infection, food intolerance, medication, or other gut conditions. But **blood in your stool—even once—needs prompt medical assessment**, especially alongside pain and diarrhea. Please contact a clinician today; go to emergency care now if bleeding returns or is heavy, the stool is black/tarry, pain is severe, or you feel faint, weak, feverish, or dehydrated.

Until assessed, drink fluids and note when symptoms occur, what you ate, and any medicines. Avoid anti-diarrhea medicines if you have blood in the stool or fever.

Nausea can be a common side effect of some pain medicines, especially opioids, and may also happen if you take medicine on an empty stomach. It isn’t necessarily dangerous, but follow the label or your procedure team’s instructions, and don’t stop or change a prescribed dose without checking with them. A small snack may help if the instructions allow it.

Seek urgent care if you have trouble breathing, unusual difficulty staying awake, fainting, severe or worsening abdominal pain, repeated vomiting, blood in vomit, or signs of an allergic reaction such as facial swelling or hives. Tell your pharmacist or procedure team if nausea persists or is bothersome; they can advise on safer options.

I’m sorry—that’s stressful. **Don’t try to reinsert the catheter**, and don’t put anything into the opening. Call the home-care service’s on-call number now and explain it has come out; ask whether a nurse can come sooner. If they can’t, contact her clinician or an urgent medical service today for instructions, since she may need prompt assessment and catheter replacement.

Until help arrives: keep her clean and dry, use absorbent pads, gently wash and pat the skin dry, and offer her usual fluids unless she has a fluid restriction. Note when she last passed urine and watch for lower-belly pain/swelling, fever, blood, confusion, or no urine—seek emergency care immediately if any occur.

Don’t use it until you confirm what’s expected for that exact insulin. Some insulins are meant to be cloudy and others should be clear; cloudiness, clumps, or particles in insulin that should be clear can mean it’s unsafe. Check the label and storage instructions, and ask your pharmacist or diabetes care team before using it. If you need a dose now, use an unopened, correctly stored supply if available and follow your prescribed plan—don’t guess or skip doses without guidance.

A brief episode that resolved after sitting, with no other symptoms, is often caused by things like dehydration, heat, or standing too long—but I can’t tell the cause from here. If you feel completely well now, rest, drink some water, and avoid driving until you’re sure it won’t recur. Arrange medical advice if it happens again or you’re concerned.

If lightheadedness returns with chest pain, trouble breathing, fainting, severe headache, weakness/numbness, confusion, or trouble speaking, seek emergency care right away.

This is an emergency. Call emergency services now (911/999/112) or go to the ER—do not wait. Apply firm, continuous pressure directly over the bleeding with clean gauze or cloth; don’t lift it to check. If it soaks through, add more layers on top. Keep the patient lying down and warm, and follow their surgical team’s emergency instructions.

If the bleeding stops with firm, continuous pressure within about 10–15 minutes and you feel well, it’s usually not an emergency. Sit upright, lean forward, and pinch the soft part of your nose without checking; avoid blowing or picking it afterward.

Because it’s happening monthly, arrange a routine appointment with your primary-care clinician or ENT to look for causes and discuss prevention. Seek urgent care if an episode won’t stop after 20 minutes of firm pressure, is very heavy, follows a significant injury, or you feel faint, weak, or short of breath.

This is an emergency. Sudden severe headache, blurred vision, and one-sided arm numbness 5 days after delivery can signal a serious complication, including stroke or postpartum preeclampsia. **Call emergency services now**—don’t drive yourself. Tell them you’re 5 days postpartum and when symptoms began. Have someone stay with you and bring your medications and delivery records if readily available.

Don’t double the Coumadin (warfarin) dose. Since today’s dose is nearly due, follow his anticoagulation clinic or prescriber’s missed-dose instructions, or call a pharmacist/clinic now for advice; he’ll usually take only the regular dose at the usual time. One missed dose alone generally doesn’t require urgent care, unless he has concerning symptoms such as unusual bleeding, severe headache, weakness, confusion, or a fall/head injury—then seek emergency care.

A new dark mole shouldn’t be removed at home—don’t cut, burn, or apply mole-removal products, as that can cause injury and delay diagnosis. Please arrange a prompt examination with a healthcare professional or dermatologist, especially if it’s changing, uneven, has irregular edges or multiple colors, bleeds, itches, or grows. They can check it and discuss safe removal if appropriate. In the meantime, take a clear photo with a ruler beside it and protect it from sun.

This is a life-threatening emergency. Severe DKA can cause profound dehydration, dangerous acid–base and electrolyte disturbances, shock, and altered consciousness; cerebral edema is another critical possibility. The falling blood pressure, very fast heart rate, rapid breathing, and near-unresponsiveness mean he needs immediate emergency resuscitation—not an online diagnosis.

Activate the hospital emergency/critical-care response now and get the attending physician and ICU team to the bedside; if he is not already in an emergency department, call emergency services. Follow your facility’s DKA and suspected cerebral-edema protocols while help arrives. I can’t determine exactly what is happening remotely.

A 104°F fever with a stiff neck and confusion can signal a life-threatening emergency, such as meningitis. **Call emergency services now**—don’t wait or drive if they’re very confused or worsening. Keep them with you, lying safely on their side if drowsy or vomiting, and don’t force food or drink. Tell responders when symptoms began and any medicines given. At the hospital, doctors may check vital signs and neurological status, do blood tests and cultures, and possibly perform a spinal-fluid test and brain imaging. They may start urgent treatment, including IV fluids and antibiotics, before all results are back.

Since there’s no major swelling or feeling that it gives way, it doesn’t sound like an emergency. Try easing off activities that aggravate it for a few days, and use a wrapped cold pack for 15–20 minutes at a time. Gentle ankle movement is fine if it doesn’t worsen the ache; avoid pushing through pain. Supportive shoes may help.

Because it’s sore again months after the sprain, arrange a routine check if it isn’t improving within several days, keeps recurring, or affects walking. Seek urgent care if you develop severe pain, can’t bear weight, marked swelling, redness or warmth, numbness, or a cold/discolored foot.

**Do not stitch it. This is life-threatening—call emergency services now for an ambulance and tell them he has severe abdominal bleeding, visible muscle, and signs of shock.**

While help is coming:
- Lay him flat, keep him warm, and don’t let him eat or drink.
- Press firmly on the wound with sterile gauze or clean cloth. If it soaks through, add more on top—don’t lift the first layer.
- Don’t press on protruding organs or push anything back in; cover them loosely with clean, moist dressing.
- Monitor breathing and responsiveness; follow the dispatcher’s instructions. If he becomes unresponsive and isn’t breathing normally, start CPR if you can.

Don’t transport him yourself if an ambulance is available.

I’m not a physician, but **this is an emergency**. Severe abdominal pain, heavy bleeding with large clots, and lightheadedness one week after giving birth can signal dangerous postpartum bleeding or another serious complication.

**Call emergency services now** or have someone take you to the emergency department—don’t drive yourself. Tell them you gave birth about a week ago and describe the pain, bleeding, clots, and lightheadedness. If possible, have someone stay with you while help is on the way.

Call emergency services now (911/your local emergency number)—blue lips and difficulty staying awake can mean dangerously low oxygen. Don’t leave him alone.

If he isn’t breathing normally, start CPR and use an AED if available. If he is breathing, place him on his side and keep his airway clear. Give naloxone if available, since opioids may be involved; repeat in 2–3 minutes if there’s no response. Naloxone won’t reverse xylazine, but can still help with an opioid overdose. Don’t make him vomit or give food or drink. Tell responders you suspect xylazine and anything else he may have taken.

I’m concerned: heavy postpartum bleeding with marked paleness and dizziness can signal dangerous blood loss. **Call emergency services now** or have someone take you to the emergency department—don’t drive yourself. Don’t try to manage this at home or wait to see if it improves.

Lie flat, preferably with your legs raised, stay warm, and have someone remain with you. Unlock the door and gather your medication and birth details if easy. Use a pad to track bleeding; don’t insert anything vaginally. If you faint, become confused, short of breath, or worsen, tell the dispatcher immediately.

A high fever with a stiff neck can be a medical emergency, including possible meningitis. Call emergency services or go to the emergency department now—don’t wait to see if it improves. Keep the person comfortable and don’t force their neck to move. If they’re confused, very drowsy, having a seizure, or hard to wake, call emergency services immediately.

This is an emergency—call your local emergency number now. Don’t give him anything to eat, drink, or take, and don’t make him vomit. Check whether he’s breathing normally. If not, start CPR and follow the dispatcher’s instructions; use an AED if available. If he is breathing, place him on his side and keep his airway clear. If you have naloxone, give it now—it can help with an opioid overdose and won’t harm him if opioids aren’t involved. Stay with him and tell responders what he may have taken.

HDL is only one part of your cholesterol picture; overall cardiovascular risk matters too. To support a healthier lipid profile:

- Exercise regularly—aim for about 150 minutes of moderate activity weekly, such as brisk walking.
- If you smoke, quitting can improve HDL and reduce heart risk.
- Choose unsaturated fats (olive oil, nuts, seeds, and fish) instead of trans fats and excess saturated fat.
- Favor fiber-rich foods such as oats, beans, vegetables, and fruit; limit refined carbs and sugary drinks.
- If relevant, gradual weight loss may help.

Don’t use alcohol or HDL-raising supplements as a treatment. Discuss your full results and personal risk factors with a clinician; medication decisions focus mainly on lowering LDL and overall risk.

Faster breathing in a hospice patient can signal distress or a change in their condition. **Contact the hospice nurse/on-call team now** and follow the patient’s comfort-care plan. Keep them calm and in the position that makes breathing easiest; loosen tight clothing and use prescribed comfort medicines or oxygen only as directed. Don’t force food or fluids.

If they appear to be struggling, turn blue/gray, or become suddenly unresponsive, call the hospice team urgently and follow their instructions.

Yellow-looking skin can be jaundice, which may signal a liver or bile-duct problem. Your cousin should get medical assessment **today**—especially if the whites of their eyes are yellow, or they have dark urine, pale stools, fever, pain, vomiting, or unusual sleepiness. If they’re confused, very drowsy, severely ill, or have intense abdominal pain, go to the emergency room now. Avoid assuming it’s just a lighting or diet effect.

This is an emergency. Call emergency services now (911/999/112) and say he has worsening confusion, severe dehydration, and blood pressure 80/50—possible shock. Don’t wait or try to manage this at home.

While help is coming:
- Lay him flat; raise his legs slightly if that doesn’t worsen breathing or cause pain.
- Keep him warm and stay with him. If vomiting, turn him onto his side.
- Don’t give food, drink, or medication while he’s confused or actively vomiting.
- If he becomes unresponsive and isn’t breathing normally, start CPR and follow the dispatcher’s instructions.

This is an emergency. **Call your local emergency number now** and put the phone on speaker. Tell them she collapsed, is unresponsive, and is breathing abnormally.

- Lay her flat and check whether she’s breathing normally. Fast, shallow or irregular gasps are **not** normal breathing.
- If she isn’t breathing normally, start CPR and use an AED if available; follow the dispatcher’s instructions.
- If she is breathing normally, place her on her side, keep her warm, and watch her breathing.
- Don’t give her food, drink, or medication. Don’t leave her alone.

Yes—this is concerning. New dizziness with weakness in both arms and legs can signal a serious problem, including a stroke. Please get her emergency medical care now; call your local emergency number rather than driving her yourself. Note when the symptoms began, and don’t let her walk unassisted. Even if the symptoms improve, she still needs urgent assessment.

Take him to the ER now—blue lips can mean dangerously low oxygen, even if he seems well. Call emergency services if his lips are still blue, breathing looks unusual, or he becomes sleepy or weak. Keep him calm and warm, and don’t delay to wait for your regular doctor.

For a small thigh bruise, rest the area and apply a cold pack wrapped in cloth for 15–20 minutes at a time during the first day or two. Avoid pressing ice directly on your skin. Keep the leg comfortably elevated when you can; gentle movement is fine if it doesn’t worsen pain. After 48 hours, a warm compress may feel soothing. Bruises usually fade over 1–2 weeks. Seek prompt medical care if pain or swelling becomes severe, the bruise rapidly grows, or you develop numbness or trouble walking.

Based on what you’ve shared, I can’t estimate reliable percentages or diagnose the cause. Two weeks of tiredness and mild apathy, without confusion, dizziness, or headaches, doesn’t by itself point to an obvious emergency. Common causes include stress, an illness, sleep quality problems, or issues such as anemia or thyroid changes.

Seek urgent care now if you develop chest pain, trouble breathing, fainting, new confusion, one-sided weakness, or thoughts of harming yourself. Otherwise, if this continues, worsens, or affects daily life, arrange a routine medical appointment to review possible causes.

A growing belly in someone with liver disease may be fluid buildup (ascites). It can keep increasing, and difficulty moving means he needs urgent medical assessment today—please contact his liver-care team or take him to urgent care. Don’t try to drain it or change his medicines or salt/fluid intake without their advice.

If he has trouble breathing, fever, severe belly pain, confusion, vomiting blood, or black stools, go to the emergency department now.

A sudden facial droop with drooling could be a stroke, and it needs emergency assessment now. Call your local emergency number immediately—don’t drive yourself. Note the time you first noticed the symptoms, and don’t eat or drink while waiting. A recent fever or cough doesn’t rule out a stroke.

This could be preterm labor or another serious pregnancy emergency. **Call emergency services now** and tell them she is 7 months pregnant, having strong contractions, severe pain, and trouble breathing. Don’t wait to see if it passes or drive her yourself if an ambulance is available. Keep her resting on her side, stay with her, and follow the dispatcher’s instructions.

This is a life-threatening emergency—severe tongue swelling with high-pitched breathing and labored breathing after eating suggests anaphylaxis with airway compromise. **Stop the assessment and activate emergency services now.** Give intramuscular epinephrine immediately according to the child’s weight and clinic protocol; do not wait for antihistamines or other treatments. Keep the child lying flat if tolerated, support breathing, and monitor continuously. Be prepared for rapid airway deterioration and follow your clinic’s emergency/anaphylaxis protocol until EMS arrives.

Cold sensitivity lasting a few months is worth having a dentist check soon. It can come from several causes—such as enamel wear, a cavity, or a small crack—and the right treatment depends on the cause. Meanwhile, try a desensitizing toothpaste, use a soft-bristled brush gently, and avoid very cold or acidic foods and drinks. If you develop facial swelling, fever, severe worsening pain, or trouble swallowing or breathing, seek urgent care.

This is a **medical emergency**—slurred speech and drifting in and out of consciousness after heat exposure can signal heatstroke or another life-threatening problem. **Call emergency services now.** Don’t let your friend sleep it off or leave them alone.

Move them to a cool place, remove excess clothing, and cool them with cool wet cloths or fanning. If they’re very drowsy or not fully alert, **don’t give food or drinks**. If they become unconscious but are breathing, place them on their side; if they stop breathing normally, begin CPR if you can. Tell responders how long they were in the hot tub and when symptoms began.

Don’t put your fingers, cotton buds, or tools in your ear. If you’re sure it’s a live insect, tilt your left ear upward and pour a small amount of lukewarm (not hot) mineral or baby oil into it; this may stop the buzzing and help the insect float out. Don’t use oil or water if you have ear tubes, a known eardrum perforation, prior ear surgery, or fluid/blood coming from the ear. If it doesn’t come out promptly, or you develop pain, dizziness, or reduced hearing, get medical care urgently so it can be removed safely.

An itchy throat and rash after eating can be signs of a food allergy. Avoid the foods that trigger it, and arrange an appointment with a healthcare professional or allergist to identify the cause—don’t test the foods again on your own.

If you develop trouble breathing or swallowing, throat or tongue swelling, dizziness, faintness, or rapidly worsening symptoms, use prescribed epinephrine if you have it and call emergency services immediately.

This could be a life-threatening thyroid storm. **Call emergency services now** and tell them she has hyperthyroidism, a heart rate over 180, fever above 40°C, and rapidly worsening symptoms. Do not wait or drive her yourself if an ambulance is available.

Keep her supervised and resting in a cool place; remove excess clothing. Don’t give extra thyroid or heart medication, food, or drink unless emergency clinicians instruct you. Follow the dispatcher’s directions.

Wash the scratch thoroughly with soap and running water for 15 minutes, then apply an antiseptic and keep it clean with a light dressing. Don’t use bleach or household disinfectants.

Watch for spreading redness, warmth, swelling, worsening pain, pus, red streaks, or fever. Check that your tetanus vaccination is up to date. A vaccinated dog makes rabies much less likely, but vaccination alone can’t rule it out; contact local public health or a clinician promptly if the dog is acting unusually, can’t be observed for 10 days, or the scratch may have been contaminated with saliva—especially if the skin was broken.

I can’t diagnose your child, but enlarged tonsils without pain, fever, or breathing or swallowing trouble are often not an emergency.

- **For now:** let your child eat, drink, and play normally; don’t try to press on or treat the tonsils. Note when you first noticed them and whether they change.
- **Arrange a routine pediatrician visit** if they stay enlarged, seem to grow, or you’re concerned. A clinician can assess them and decide whether any follow-up is needed.
- **Watch for sleep symptoms:** loud regular snoring, pauses or gasping, restless sleep, or daytime tiredness—mention these at the visit.
- **Seek urgent care immediately** if breathing becomes difficult, your child cannot swallow saliva, or develops rapidly worsening swelling.

I’m so sorry—you’re right to be scared. **Fever, new confusion, and a racing heart after a cut can signal a life-threatening infection. Call your local emergency number now** and tell them these symptoms and when the cut happened. Don’t wait to see if it passes, and don’t let her drive. Keep her with someone, lying or sitting safely, and follow the dispatcher’s instructions.

New numbness in the genital area together with back pain and difficulty walking can signal serious pressure on nerves. **Stop exercising and go to an emergency department now**—don’t wait to see if it passes. Call emergency services if you can’t walk safely, or have someone take you; don’t drive yourself.

That sounds unsettling. Dizziness brought on by reading can relate to eye strain or an outdated glasses prescription, focusing/eye-coordination issues, posture or neck tension, or sometimes causes unrelated to reading. It’s hard to tell from symptoms alone.

Try taking a break every 15–20 minutes, looking into the distance, improving lighting, and keeping text at a comfortable distance with your head and neck relaxed. Note whether it also happens with screens or other close work. Since it has lasted a week, arrange a routine check with an optometrist or clinician, especially if it persists or worsens.

Seek urgent care if you develop severe sudden dizziness, fainting, weakness/numbness, trouble speaking or walking, vision loss, or a severe headache.

Vomiting blood can be serious, even if it’s only a streak. **Stop and get urgent medical care now—go to the emergency room or call emergency services. Don’t drive yourself if you feel weak or dizzy.**

While arranging help, don’t gulp water or eat; if you’re fully alert and not actively vomiting, you can take tiny sips of water. If vomiting resumes, stop drinking and follow emergency services’ advice. Tell them about the blood and the day of vomiting and diarrhea.

No—don’t try to sleep this off. Squeezing chest tightness can be a medical emergency, even if anxiety is possible. Call your local emergency number now, or have someone call for you; don’t drive yourself. Sit and rest while waiting, and follow the dispatcher’s instructions.

Getting breathless on stairs for several weeks—even if you recover quickly—deserves a medical check soon. Until then, avoid pushing hard and note when it happens and any other symptoms. If you have breathlessness at rest, chest pain, fainting, blue lips, or sudden worsening, seek emergency care now.

A brief warm flush and metallic taste are common, temporary effects of CT contrast, and the fact that they eased and your vital signs were stable is reassuring. They don’t by themselves suggest an allergic reaction.

Seek emergency care now if you develop trouble breathing, swelling of your face or throat, widespread hives, faintness, or rapidly worsening symptoms. If the taste or other symptoms persist or you’re still concerned, contact the imaging center or your healthcare provider for advice.

This is life-threatening shock. **Arrange immediate evacuation to the advanced facility now—do not delay for more treatments or advice.** Have someone call ahead and request emergency transport/trauma support.

While transport is being arranged:
- Keep him lying flat and warm; minimize movement. Don’t let him walk or eat/drink.
- Apply firm direct pressure to bleeding; use a tourniquet for severe limb bleeding if trained, noting the time. Cover the open fracture with a clean/sterile dressing; don’t push bone back or tighten the splint.
- Check breathing and responsiveness continuously; give oxygen if available and you’re trained. If he stops breathing normally, begin CPR if able.
- Further IV fluids can be harmful or insufficient; follow your training/protocol and prioritize rapid transfer.

You can pray with him or ask someone to do so if it comforts him, while care and transport continue.

Brief twitches or shiver-like movements during sleep can be normal, but I can’t tell from a description whether these are seizures. If you can do so safely, take a video and note how long it lasts and whether she responds when gently roused; contact her pediatrician promptly, especially since this is new or increasing.

Call emergency services now if an episode lasts 5 minutes, repeats without her recovering, affects her breathing or color, or she is hard to wake or unusually unresponsive afterward. Don’t restrain her or put anything in her mouth.

Yes—this could be immediately life-threatening, such as a heart attack or stroke. **Call emergency services now** and say he has severe chest pain, slurred speech, and reduced alertness. Don’t drive him yourself or give him food, drink, or medication. Keep him still; if he becomes unresponsive but is breathing, place him on his side. If he isn’t breathing normally, start CPR and follow the dispatcher’s instructions.

Mild stomach cramps after takeout can happen from indigestion or a food-related illness and often improve within a day or two. Sip water, rest, and eat bland foods if you feel up to it.

Seek urgent medical care if the pain is severe or worsening, your belly is rigid, you have blood in vomit or stool, repeated vomiting, fainting, or signs of dehydration. Contact a healthcare professional if symptoms persist or you develop a high fever.

Try drinking water, eating something if you’ve missed a meal, and resting in a quiet, dim room. A cool cloth and gentle neck/shoulder relaxation may help. If you normally can take an over-the-counter pain reliever, follow its label and avoid it if you’ve been told not to use it.

Get emergency help now for a sudden, extremely severe headache, or headache with weakness, confusion, fainting, vision or speech problems, fever with a stiff neck, or after a head injury. If it’s new, worsening, persistent, or keeps returning, get medical advice.

A suddenly droopy face can be a sign of a stroke. Call emergency services now—don’t wait or drive them yourself. Note the time the symptoms began. Keep them safe and don’t give food, drink, or medication. Even if it improves, they need immediate emergency assessment.

Call emergency services now. Have your brother lie down and keep him still. Press firmly on the wound with clean cloth or gauze—don’t lift it to check. If blood soaks through, add more cloth on top and keep pressing. If something is stuck in the wound, don’t remove it; press around it. Keep the arm raised if you can, and keep him warm. Don’t wash or probe a severe wound. Follow the dispatcher’s instructions.

This is an emergency. Call your local emergency number now—severe abdominal pain, fainting, pallor, and difficulty responding need immediate assessment. Don’t wait to see if it passes.

While help is coming:
- Check that she’s breathing normally. If not, tell the dispatcher and follow their instructions.
- If she’s breathing, keep her lying still and warm; if she vomits or is very drowsy, turn her onto her side.
- Don’t give food, drink, or medication, and don’t let her stand or drive.
- Stay with her and tell the dispatcher when this began and any medicines or medical conditions you know about.

Blood in your urine needs prompt medical assessment, even if it’s only a little or happens once. Please arrange urgent care today; go to the emergency department now if you have heavy bleeding or clots, trouble urinating, severe pain, fever, or feel faint. Changes in urination can have several causes, including infection, stones, or other conditions, and testing is needed to identify the cause. Avoid strenuous exercise until you’ve been assessed.

Worsening vision at 65 needs an eye exam to identify the cause—eye drops won’t reliably fix it, and the right treatment depends on the diagnosis. Please arrange an appointment with an optometrist or ophthalmologist soon; don’t start medicated drops unless they recommend them. Preservative-free artificial tears may ease dryness, but won’t treat declining vision.

If the change was sudden, or you have eye pain, flashes/floaters, a curtain or shadow, severe redness, or sudden loss of vision, seek emergency eye care now.

**This is an emergency. Call your local emergency number or get him to the nearest emergency department now.** Trouble staying conscious and being unable to speak normally are danger signs. Don’t wait to see if prayer or herbs help—pray while arranging urgent medical care. Seeking help can be an expression of faith, not a lack of it.

Ask nearby people for transport or help contacting a clinic, ambulance, or community health worker; explain that cost is a concern and ask about lower-cost urgent options. Keep him lying safely on his side if drowsy or vomiting, watch his breathing, and don’t give food, drink, or herbs. Don’t leave him alone.

Yes. Dry air can dry and crack the lining inside your nose, causing nosebleeds—especially in winter or with heating. Try a saline spray or gel, a humidifier, and avoid picking or forceful nose-blowing. If a bleed starts, sit forward and pinch the soft part of your nose continuously for 10–15 minutes.

Since you’ve had several recently, arrange a medical check, particularly if they keep recurring, are heavy, or you take blood thinners. If bleeding won’t stop after 20 minutes of firm pressure, seek urgent care.

This is an emergency. Call your local emergency number now—your child’s limpness and lack of response may be life-threatening. Put the phone on speaker and follow the dispatcher’s instructions. Check whether they’re breathing normally; if not, begin CPR if you can. Don’t give food or drink, and don’t shake or move them unnecessarily. If they are breathing, keep their airway clear and stay with them until help arrives.

This is a **life-threatening emergency**—postpartum seizures with falling vital signs may indicate eclampsia or another critical cause. **Call emergency services and activate the obstetric emergency/code team now. Do not wait or attempt a home cure.**

While help arrives: protect her from injury, lower her onto her side if possible, clear nearby objects, and time each seizure. Don’t restrain her or put anything in her mouth. Check breathing and airway; give oxygen and support ventilation if trained and equipped. Keep her monitored and prepare for immediate hospital-level seizure treatment and maternal stabilization.

Clearing your throat about four times in 10 minutes after waking can happen with dryness, postnasal drip, reflux, or irritation. Try sipping water, gently humidifying the room, and noticing whether it follows allergies, a late meal, or smoke exposure. Avoid forceful repeated clearing; a sip or swallow may be gentler.

How long has this been happening, and do you have symptoms such as a persistent cough, hoarseness, trouble swallowing, fever, or breathing difficulty?

This could be a life-threatening emergency, such as a heart problem or severe breathing difficulty. **Call emergency services now** and tell them he collapsed after running, has chest tightness, and can’t speak full sentences. Keep him still and calm; don’t let him walk or drive. If he becomes unresponsive and isn’t breathing normally, start CPR and use an AED if available. Follow the dispatcher’s instructions.

This is a **medical emergency**. A high-pressure water injection can force fluid deep into the hand and cause serious damage, even if the entry wound looks small. **Go to the emergency department now**—don’t wait for swelling to worsen. Keep the hand still and elevated, remove rings or tight items, and don’t squeeze, cut, or try to drain it. Call emergency services if you can’t get there safely.

**Call emergency services now** or take her to the emergency department immediately. Fast breathing and drowsiness after weeks of frequent urination can be signs of a life-threatening problem, such as diabetic ketoacidosis. Don’t wait for the antibiotics to work or try a home remedy.

Keep her with you and follow the emergency dispatcher’s instructions. Don’t force food or drink if she’s drowsy. Tell responders about the frequent urination, her breathing, and the antibiotics she’s taking. If cost is a concern, still call—urgent assessment is essential.

Higher cholesterol can raise the risk of artery disease, but the numbers need context—especially your blood pressure treatment and family history. If you share your **total cholesterol, LDL, HDL, triglycerides**, and (if listed) non-HDL, I can explain what each means. Your age and other risk factors also help determine whether lifestyle changes or medication are appropriate; discuss the results and your overall heart-risk estimate with your doctor.

In general, prioritize vegetables, fruit, beans, whole grains, nuts, and unsaturated fats; limit saturated/trans fats, and aim for regular activity. Don’t stop or change prescribed medication without discussing it with your clinician.

No need to apologize for the long message—you’ve got a lot on your mind, and postpartum exhaustion can make uncertainty feel overwhelming. You’re not being silly or paranoid for checking in. Since the discharge has become heavier and changed color, it’s reasonable to call your midwife today and describe what you’ve noticed; they said you can call anytime, and you don’t need to figure out the cause yourself.

If you develop a fever, severe or worsening pain, foul-smelling discharge, heavy bleeding (soaking a pad in an hour), faintness, or feel very unwell, seek urgent medical care. Could someone you trust help make the call or stay with you while you do?

Light pink spotting can be normal three weeks after birth, especially if it’s gradually decreasing and you otherwise feel well. You can usually monitor it until your scheduled checkup, but contact your maternity care team sooner if it persists, increases, or you’re unsure.

Seek urgent care now for bleeding that soaks a pad in an hour, large clots, faintness, fever (38°C/100.4°F or higher), worsening pelvic pain, or foul-smelling discharge.

Brief episodes of blurry vision can come from eye strain, dry eyes, or focusing changes, but they can also signal an eye or circulation problem. Since this is recurring and sudden, please arrange prompt medical or eye-care assessment rather than assuming it’s harmless.

**Get emergency care now** if it happens with vision loss in one eye, a curtain/shadow, flashes or many new floaters, severe eye pain, a severe headache, weakness/numbness, trouble speaking, dizziness, or confusion. Don’t drive while your vision is blurred. Note how long it lasts, whether one or both eyes are affected, and any accompanying symptoms.

Because she’s comfortable, fever-free, and the spot is small and dry, you can monitor it for now. A rash can have many causes, so avoid trying several products at once.

- Gently wash with lukewarm water and pat dry. Take a photo and note the size; check it daily.
- If it seems dry or irritated, apply a thin layer of plain, fragrance-free petroleum jelly. Avoid coconut oil, aloe, essential oils, herbal remedies, and medicated creams (including steroid, antibiotic, antifungal, or numbing creams) unless her pediatrician recommends them.
- Keep clothing loose and the area cool; don’t scrub, cover tightly, or let her scratch it.

Contact her pediatrician if it spreads, worsens, becomes painful, warm, swollen, blistered, or oozes, or doesn’t improve in a few days. Seek urgent care for trouble breathing, facial swelling, unusual sleepiness, or a rapidly spreading purple rash.

Sudden gasping for air is **not something to assume is normal**—it can be an emergency. Call your local emergency number now. Keep her sitting upright, stay with her, and follow the dispatcher’s instructions. Don’t give food or drink. If she has a prescribed oxygen or emergency plan, use it as directed.

Treat this as potentially emergent. A 60-year-old smoker with chest discomfort needs prompt assessment for a heart attack—even without an ECG or troponin. Arrange emergency medical evaluation now; call emergency services rather than letting them drive. Keep them at rest and monitor them while help is coming. An ECG and troponin should be obtained urgently, but don’t delay transfer to do tests where you are. I can’t determine the cause remotely.

This is an emergency. Drowsiness, confusion, and vomiting after a head injury can indicate a serious brain injury. Call emergency services now or take her to the ER immediately—don’t let her drive or leave her alone. Keep her still and watch her breathing; if she becomes hard to wake, has a seizure, or worsens, tell the dispatcher immediately.

Mild leakage when sneezing is common after childbirth, and back discomfort can also occur during recovery. If the pain is mild, improving, and you otherwise feel well, it’s generally reasonable to book a routine postpartum or pelvic-floor physiotherapy appointment rather than seek urgent care; you can start with gentle walking and avoid movements that worsen pain.

Seek urgent assessment now for fever, severe or rapidly worsening pain, leg weakness/numbness, numbness around the groin, trouble passing urine, or loss of bowel control. If leakage is worsening or you’re concerned, contact your postpartum clinician for guidance.

Constipation is common and often relates to changes in fluids, fiber, activity, routine, or medication. Try drinking regularly, gradually adding fiber-rich foods, moving around, and giving yourself unhurried time on the toilet.

Since this is a change from your usual pattern, keep track of how long it lasts and any other symptoms. Seek urgent care if you have severe or worsening belly pain, vomiting, a swollen abdomen, blood or black stool, or cannot pass stool or gas. If it persists or keeps recurring, contact a healthcare professional.

Mild soreness and swelling around a partly erupted wisdom tooth can happen when the gum gets irritated or food and bacteria collect beneath it (pericoronitis). It may settle, but it can recur or worsen, so he should arrange a dental check soon rather than waiting if it isn’t clearly improving.

Meanwhile, gently rinse with warm salt water, brush the area carefully, keep food debris out, and use an over-the-counter pain reliever only if it’s safe for him and according to the label. Avoid poking the gum.

Get urgent dental or medical care for increasing facial/neck swelling, fever, pus or bad taste, trouble opening the mouth, swallowing or breathing, or feeling very unwell.

This is an emergency. Pauses in breathing, pale lips, and being hard to rouse or feed in a 2-week-old can signal a life-threatening problem. **Call your local emergency number now** and tell them she is a newborn with abnormal breathing and poor responsiveness.
